<P>16. <B>To coole</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Something seems to be wanting. The <I>bellows</I> and <I>fan,</I>
being commonly used for contrary purposes, were probably opposed by the author,
who might perhaps have written, &lquo;<I>To kindle and</I> to cool.&rquo; <SC>M. Mason</SC>: Johnson's
amendment is unnecessary. The bellows and the fan have the same effects. When
applied to the fire, they increase it; but when applied to any warm substance, they
cool it. <SC>Malone</SC>: The text is undoubtedly right. The following lines in Spenser's
<I>Faerie Queene</I> at once support and explain it, &lquo;But to delay the heat, least by mis-
chaunce It might breake out, and set the whole on fire, There added was by goodly
ordinaunce, An huge great paire of bellowes, which did styre Continually, and cool-
ing breath inspyre.&rquo;&mdash;II, Cant. ix, 267. <SC>Staunton</SC> (<I>Athen.</I> 12 Apr. 1873): Some-
thing appears to have been lost; but Johnson's remedy stretches out the line beyond
all measure. We might better read, &lquo;To <I>heat</I> and cool,&rquo;&mdash;citing in confirmation, &lquo;To
<I>glow</I> the delicate cheeks which they did <I>cool.</I>&rquo;&mdash;II, ii, 239.
<P>16. <B>Gypsies Lust</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: &lquo;Gipsy&rquo; is here used both in the original meaning
for an <I>&AElig;gyptian,</I> and in its accidental sense for a <I>bad woman.</I> <SC>Irving's Ed.</SC>: No
metaphor, as all who know anything of the gipsies know well, could be less exact
than that which takes their women as a symbol of lust. They might much more
correctly stand as a symbol of chastity.

<P>171. In <I>Notes and Queries,</I> I, iii, 498, <SC>A. E. Brae</SC> contended that in both instances
Shakespeare used the word as the Latins, or at least Ovid, used <I>triplex,</I> and herein
lay a proof of Shakespeare's learning. But when Ovid represents (<I>Ibis,</I> 76) the
Fates as spinning (only Lachesis spun) <I>triplici pollice,</I> it is to be feared that he
is in the same condemnation with Shakespeare. <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 62) devotes
a section to instances of an &lquo;inaccurate use of words in Shakespeare, some of them
owing to his imperfect scholarship (imperfect, I say, for he was not an ignorant man
even in this point), and others common to him with his contemporaries.&rquo; Some of
these instances are &lquo;eternal&rquo; for <I>infernal,</I> &lquo;imperious&rquo; for <I>imperial,</I> &lquo;ceremonies&rquo; for
<I>omens,</I> &lquo;temporary&rquo; for <I>temporal,</I> the present &lquo;triple&rquo; for <I>third,</I> and again in this play
&lquo;competitor&rquo; for <I>colleague</I> (I, iv, 5; V, i, 52), &lquo;important&rquo; for <I>importunate,</I> etc.
The effect of this list is cumulative, and possibly it is therefore wisest to acknowledge
at once that Shakespeare has here blundered. At the same time, might we not admit
that after Shakespeare has used a word twice in an intelligible though illogical sense,
the word might as well be adopted into the language for daily use? It would
have a paternity which many a perfectly legitimate word might be content to own.
&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>22. <B>Strumpets Foole</B>] <SC>Douce</SC> (ii, 73): Many ancient prints conduce to show
that women of this description were attended by buffoons; and there is good reason
for supposing, partly from the same kind of evidence, that in their houses such
characters were maintained to amuse the guests by their broad jokes and seasonable
antics. [<SC>Warburton</SC>, in the belief that the metaphor, introduced by &lquo;Pillar,&rquo; needed
an antithesis, asserted that we should here, for &lquo;Foole,&rquo; read <I>stool,</I> because &lquo;women
of this description&rquo; sometimes sat &lquo;in the laps of their lovers.&rquo; Strangely enough,
<SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 63) had &lquo;no doubt&rquo; that Warburton was right, and believes &lquo;that
&ldquo;pillar&rdquo; requires it.&rquo; To Walker's editor, <SC>Lettsom</SC>, the emendation &lquo;appears
very doubtful.&rquo; <SC>Grey</SC> (ii, 190) suggested a change, which he &lquo;imagines would be
as proper,&rquo; namely: <I>strumpet's tool.</I> It was reserved to <SC>Coleridge</SC> to put the
question at rest at once and for ever. &lquo;Warburton's conjecture is ingenious,&rquo; he says
(p. 317), &lquo;and would be a probable reading, if the scene opening had discovered
Antony with Cleopatra on his lap. But, represented as he is walking and jesting
with her, &ldquo;fool&rdquo; must be the word. Warburton's objection is shallow, and implies
that he confounded the dramatic with the epic style. The &ldquo;pillar&rdquo; of a state is so
common a metaphor as to have lost the image in the thing meant to be imaged.&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>23. <B>Cleo. If it be,</B> etc.] <SC>Hazlitt</SC> (p. 97): The character of Cleopatra is a master-
piece. What an extreme contrast it affords to Imogen! One would think it almost
impossible for the same person to have drawn both. She is voluptuous, ostentatious,
conscious, boastful of her charms, haughty, tyrannical, fickle. The luxurious pomp
and gorgeous extravagance of the Egyptian queen are displayed in all their force and
lustre, as well as the irregular grandeur of the soul of Mark Antony. Take only the
first four lines that they speak as an example of the regal style of love-making.

<P>Mark Antony, as delineated by Shakespeare, reminds me of the Farnese Hercules.
There is an ostentatious display of power, an exaggerated grandeur, a colossal effect
in the whole conception, sustained throughout in the pomp of the language, which
seems, as it flows along, to resound with the clang of arms and the music of the
revel. The coarseness and violence of the historic portrait are a little kept down;
but every word which Antony utters is characteristic of the arrogant but magnani-
mous Roman, who &lquo;with half the bulk o' the world played as he pleased,&rquo; and was
himself the sport of a host of mad (and bad) passions, and the slave of a woman.
[Everyone will recall Romeo's impassioned, &lquo;They are but beggars that can count
their worth&rquo; (II, vi, 32), and Claudio's, &lquo;I were but little happy, if I could say how
much&rquo; (<I>Much Ado,</I> II, i, 292). <SC>Steevens</SC> gives, from Theobald, without acknowl-
edgement, a quotation from Ovid (<I>Meta.</I> xiii, 824) which is possibly parallel. It is
where Polyphemus is boasting to Galatea of his wealth in flocks and herds;&mdash;&lquo;All
this flock is my own; many others are roaming the valleys; Many are hid in the
forest, and many are stabled in caverns. Should you ask how many there are, I
should not be able to tell you. To number the tale of his flock is ever the mark of
a poor man.&rquo; &lquo;Hoc pecus omne meum est: multae quoque vallibus errant; Multas
silva tegit: multae stabulantur in antris: Nec, si forte roges, possim tibi dicere,
quot sint. Pauperis est numerare pecus.&rquo; Golding's translation (p. 170 <I>verso</I>), more
vigorous than mine, is as follows:&mdash;&lquo;This Cattell heere is all myne owne. And
many mo besyde Doo eyther in the bottoms feede, or in the woodes them hyde, And
many standing at theyr stalles doo in my Caue abyde. The number of them (if a
man should ask) I cannot showe. Tush beggars of theyr Cattell vse the number for
too knowe.&rquo; Steevens quotes also from an Epigram, wholly apposite, where Martial
(Bk. vi, No. 34) begs for kisses, and in answer to the question &lquo;how many?&rquo; answers,
&lquo;bid me number ocean's waves, or the shells scattered on the &AElig;gean shore, or the
number of bees wandering on the Cecropian mount, or the number of voices and
applauding hands when the people catch sight of C&aelig;sar's face in the crowded theatre.
I do not want as many as the clever Catullus begged from Lesbia, that is, any definite
number, however vast, because &lquo;pauca cupit, qui numerare potest.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>25. <B>Ile,</B> etc.] <SC>Hartley Coleridge</SC> (ii, 183): If Antony owed to Cleopatra the
loss of empire, he is indebted to her for less hateful renown than would else have
clung to him. Shakespeare and Dryden make the Philippics forgotten, and the
murderer of Cicero is lost in the lover of Cleopatra.
<P>25. <B>bourne</B>] <SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D.</I>): Early modern English <I>borne,</I> apparently equiv-
alent to Old Fr. <I>bodne, bone, boune.</I> In English in Lord Berners, and in Shakespeare
(seven times), then apparently not till the 18th century; the modern use being due
to Shakespeare, and in a large number of cases directly alluding to the passage in
<I>Hamlet.</I> 2. A bound, a limit [as in the present line]. 3. In Shakespeare's famous
passage, <I>Hamlet,</I> III, i, 79, &lquo;Borne&rquo; (Qq), probably meant the &lquo;frontier or pale&rquo;
of a country; but has been associated contextually with the goal of a traveller's
course.

at a greater distance than the present visible universe affords.

<P>30. <B>Grates me, the summe</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Be brief, <I>sum</I> thy business in a few words.
<SC>A. E. Thiselton</SC> (p. 7) believes that here is an instance where a comma indicates
merely a grammatical inversion of the sentence and that the phrase is, in fact, &lquo;The
sum grates me.&rquo; The meaning is the same, whatever the punctuation, namely, that
the sum, and not the particulars, of the news is to be delivered. If there be, how-
ever, an inversion, as Mr Thiselton contends, it is used for dramatic effect, and, it
seems to me, that this effect will be heightened in proportion as the punctuation is
emphatic, even to the conversion, as in the majority of modern texts, of the comma
into a full stop. Time should be given to Anthony at least to stamp his $oot with
vexation. He is too impatient to care for grammar, and any addition, such as &lquo;It&rquo; or
&lquo;'T&rquo; weakens the rasping harshness of &lquo;Grates,&rquo; which is a relief and a satisfaction
to his vexed soul.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>31. <B>them</B>] <SC>Malone</SC> interprets this as referring to the &lquo;newes,&rquo; and he may be
right; as he says, &lquo;news&rquo; may be plural. But Cleopatra, in lines 42 and 45, speaks
of the &lquo;messengers,&rquo; and, in line 62, of the &lquo;Ambassadors.&rquo; Although only &lquo;<I>a</I>&rquo;
messenger enters, it is not impossible that others were seen approaching; or, what is
more likely, by exaggerating the number, Cleopatra magnifies the importance of the
news, and veils her jealousy of any control over Anthony greater than her own, in
stinging taunts at his subordination to a shirll-tongued woman and a beardless boy.&mdash;
<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>31. <B>Anthony</B>] This spelling is as invariable in this play as the spelling &lquo;Antony&rquo;
is in <I>Julius C&aelig;sar.</I>
<P>32. <B>Fuluia</B>] <SC>Leonhard Schmitz</SC> (Smith's <I>Dict.</I>): Fulvia was first married to
P. Clodius, by whom she had a daughter, Claudia, afterwards the wife of C&aelig;sar
Octavius. When Clodius was murdered, she married C. Scribonius Curio; and after
his fall in Africa, she lived for some years as a widow, until about <SC>b.c.</SC> 44 she mar-
ried M. Antony, by whom she became the mother of two sons. Up to the time of
her marrying Antony, she had been a woman of most dissolute conduct, but hence-
forth she clung to Antony with the most passionate attachment, and her only ambition
was to see her husband occupy the first place in the republic, at whatever cost that
position might be purchased. When Antony was declared a public enemy, she
addressed the most humble entreaties to the Senate, praying that they might alter
their resolution. Her brutal conduct during the fearful proscriptions of <SC>b.c.</SC> 43 is
well known; she gazed with delight upon the head of Cicero, the victim of her
husband. In <SC>b.c.</SC> 40, while Antony was revelling with Cleopatra in all the luxuries
of the East, Fulvia, stimulated partly by jealousy and the desire of drawing Antony

<P>back to Italy, and partly by her hostility towards Octavius, resolved upon raising a
commotion in Italy. She induced L. Antonius, her husband's brother, to come for-
ward as the protector of those who were oppressed and reduced to poverty by the colo-
nies of Octavius. He took his post at Praeneste whither he was followed by Fulvia.
She afterwards followed him to Perusia, and endeavoured to rouse the inhabitants of
the north of Italy to assist him, while he was besieged at Perusia by Octavius. When
Perusia fell into the hands of Octavius, by the treachery of L. Antonius, Fulvia was
permitted to escape, and went to Brundusium, where she embarked for Greece. Her
husband, who had in the meantime been informed of the war of Perusia and its result,
was on his way to Italy. He met Fulvia at Athens, and censured her severely for
having caused the disturbance. It is said that, from grief at his rough treatment, she
was taken ill, and in this state he left her at Sicyon while he went to Brundusium.
Her feelings were so deeply wounded by her husband's conduct, that she took no
care of herself, and soon after died at Sicyon, <SC>b.c.</SC> 40. The news of her death came
very opportunely for the Triumvirs, who now formed a reconciliation, which was
cemented by Antony marrying the noble-minded Octavia.

<P>36. <B>damne</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii): The MS alters &lquo;damne&rquo; to <I>doom;</I> and although

have done so even in the time of Shakespeare, yet we make no change, recollecting
that the heroine, in other places, sometimes errs on the score of delicacy, and that
&lquo;damn&rquo; is the more expressive word, which the poet, on that very account, may have
preferred. Still &lquo;damn&rquo; and <I>doom</I> would be spelt with the same letters in short-
hand, and the transcriber may have misread his note.

<P>47. <B>raing'd</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: Taken from the Roman custom of raising triumphal
arches to perpetuate their victories.&mdash;[Hereupon Warburton cannot refrain from a
stroke of smug self-praise by exclaiming, &lquo;extremely noble!&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: I
am in doubt whether Shakespeare had any idea but of a fabric standing on pillars.
It is not easy to guess how Dr Warburton missed this opportunity of inserting a
French word, by reading <I>derang'd.</I> Which, if <I>deranged</I> were an English word,
would be preferable both to <I>raised</I> and <I>rang'd.</I>&mdash;[This conjecture was not re-
peated in the <I>Var.</I> of 1773, where Johnson was associated as an editor with
Steevens. It is, therefore, to be assumed that it was charitably withdrawn.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC> (i, 26): That is, orderly ranged; whose parts are now entire and dis-
tinct, like a number of well-built edifices.&mdash;[Capell, followed by Malone, quotes as
parallel &lquo;bury all, which yet distinctly ranges, in heaps and piles of ruins.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Cor.</I> III,
i, 206. But <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>) differentiates both this use in <I>Cor.</I> and also, &lquo;whatso-
ever comes athwart his affection ranges evenly with mine,&rquo; in <I>Much Ado,</I> II, ii, 7,
quoted by Steevens, from the use of the word in the present line,&mdash;and, I think,
properly. Capell's interpretation seems to be just. Compare &lquo;whose several ranges,&rquo;
III, xiii, 7, that is, whose several ranks of war.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>with that wherewith Northcote said he mixed his colours: &lquo;brains,&rquo; will supply an
actor with the appropriate &lquo;business.&rquo; In the present line, after &lquo;thus,&rquo; <SC>Pope</SC> inserted
the stage-direction &lquo;<I>embracing,</I>&rquo; and has been followed by every editor, I think, from
that day to this. I do not forget how much more childlike than at present were the
men and women of aforetime, whether in the days of the C&aelig;sars or in the days of
Elizabeth, in the outward expression of their emotion, by embracing, by kissing, or by
the enviable gift, at command, of profuse and prolonged tears. But even with this in
mind, is it to be considered likely that Anthony would here publicly kiss, embrace,
or even touch Cleopatra? She was wrangling with him,&mdash;teasing him almost past
endurance, determined to obtain from him some assurance that, whatever the mes-
sage $rom Rome, he would not leave her; and is it in character that she should
tamely submit to be &lquo;embraced?&rquo; and then, when released from Anthony's arms,
where she had lain like an unresisting dove, renew the wrangling which this
&lquo;embrace&rquo; had interrupted? All wrangling thereafter would be absolutely stingless.
They were not standing side by side. Quarrels are not so conducted. They were
facing each other, and, I imagine, by some such gesture as an obeisance and a sweep-
ing wave of both hands toward her,&mdash;a not uncommon mode of illustrating &lquo;thus,&rquo;
&mdash;he showed that his whole existence with her, day by day and hour by hour, was
the true nobleness of life, compared to which kingdoms are clay. In speaking above
of stage-directions, I refer to situations where a key is urgently needed. There are,
in the Ff and Qq, many insertions, such as &lquo;<I>They all start.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<I>Rich. III:</I> II, i, 79,
etc., which are good, but not essential; experienced actors do not need to be thus
instructed.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

himself, but stirr'd by Cleopatra,&rquo; and marks it as <I>Aside.</I> <SC>Heath</SC> (p. 448) thinks
this emendation of Upton &lquo;can admit of no dispute.&rquo; <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 26): Cleopatra
checks herself for asking so idle a question as that about Fulvia, knowing as she
(forsooth) did, that Antony would be Antony; and is there stopped by a reply of
most exquisite delicacy,&mdash;&lquo;But, stirr'd by Cleopatra,&rquo;&mdash;who can say what he will
be? for that is left to be indicated by the tone in which the words are delivered, and
the action and look that accompanies them. <SC>Johnson</SC>: &lquo;But,&rquo; in this passage, seems
to have the old Saxon signification of <I>without, unless, except.</I> Antony, says the
Queen, will recollect his thoughts. <I>Unless</I> kept, he replies, in commotion by Cleo-
patra. [Emphatically, this is to me &lquo;obscurum per obscurius.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>M. Mason</SC>
seems as wide of the mark as Dr Johnson. He observes that &lquo;by &ldquo;Antony will be
himself,&rdquo; Cleopatra means to say, &ldquo;that Antony will act like the joint sovereign of
the world, and follow his own inclinations, without regard to the mandates of C&aelig;sar,
or the anger of Fulvia.&rdquo; To which he replies, &ldquo;If but stirr'd by Cleopatra;&rdquo; that
is, &ldquo;if moved to it in the slightest degree by her.&rdquo; &rquo; <SC>Singer</SC> &lquo;believes Mason's
explanation to be nearly correct; Antony will be himself without regard to C&aelig;sar
or Fulvia. <I>Add</I> if <I>moved to it</I> by Cleopatra.&rquo; <SC>Nares</SC> (<I>s. v.</I> But): Antony's reply
may either mean, &lquo;<I>but</I> Cleopatra will have the merit of moving him to be so;&rquo; or
&lquo;moved <I>only</I> by Cleopatra.&rquo; <SC>Knight</SC>, after giving the explanations of Johnson and
M. Mason, justly says, &lquo;Surely the meaning is more obvious;&rquo; he then gives what
seems to me to be the true interpretation: &lquo;Antony accepts Cleopatra's belief of what
he will be. He will be himself; but still under the influence of Cleopatra; and to
show what that influence is, he continues, &ldquo;Now for the love of Love,&rdquo; etc.&rquo;
<SC>Abbott</SC> quotes this passage under &sect; 128, and gives the meaning of &lquo;but&rquo; as equiv-
alent to &lquo;<I>not except</I> stirr'd,&rquo; &lquo;<I>only</I> if stirr'd,&rquo;&mdash;a meaning which is to me more
than doubtful. The whole difficulty arises, I think, from failing to apprehend the
meaning of Cleopatra's last words. &lquo;I'll seem the fool I am not,&rquo; she says, and then
adds contemptuously, &lquo;Antony will be the fool he really is.&rquo; He parries the stab,
and tries, unsuccessfully, to propitiate her by acknowledging that he will be that
same fool, but stirr'd to his very soul by love for Cleopatra. Then follows the
exquisite music of the next four lines, to which there came in reply only the exasper-
ating parrot-cry, &lquo;Hear the ambassadors!&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>61. <B>now</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: We should read <I>new;</I> a sentiment much in character

force, for the reasonableness of what is then spoken is all wrapped up in it: by &lquo;now&rquo;
is insinuated the speaker's own advanced age, and that of the lady addressed to;
which, in the opinion of persons like them, makes it proper that no time be lost in
the pursuing of what they call&mdash;pleasures. <SC>Johnson</SC> adopted an original punc-
tuation, without comment.

<P><B>Scene ii</B>] <SC>Delius</SC> (<I>Sh. Jahrbuch,</I> V, 267): The frivolous conversation of Cleo-
patra's court, expressive of the thoughtless life there, is carried on in prose. The sooth-
sayer, in expounding the value of his prophecies, is the only one who uses blank
verse. On the appearance of the impassioned Cleopatra language assumes a higher
strain and blank verse is then used by the others. In the dialogue, at the con-
clusion of the Scene, between Antony and his trusty Enobarbus, the latter as the
representative of the more elevated humour of the play, speaks in prose, in which
his satirical remarks on Cleopatra and Fulvia are certainly appropriate. Antony
himself barely responds to this mood and style of his friend.
<P>1. <B>Lamprius, . . . Rannius, Lucillius</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: It is not impossible, indeed,
that &lquo;Lamprius, Rannius, Lucillius,&rquo; might have been speakers in this scene as it
was first written down by Shakespeare, who afterwards thought proper to omit their
speeches, though at the same time he forgot to erase their names as originally
announced at their collective entrance. [In <I>Much Ado,</I> there is a character, Inno-
gen, who is set down in the Dramatis Person&aelig;, and enumerated among those who
enter at the beginning of the Second Act, and yet she speaks no word throughout
the play. See <I>Appendix,</I> <SC>Wyndham</SC>, p. 487.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>4. <B>sweet Alexas</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii) reads &lquo;<I>most</I> sweet Alexas,&rquo; in accordance
with a marginal note in his Second Folio; &lquo;by what follows,&rquo; he says, &lquo;&ldquo;most&rdquo; is
clearly required, and we may be sure that it had, in some way, escaped in the press.&rquo;
[It cannot be denied that the addition, <I>most,</I> is an improvement; not absolutely
necessary, but still an improvement. The next words &lquo;most <I>anything</I> Alexas&rquo;
seem almost to demand it. To improve Shakespeare, however, is no more justifiable
than to deface him.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>7. <B>which you say, must change his Hornes with Garlands</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: We

<C>[7. <B>which you say, must change his Hornes with Garlands.</B>]</C>
<P>must restore, &lquo;must <I>charge</I> his horns,&rquo; that is, must be an honourable cuckold, must
have his horns hung with garlands. <I>Charge</I> and &lquo;change&rquo; frequently usurp each
other's place in our Author's old editions. [Theobald hereupon adds, with his charac-
teristic scrupulous honesty,&mdash;an honesty Warburton knew not,&mdash;&lquo;I ought to take
notice, that Mr Warburton likewise started this emendation.&rquo; In Warburton's own
edition, no such scruples harassed him. He gave the emendation as wholly his
own.] <SC>Upton</SC> (p. 304) quotes this passage as an instance where Shakespeare uses
&lquo;change&rquo; in its secondary sense of <I>new dress and adorn.</I> <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 27, adopting
<I>charge</I>): That is, dress them up &lquo;with garlands,&rquo; set them forth gayly; a wanton
thought, that suits perfectly the person it comes from, and is expressed in words
equally wanton. [Theobald's] very slight change is necessary. <SC>Johnson</SC>: I am in
doubt whether to &lquo;change&rquo; is not merely to <I>dress,</I> or to <I>dress with changes of</I> gar-
lands. <SC>Malone</SC>: I think the reading, originally introduced by Theobald [<I>charge</I>],
is the true one, because it affords a clear sense; whilst, on the other hand, the read-
ing of the old copy affords none: for supposing <I>change with</I> to mean <I>exchange for,</I>
what idea is conveyed by this passage? and what other sense can these words bear?
The substantive <I>change</I> being formerly used to signify <I>variety</I> (as <I>change</I> of clothes,
of honours, etc.) proves nothing: <I>change of clothes</I> or <I>linen</I> necessarily imports more
than one; but the thing sought for is the meaning of the <I>verb</I> to &lquo;change,&rquo; and no
proof is produced to show that it signified to <I>dress</I>; or that it had any other meaning
than to <I>exchange.</I> Charmian is talking of her <I>future</I> husband, who certainly could
not change his horns, <I>at present,</I> for garlands, or any thing else, having not yet
obtained them; nor could she mean, that when he did get them, he should &lquo;change&rquo;
or part with them, for garlands: but he might <I>charge</I> his horns, when he should
marry Charmian, with garlands: for having once got them, she intended, we may
suppose, that he should wear them <I>contentedly</I> for life. The same mistake happened
in <I>Cor.</I> V, iii, 152, where the same correction was made by Warburton, and adopted
by all subsequent editors: &lquo;And yet to <I>charge</I> thy sulphur with a bolt.&rquo; <SC>Steevens</SC>:
&lquo;To change his horns <I>with</I> (i. e. for) garlands&rquo; signifies, to be a triumphant cuck-
old; a cuckold who will consider his state as an honourable one. We are not to
look for serious argument in such a &lquo;skipping dialogue&rquo; as that before us. <SC>Knight</SC>
stands loyally by the First Folio, and interprets &lquo;change&rquo; by &lquo;<I>vary&mdash;give a different
appearance to.</I>&rquo; <SC>Staunton</SC> follows Knight, and suggests that &lquo;change&rquo; &lquo;may mean
to <I>vary</I> or <I>garnish. Charge</I> is certainly very plausible.&rquo; W. W[<SC>illiams</SC>] (<I>Parth-
enon,</I> 17 May, 1862): It seems to me that when Warburton offered an explanation
of Shakespeare's meaning, he also well-nigh restored, unconsciously, the very words
of the dramatist. He says the horns of Charmian's husband must be &lquo;hung about&rquo;
with garlands. Now <I>hang</I> was anciently spelt <I>hange,</I> and, although this orthography
was dying out at the date of this tragedy, the omission or insertion of the final <I>e</I>
depended pretty much on the caprice of the compositor. It can scarcely then be
deemed unreasonable to conclude that the play-house copy from which this tragedy
was probably printed would have shown Shakespeare's words to have been &lquo;must
<I>hange</I> his Horns with Garlands.&rquo; . . . The insertion of a superfluous initial letter
was equally likely as a source of error . . . We find in the old copies of this play, &lquo;'<I>t</I>is
well,&rquo; where Shakespeare must have written &lquo;is well,&rquo; and &lquo;<I>s</I>tow me after&rquo; for &lquo;<I>tow</I>
me after.&rquo; <SC>Staunton</SC> (<I>Athen&aelig;um,</I> 12 April, 1873): &lquo;Change&rquo; is unquestionably a
misprint for <I>chain</I>&mdash;of old spelt <I>chayne.</I> The allusion is to the sacrificial ox, whose
horns were wreathed with flowers. [It is to be regretted that Staunton did not know

<P>27. <B>my Liuer</B>] <SC>M. Mason</SC>: The liver was considered as the seat of desire. In
answer to the Soothsayer, who tells her she shall be very loving, she says, &lquo;she had
rather heat her liver by drinking, if it was to be heated.&rquo;
<P>29-33. <B>Let mee bc married . . . Octauius C&aelig;sar</B>] <SC>Th. Zielinski</SC> (<I>Philologus,</I>
p. 19): Shakespeare imagined Charmion as younger than her mistress; the age of
fifty, then, would bring her to the birth of Christ. Is it clear who that child is &lquo;to
whom Herode of Iewry may do homage&rquo;? In Matthew, ii, 8, Herod himself says
&lquo;Go and search diligently for the young child; and when ye have found him, bring
me word again, that I may come and worship him also.&rquo; And to whom does he say
this? To the &lquo;Holy Three Kings.&rquo; Are not these the same that are included in
the list of Charmion's wishes? The fancy deserves a Mystery:&mdash;wife to the Holy
Three Kings, the mother of God, and, withal, Empress of Rome. [It is by no
means easy to disprove this interpretation, which at first decidedly shocks us. It is
unavailing to appeal to the text of the Scriptures, where, in the Bishop's Bible of
1568,&mdash;the Version used by Shakespeare,&mdash;the Magi are termed, not Kings but &lquo;Wise
men&rquo;; these Wise men had been called &lquo;Kings&rquo; centuries before Shakespeare was
born, and as such had been familiar characters in Christmas carols throughout
England, and, possibly, are so, to this day. It is also possible that any allusion
whatever to &lquo;Three Kings&rquo; would at once have suggested to Shakespeare's audience
the &lquo;three wise men.&rquo; Furthermore, the &lquo;Three Kings&rquo; must here be considered as
a unit or as a single group; Charmian was to be married to them all at once or in one
forenoon. This play opens in <SC>b.c.</SC> 40 and extends to <SC>b.c.</SC> 32; if Charmian be now
eighteen or twenty, she will be fifty in the year when Christ was born. The refer-
ences to Herod and the verse in Matthew are a little staggering. I do not like this
interpretation; it more than grates me. It imparts to Charmian's words an air of
frivolous irreverence, which is to me un-Shakespearian. But there is never anything
uttered at random by any of Shakespeare's characters, and the chances are many
against this wish of Charmian's being spoken at haphazard and tallying at the same
time so exactly with dates. Whenever an allusion is thrown out, we must catch it
of ourselves; Shakespeare will not point it out to us. It is to be feared that there
is many an allusion in his plays, less pointed than this, which critics have accepted
and approved.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

Herod was always one of the personages in the Mysteries of our early stage, on which

<P>he was constantly represented as a fierce, haughty, blustering tyrant, so that &lquo;Herod
of Jewry&rquo; became a common proverb, expressive of turbulence and rage. Thus,
Hamlet says of a ranting player, that he &lquo;<I>out-herods</I> Herod.&rquo; And, in this tragedy,
Alexas tells Cleopatra [III, iii, 6] that &lquo;not even <I>Herod of Jewry</I> dare look upon
her when she is angry;&rquo; i. e. not even a man as fierce as Herod. According to this
explanation, the sense of the present passage will be&mdash;Charmian wishes for a son
who may arrive at such power and dominion that the proudest and fiercest monarchs
of the earth may be brought under his yoke. [That this is the specific, theatrical
Herod to whom Charmian refers has been universally accepted, and will probably so
remain, in spite of the preceding ingenious note.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>42. <B>Witch</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> ii, 88): &lquo;Witch&rquo; in the sense of a male sorcerer, or
without any specific reference to sex, frequently occurs in the old writers [whereof
many examples follow. In <I>Wint. Tale,</I> Leontes calls Paulina a &lquo;witch&rquo; and to
add to it an especial roughness, calls her a &lquo;mankind witch.&rquo; Walker concludes
his article with a quotation from Minsheu's <I>Guide into the tongues,</I> 1617 (s. v. Con-
iuration) where the difference is set forth &lquo;betueene Conjuration, Witchcraft, and
Inchantment;&rquo;&mdash;&lquo;the <I>Coniurer</I> seemeth by praiers and inuocation of <I>Gods</I> powerfull
names, to compell the <I>Diuell</I> to say or doe what he commandeth him: The <I>Witch</I>
dealeth rather by a friendly and voluntarie conference or agreement betweene him or
her and the <I>Diuell</I> or <I>Familiar,</I> to haue his or her turne serued in <I>lieu</I> or stead of
blood, or other gift offered vnto him, especially of his or her soule: So that a <I>Con-
iurer</I> compacts for curiositie to know secrets, and worke maruels; and the <I>Witch</I> of
meere malice to doe mischiefe: And both these differ from <I>Inchaunters</I> or <I>Sorcerers,</I>
because the former two haue personall conference with the <I>Diuell,</I> and the other
meddles but with <I>Medicines</I> and ceremoniall formes of words called <I>Charmes,</I> with-
out apparition.&rquo; Walker quotes only a portion of the foregoing, but the whole of it
seems interesting. <SC>J. Churton Collins</SC> (Note in <I>The Pinner of Wakefield,</I> III,
ii, 703) quotes from Latimer: &lquo;We run hither and thither to witches or sorcerers
whom we call wise men.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Sermons preached in Lincolnshire,</I> V. (ed. not given).
In the edition of 1572, however, this passage runs, &lquo;we runne hither and thither to
wyssardes, or sorcerers, whome we call wyse men.&rquo;&mdash;Fol. 98, <I>verso.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>49-51. <B>There's . . . Soothsay</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 18) reads &lquo;There is&rquo; and
divides the lines thus:&mdash;&lquo;chastity,&rquo; &lquo;Nilus&rquo;&mdash;&lquo;bedfellow.&rquo; &lquo;Nilus,&rquo; he observes,
&lquo;surely indicates verse.&rquo; But why does he begin and end with these two or three
lines?&mdash;an oasis of verse in a desert of prose. Is it to be imagined that Shakespeare
would have contemplated with pleasure such patchwork? Especially, since, in order
to be appreciated, it must be seen on the printed page, a pleasure, which, in this
play, Shakespeare probably never enjoyed. And in the meantime what becomes of
Delius's fine-spun theory in regard to prose and verse? Every line of this portion
of the scene must be stark prose, or for poor Delius, &lquo;all's had, nought's spent.&rquo; We
have read our Shakespeare to little advantage unless we have acquired from him a
liberality as free as the air, that chartered libertine, and these theories (the very word
becomes repulsive!) are sent to put that liberality to the test.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P><I>the True Reading of Shakespeare in all the Editions ever yet publish'd.</I> The volume
which followed did not belie this unfortunate title-page; it achieved Pope's undying
enmity, and, for its author, a chief place in <I>The Dunciad.</I> In reference to the pres-
ent passage Theobald says (p. 157) in substance:&mdash;&lquo;The fact is evidently this:
Alexas brings a fortune-teller to Iras and Charmian, and says himself, &ldquo;We'll know
all our fortunes.&rdquo; Well; the Soothsayer begins with the women; and some jokes
pass upon the subject of husbands and chastity: after which, the women hoping for
the satisfaction of having something to laugh at in Alexas's fortune, call him to hold
out his hand, and wish heartily that he may have the prognostication of cuckoldom
upon him. The whole speech, therefore, must be placed to Charmian. There needs
no stronger proof of this being a true correction, than the observations which Alexas
immediately subjoins on their wishes and zeal to hear him abused.&rquo; Theobald's
<I>Shakespeare Restored</I> was published in 1726; two years afterward appeared Pope's
<I>Second Edition</I> wherein the Editor was forced to adopt many, very many of Theo-
bald's corrections. It looks, in the present passage, as though Pope, smarting under
the judicious slashes which Theobald administered, was determined to adopt as little
of Theobald's emendation as possible. He therefore omitted the name &lquo;Alexas&rquo;
altogether, and by Italics tried to make Charmian's speech apply to him, thus:
&lquo;<I>Char.</I> Our worser thoughts heav'ns mend. Come, <I>his</I> fortune, <I>his</I> fortune.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>65. <B>that cannot go</B>] That is, that cannot have children. See <I>N. E. D.</I> s. v. 7.
<P>71, 72. <B>prayer of the people</B>] <SC>Thiselton</SC> (p. 9): This seems to mean &lquo;that
universal prayer.&rquo;
<P>74, 75. <B>decorum</B>] Both here and in V, ii, 21, the compositors give this word in
Italics, as an indication that it had not yet been adopted into the language. Herein
they seem to have followed the prevailing fashion. In a majority of the examples,
gathered by the <I>N. E. D.</I> extending from Ascham's <I>Scholemaster,</I> in 1568, down to
Shakespeare's time, the word is similarly italicised; and the <I>Text. Notes</I> above, show
that the practice was kept up in all the early editions down to, and including, John-
son's.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>113. <B>Euphrates</B>] The <I>Text. Notes</I> give Keightley's division of these lines, but it

&lquo;Euphr&abreve;tes&rquo; that he reads &lquo;Euphrates <I>and.</I>&rquo; <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.</I> 172) shows by

<P>124. <B>our quicke windes</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: We should read <I>minds.</I> The <I>m</I> was
accidentally turned the wrong way at the press. The sense is this: While the active
principle within us lies immerged in sloth and luxury, we bring forth vices instead
of virtues, weeds instead of flowers and fruits: But the laying before us our ill
condition plainly and honestly is, as it were, the first culture of the mind, which
gives hope of a future harvest. This he says to encourage the messenger to hide
nothing from him. <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 27): By &lquo;winds&rquo; are meant&mdash;friends; persons so
truly such, as to remind those they love of their faults; the observation is certainly
just; and the metaphor in which it is wrap'd, a physical truth; and that this is a
true interpretation, is clear from what immediately follows,&mdash;&lquo;and our ills told us,
Is as our earing;&rquo; i. e.&mdash;and the telling us our ills or ill actions, is a kind of culture
to minds that lie waste;&mdash;still pursuing the image he had borrowed from husbandry.
<SC>Johnson</SC> [reading &lquo;winds&rquo;]: The sense is, that man, not agitated by censure, like
soil not ventilated by <I>quick winds,</I> produces more evil than good. <SC>Blackstone</SC>: I
suspect that <I>quick winds</I> is, or is a corruption of, some provincial word, signifying
either <I>arable lands,</I> or the <I>instruments of husbandry</I> used in tilling them. <SC>Steevens</SC>:

<CC>
<C><B>[124. our quicke windes]</B></C>
<P>This conjecture is well founded. The ridges left in lands turned up by the plough,
that they may sweeten during their fallow state, are still called <I>wind</I>-rows. <I>Quick
winds,</I> I suppose to be the same as <I>teeming fallows</I>; for such <I>fallows</I> are always
<I>fruitful</I> in <I>weeds.</I> <SC>Henley</SC>: When the &lquo;quick winds lie still,&rquo; that is, <I>in a mild
winter,</I> those weeds which &lquo;the tyrannous breathings of the north&rquo; would have cut
off, will continue to grow and seed, to the no small detriment of the crop to follow.
<SC>M. Mason</SC>: The words <I>lie still,</I> are opposed to <I>earing; quick</I> means pregnant; and
the sense of the passage is: &lquo;When our pregnant <I>minds</I> lie idle and untilled, they
bring forth weeds; but the telling us of our faults is a kind of culture to them.&rquo; The
pronoun <I>our</I> before <I>quick,</I> shows that the substantive to which it refers must be some-
thing belonging to us, not merely an external object, as the <I>wind</I> is. To talk of
<I>quick</I> winds lying <I>still,</I> is little better than nonsense. <SC>Malone</SC>: Dr Johnson's
explanation is certainly true of <I>soil,</I> but where did Dr Johnson find the word <I>soil</I> in
this passage? He found only <I>winds,</I> and was forced to substitute <I>soil ventilated by
winds</I> in the room of the word in the old copy; as Mr Steevens, in order to extract
a meaning from it, supposes <I>winds</I> to mean to <I>fallows,</I> because &lquo;the ridges left in
lands turned up by the plough, are termed <I>wind</I>-rows;&rquo; though surely the obvious
explication of the latter word, <I>rows exposed to the wind,</I> is the true one. Hence the
rows of new-mown grass laid in heaps to dry, are also called <I>wind-rows.</I> Our <I>quick</I>
minds, means, our lively, apprehensive minds. So, in <I>2 Hen. IV:</I> IV, iii, 107: &lquo;It
ascends me into <I>the brain;</I>&mdash;makes it apprehensive, <I>quick,</I> forgetive.&rquo; Again, in
this play: &lquo;The <I>quick</I> comedians,&rquo; etc. The same error is found in <I>King John,</I> V,
vii, 16 where we have, in the only authentick copy: &lquo;Death, having prey'd upon the
outward parts, Leaves them invisible; and his siege is now Against the <I>wind.</I>&rquo;
Again, in <I>Tro. and Cress.</I> F<SUB>2</SUB>F<SUB>3</SUB>F<SUB>4</SUB>: &lquo;Let it be call'd the <I>mild</I> and wand'ring flood.&rquo;
<SC>Knight</SC> [reading &lquo;winds&rquo;]: When do we &lquo;bring forth weeds&rquo;? In a heavy and
moist season, when there are no &lquo;quick winds&rquo; to mellow the earth, to dry up the
exuberant moisture, to fit it for the plough. The poet knew the old proverb of the
worth of a bushel of March dust; but &lquo;the winds of March,&rquo; rough and unpleasant
as they are, he knew also produced this good. The quick winds then are the voices
which bring us true reports to put an end to our inaction. When these winds lie
still we bring forth weeds. But the metaphor is carried farther: the winds have
rendered the soil fit for the plough; but the knowledge of our own faults,&mdash;ills,&mdash;
is as the ploughing itself,&mdash;the &lquo;earing.&rquo; <SC>Collier</SC> [reading &lquo;winds&rquo;]: Perhaps
&lquo;winds&rquo; ought to be spelt <I>wints,</I> which in Kent and Sussex is an agricultural term
(in other parts of the country called a <I>bout</I>), meaning &lquo;two furrows ploughed by the
horses going to one end of the field and back again.&rquo; See Cooper's <I>Sussex Glossary,</I>
1836; also Holloway's <I>General Provincial Dictionary,</I> 1838. &lquo;Our quick winds,&rquo;
therefore, is to be understood as our <I>productive soil.</I> &lquo;Earing&rquo; is ploughing; and its
use shows that Anthony had agriculture in his thoughts, with reference to &lquo;winds&rquo;
or <I>wints.</I> <SC>Staunton</SC> [reading &lquo;winds&rquo;]: Warburton's change is, perhaps, without
necessity. &lquo;Quick winds&rquo; may mean <I>quickening winds,</I> and Johnson's explanation
of the passage is possibly the true one. <SC>Deighton</SC> [reading <I>winds</I>]: It is when our
active minds are allowed to lie untilled by wholesome truths that they shoot up
noxious growths, and the telling us of our faults is as the ploughing of the soil which
roots up such growths. [To me an insuperable difficulty in accepting &lquo;winds&rquo; is the
possessive pronoun &lquo;our.&rquo; I do not know what these winds are, which we possess
and, if quiescent, suffer us to bring forth weeds. The agency of our reformation comes

<P>143. <B>Spirit</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 201) includes this &lquo;Spirit&rquo; in his list of numerous
passages &lquo;in which the disyllabic pronunciation of <I>spirit</I> renders a line positively
unmetrical or inharmonious to a degree beyond what the poet's ear could possibly
have tolerated.&rquo; [From childhood we have been so accustomed to regard <I>sprite</I> as
the name of a goblin, that its introduction in a solemn line like the present could
hardly fail to have a jarring effect, for which metrical smoothness would be hardly a
sufficient compensation.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>145. <B>The present pleasure,</B> etc.] <SC>Warburton</SC>: The allusion is to the sun's
diurnal course; which rising in the <I>east,</I> and by <I>revolution lowering,</I> or setting in the
<I>west,</I> becomes <I>the opposite of itself.</I> [<SC>Rolfe</SC> thinks that there is an allusion rather to
the turning of a wheel, probably suggested by the familiar &lquo;wheel of Fortune.&rquo;]
<SC>Johnson</SC>: This is an obscure passage. The explanation which Dr Warburton has
offered is such, that I can add nothing to it; yet, perhaps, Shakespeare, who was
less learned than his commentator, meant only, that our pleasures, as they are
<I>revolved</I> in the mind, turn to pain. <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 28): The sentiment contained in
the passage that begins with these words is, in the main, no other than that con-
tain'd in the general maxim preceding it, and in the reflections with which it is fol-
lowed. <SC>Tollet</SC>: I rather understand the passage thus: &lquo;What we often cast from
us in contempt we wish again for, and what is at present our greatest pleasure, lowers
in our estimation by the revolution of time; or by a frequent return of possession
becomes undesirable and disagreeable.&rquo; <SC>Steevens</SC>: I believe <I>revolution</I> means
change of circumstances. This sense appears to remove every difficulty from the
passage.&mdash;&lquo;The pleasure of to-day, by revolution of events and change of circum-
stances, often loses all its value to us, and becomes to-morrow a pain.&rquo; [<SC>Knight</SC>
and <SC>Deighton</SC> adopt this interpretation of Steevens.]

<P>146. <B>By reuolution lowring</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii. Reading &lquo;By repetition sour-
ing&rquo;): Our text has been furnished here by the MS and we cannot doubt that it is
what the poet wrote. The meaning of course is, that pleasure, souring by repetition,
becomes the reverse of itself. The old compositor misread &lquo;repetition&rquo; <I>revolution,</I>
and &lquo;sowering&rquo; (as the word was then often spelt) <I>lowering,</I> and thus made almost
nonsense of the whole passage. The restoration by the old annotator can hardly
have been a mere guess. [We are willing, all of us, upon a compelling occasion, to
listen with condescending benignity to almost any emendation of the text of Shake-
speare, but&mdash;we must draw the line at <I>souring,</I>&mdash;a repulsive word, and worse than a
wilderness of flies in the apothecary's ointment. In his <I>Third Edition</I> Collier
returned to the received text, but remarked in a footnote that the reading of the MS
&lquo;is perhaps right.&rquo; See note on <SC>Daniel's</SC> <I>Cleopatra, Appendix,</I> p. 515.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>148. <B>could plucke</B>] <SC>Heath</SC>: The verb <I>could</I> hath a peculiar signification in this
place; it doth not denote <I>power</I> but <I>inclination.</I> The sense is, &lquo;the hand that drove
her off would now willingly pluck her back again.&rquo;
<P>150. <B>harmes, more</B>] I doubt the propriety of this comma, which has been uni-
formly adopted, I believe. I think the sense is: My idleness hatches ten thousand
more unknown harms than the ills I see at hand.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>153. <B>How now</B>] <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Notes,</I> p. 150): It would be impossible, I presume, to
point out, in any old writer, an instance of &lquo;How now!&rquo; used as <I>the exclamation of
a person summoning another into his presence.</I> Here the right reading is indubitably,
&mdash;&lquo;<I>Ho,</I> Enobarbus!&rquo; I have already shewn [in a note on <I>Love's Lab. Lost,</I> V, ii,
45, quoted <I>ad loc.</I> in this edition&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] that &lquo;<I>ho</I>&rquo; was very frequently spelt &lquo;<I>how:</I>&rquo;
and the probability is that in the present passage the author's manuscript had &lquo;<I>how:</I>&rquo;
to which either some transcriber or the original compositor, who did not understand
what was meant, added &lquo;now&rquo; (making the line over-measure). [Dyce in his
edition, printed four years after his <I>Notes,</I> acknowledged that he was unaware, when
he wrote the foregoing note, that he had been therein anticipated by Capell.]

&lquo;It&rquo; stands for&mdash;this action of theirs: His &lquo;tailors&rquo; are women, the artificers of other
women; and in that lies the comfort he speaks of; for &lquo;when old robes are worn
out,&rquo; that is&mdash;when an old wife is carried to her grave, &lquo;there are members&rquo; (<I>videlicet,</I>

deities are pleased to take a man's wife from him, this act of theirs makes them
appear to man like the tailors of the earth: affording this comfortable reflection, that
the deities have made other women to supply the place of his former wife; as the
tailor, when one robe is worn out, supplies him with another. <SC>Anon</SC>. [<I>Var.</I> '21]:
The meaning is this&mdash;&lquo;As the gods have been pleased to take away your wife

him to them, or putting him upon using their service. The shrewd humourist means
to insinuate, I take it, that a wife of long standing is something like an out-worn
dress; and that a change every little while in that behalf is as pleasant as having a
new suit of clothes. Was the naughty wag an advocate of free-love? Antony winces
under the cutting irony of his talk. <SC>Deighton</SC> detects in &lquo;there are members&rquo; a
&lquo;probable allusion to the scriptural narrative of Eve being made out of one of

<P>202. <B>Expedience</B>] <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>) gives to this word the two meanings of 1)

Hen. IV:</I> I, i, 33; and the present line. So nice is the distinction between these
two meanings that it is not easy to decide that the present instance does not come
under the head of <I>haste.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>203. <B>loue</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 28): They who alter'd &lquo;love&rquo; into <I>leave</I> had not reflected
sufficiently, who the person is that they gave it to: the person is Antony; Antony
coming to himself, and beginning to think rather seriously; who, in that disposition,
must be suppos'd to consider his own dignity, of which the word <I>leave</I> is an evident
breach; it seems indeed to have been avoided with some study; and &lquo;love,&rquo; a less
natural expression, substituted for it: the sense we must take the words in, is as fol-
lows:&mdash;and get her, whose love is so great for me, to consent to my parting. <SC>Malone</SC>:
If the old copy be right, the words must mean, I will get her love to permit and
endure our separation. But the word <I>get</I> connects much more naturally with the
word <I>leave</I> than with <I>love.</I> The same error has happened in <I>Tit. And.</I> and there-
fore I have no longer any doubt that <I>leave</I> was Shakespeare's word. In that play
we find: &lquo;He <I>loves</I> his pledges dearer than his life,&rquo; instead of&mdash;&lquo;He <I>leaves.</I>&rquo;&mdash;[III,
i, 292. Dyce adopts this conclusion of Malone.] <SC>Steevens</SC>: The old reading may
mean:&mdash;&lquo;And prevail on her love to consent to our separation.&rquo; [Thus <SC>Knight</SC>
substantially. The original text is not, to me, sufficiently obscure to justify a change.
Capell's reason is weighty, and, in addition, it seems somewhat absurd in Anthony
to send notice to his officers of his intention, and to all his subordinates of his &lquo;quicke
remoue from hence,&rquo; and then to say that he would get Cleopatra's leave to depart.
&lquo;Durior lectio preferenda est.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>204. <B>more vrgent touches</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Things that touch me more sensibly,
more pressing motives.
<P>206. <B>our contriuing Friends</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 163): &lquo;Contriving&rquo; here is not
<I>managing</I> or <I>plotting,</I> but <I>sojourning; conterentes tempus.</I> See <I>Tam. Shr.</I> I, ii.
<SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D. s. v.</I> Contrive, v<SUP>2</SUP>. obs.): Apparently irregularly formed on Latin
<I>contrivi,</I> pret. of <I>conterere</I> to wear away; cf. <I>contrite, contrition;</I> perhaps associated
by translators with &lquo;contrive&rquo; to invent, etc. <I>Transitive.</I> To wear down, wear
away, consume, spend; to pass, employ (time). Cf. &lquo;Please ye we may contrive
this afternoon.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Tam. Shr.</I> I, ii, 276. [The context is not, I think, in Walker's
favour. It was not for the sake of Anthony's company that his friends, who happened
to be sojourning in Rome, petitioned him at home, but much was breeding that might
endanger the sides of the world, and Anthony's presence was needed to encourage
those friends, who were looking after his interests. This seems, I think, to favour
the usual meaning of &lquo;contriving.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>206. <B>Rome</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 163): Pronounce &lquo;Rome,&rquo; as usual, <I>Room</I>; this
removes the jingle between &lquo;Rome&rquo; and &lquo;home.&rquo;
<P>207. <B>Petition vs at home</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Wish us at home; call for us to reside at

<P>3. <B>since</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 62): &lquo;Since&rquo; when used adverbially as well as conjunction-
ally, frequently takes the verb in the simple past where we use the complete <I>present,</I>
[as in the present phrase]. This is in accordance with an original meaning of the
word, <I>later</I> (&lquo;sith&rquo;). We should still say, &lquo;I never saw him <I>after</I> that;&rquo; and &lquo;since&rquo;
has the meaning of <I>after.</I> [See also &sect; 347, for examples of the simple past, &lquo;did&rquo; for
complete present with &lquo;since,&rquo; etc.]

<P>6. <B>I did not send you</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: You must go as if you came without my order

love, which is possible, though doubtful&rquo;; &lquo;if you <I>did</I> love&rquo; means &lquo;if you loved,
which is evidently not the case.&rquo;

<P>14. <B>teachest like a foole:the way,</B> etc.] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii) claims for his punc-
tuation (also that of his MS) a priority over all editions; the <I>Text. Notes</I> show that
it had been adopted by Johnson. Collier, with pardonable zeal, pronounces the
punctuation of his MS a decided improvement on that of the Folio, of which, he
says, &lquo;there can be no dispute that [its] mode of pointing the passage is wrong,&rquo;&mdash;
an assertion, on the part of a veteran editor, so strange, that though it stands off as
gross as black and white, my eye will scarcely see it. As if there were a phrase, a
word, a comma in Shakespeare about which &lquo;there can be no dispute&rquo;! And,
moreover, Collier was unfortunate in making so extravagant a claim for his MS in
this passage, of all passages, where the majority of editors in favour of the original
punctuation is so very heavy. The majority has not erred, I think. Never would
Cleopatra have uttered so tame, so dispassionate a sentence as that which Collier and
his MS offer to us: &lquo;thou teachest, like a fool, the way to lose him.&rquo; If the Folio
err in punctuation, it errs on the side of moderation. Instead of a colon after &lquo;foole,&rquo;
I think a period would be better.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>15. <B>too farre</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 434) holds this to be a compound epithet: <I>too-far.</I>
<P>15. <B>wish forbeare</B>] <SC>Staunton</SC>: That is, I commend forbearance. <SC>Keightley</SC>
(<I>Exp.</I> 311): &lquo;Wish&rquo; here signifies <I>recommend, advise.</I> I think we should read
&lquo;wish <I>you</I>&rquo; [so reads Keightley's text], as it is always followed by its object when
used in this sense. <SC>John Hunter</SC>: Forbear is my wish. The verb &lquo;forbear&rquo; is
here in the imperative mood. <SC>Deighton</SC>: An elliptical expression for &lquo;I should
like to see you forbear to try him so far.&rquo; [The paraphrases just given are all of
them obvious, but none of them supplies the strength, which the weak expression,
&lquo;I wish, forbear&rquo; lacks. It is this weakness, this childishness, almost infantile,
which renders the words suspicious, so it seems to me. Nicholson's conjecture,
recorded in the <I>Cam. Ed.,</I> &lquo;the wish forbear&rquo; is plausible, and is certainly stronger
than the weak &lquo;I wish.&rquo; It is better than his alternative conjecture, &lquo;your wish,
forbear.&rquo; Weakness is, however, no sufficient ground for disturbing the text.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>19. <B>sullen</B>] Into this word we may read all the moods most unlovely in woman,
from waspishness to gloomy malignity. &lquo;O!&rquo; exclaims Coleridge, &lquo;the instinctive
propriety of Shakespeare in the choice of words.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>27. <B>that same eye ther's some good news</B>] This is a wilful and highly irritating
misinterpretation of Anthony's expression. His looks had been, of course, downcast,
as befitted words which he was &lquo;sorry to breathe.&rquo; Cleopatra had instantly divined
his &lquo;purpose,&rquo; and conjectured the purport of his message from Rome; she resolved,
therefore, that before Anthony could declare it, he should be &lquo;chafed&rquo; almost beyond
endurance; then, by tenderly yielding, she knew that she could bind him to her
more strongly than ever. She begins, accordingly, by wilfully misinterpreting his
looks.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>28. <B>What sayes the married woman you may goe?</B>] <SC>Thiselton</SC> (p. 9): To
punctuate this line as it is done both in the Globe and Oxford editions is to spoil the
antithesis between it and the next. &lquo;What&rquo; is exclamatory and expresses surprise:
&lquo;you don't mean to tell me.&rquo; It is to be observed that Cleopatra as yet knows
nothing of the nature of the news from Rome which had aroused Anthony. She had
only concluded &lquo;A Romane thought hath strooke him&rquo; from a sudden subsidence of
his mirth, and she infers that the news probably involves his speedy departure, and
is really welcome to him as importing reconciliation with C&aelig;sar. Fulvia and Lucius
had been at war with the latter, and Cleopatra believes or pretends to believe that it
has been Fulvia's wish that Anthony should keep out of the way, and that it was
merely owing to this that he was able to dance attendance on herself. [Rowe's
division of the line seems to me to be right; but the interrogation mark of the Folios
at the end should have been retained. The line contains the two questions: &lquo;What
says the married woman?&rquo; and, in effect, &lquo;Does she give you leave to go?&rquo; Then
follows the antithesis, &lquo;Would she had never given you leave to come!&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>28, 29. <B>What sayes the married woman . . . leaue to come</B>] <SC>Th. Zielinski</SC>
(<I>Philologus,</I> 1905, Bd. lxiv, Hft. i, p. 17): In this farewell scene between Anthony
and Cleopatra Shakespeare had in mind Ovid's <I>Epistle of Dido to &AElig;neas.</I> First of
all, the situations are exactly analogous, as every one may see at once; even the
Poet himself acknowledges it, where he says: &lquo;Dido and her &AElig;neas shall want
troops.&rquo; etc. IV, xiv, 64. Shakespeare's Cleopatra is developed psychologically, not
from the Vergilian, but from the Ovidian Dido; from the latter she derives her
nervousness, although she derives from the English poet,&mdash;or rather from Plutarch,
&mdash;that fatal admixture of instinctive, foxlike slyness, which Ovid's heroine lacks.
Special points of resemblance the student will find for himself; the most noteworthy

<P>40. <B>Riotous madnesse</B>] This is her own self-reproach.
<P>49. <B>browes bent</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: That is, the arch of the eye-brows. So, in <I>King
John:</I> &lquo;Why do you bend such solemn brows on me?&rquo;&mdash;IV, ii, 90. <SC>Schmidt</SC>
(<I>Lex. s. v.</I> Bent. 3) interprets it as meaning the whole forehead.
<P>49. <B>none our parts</B>] For other instances of the use of certain adjectives, like
&lquo;none,&rquo; as &lquo;pronouns, in a manner different from modern usage,&rquo; see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 12.
<P>50. <B>race of Heauen</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: That is, had a smack or flavour of heaven.
<SC>Johnson</SC>: &lquo;Race&rquo; is well explained by Warburton; the &lquo;race&rquo; of wine is the taste
of the soil. <SC>Malone</SC>: I am not sure the poet did not mean, &lquo;was of heavenly origin.&rquo;
<SC>John Hunter</SC>: &lquo;Race&rquo; is a suspicious word here, for which I would venture to sub-
stitute <I>trace. . . .</I> It should be remarked, however, that &lquo;race&rquo; had for one of its
meanings <I>smack</I> or <I>relish.</I> [Between the two interpretations of Warburton and
Malone subsequent editors have been pretty evenly divided. Warburton carelessly
wrote &lquo;<I>had</I> a smack&rquo; instead of &lquo;<I>was</I> a smack;&rquo; possibly, this weakened his general
acceptance, but needlessly, I think. &lquo;Race&rquo; was undoubtedly applied, in Shake-
speare's day, to the flavour of wine. <SC>Craigie</SC> (<I>N. E. D. s. v.</I> Race, <I>sb.</I><SUP>2</SUP> 10) gives
among others a quotation from Massinger: &lquo;A pipe of rich Canary . . . Is it of the
right race.&rquo;&mdash;<I>New Way,</I> I, iii. This justifies Warburton's interpretation of <I>flavour.</I>
Cleopatra says, in effect, there was no single feature, however insignificant, but was
of a flavour, or, was the very flavour of heaven. The objection to Malone's inter-
pretation seems to me to lie in the difficulty of accepting any one single feature as
a &lquo;race&rquo; whether of heaven or of earth.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>67. <B>present state, whose Numbers threaten</B>] <SC>Staunton</SC> (<I>Athen.</I> 12 April,

threaten&rquo;? &lquo;Numbers&rquo; was a term commonly used to express an armed force; and
the next line,&mdash;&lquo;quietness grown sick of rest,&rquo;&mdash;bespeaks an antithesis between
Peace and War. Compare the whole speech, where the sentences are framed short
and magniloquent, to imitate the &lquo;Asiatic&rquo; style, which, as Shakespeare learned from
Plutarch, Antony affected. [See <I>Appendix, Plutarch.</I>]

<P>69. <B>more particular</B>] That is, what is more especially my own personal, private

B, &dagger; 6) quotes from the first line of Heminge and Condell's <I>Epistle Dedicatorie</I> in
the First Folio: &lquo;Whilst we studie to be thankful in our particular,&rquo; etc. <SC>Schmidt</SC>
(<I>Lex.</I>) gives &lquo;who loved him in a most dear particular,&mdash;<I>Cor.</I> V, i, 3, where it is
&lquo;dear&rquo; that is compared, not &lquo;particular.&rquo; See IV, ix, 24, &lquo;in thine own particular,&rquo;
where it means, &lquo;in thine own special person.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>70. <B>should safe my going</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 290): It may be said that any noun or
adjective could be converted into a verb by the Elizabethan authors, generally in an
active signification [as &lquo;safe&rquo; in this present line, where the meaning is], &lquo;make my
departure unsuspected by you of dangerous consequences.&rquo;
<P>73. <B>Can Fuluia dye?</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: That Fulvia was mortal, Cleopatra could have
no reason to doubt; the meaning therefore of her question seems to be: &lquo;Will there
ever be an end of your excuses? As often as you want to leave me, will not some
Fulvia, some new pretext be found for your departure?&rquo; She has already said that
though age could not exempt her from follies, at least it freed her from a childish
belief in all he says. <SC>Ritson</SC>: I am inclined to think, that Cleopatra means no
more than&mdash;Is it possible that Fulvia should die? I will not believe it. <SC>Malone</SC>:
Though age has not exempted me from folly, I am not so childish, as to have appre-
hensions from a rival that is no more. And is Fulvia dead indeed? Such, I think,
is the meaning. <SC>Mrs Jameson</SC> (ii, 128): Cleopatra recovers her dignity for a
moment at the news of Fulvia's death, as if roused by a blow. And then follows
the artful mockery with which she tempts and provokes him, in order to discover
whether he regrets his wife. [It is extremely difficult to decide on which one of
these three words the emphasis should be laid; each can appropriately bear it. It
is even more difficult than Lady Macbeth's, &lquo;We fail!&rquo; Possibly, none should be
emphasized, but each uttered slowly, after a pause, as though the speaker were
revolving many things in her mind.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>76. <B>at the last, best,</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: This conjugal tribute to the memory of Fulvia
may be illustrated by Malcolm's eulogium on the Thane of Cawdor: &lquo;nothing in
his life Became him, like the leaving it.&rquo;&mdash;I, iv, 7. <SC>Boswell</SC>: Surely it means her
death was the best thing I have known of her, as it checked her <I>garboils.</I> <SC>Irving
Edition</SC>: Antony evidently means either, &lquo;in the last part of the letter is the best
news,&rquo; or &lquo;the best thing she ever did was her last act, that is, her leaving me.&rquo;
<SC>Rolfe</SC>: These words probably refer to the last part of the letter, or that giving the
good news of Fulvia's death. <SC>Staunton</SC>: The commentators will have the word
&lquo;best&rquo; to relate to the &lquo;good end&rquo; made by Fulvia. But it is no more than an
epithet of endearment which Anthony applies to Cleopatra;&mdash;read at your leisure the
trouble she awakened; and then at the last, <I>my best one,</I> see when and where she
died. [Of course, after &lquo;best&rquo; Staunton's text has the comma, of the Folio.] <SC>Staun-
ton</SC> (<I>Athen.</I> 12 April, 1873): Very many years ago I protested against the error
modern editors had committed in altering the punctuation of the old copy by placing
a colon or semi-colon after &lquo;best,&rquo; and interpreting it to mean that Fulvia's death
was the most becoming act of her life; or that the intelligence of her decease was
the best part of the news. I showed conclusively, as it appeared to me, that &lquo;best&rquo;
in this place was simply a term of endearment, like &lquo;sweet,&rquo; or &lquo;love,&rquo; or &lquo;dear;&rquo;
the construction being,&mdash;&lquo;read in these letters all the turmoils she provoked, and, at
the last, <I>my best one,</I> read when and where she died.&rquo; It seemed to me incredible
that there could be any question as to this, the obvious meaning, being accepted as
the true one, when it was once explained. I did not then know that young ignorance
and old prejudice were not the only or the worst foes a modern restoration of Shake-
speare's language had to overcome. I had to learn that the most implacable opponents
of all improvements in Shakespeare's text in these days were to be found among
Shakespeare's editors. This use of &lquo;best,&rquo; or of analogous epithets, is very common
with our early poets. Compare&mdash;&lquo;but that I love thee, <I>best, O most best!</I> believe it.&rquo;
&mdash;<I>Hamlet,</I> III, ii; &lquo;Gallus, Tibullus, and the <I>best-best</I> C&aelig;sar.&rquo;&mdash;Jonson's <I>Poetaster,</I>
V, i; &lquo;Believe me, Philomuse, i&rquo; faith thou must, The <I>best-best</I> seale of wit is wit's
distrust.&rquo;&mdash;Introd. to Marston's <I>What you Will;</I> &lquo;Be she with that goodness blest
Which may merit name of <I>best.</I>&rquo;&mdash;George Wither's song, &lquo;<I>Shall I wasting in despair;</I>
&lquo;&mdash;<I>kind,</I> forgive me: Make me not sick in health.&rquo;&mdash;<I>The Revenger's Tragedy;</I>
&lquo;&mdash;But, last, <I>good,</I> thy humour.&rquo;&mdash;Induct. to Marston's <I>Antonio and Mellida,</I> where
the turn of expression is precisely the same as&mdash;&lquo;at the last, best, see when,&rquo; etc.
[Staunton overlooked Florizel's enamoured words &lquo;When you do speak, sweet, I'ld
have you do it ever&rquo;? Had we only dutifully followed the Folio, and disregarded
Capell's unfortunate colon, there would never have been, I think, any doubt as to
the comprehension of Anthony's epithet &lquo;best,&rquo; which harmonizes with his eagerness
to propitiate her whom he had already called his &lquo;Queen.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>84. <B>th'aduice. By</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 508) in order to complete the metre, suggests,

immediately ruinates the good suggestion by adding: &lquo;but &ldquo;vice&rdquo; or &ldquo;by&rdquo; may be
prolonged.&rquo; It were better far, brazenly to insert, like Steevens, a superfluous <I>Now,</I>
or even a whole Dictionary, than weakly to quaver out &lquo;vice&rquo; or &lquo;By.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>87. <B>affects</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> ii, 128) in his Article to show that &lquo;<I>s</I> is not infre-
quently substituted for <I>st</I> in the second person singular of the verb&rquo; has the follow-
ing: &lquo;<I>Qu&aelig;re,</I> therefore, in cases where <I>st</I> would produce extreme harshness, and
where at the same time the old copies have <I>s,</I> whether we ought not to write the
latter. (In the north of England, and in Scotland (see, for example, Burns <I>passim</I>),
<I>s</I> for <I>st</I> in the second person seems to be the rule.)&rquo; [The propriety of Walker's
suggestion can hardly be questioned, I think. There are instances where it is almost
impossible to pronounce the full form in <I>st</I> and at the same time impart any smooth-
ness whatever to the verse. In the well-known line where Hamlet asks the Ghost
why &lquo;thou dead corse again in complete steel <I>Revisitest thus</I> the glimpses of the
moon,&rquo; can cacophony further go? Thus to pronounce these two words is to pay too
dear a price for grammar. Again in <I>Lear,</I> where the old demented king says &lquo;thou
hotly <I>lustest to</I> use.&rquo; In both cases we are forced to use the forms in the Folio and
say &lquo;Revisits thus&rquo; and &lquo;lusts to.&rquo; Thus, too, in the present line, an ear that would
shrink under &lquo;affects&rquo; for <I>affectest</I> is too grammatical to be of use to anybody, much
less to its owner. When Heine said that to his ears the English language sounded
like the harsh notes of sea-mews, I think he must have had in memory some of the
second person singulars of verbs ending in <I>t.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>92. <B>euidence</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii): There can be no hesitation in adopting here the
excellent emendation of the MS, viz.: <I>credence</I> for &lquo;evidence&rquo;; it suits both measure
and meaning admirably; for the sake of the metre &lquo;evidence&rquo; [must be pronounced]
<I>ev'dence.</I> Cleopatra was not to give <I>evidence,</I> but belief, to the affection of Antony.
<SC>Singer</SC> (<I>Sh. Vind.</I> 289): The substitution of <I>credence</I> would be specious, but that
the occurrence of &lquo;trial,&rquo; in the next line, shows that the old text is right. Cleopatra
had just cast a doubt on Antony's love; he bids her give &lquo;true evidence&rquo; in favour
of it, not bear false witness against it, as she had done. <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Strict.</I> 201) quotes
with approval this note of Singer, and adds: Compare &lquo;Proceed no straiter 'gainst
our uncle Gloster Than from <I>true evidence,</I>&rquo; etc.&mdash;<I>2 Hen. VI:</I> III, ii. &lquo;Give true
evidence&rquo; is &lquo;Bear true witness;&rquo; but what is &lquo;Give <I>true credence</I>&rquo;? <SC>Staunton</SC>:
Mr Collier's annotator . . . would poorly read <I>credence,</I> which, like many of his sug-
gestions, is very specious and quite wrong. The meaning of Antony is this,&mdash;&lquo;For-
bear these taunts, and demonstrate to the world your confidence in my love by sub-
mitting it freely to the <I>trial</I> of absence.&rquo;
<P>92. <B>to his</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.</I> 77) recommends that these two words should be
written, <I>to's.</I> Could Walker have vainly imagined that by writing these words thus
the rhythmical flow of the line would be promoted? If <I>to's</I> represents one sound,
why should it not be written honestly <I>tos?</I> Does not the apostrophe by indicating an
omission equally indicate a pause long enough to show that <I>to's</I> is not <I>tos?</I> And if
there is to be a pause, however brief, it is a pause long enough to give a breathing
and say <I>to his.</I> No flow of rhythm can compensate, to my ear at least, for such slip-
shod pronunciation of English as <I>to's.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

to me as Antony is, and I forget everything.&rquo; <I>Oblivion,</I> I believe, is boldly used
for <I>a memory apt to be deceitful. . . .</I> Mr Edwards has proposed in his MS notes: &lquo;Oh
<I>me!</I> oblivion is a very Antony,&rquo; etc. <SC>Henley</SC>: Perhaps nothing is more necessary
here than a change of punctuation; <I>O my!</I> being still an exclamation frequently used
in the west of England. <SC>M. Mason</SC>: The sense of the passage appears to me to be
this: &lquo;O, my oblivion! as if it were another Antony, possesses me so entirely, that
I quite forget myself.&rquo; [Steevens's paraphrase of &lquo;my oblivion is a very Antony&rquo; is
possibly just; but may it not be that Cleopatra means that she is so utterly lost, heart
and soul and mind and strength, in Anthony, that even her forgetfulness is become a
part of him, and that her own individual self is all forgotten? See V, ii, 106.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>114-116. <B>But that . . . it selfe</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: That is, But that your charms
hold me, who am the <I>greatest</I> fool on earth, in chains, I should have adjudged you
to be the <I>greatest.</I> That this is the sense is shown by her answer: &lquo;'Tis sweating
labour, To bear such <I>idleness so near the heart,</I> As Cleopatra this&mdash;.&rquo; <SC>Heath</SC> (p.
450): I apprehend the sense is this; <I>Ant.</I> If I were not sufficiently acquainted with
you to know, that you have so perfect a command of your own disposition, as to be
able to put on or dismiss idleness, or childish frowardness, at pleasure, I should take
you, from your present behaviour, for childishness itself. <I>Cleo.</I> As much idleness as
you are pleased to call my present disposition, it is sweating labour to bear such idle-
ness so near the heart, as I do this which you reproach me with. <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 29): Did
I not know, says Antony, what a mistress you are in the arts of dissembling, and of
counterfeiting any idle humour you please, I should take the wantonness of your
present behaviour for real wantonness, and accuse you of little feeling; and with this
interpretation, the answer of Cleopatra quadrates perfectly; for it amounts to an
avowal&mdash;that she had indeed been acting a part, and that with the greatest con-
straint, and most painfully to herself; her motive, as she would have it thought,&mdash;to
keep up Antony's spirits, and her own, in such a trying juncture as this of their
parting. <SC>Steevens</SC>: Warburton's explanation is a very coarse one. The sense
may be:&mdash;But that your queenship chooses idleness for the subject of your conver-
sation, I should take you for idleness itself. Or an antithesis may be designed between
<I>royalty</I> and <I>subject.</I> But that I know you to be a queen, and that your royalty holds
idleness in subjection to you, exalting you far above its influence, I should suppose
you to be the very genius of idleness itself. <SC>Malone</SC>: But perhaps <I>your subject</I>
rather means, whom being in subjection to you, you can command at pleasure, &lquo;to
do your bidding,&rquo; to assume the airs of coquetry, etc. Were not this coquet one of
your attendants, I should suppose you yourself were this capricious being. <SC>Hud-
son</SC>: &lquo;Idleness&rquo; here means idle or sportive and unmeaning <I>talk.</I> And there is an
antithesis between &lquo;royalty&rquo; and &lquo;subject.&rquo; So the sense is, &lquo;But that you are queen
over your passion for idle discourse, and can command it as your subject, assuming
it and laying it aside when you choose, I should think you the very genius of idleness
itself.&rquo; <SC>Rolfe</SC>: But that your sovereignty can make frivolousness subservient to your
purpose, I should take you for frivolousness itself.

<P>noun substantive,&mdash;is remarkably frequent in the Folio. Those who are conversant

<P>16, 17. <B>Hereditarie, Rather than purchaste</B>] <SC>Lord Campbell</SC> (p. 117): That
is to say, they are taken by <I>descent,</I> not by <I>purchase. Lay gents</I> (viz., all except
lawyers) understand by &lquo;purchase&rquo; buying for a sum of money, called the price; but
lawyers consider that &lquo;purchase&rquo; is opposed to <I>descent,</I>&mdash;that all things come to the
owner either by <I>descent</I> or by <I>purchase,</I> and that whatever does not come through
operation of law by <I>descent</I> is <I>purchased,</I> although it may be the free gift of a donor.
Thus, if land be devised to A. in fee, he takes by <I>purchase,</I> or to B. for life, remainder
to A. and his heirs, B. being a stranger to A., A. takes by <I>purchase;</I> but upon the
death of A., his eldest son would take by <I>descent.</I> So in <I>2 Hen. IV:</I> IV, iv, the
King, who had usurped the crown, says to the Prince of Wales:&mdash;&lquo;For what in me
was purchas'd Falls upon thee in a more fairer sort.&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> I took by <I>purchase,</I> you will
take by <I>descent.</I>
<P>19, 20. <B>You are . . . Ptolomy</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 295): Arrange, perhaps,&mdash;
&lquo;You are too indulgent: Let's grant 'tis not amiss &verbar; To tumble on the bed of Ptolemy.&rquo;
<P>21. <B>a Mirth</B>] For a merry joke. <SC>Deighton</SC>: It seems doubtful whether &lquo;To
give a kingdom&rquo; means to bestow a kingdom on his entertainer, or to squander the
wealth of a kingdom in a single feast.

&lquo;<I>As,</I>&rquo; equivalent to <I>as regards which, though, for,</I> was sometimes used parenthetically

<P>27. <B>his foyles</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: For the emendation now made [<I>soils</I>] I am answer-
able. In the MSS of our author's time, <I>$</I> and <I>f</I> are often undistinguishable, and no
two letters are so often confounded at the press. Shakespeare has so regularly used
this word in the sense required here, that there cannot, I imagine, be the smallest
doubt of the justness of this emendation. So, in Hamlet: [Hereupon Malone gives
examples of <I>soil</I> from <I>Hamlet, Love's Lab. L., Meas. for Meas., 2 Hen. IV,</I> and,
doubtless, a <I>Concordance</I> would $urnish many more.] <SC>Steevens</SC>: If &lquo;foils&rquo; be inad-
missible (which I question), we might read&mdash;<I>fails.</I> In <I>The Winter's Tale,</I> we meet
with this substantive, which signifies omission, or non-performance: &lquo;Mark, and per-
form it. See'st thou? for the fail Of any point in't, shall not only be Death to thy-
self,&rquo; etc. Yet, on the whole, I prefer Malone's conjecture. <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii):
Malone and modern editors have altered &lquo;foils&rquo; to <I>soils,</I> without sufficient necessity;
the &lquo;foils&rquo; of Anthony are his vices, his <I>foibles</I> (possibly Shakespeare's word, though,
according to our dictionaries, not so old), which <I>foil,</I> or defeat, the exercise of our
virtues. [I fail to perceive any gain in substituting <I>soils</I> for &lquo;foils.&rquo; &lquo;Foils&rquo; is a
synonym of <I>soils,</I> and has all its strength. <SC>Bradley</SC> (<I>N. E. D. s. v.</I> Foil, <I>sb.</I><SUP>2</SUP>, 2. &dagger; b)
gives as its definition &lquo;A disgrace, stigma. With mixture of the sense of <I>Foil, v.</I><SUP>1</SUP>, 6.
which means To foul, defile, pollute. In material and immaterial sense.&rquo; <SC>Schmidt</SC>
(<I>Lex.</I>) also gives a definition of &lquo;foil&rquo; as &lquo;blemish, shortcoming&rquo; and quotes the
present passage as an example. With such evidence before us, is there any sufficient
reason why we should discard Shakespeare's word and adopt Malone's?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

much burden upon us.
