<P>31. <B>confound</B>] See note on &lquo;confound&rquo; I, i, 59.
<P>33-36. <B>'tis to be chid: As we,</B> etc.] <SC>Heath</SC> (p. 451): As we rate boys, who,
when they have attained a sufficient maturity of knowledge to regulate their own
conduct, sacrifice to their present pleasure, the experience they have had of the ill
consequences which will certainly follow from such indulgence, and thus rebel
against their own judgment. According to Hanmer's reading, the fault of the boy is
said to proceed from the immaturity of his knowledge, that is, want of sufficient
experience to teach him that knowledge, at the same time that he is said to have that
experience, and to act in contradiction to it, and to his judgment founded upon it.
<SC>Capell</SC> (i, 30): &lquo;Being mature&rquo; has been chang'd into&mdash;<I>immature</I>: but &lquo;boys&rquo; are
not usually &lquo;rated&rquo; for faults before they are of years to know better; nor can they
&lquo;rebel to judgment,&rquo; till such time as they have some. <SC>Johnson</SC>: By &lquo;boys mature in
knowledge&rquo; are meant, boys old enough to know their duty. <SC>R. G. White</SC> (ed. i):
Hanmer's reading, &lquo;<I>immature</I> in knowledge&rquo; is most plausible. For boys are not
mature in anything, and least in knowledge; and were they mature they would not
pawn their experience to their present pleasure; or at least their so doing would not
be chosen as an illustration here. Without an equivalent to Hanmer's too great
change, the passage appears to be inexplicable. <SC>Daniel</SC> (p. 80): Read these four
lines thus: &lquo;&mdash;&mdash; <I>he's</I> to be chid As we rate boys, who, being mature in knowledge,
<I>Pawns his</I> experience to <I>his</I> present pleasure, And so <I>rebels</I> to judgment.&rquo; Boys are
not mature in knowledge, and cannot pawn experience nor rebel against judgment
they do not possess; but Antony being so, and doing thus, is to be chidden as a boy.
J[<SC>oseph</SC>] C[<SC>rosby</SC>] (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> V, vii, 464, 1877): The only objection to Daniel's
emendation is that it makes no less than five changes in the original text. But the
same sense and construction may be obtained by only one alteration, and that a
very slight one,&mdash;viz. by reading <I>They're</I> for &lquo;'tis,&rquo;&mdash;placing the parenthetical clause
between dashes, and closing the first sentence with a note of exclamation after &lquo;ours,&rquo;
thus:&mdash;&lquo;As his own state and ours! <I>They're</I> to be chid&mdash;As we rate boys&mdash;who,

less difficulty in these lines had they only followed the punctuation of the Folio, with
a colon after &lquo;chid,&rquo; instead of adopting Capell's text where is no punctuation after

is an elastic term. Later on, Anthony calls C&aelig;sar a &lquo;boy.&rquo; Compared with
Anthony's fifty-two years thirty-two years may well be a boy's span, and can any
one say that such a &lquo;boy&rquo; might not be mature enough to recognize the folly of pawn-
ing experience to present pleasure? The old shepherd in <I>The Winter's Tale</I> thought
that youths of three-and-twenty knew too much.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>51. <B>Comes fear'd, by being lack'd</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: Let us examine the sense of
this in plain prose: &lquo;The earliest histories inform us, that the man in supreme com-
mand was always wish'd to gain that command, till he had obtain'd it. And he,
whom the multitude has contentedly seen in a low condition, when he begins to be
wanted by them, becomes to be &ldquo;fear'd&rdquo; by them.&rquo; But do the multitude fear a
man because they want him? Certainly, we must read: &lquo;Comes <I>dear'd,</I> by being
lacked,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> endear'd, a favourite to them. Besides, the context requires this read-
ing; for it was not fear, but love, that made the people flock to young Pompey and
what occasioned this reflection. So in <I>Coriolanus:</I> &lquo;I shall be <I>lov'd,</I> when I am
lack'd.&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC>: Something, however, is yet wanting. What is the meaning of
&mdash;&lquo;ne'er lov'd till <I>ne'er</I> worth love?&rquo; I suppose that the second &lquo;ne'er&rquo; was inad-
vertently repeated at the press, and that we should read &lquo;till <I>not</I> worth love.&rquo;
<SC>Knight</SC> [who follows the Folio]: The general reading is <I>dear'd.</I> But it must be
remembered that C&aelig;sar is speaking; and that, in the notions of one who aims at
supreme authority, to be feared and to be loved are pretty synonymous. <SC>Collier</SC>
(ed. i, also following the Folio): Warburton's alteration is plausible, but does not
seem necessary. C&aelig;sar may mean, that Pompey, by being so much backed by the
people, has become powerful, and is therefore &lquo;fear'd.&rquo; <I>Ibid.</I> (ed. ii, adopting <I>lov'd</I>
from his MS): We accept the emendation of the MS with confidence, not lessened
by the Shakespearian alliteration thus afforded. The meaning is too plain to need ex-
planation. [In his <I>Third Edition</I> <SC>Collier</SC> adopted Warburton's <I>dear'd.</I>] <SC>J. Crosby</SC>
(<I>Shakespeariana,</I> Dec. 1883, p. 46) suggests that &lquo;fear'd&rquo; should be &lquo;spelt <I>'feer'd,</I>
abbreviated from <I>affeer'd, i. e.,</I> estimated at its true worth, appraised, <I>valued.</I>&rquo;
[This suggestion would be almost conclusive, were it possible to find a single instance
where <I>affeer</I> is abbreviated to <I>'feer,</I> or where even any of the word's modifications
is so abbreviated. Not an instance is to be found, I think, in the <I>N. E. D.</I> nor
in <SC>Wright's</SC> <I>English Dialect Dictionary,</I> where such an abbreviation could not
fail to be given, if it had been ever used in any English dialect. C&aelig;sar is in a
bitter mood. To his vexation over Anthony's misdoings is now added the morti-
fying news that those whose love for him had changed to fear were flocking to
Pompey. Whereupon he begins to moralize and says that he ought to have known
that this would be so, because from time immemorial he who is in power was loved
up to the very moment when he attained that power. Then he became feared and
people deserted him (just as they had deserted him for Pompey). Next, through
this desertion, he becomes an ebb'd man. And this ebb'd man (again a victim of
popular caprice, and now loved when all his power is gone and there is no longer
profit in loving him), by being missed and wanted again by the people, comes again
to be feared. Thus the common people go to and back, hither and yon, like a vaga-
bond flag on the stream. If this interpretation be just, Warburton's emendation,
<I>dear'd,</I> is needless, and the text of the Folio may be vindicated.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>53. <B>lacking</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: The addition of a single letter [to the word in the
Folio] will not only give us good sense, but the genuine word of our author into the
bargain:&mdash;&lquo;<I>Lackeying</I> the varying Tide,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> floating backwards and forwards with
the variation of the tide, like a page, or lacquey, at his master's heels. <SC>Steevens</SC>:
Compare Chapman's <I>Iliad</I>: &lquo;My guide to Argos, either shipp'd, or lackeying by thy
side,&rquo; Bk. 24th, [line 392.] Again, &lquo;&mdash;who would willingly Lackey along so vast a
lake of brine.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Odyssey,</I> Bk. 5, [line 130.] Again in Marston's <I>Antonio and Mel-
lida,</I> 1602: &lquo;O that our power Could lackie or keep wing with our desires.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Second
Part, Prologue.</I> <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. i): Southern in his Folio, 1685, altered &lquo;lacking&rquo;
to <I>backing.</I> <SC>Halliwell</SC> (<I>Notes,</I> etc. p. 13): &lquo;Lacking&rquo; is rather a variation of form
than an error. The same orthography occurs in a MS dated 1615, quoted by Haw-
kins, in his edition of Ruggle's <I>Ignoramus,</I> 1787, Appendix, p. 120. <SC>J. Churton
Collins</SC> (p. 299): Theobald gave us back one of the finest onomatop&oelig;ic lines in
Shakespeare:&mdash;G&macr;oes &macr;to a&breve;nd b&macr;ack l&macr;ack&breve;eyi&breve;ng th&breve;e v&macr;ar&breve;yi&breve;ng &macr;tide.
<P>55. <B>Mes.</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: Perhaps another Messenger should be noted here, as enter-
ing with fresh news. <SC>Heyse</SC> (p. 146) makes the same suggestion, &lquo;inasmuch as
C&aelig;sar had been assured that he should &ldquo;every hour have report How 'tis abroad.&rdquo;
That this second messenger brings nothing absolutely new is no more than is to be
expected from reports every hour.&rquo;
<P>57. <B>eare</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: To &lquo;ear&rquo; is to <I>plough</I>; a common metaphor.
<P>60. <B>Lacke blood to think e on't</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Turn pale at the thought of it.
<P>60. <B>flush youth</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: That is, youth ripened to manhood; youth whose
blood is at the flow.

<P>65. <B>Vassailes</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: <I>Wassel</I> is here put for intemperance in general. <SC>Hen-
ley</SC>: &lquo;Vassals&rquo; is, without question, the true reading. <SC>Knight</SC>: Wassal is em-
ployed by Shakspere in the strict meaning of drunken revelry; and that could
scarcely be called &lquo;lascivious.&rquo; On the contrary, &lquo;leave thy lascivious <I>vassals</I>&rquo;
expresses C&aelig;sar's contempt for Cleopatra and her minions, who were strictly the vas-
sals of Antony, the queen being one of his tributaries. <SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. ii): Knight
prints &lquo;vassals,&rquo; though the rest of the speech so distinctly shows that here <I>wassails</I>
and not &lquo;vassals&rquo; are in question. <SC>Collier</SC>: Either reading may be right; but
<I>vassal</I> was not usually, though sometimes, spelt <I>vassaile,</I> and nothing is more likely
than that the old compositor should use <I>v</I> for <I>w.</I> C&aelig;sar has previously accused
Antony of &lquo;tippling with a slave,&rquo; and &lquo;reeling the streets at noon,&rquo; which counte-
nances <I>wassails</I> as an old drinking term; and, in addition, we may state that &lquo;vas-
sailes&rquo; is amended to <I>wassails</I> in the MS. [According to Bartlett's <I>Concordance,</I>
&lquo;vassal&rquo; or &lquo;vassals&rquo; occurs twenty times elsewhere in Shakespeare, which added
to the present instance make twenty-one; of this number three occur in the present
play; in a third of the instances it is spelt in the Folio <I>vassaile</I> or <I>vassailes;</I> it is
also so spelt in <I>Sonnet 58.</I> In none of these instances, except in the present, has
there been any suggestion of <I>wassail;</I> nor can I see any necessity for such a sugges-
tion here, in spite of the dogmatic assertion of Dyce, whose note, to my regret, I do
not comprehend. It is really not clear to me that Anthony ought to leave his revelry
in Egypt, because &lquo;the rest of the speech so distinctly shows&rquo; that some time pre-
viously, at Modena, he drank gilded puddles and browsed on bark. The adjective
which qualifies &lquo;vassailes,&rquo; seems to me to be far more appropriate to humankind than
to drinking bouts. In the present play, it is spelt &lquo;vassaile,&rquo; II, vi, 71, and &lquo;vassal,&rquo;
V, ii, 35. It is to be borne in mind that the spelling of the compositors of the Folio
is so lawless, that any appeal to its uniformity is generally useless.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>4. <B>Ha, ha.</B>] It is not easy to decide how this exclamation should be spelt, expres-
sive as it is of mingled weariness and impatience. What is, possibly, the modern
equivalent was spelt by Shakespeare's compositors five times &lquo;heigh ho&rquo; and once &lquo;hey
ho.&rquo; I say &lquo;modern equivalent&rquo; because Shakespeare does not always employ it to
express weariness, for example, in the song in <I>As You Like It,</I> &lquo;Then heigh ho, the
holly, This life is most jolly.&rquo; In the present instance, howsoever it be spelt, it is
not laughter, any more than is Othello's agonized, &lquo;Ha, ha, false to me?&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>4. <B>giue me to drinke</B>] <SC>Deighton</SC>: Not &lquo;give me mandragora to drink,&rquo; but &lquo;enable
me, put it in my power, to drink mandragora,&rquo; as in <I>Othello,</I> II, iii, 209, &lquo;<I>Give me
to know</I> How this foul rout began.&rquo; [I think these two instances are hardly parallel.
Othello demands certain information and follows up this demand with direct ques-
tions. Cleopatra gives a command which she does not expect to be obeyed; and
would probably have refused the smallest sip, had mandragora been really brought to
her.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>4. <B>Mandragoru</B>] In the <I>Text. Notes</I> of the <I>Cam. Ed.</I> &lquo;Mandragora&rquo; is given as
the word in F<SUB>1</SUB>. This is possibly an instance, among many, of a variation in copies
of the same edition. It is clearly &lquo;Mandragoru&rquo; in my copy of F<SUB>1</SUB>; it is so also in
Vernor and Hood's <I>Reprint</I> of 1807; in Booth's <I>Reprint,</I> and in Staunton's <I>Photo-
lithograph.</I> It is a matter of very small importance, and serves only as a warning
against a reliance, too implicit, on the spelling of Shakespeare's compositors.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>4. <B>Mandragoru</B>] &lquo;Mandragora hath that name, for it beareth apples with great
savour of the greatnesse of the apples of <I>Macian,</I> and is called <I>Malum terre</I> among
Latines. And Poets call it <I>Antropomoros,</I> for the root thereof is some deale shapen
as a man: the rinde thereof medled with Wine is giuen to them to drinke that shall
be cut in the body, for they shuld sleepe and not feele the sore cutting. . . . And
<I>Diosco.</I> saith, that <I>Mandragora</I> is a sleeping hearbe. . . . For the rindes thereof sod
in Wine, cause sleepe, <I>&amp;</I> abateth all manner sorenesse: and so that time a man
feeleth vnneth, though he bee cut.&rquo;&mdash;Batman <I>vppon Bartholome,</I> 1582, Liber XVII,
Chap. 104, p. 304. Page after page could be quoted of the superstitions which have
clustered about this plant. All that Cleopatra cared for here and now was its nar-
cotic power, and that quality is all that a note need set forth. Therefore it is, that
only the foregoing extract from Bartholome is given,&mdash;a book probably less accessible
to the general reader than many another. Should a student wish, however, to pur-
sue the subject further, he is referred to:&mdash; Lyte's trans. of Dodoens, ed. 1578, p.
437; Holland's <I>Plinie,</I> tome II, bk. xxv, ch. 13, ed. 1634; Gerarde's <I>Herball,</I> p.
351, ed. 1633; Lupton's <I>Thousand Notable things of sundrie sortes,</I> Third Booke,
43, ed. 1627 (where directions may be found &lquo;to make a counterfet Mandrage, which
hath been sold by deceiuers, for much money&rquo;); Nares, <I>s. v.;</I> Ellacombe, <I>Plant
Lore,</I> p. 117; Grindon, <I>Shakspere Flora,</I> p. 290; Seager, <I>Natural History in Shake-
speare's Time,</I> p. 195; or <I>Othello,</I> III, iii, 384; <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I> IV, iii, 47 of this
Edition. Finally, there is an exhaustive discussion of it, historically and botanically,
by Prof. <SC>Ferd. Cohn</SC> in the <I>F&uuml;nfundsechzigster Jahres-Bericht der Schlesischen
Gesellschaft f. vaterl&auml;ndische Cultur,</I> Breslau, 1888, p. 285.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P><SC>Mrs Jameson</SC> (p. 130): Finer still are the workings of her variable mind and
lively imagination, after Antony's departure; her fond repining at his absence, her
violent spirit, her right royal wilfulness and impatience, as if it were a wrong to her
majesty, an insult to her sceptre, that there should exist in her despite such things as
space and time; and high treason to her sovereign power, to dare to remember what
she chooses to forget.
<P>6, 7. <B>this great gap of time: My Anthony is away</B>] The modern punctuation,
either with or without a comma after &lquo;time,&rquo; is, I think, much to be preferred to the
colon of the Folio, and yet it does not convey exactly the meaning of the Folio.
According to the Folio, Cleopatra seems to say in effect, &lquo;That I might sleep out
this great gap of time. Cannot you understand? My Anthony is away.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>9. <B>O 'tis Treason</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC> deemed this phrase &lquo;cold and unmetrical,&rquo; he,
therefore omitted &lquo;'tis.&rquo; <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 295) agreed with him in the omission.
And both were anticipated by <SC>Capell</SC>.
<P>16. <B>May not flye forth of Egypt</B>] For several other examples of this somewhat
unusual form, &lquo;forth of,&rquo; see <SC>Franz</SC>, &sect; 388, <I>e</I>): Compare also, IV, x, 9, &lquo;They have
put forth the Hauen,&rquo; where &lquo;forth&rquo; is a true preposition.

<P>28. <B>the Arme</B>] <SC>Collier</SC>: By &lquo;arm&rquo; is probably to be understood <I>weapon.</I>
<P>29. <B>Burganet</B>] <SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D.</I>): An adaptation of Old French <I>bourguig-
notte,</I> apparently formed on <I>Bourgogne,</I> Burgundy. b. A helmet with a visor, so
fitted to the gorget or neck-piece, that the head could be turned without exposing
the neck.
<P>29. <B>men</B>] Although the reading of the First Folio should not be disturbed, the
reading of the Folios, &lquo;man,&rquo; with its all-embracing scope seems the finer; Anthony is
the demi-Atlas of the earth, the arm and burgonet of all the inhabitants thereof.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>29. <B>Hee's speaking now,</B> etc.] <SC>Hazlitt</SC> (p. 97): Few things in Shakespear
(and we know of nothing in any other author like them) have more of that local
truth of imagination and character than the passage in which Cleopatra is represented
conjecturing what were the employments of Antony in his absence. &lquo;He's speaking
now, or murmuring&mdash;<I>Where's my serpent of old Nile?</I>&rquo; Or again, when she says to
Antony, after the defeat at Actium, and his summoning up resolution to risk another
fight&mdash;&lquo;It is my birth-day; I had thought to have held it poor; but since my lord
is Antony again, I will be Cleopatra.&rquo; [This &lquo;birthday,&rquo; Shakespeare found in
Plutarch.]
<P>31, 32. <B>cals me:</B>) <B>. . . Thinke</B>] <SC>Keightley</SC> (<I>Exp.</I> 312): &lquo;For so he calls me&mdash;
Now I feed myself With most delicious poison&mdash;thinks on me,&rquo; etc. It is thus I would
give force to the passage. The appeal to those present is feeble. [In considering
&lquo;Now I feed myself With most delicious poison&rquo; as parenthetical, Keightley is
anticipated by Capell. What Keightley may gain in force by continuing in <I>thinks</I>
the nominative of &lquo;calls,&rquo; does he not lose in elegance by adopting a commercial style
in omitting <I>he?</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>then does she mention it as a wonder that he should say such rapturous things of her
in her decline of life? No, Antony's speech should be continued as the metaphor
is: &lquo;Where's my serpent of old Nile?&mdash;Now I feed myself With most delicious

almost needless to remark that no one has ever adopted this arrangement.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>32. <B>most delicious poyson</B>] It is poison because the reminiscence &lquo;works like
madness in her veins.&rquo;
<P>32-34. <B>Thinke on me . . . wrinkled deepe in time</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>, in his first
edition included these lines in quotation marks, for which he has nowhere, that I
can find, offered any explanation. It is not his custom so to mark mnemonic lines;
only Pope and Warburton thus mark them. They were not repeated in his <I>Second
Edition.</I>
<P>33. <B>with Ph&oelig;bus amorous pinches blacke</B>] <SC>Hazlitt</SC> (<I>Elizabethan Literature,</I>
p. 52, ed. 1869) says that this line of Cleopatra is the same as the following exclam-
ation of Eleazer, the Moor, in <I>Lust's Dominion</I>:&mdash;&lquo;Now by the proud complexion
of my cheeks, Ta'en from the kisses of the amorous sun.&rquo;&mdash;III, iv, p. 140, ed. Haz.
Dodsley. Collier thinks that <I>Lust's Dominion</I> was probably written in 1599&mdash;1600.
There is, however, but little parallelism between the two passages. It is only by a
flight of fancy that &lquo;kisses&rquo; can turn a fair cheek black (they generally turn it red),
but an &lquo;amorous pinch&rquo; is a &lquo;feeling disputation&rquo; which is sure to be followed by
black traces.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>34. <B>wrinkled deepe in time.</B>] It is almost impossible to accept the interrogation
mark which a large majority of editors have followed Rowe in placing at the end of
this sentence. Cleopatra is wrapt out of herself by the delicious poison, and apostro-
phises the absent Anthony, just as, in the next line, she apostrophises the dead
C&aelig;sar.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>34. <B>Broad-fronted C&aelig;sar</B>] <SC>Seward</SC> (<I>Preface to Beaumont &amp; Fletcher,</I> p. lxvi):
Is there the least ground from Medals, Statues, or History for this description of
C&aelig;sar? No, but the very reverse. Look on his medals, and particularly on the fine
bronze at Dr Mead's, and you'll find that he has a remarkably <I>sharp forehead.</I> But
there is a peculiarity in C&aelig;sar's <I>forehead</I> mentioned by all Historians, and con-
firmed by medals and statues. He was <I>bald,</I> and boasted that he would cover his
temples with laurels instead of hair; and, for that purpose, after he was Dictator, con-
stantly wore his laurel-crown. I read therefore, &lquo;<I>Bald</I>-fronted C&aelig;sar.&rquo; <SC>Henley</SC>
sees in &lquo;broad-fronted&rquo; the very allusion to baldness which Seward denies.
<P>38. <B>Aspect</B>] For a list of other words &lquo;in which the accent is nearer the end than
with us,&rquo; see <SC>Abbott,</SC> &sect; 490.

<P>43, 44. <B>that great Med'cine hath With his Tinct gilded thee</B>] There seems
to have been, of old, some nicety observed in the spelling of <I>Medicine.</I> Hanmer
here spells it &lquo;Med'cin,&rquo; and Capell, who in his text spells it, &lquo;Med'cine,&rquo; as it is in
the Folio, says in his Notes that it should have been spelt <I>Med'cin,</I> because &lquo;the
appellation is given to Antony, as being the curer of all her sorrows.&rquo; On the other
hand, Hanmer in <I>All's Well,</I> II, i, 74, &lquo;I have seen a medicine That's able to
breathe life into a stone,&rquo; spells the word in question, <I>Medecine,</I> and, in a note, says
it is &lquo;here put for a <I>She-physician.</I>&rquo; So that according to Hanmer, we have <I>Med'cin,</I>
masculine, <I>Medecine,</I> feminine. <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 295) also thinks that &lquo;medi-
cine&rquo; in the present passage means <I>physician.</I> <SC>Johnson</SC> comes nearer the truth, I
think, when he says that there is here an allusion &lquo;to the philosophers stone, which,
by its touch, converts base metal into gold. The Alchemists call the matter, what-
ever it may be, by which they perform transmutation, a <I>medicine.</I>&rquo; The particular
&lquo;medicine&rquo; Cleopatra refers to, is, I think, the <I>elixir vitae,</I> which is what Anthony
certainly was to her, and into this elixir, gold enters as an essential ingredient, hence
the word &lquo;gilded.&rquo; There would have been no thought that Anthony was himself
the physician, I think, had the use of <I>its</I> been so common that Cleopatra could have
said &lquo;that great medicine hath With <I>its</I> tinct gilded thee.&rquo; As to any distinction
between <I>Med'cin</I> and <I>Med'cine,</I> if there be a reference to it in the <I>N. E. D.,</I> it has
escaped me.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

pardon? Grammar is on his side, and the truth of construction; But where find a
reason why a pearl should be called so? The pearl is met with in oisters that are

has a kind of growth in the shell it adheres to; which growth is effected by the
accession of coat after coat, one enclosing other in the manner of onions: Now, is it
too great a liberty for a poet to say of it,&mdash;that the fish it's mother forms those coats
by a repetition of touchings, which he calls&mdash;&lquo;kisses?&rquo; if this will not be allow'd of,
a better solution must be sought for; and no such offers itself at present. This cir-
cumstance of the pearl is not in Plutarch: but there is mention in Pliny&mdash;of a pearl

<P>52. <B>at whose foote</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC> (ed. i): This has relation neither to Cleopatra,

<P>53. <B>peece</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: This expression of &lquo;piecing her throne&rquo; is indeed
tolerable; but barely so. No bungling carpenter could have expressed his labour
worse. I suspect that Shakespeare wrote, &lquo;I will <I>pace</I> Her opulent throne,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> I
will erect an imperial throne for her, and every step up to it shall be a kingdom. The
expression is noble, and the idea vastly magnificent. <SC>Seward</SC> (<I>Preface,</I> p. lxvii):
To <I>piece,</I> to this day signifies to join two pieces together, or to fasten new parts
to anything, as to <I>piece a rope,</I> to <I>piece a beam.</I> I will join new kingdoms to her
Dominions, and make her Queen of Asia as well as Egypt. <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex. s. v.</I>
Piece, vb. 3) to the same effect furnishes the following:&mdash;&lquo;all of it with our dis-
pleasure pieced.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Lear,</I> I, i, 203; &lquo;I twice five hundred and their friends to piece
'em.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Cor.</I> II, iii, 220; and two or three other examples.
<P>54. <B>opulent</B>] <SC>Deighton</SC>: It is perhaps doubtful whether this means &lquo;already
opulent,&rquo; or &lquo;which shall thereby be made opulent.&rquo;

nifies <I>thin-shouldered,</I> which we know to be one of the principal beauties of a horse.

<C>[56. <B>an Arme-gaunt Steede</B>]</C>
<P>Mr Warburton here seems to have stolen Don Quixote's Rosinante, to mount the demi-
Atlas of <I>this</I> earth. . . . However, he seems to have matched him well, with one from
Fairfax who is <I>stall-worn. . . .</I> But Mr Warburton, who made this match, has played
us a Yorkshire trick; and the odds are prodigiously on old Fairfax's side; for when
I come to look upon him in his stable, he is really not a <I>stall-worn,</I> but a <I>stalworth</I>
steed; now <I>stalworth</I> or <I>stalwart,</I> signifies <I>bold, courageous, strong.</I> <SC>Heath</SC> (p.
452): &lquo;Arm-gaunt&rquo; is in my apprehension, a steed whose armour fitted him, and set
close about him. <SC>Johnson</SC>: <I>Arm</I> is the Teutonick word for <I>want,</I> or <I>poverty.</I>
&lquo;Arm-gaunt&rquo; may be therefore an old word, signifying <I>lean</I> for <I>want,</I> ill fed.
Edwards's observation, that a worn-out horse is not proper for Atlas to mount in
battle, is impertinent; the horse here mentioned seems to be a post-horse, rather than
a war-horse. Yet as &lquo;arm-gaunt&rquo; seems not intended to imply any defect, it perhaps
means, a horse so slender that a man might clasp him, and therefore formed for
expedition. <SC>Malone</SC>: On this passage, which I believe to be corrupt, I have
nothing satisfactory to propose. It is clear that whatever epithet was used, it was
intended as descriptive of a beautiful horse, such (we may presume) as our author
has described in his Venus and Adonis. <SC>M. Mason</SC>: I should amend by reading:
&lquo;a <I>termagant</I> steed, <I>That</I> neigh'd,&rquo; etc. <I>Termagant</I> means <I>furious.</I> So Douglas,
in <I>Henry IV.</I> is called the <I>termagant</I> Scot, an epithet that agrees well with the
steed's neighing so high. Besides, by saying that Antony mounted composedly a
horse of such mettle, Alexas presents Cleopatra with a flattering image of her hero,
which his mounting slowly a jaded post-horse, would not have done. <SC>Steevens</SC>:
When I first met with Mason's conjecture, I own I was startled at his boldness; but
that I have since been reconciled to it, its appearance in the present text of Shak-
speare will sufficiently prove. The sobriety displayed by Antony in mounting a steed
of temper so opposite, reminds us of a similar contrast in Addison's celebrated com-
parison of the Angel: &lquo;<I>Calm</I> and <I>serene</I> he drives the furious blast.&rquo; <SC>Boswell</SC>:
May I be permitted to throw out a conjecture, as to which I myself have no great con-
fidence. <I>Gaunt</I> is certainly <I>thin;</I> but as it is generally used in speaking of animals
made <I>savage by hunger,</I> such as a <I>gaunt</I> wolf, a <I>gaunt</I> mastiff, it is possible that it
may derivatively have acquired the sense of fierce, and an <I>arm-gaunt</I> steed may
signify a steed looking fierce in armour. <SC>Nares</SC> (<I>Gloss. s. v.</I>): It seems to me that
Warburton though he failed in his proof, gave the interpretation best suited to the
text, <I>worn by military service.</I> This implies the military activity of the master; all
the rest of the senses are reproachful, and are therefore inconsistent with the speech
which is made to display the gallantry of a lover to his mistress. <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Notes,</I> p.
151) quotes Nares with approval, and adds that he has not the slightest doubt that
Collier's MS and Hanmer were right in their &lquo;arm-<I>girt.</I>&rquo; <SC>Knight</SC>: &lquo;Arm-gaunt&rquo; con-
veys the notion of a steed fierce and terrible in armour; and the epithet therefore is not
to be lightly replaced by any other. <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. i): &lquo;That is, a horse which had
perhaps become gaunt by bearing arms. However this is doubtful.&rquo; <SC>Collier</SC> in his
<I>Second Edition</I> adopted the change of his MS, <I>arm-girt,</I> &lquo;which accords with Han-
mer's suggestion: <I>arm-girt</I> is, of course, girded with armour.&rquo; In his <I>Third Edition,</I>
he discarded <I>arm-girt</I> and returned to &lquo;arm-gaunt&rquo; which, he says, &lquo;is very intelli-
gible, and not less forcible.&rquo; W. N. L[<SC>ettsom</SC>?] (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> I, vii, 378, 1853):
This appears to me a mere misprint for <I>rampaunt,</I> but whether <I>rampaunt</I> was Shake-
speare's word or a transcriber's sophistication for <I>ramping</I> is more than I can under-
take to determine. . . . At one period to <I>ramp</I> and to <I>prance</I> seem to have been

<P>synonymous. Spenser makes the horses of night &lquo;fiercely ramp,&rquo; and Surrey exhibits
a <I>prancing</I> lion. <SC>R. G. White</SC> (<I>Sh.'s Scholar,</I> 1854, p. 448) made the same emen-
dation. <SC>Perring</SC> (p. 436) also approves, and, on the supposition that the phrase
originally stood <I>on a rampaunt,</I> furnishes an imaginary genealogy of the word as we
now have it, thus:&mdash;<I>arampaunt, aramgaunt, armgaunt.</I> <SC>Singer</SC>: The epithet,
<I>arrogant</I> [adopted in Singer's text], is the happy suggestion of Mr Boaden, and is to
be preferred, both on account of its more striking propriety and because it admits of
the original article, &lquo;an&rquo; retaining its place before it. <SC>R. G. White</SC>: Being able to
discover no meaning in &lquo;arme-gaunt,&rquo; I hardly hesitate to substitute Hanmer's <I>arm-
girt.</I> <SC>Halliwell</SC>: &lquo;Arm-gaunt,&rquo; that is, a steed as thin as one's arm, one worn
lean and thin by excessive service in war. Chaucer has a similar compound, <I>arm-
grete,</I> as large as the arm,&mdash;&lquo;His lange heer y-kempt byhynd his bak, As eny raven
fether it schon for blak. A wrethe of gold arm-gret, and huge of wighte, upon his
heed,&rquo; etc.&mdash;[<I>The Knightes Tale,</I> line 1285, ed. Morris.] <SC>Staunton</SC>: If the original
lection be genuine, which we doubt, &lquo;gaunt&rquo; must be understood to mean <I>fierce, eager.</I>
<SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 297) adopts Mason's &lquo;<I>termagant,</I> of course,&rquo; and adds, &lquo;<I>Terma-
gant</I> may have been written <I>tearmagant,</I> as <I>cleargie,</I> and some other old forms, among
the rest <I>tearme. . . .</I> But I rather think it was written <I>tarmagaunt.</I> Hamlet of 1603,
&mdash;&ldquo;I would have such a fellow whipt, for o'redoing tarmagant.&rdquo; . . . The old
spellings, &ldquo;Arme-gaunt&rdquo; and <I>tarmagaunt</I> render the mistake easily intelligible.&rquo;
<SC>Lettsom</SC> (Walker's editor) in a footnote to the foregoing, &lquo;confesses that he cannot
agree with Walker in his approbation of Mason,&rquo; and justly says that, &lquo;<I>Termagant</I> in
the sense of <I>violent</I> is essentially a comic word.&rquo; <SC>Dyce</SC> rehearses various emendations,
without expressing any opinion other than that Mason's <I>termagant</I> is &lquo;very bad.&rquo;
<SC>Keightley</SC> (<I>Exp.</I> 312): The best correction seems to be that of Boaden and myself,
<I>arrogant;</I> we might also read <I>ardent;</I> or <I>angry.</I> I had, like M. Mason, conjectured
<I>termagant;</I> but that term is never applied to an animal. <SC>John Hunter</SC>: We
think &lquo;arm-gaunt&rquo; refers to the angular parts of the horse's armour, as resembling
the projecting bones of a lean or gaunt animal. <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>): There is in old
English another &lquo;gaunt,&rquo; the German <I>ganz,</I> signifying <I>whole, healthful, lusty,</I> and
&lquo;arm-gaunt&rquo; may mean completely armed, harnessed, or rather: lusty in arms, full
of life and spirits even under the weight of arms. <SC>R. M. Spence</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 1878,
V, x, 244): Of the one adjective I make two, &lquo;arm'd gaunt.&rquo; I regard it as an error
not of sight but of hearing. Let any one pronounce the two words, and, unless his
utterance be more than ordinarily distinct, ten to one his <I>arm'd gaunt</I> will reach the
ear of his auditor as <I>arm-gaunt.</I> In this case the printer has only too faithfully fol-
lowed the amanuensis. J. D. (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 1879, V, xii, 163) on the authority of
<I>The Gentleman's Dictionary,</I> 1705, accepts <I>arm</I> as denoting in Shakespeare's time,
&lquo;the fore-thigh, or upper part of the fore-leg of a horse. &ldquo;Arm-gaunt&rdquo; means, there-
fore,&rquo; he says, &lquo;slender in the fore-thigh, or fore-leg, and is equivalent to <I>high-bred.</I>&rquo;
<SC>B. Nicholson</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 1892, VIII, i, 182) suggests that <I>gaunt</I> might have been
the perfect participle <I>gaunted,</I> where the final <I>-ed</I> had been absorbed in the final <I>t</I> of
<I>gaunt,</I> and inasmuch as this, &lquo;as shown by <I>gauntlet,</I> is derived from the French <I>gant,</I>
&ldquo;arm-gaunt&rdquo; is <I>armour-gloved.</I> A poetic metaphor, and one which beautifully
expresses how the armourer so metal-gloved his steed as not to impede any of his
natural actions.&rquo; <SC>Rolfe</SC>: I have no doubt that it is a misprint. The poet's word
was not improbably <I>rampaunt,</I> though the article &lquo;an&rquo; favours <I>arrogant.</I> <SC>Murray</SC>
(<I>N. E. D. s. v.</I> Arm. <I>sb</I><SUP>1</SUP>, III): Meaning not certainly known. ? with gaunt limbs.

<P>[If &lquo;Arme-gaunt&rquo; be not a misprint, it is so near it that it might as well be one out-
right, and live up to its character. Some of the best editors and critics have so
deemed it. In view of the formidable, not to say appalling combination of equine
qualities and armourer's art which has been detected in this adjective, Anthony would
have been more than mortal had he not approached his steed with extreme caution,
and mounted it &lquo;soberly.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>58. <B>Was beastly dumbe by him</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: Alexas means, the horse made
such a neighing, that if he had spoke he could not have been heard. I suspect the
poet wrote, &lquo;Was beastly <I>dumb'd</I> by him,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> put to silence. Thus in <I>Pericles,</I> V,
Prologue 5, &lquo;Deep clerks she dumbs.&rquo; <SC>Warburton</SC>: Shakespeare wrote: &lquo;Who
neigh'd so <I>loud,</I> that what I would have spoke Was beastly <I>done</I> by him,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> the
sense of what I would have spoke the horse declared, tho' in inarticulate sounds.
[No space on any page can be so precious that room should not be found on it for
this Warburtonian gem.] <SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Emend.</I> p. 488): The MS gives, &lquo;Was <I>boast-
fully</I> dumb'd by him.&rquo; One slight objection to this change is that <I>boastfully</I> must be
read as a disyllable, and such is the case with various words. . . . <I>Boastfully</I> might
be, and probably was, misprinted &lquo;beastly.&rquo; <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Notes,</I> p. 152): But why did
the MS alter &lquo;beastly&rquo; to <I>boastfully</I> (which I should have thought nobody <I>could</I>
&lquo;read as a disyllable,&rquo; had not Mr Collier declared that it &lquo;<I>must</I> be read as such&rquo;)?
Merely because he happened not to perceive the meaning which Shakespeare evidently
intended &lquo;beastly&rquo; to convey, viz. <I>in the manner of a beast,</I>&mdash;i. e. <I>by inarticulate
sounds</I> which rendered vain all attempts at speaking on the part of Alexas. <SC>Singer</SC>:
&lquo;Dumbe&rquo; was altered by Theobald without necessity. The <I>arrogant</I> steed, says
Alexas, would let no sound be heard but his own, he neighed so loud that what I
would have spoke was made unintelligible, no better than the sound of a dumb
animal. <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> ii, 61) gives the present &lquo;dumbe&rquo; as the first example
under his &lquo;Article, lxii,&rquo; which treats of &lquo;final <I>d</I> and final <I>e</I> confounded.&rquo; He con-
cludes, of course, that the true word is <I>dumb'd.</I> This confusion he attributes mainly
(and his editor, Lettsom, agrees with him) to some peculiarity in the old method of
writing the final <I>e</I> or <I>d.</I> This may be so, but in a number of cases, this confusion is
due, I think, either to the imperfect pronunciation of the reader who read aloud the
copy to the compositor, or else to the failure of the compositor to catch the reader's
full pronunciation. See &lquo;vouchsafe,&rquo; I, iv, 10; &lquo;Tawny fine,&rquo; II, v, 16, and &lquo;Or
looke on thine,&rquo; V, i, 49.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>59. <B>What was he sad, or merry?</B>] Neither the punctuation of the Folio nor
that of Rowe, which has been almost uniformly followed, seems to me quite correct.
I should prefer, as more natural, &lquo;What was he, sad or merry?&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>68. <B>mingle</B>] For many other words similarly used as nouns, see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 451.
<P>68. <B>Bee'st thou</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 298): <I>Be, Beest,</I> etc. were used in Anglo-Saxon
generally in a future sense. Hence, since the future and subjunctive are closely
connected in meaning, <I>be</I> assumed an exclusively subjunctive use; and this was so
common, that we not only find &lquo;if it <I>be</I>&rquo; (which might represent the proper inflected
subjunctive of <I>be</I>), but also &lquo;if thou <I>beest,</I>&rquo; where the indicative is used subjunctively.
<P>70. <B>So do's it no mans else</B>] That is, &lquo;So does it <I>as</I> no man else.&rquo; For other
examples of the omission of <I>as,</I> see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 281. &lquo;Mans&rquo; is here one of the very
many instances gathered by <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 240) of &lquo;the final <I>s</I> interpolated and
omitted in the First Folio,&rquo; see I, iv, 11.
<P>73, 74. <B>Who's borne that day, . . . shall dye a Begger</B>] There is no hidden
meaning here, I think; it is simply that the day shall be ill-omened, or as Constance
says in <I>King John,</I> &lquo;This day all things begun, come to ill end.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>82. <B>Parago nagaine</B>:] <SC>Thiselton</SC> (p. 10): The colon after &lquo;againe&rquo; was prob-
ably deliberately placed there to indicate by a pause a special emphasis on the suc-
ceeding &lquo;My man of men.&rquo;

<P>86-88. <B>My Sallad dayes, When I was greene in iudgement, cold in blood,
To say, as I saide then.</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC> questions the propriety of &lquo;sallad,&rquo; and calcu-
lates the age of Cleopatra, when she was in love with C&aelig;sar, to be twenty years.
He then goes on to say that, &lquo;If an &AElig;gyptian could at those years have reason to
complain of coldness of blood, she must have a very particular constitution.&rquo; But he
concludes by upholding Shakespeare, who found his authority in Plutarch's report that
Cleopatra was &lquo;but a young thing&rquo; when she knew C&aelig;sar and Pompey, and that she
fell in love with Anthony in the prime of her beauty. (See <I>Appendix, Plutarch.</I>) <SC>War-
burton</SC> inflicts what it is difficult to regard as other than an injury to the text, by giving
what he calls, &lquo;Shakespear's best justification&rquo; in &lquo;restoring his own sense, which is
done merely by a different pointing:&mdash;&ldquo;My sallad days: When I was green in
judgment. Cold in blood! To say as I said then.&rdquo; <I>Cold in blood,</I> is an upbraid-
ing expostulation to her maid. <I>Those,</I> says she, <I>were my sallad days, when I was
green in judgment; but your blood is as cold as my judgment, if you have the same
opinion of things now as I had then.</I>&rquo; This punctuation, and interpretation have been
substantially followed down to this very hour. <SC>Boswell</SC> remarks that &lquo;<I>cold</I> and
<I>green</I> seem to be suggested by the metaphor <I>sallad</I> days.&rquo; Wherein he is right; what
he should have added is that both apply, not to Charmian, but to Cleopatra. What to
her was the temperature of Charmian's blood? The coldness had been her own, and
she was finding excuses for having &lquo;ever loved C&aelig;sar so.&rquo; If those were her sallad
days they were as inevitably both green and cold. The abruptness of the phrase, &lquo;To
say, as I said then!&rquo; intensifies its scorn. It is parallel to her reply in a previous
scene, &lquo;Thou teachest like a fool! The way to lose him!&rquo; and in a succeeding
scene, &lquo;so tart a favour To trumpet such good tidings.&rquo;&mdash;II, v, 48; and in Enobar-
bus's speech, &lquo;That he should dreame . . . the full C&aelig;sar will answer his emptinesse.&rquo;
&mdash;III, xiii, 39. Hanmer's punctuation seems to me exactly right: &lquo;My sallad days!
When I was green in judgment, cold in blood! To say, as I said then!&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>90, 91. <B>Ile vnpeople Egypt</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: By sending out messengers.

<P>1. <B>Menecrates, and Menas</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: The persons are so named in the first
edition. I know not why Menecrates appears; Menas can do all without him. [In
the following note, Capell endeavours to prove that a judicious discrimination will
distinguish Menas from Menecrates; that &lquo;<I>Mene,</I>&rquo; in line 5, should be <I>Menas;</I> and
that, furthermore, Warburton's emendation, <I>delay's</I> for &lquo;decayes&rquo; is just.] <SC>Capell</SC>
(i, 31): All the speeches in this scene, except one by Varrius, are given by the Folios
to Pompey and Menecrates only; this was such a palpable error with respect to one
of them [line 49] that it stands corrected in all the moderns, and of that speech
<I>Menas</I> is made the speaker, and so he <I>should</I> be of [that in line 5]. A little reflec-
tion upon the characters of the parties in question, will set the whole of this scene
in the clearest light; and shew, withal, the propriety of both these corrections
[namely, <I>Menas</I> for <I>Mene.</I> in line 5, and Warburton's <I>delay's</I>]: The character of
Pompey is mark'd by&mdash;a high sense of honour; and by a natural honesty, join'd
with irresolution and a backwardness to engage in great actions: that of Menas has
nothing particular, but that he is Pompey's fast friend: Menecrates is also his friend;
but not in favour, like Menas, from being discontented, and disapproving his patron's
conduct: Thus stated, the characters themselves will point out who the speeches
belong to: he who speaks in the second agrees with Pompey, in thinking&mdash;that the
gods would befriend them at last; but, delivering his opinion in the form of a maxim,
&lquo;what they do delay, they not deny,&rquo; the other takes occasion from one of those
words to tell him&mdash;that there was a delay which he should make his chief petition
to heaven, meaning&mdash;a delay of the preparations against him: this is taken up by
Menecrates, whose dissent is worded also in maxims, a respectful way of expressing
dissent; intimating by them,&mdash;that his opinion was rather, that Pompey himself
should prepare, and attack the triumvirs before their whole strength was gather'd
together: and this speech of Menecrates is a most unanswerable argument in favour
of the latter amendment [<I>delay's</I>], and no small one in that of the first [<I>Menas</I> for
<I>Mene.</I>]; for, unless <I>delay's</I> be admitted, no reason can be assign'd for making the
reflections contain'd in it; and, if he be the maker of them, he could not be so of
that in the other speech, their tendencies being so contrary. <SC>Malone</SC>: I have given
the first two speeches to Menecrates, and the rest to Menas. It is a matter of little
consequence. [For Johnson's suggestion that this Scene might be included in the
First Act, see the beginning of the next Scene.]

<P>7. <B>decayes</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: This nonsense should read thus: <I>delay's.</I> Menecrates
had said, &lquo;The Gods do not deny that which they delay.&rquo; The other turns his words
to a different meaning, and replies, &lquo;Delay is the very thing we beg of them,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> the
delay of our enemies in making preparations against us; which he explains after-
wards, by saying Mark Antony was tied up by lust in Egypt; C&aelig;sar by avarice
at Rome; and Lepidus employed in keeping well with both. [This emendation of
Warburton would have been relegated to the <I>Text. Notes,</I> had it not beguiled as
sensible an editor as Capell.] <SC>Heath</SC>: (p. 453): This emendation of Mr War-
burton's is certainly nonsense, whatever becomes of the common text which he is
pleased to call so. Who ever prayed for success in any enterprize, and at the same
time prayed that that success might be delayed as long as he should pray for it?
Besides the reply of Menecrates plainly implies that delay was not the thing sued
for; but something else which was for the present denied; which could not be
delay, since Pompey was already in possession of that, but must be the attainment
of the empire. The ancient reading is undoubtedly the true one. The sense is,
While we are wearying the Gods with prayers, the very thing we are praying for,
that is the empire, is falling into decay and ruin by the ill conduct of my competitors,
by the luxurious indolence of Antony, the avaricious extortions of C&aelig;sar, and by the
insincerity and private views of all the three triumvirs. <SC>Johnson</SC>: The meaning is,
&lquo;While we are praying, the thing for which we pray is <I>losing its value.</I>&rquo;

<P>15, 16. <B>My powers are Cressent, and my Auguring hope Sayes it will
come to'th'full</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: What does the relative &lquo;it&rquo; refer to? It cannot in
<I>sense</I> relate to &lquo;hope&rquo;, nor in <I>concord</I> to &lquo;powers.&rquo; It is evident beyond a doubt, that
the poet's allusion is to the moon; and that Pompey would say, He is yet but a half-
moon, or <I>crescent;</I> but his hopes tell him, that crescent will come to a <I>full</I> orb. <SC>Dyce</SC>:
Theobald's change though adopted by all his successors, except Mr Collier, appears
to me a very hasty alteration:&mdash;our old writers frequently make &lquo;it&rquo; refer to a pre-
ceding plural substantive. [It is to be regretted that Dyce did not give some of
these instances. It is probable that in all of them there would have been found
some noun, in the singular, interposed between the plural antecedent and its singular
relative, whereby the relative becomes singular by attraction. In the present case,
&lquo;it&rquo; refers to &lquo;powers,&rquo; but &lquo;crescent,&rquo; although an adjective, is, in the imagination
of the speaker, a singular and, consequently, by its proximity, throws the relative &lquo;it&rquo;
into the singular also.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>28. <B>soften thy wand lip</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC> (Nichols, ii, 501) &lquo;suspects&rquo; that &lquo;wand,&rquo;
or as he has it in his text, after Pope, <I>wan,</I> should be <I>warm,</I> but as he made no
later allusion to this conjecture, it is to be inferred that he withdrew it. <SC>Johnson</SC>
makes the same conjecture, as well as &lquo;perhaps, <I>fond.</I>&rquo; <SC>Steevens</SC>: &lquo;Wand,&rquo; if it
stand, is either a corruption of <I>wan,</I> the adjective, or a contraction of <I>wanned,</I> or
<I>made wan,</I> a participle. So, in <I>Hamlet</I>: &lquo;That, from her working, all his visage
<I>wan'd.</I>&rquo; Again, in Beau. and Fl. <I>Queen of Corinth</I>: &lquo;Now you look <I>wan</I> and
pale; <I>lips'</I> ghosts you are.&rquo; [IV, i.] Or perhaps <I>waned</I> lip, <I>i. e. decreased,</I> like the
moon, in its beauty. Yet this expression of Pompey's, perhaps, after all, implies a
wish only, that every charm of love may confer additional softness on the lips
of Cleopatra: <I>i. e.</I> that her beauty may improve to the ruin of her lover; or, as
Ritson expresses the same idea, that &lquo;her <I>lip,</I> which was become <I>pale</I> and <I>dry</I> with
<I>age,</I> may recover the <I>colour</I> and <I>softness</I> of her <I>sallad</I> days.&rquo; The epithet <I>wan</I> might
indeed have been added, only to show the speaker's private contempt of it. <SC>Percy</SC>:
Shakspeare's orthography often adds a <I>d</I> at the end of a word. Thus, &lquo;vile&rquo; is (in
the old editions) everywhere spelt <I>vild.</I> &lquo;Laund&rquo; is given instead of <I>lawn:</I> why not
therefore <I>wand</I> for <I>wan</I> here? If this however should not be accepted, suppose we
read with the addition only of an apostrophe, <I>wan'd; i. e. waned,</I> declined, gone off
from its perfection; comparing Cleopatra's beauty to the moon past the full. <SC>Collier</SC>
(ed. i): It may be doubted whether &lquo;wand&rquo; and &lquo;lip&rquo; ought not to be united by a
hyphen; &lquo;wand&rquo; probably has reference to Cleopatra's power of enchantment,&mdash;that
her lip is as potent as a magician's wand; and this construction seems warranted by
what immediately follows: &lquo;Let <I>witchcraft</I> join with beauty.&rquo; &lquo;Wand&rquo; is the
&lquo;witchcraft&rquo; and &lquo;lip&rquo; the &lquo;beauty.&rquo; <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Remarks,</I> p. 245): What Mr Collier
says here about Cleopatra's &lquo;wand-lip,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> lip as potent as a magician's wand,
cannot be allowed the merit of originality; at least, it had been previously said in that
mass of folly, ignorance, and conceit, Jackson's <I>Shakespeare's Genius Justified;</I> and
one can hardly suppose that such a wild fancy would spring up spontaneously in the
brains of two commentators. Not even in Lycophron, the most enigmatical of poets,
is there any expression half so far-fetched or so strangely compounded as <I>wand-lip!</I>
Whether the word be written <I>wand</I> or <I>wan'd,</I> it is evidently the past participle of the
verb <I>wane;</I> Cleopatra herself has previously touched on the decrease of her beauty:
&lquo;with Ph&oelig;bus' amorous pinches black And <I>wrinkled deep in time.</I>&rquo; <SC>Collier</SC>, in his
<I>Second Edition</I> makes no allusion to his extravagant suggestion of a wizard's wand,
&mdash;it cannot be enlivening to be coupled with Zachary Jackson,&mdash;but restricts himself
to recording that his MS has <I>warm,</I> and the safe remark that &lquo;&ldquo;wan'd&rdquo; ought prob-
ably to be taken as <I>waned, i. e.</I> a lip that is on the wane.&rquo; <SC>Keightley's</SC> text reads
<I>wanton</I> &lquo;in the sense of soft, yielding, like &ldquo;the wanton rushes,&rdquo;&mdash;<I>1 Hen. IV:</I> III, i,&rquo;
and he &lquo;strongly suspects [<I>Exp.</I> p. 313] that the poet's word may have been <I>tann'd,</I>
spelt of course <I>tand.</I> She is more than once called gypsy; she has &ldquo;a tawny front.&rdquo;&rquo;

<P>[Keightley's <I>tann'd</I> can be upheld only at the expense of physiology; there are, I
believe, no pigmentary cells in the lips which can be affected by the sun's rays. I
cannot accept Dyce's assertion that &lquo;wand&rquo; is &lquo;evidently the past participle of the
verb <I>wane.</I>&rquo; I see no reason why it should not be the same &lquo;wand&rquo; which the
Quartos give us in <I>Hamlet,</I> &lquo;all his visage wand&rquo; (II, ii, 527) where almost every
modern editor to the complete satisfaction of himself and of his readers prints <I>wann'd</I>
that is, <I>made wan.</I> And, moreover, this interpretation is not lacking in fitness.
Cleopatra's lips, at the age of thirty-eight, as has been suggested, could hardly be as
&lquo;ripe in show&rquo; as the lips of Helena, &lquo;those kissing cherries&rquo; as Demetrius calls
them; and it is to be remembered that it is not an admirer of Cleopatra that terms
her lips wan. To Anthony, one kiss from them, wan'd or not, &lquo;repaid all that he
had lost.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>30. <B>Tye vp the Libertine in a field of Feasts</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii): The MS
thus alters this line:&mdash;&lquo;<I>Lay</I> up the libertine in a <I>flood</I> of feasts;&rquo; but we do not feel
warranted in deserting the old editions, although it is true that in <I>Othello,</I> I, i, we have
seen &lquo;Laying&rquo; misprinted <I>Tying,</I> as here <I>Lay</I> may have been misprinted &lquo;Tie.&rquo; As
to &lquo;field of feasts&rquo; we hardly know what is to be understood by the expression, but
&lquo;<I>flood</I> of feasts&rquo; seems almost equally objectionable, though intelligible; however,
if any part of this play, as published, were derived from shorthand notes, &lquo;field&rquo; and
<I>flood</I> would be spelt with the same letters, and hence possibly the confusion.
W. W[<SC>illiams</SC>] (<I>Parthenon,</I> 17 May, 1862): Assuredly, Shakespeare has no meta-
phor similar [to &lquo;field of feasts&rquo;] throughout his works. &lquo;Field&rquo; is defined by John-
son as being strictly &lquo;ground not inclosed, the open country;&rquo; and to &lquo;tie,&rquo; he tells
us, is &lquo;to constrain or confine, <I>up</I> being little more than an emphatical addition.&rquo;
Pompey, wishing to fasten Antony to a particular spot, would scarcely desire the
security of an <I>open</I> space. But there is a word, for which, by a very probable mis-
reading, &lquo;field&rquo; may have been substituted. <I>Fold,</I> says Johnson, is an &lquo;enclosure of
any kind,&rquo; and a fold would therefore exactly suit Pompey's purpose. The most
rigid foliantist cannot object to weigh for a moment whether the true meaning may
not be,&mdash;&lquo;Tie up the libertine in a <I>fold</I> of feasts.&rquo; We have then a figure of which
Shakespeare is particularly fond. . . . A reference to a <I>Concordance</I> will save me any
parade of confirmatory passages. [The phrase is certainly obscure, and yet I venture
to think that the Folio needs no alteration. Pompey's train of thought is, let me
imagine, somewhat as follows: At all hazards, Anthony must be kept in Egypt, a
prisoner to his passions; within this boundary the libertine must be tied up. But
the very idea of a libertine involves a certain freedom of motion; a libertine cannot
be tied up to a single feast, else he would cease to be a libertine in feasts; there must
be many feasts; in using the word &lquo;libertine&rquo; there may have then crept into Shake-
speare's mind that charming simile which elsewhere he twice uses, whereby the air
becomes a &lquo;chartered libertine,&rquo; blowing wheresoever it pleases, over hill and dale,
and a single feast hereby expands, in imagination, into a whole field of feasts.
Some limitations there must be; what better than a field of vague extent, wherein
a libertine could be confined and indulge in endless feasting, day and night.

<P>30. <B>Libertine</B>] There is one Article in Walker's <I>Versification</I> (XL, p. 201) which,
for the sake of that fine scholar's reputation, even his admirers would, I think, like to
see expunged. Its title is: &lquo;The <I>i</I> in <I>-ity</I> is almost uniformly dropt in pronunciation,&rquo;
and, in proof, he quotes upwards of twenty instances where he assumes that this
barbarous pronunciation must be adopted. Apparently, warming with his subject, he
goes from bad to worse until, toward the close, he recommends such words as <I>hostil'ty,
virgin'ty, pur'ty</I> and &lquo;suspects that the Elizabethan poets extended this rule to all
substantives ending in <I>-ty,</I> as <I>honesty, liberty, poverty,</I> etc. Hence it is that <I>majesty</I>
is almost uniformly a disyllable in Shakespeare.&rquo; His last quotation is this present
line, wherein he asserts that &lquo;libertine&rquo; is &lquo;used in the same way,&rquo; and, therefore,
to be pronounced <I>lib' tine.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>31. <B>Epicurean</B>] In Greek names, Shakespeare usually followed, not the Latin, but
the Greek accent, which was the method of Reuchlin, the accepted authority of his
day; thus, <G>*)erikou/peios</G>. Thus, too, <G>*bapabba_s</G> in <I>The Mer. of Ven.</I> Walker overlooked
this fact, which would have spared him trouble in compiling his Article XLII, <I>Vers.</I>
p. 211. &lquo;Euphrates&rquo; in I, ii, 113, is an exception.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>33. <B>feeding may prorogue his Honour</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: This undoubtedly means
&lquo;to delay his sense of honour from exerting itself till he become habitually sluggish.&rquo;
<SC>Deighton</SC>: To &lquo;prorogue,&rquo; from Lat. <I>pro,</I> publicly, and <I>rogare,</I> to ask (the tech-
nical term for proposing a measure to a legislative body), properly means to propose
a further extension of office, thence to carry forward from one meeting to another, and
so to defer. <SC>Staunton</SC>: Shakespeare certainly uses &lquo;prorogue&rquo; here, as he employs
it in <I>Pericles,</I> V, i, 24, &lquo;nor taken sustenance But to prorogue his grief,&rquo;&mdash;in the sense
of <I>deaden</I> or <I>benumb.</I>
<P>34. <B>Lethied dulnesse</B>] The <SC>Cam. Edd.</SC> record an Anonymous conjecture of
&lquo;<I>Lethe</I> dulness,&rquo; which seems probable. It must have been difficult for the ear of
the compositor to escape from hearing the <I>d</I> of &lquo;dulness&rquo; transferred to <I>Lethe.</I>

<P>50. <B>C&aelig;sar and Anthony shall well greet together</B>] If we accept &lquo;greet&rquo; in its
prominent sense of to <I>salute,</I> it becomes difficult to comprehend how two men can
&lquo;greet <I>together.</I>&rquo; It would be still more difficult, I think, to find, throughout English
literature, a second example of the phrase. The <I>N. E. D.</I> knows none such,&mdash;as far
as I can discover. May it not be, however, that &lquo;greet&rquo; is an error of the compositor,
who, deceived either by his mental ear or the voice of his reader, has added to the
verb <I>gree</I> the <I>t</I> of the next word, &lquo;together&rquo;? and that the true reading is &lquo;C&aelig;sar and
Anthony shall well gree together&rquo;?&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>) gives many instances, and the
<I>N. E. D.</I> still more, of the use of <I>gree</I> in the sense of <I>to agree, to be in accord,</I> etc.
The past participle, &lquo;greed&rquo; occurs in II, vi, 47, &lquo;this greed vpon, To part with
vnhackt edges,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>52. <B>wan'd vpon him</B>] See &lquo;He stayes vpon your will,&rquo; I, ii, 131.
<P>54. <B>I know not Menas,</B> etc.] <SC>Thiselton</SC> (p. 11): Modern editors have taken
great liberties with the Folio punctuation of this speech, in total disregard of the
point on which Pompey is enlarging, viz., that Anthony's accession to the side of
C&aelig;sar and Lepidus will, if it prove to be a fact, indicate the strength of Pompey's
menace. As usually punctuated the speech is self-contradictory, for Pompey is thereby
made to say first that he knows not how it is, then to explain how it is, and finally to
reassert that he knows not how it is. On the other hand, according to the Folio
punctuation, Pompey states the only possible ground that occurs to him for Anthony's
reported movements; he would rather expect Anthony to remain on quarrelsome
terms with his colleagues of the Triumvirate; he therefore awaits confirmation of the
report, holding it, if true, as a proof of his power and, at the same time, of the
necessity of using that power to the uttermost against such a combination.
<P>57. <B>pregnant</B>] <SC>Nares</SC> (<I>Gloss. s. v.</I>) discusses the various meanings of this word,
and, under the fourth head, says that it signifies &lquo;full of force or conviction, or full
of proof in itself.&rquo; This definition, <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>) quotes as the interpretation of the
word in the present passage. Nares, in conclusion, says that &lquo;this word was used
with great laxity, and sometimes abused, as fashionable terms are; but may be gener-
ally referred to the ruling sense of being full, or productive of something.&rquo;

strout, or square it, looke big on't, carrie his armes a kemboll braggadochio-like.&rquo;

<P>20. <B>Enter C&aelig;sar,</B> etc.] <SC>Knight</SC> (<I>Supp. Notice,</I> p. 356): The interview between
C&aelig;sar and Antony is most masterly. The constrained courtesy on each side&mdash;the
coldness of C&aelig;sar&mdash;the frank apologies of Antony&mdash;the suggestion of Agrippa, so
opportune, and yet apparently so unpremeditated&mdash;the ready assent of Antony&mdash;all
this&mdash;matter for rhetorical flourishes of at least five hundred lines in the hands of an
ordinary dramatist&mdash;may be read without a start or an elevation of the voice. It is
solid business throughout. Antony we might think was a changed man. Enobarbus,
who knows him, is of a different opinion.&mdash;<SC>Lloyd</SC> (p. 338): The fated superiority
of the cool and steadfast gamester for power, over the ardent and dissipated, is set
forth with admirable effect in the long scene with the Triumvirs, which never pauses,
and flags not in a line, though the subject matter is no whit more vivacious in itself
than the contents of interchanging protocols.

<P>56, 57. <B>their contestation Was Theame for you, you were the word of
warre</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: The only meaning of this can be, that the war, which Antony's
wife and brother made upon C&aelig;sar, was theme for Antony too to make war; or was the
occasion why he did make war. But this is directly contrary to the context, which
shows, Antony did neither encourage them to it, nor second them in it. We cannot
doubt then, but the poet wrote: &lquo;&mdash;and their contestation Was <I>them'd</I> for you,&rquo;
<I>i. e.</I> The pretence of the war was on your account, they took up arms in your name,
and you were made the theme and subject of their insurrection.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: I am
neither satisfied with the reading nor the emendation: <I>them'd</I> is, I think, a word
unauthorised, and very harsh. Perhaps we may read: &lquo;&mdash;their contestation <I>Had</I>
theme <I>from</I> you,&rquo; The dispute derived its subject from you. It may be corrected
by mere transposition: &lquo;&mdash;their contestation <I>You were theme for,</I> you were the
word&mdash;.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC> (i, 32): Though there can be no doubt made that [Warburton's]
emendation is just [Capell adopted it.], and his interpretation also; yet is grammar
made dreadfully free with, and the analogy of language: for, according to the latter,
<I>them'd</I> can have no other sense but&mdash;propos'd as a theme, given out as such; and
must, according to grammar, be govern'd of &lquo;contestation;&rquo; but this sense and con-
struction bring matters back nearly to the point they were in under the old reading
&mdash;&lquo;theame:&rquo; the fault is in the Poet himself, whose licence of expression is sometimes
excessive.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: &lquo;Was theme for you,&rquo; I believe, means only, &lquo;was proposed as
an example for you to follow on a yet more extensive plan;&rquo; as <I>themes</I> are given for a
writer to dilate upon. Shakspeare, however, may prove the best commentator on him-
self. Thus, in <I>Coriolanus,</I> I, i: &lquo;&mdash;throw forth greater <I>themes</I> For insurrection's argu-
ing.&rquo; Sicinius calls Coriolanus, &lquo;&mdash;the <I>theme</I> of our assembly.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: That is,
&lquo;their contestation <I>derived</I> its <I>theme</I> or subject from you; you were their word of war;&rquo;
this affords a clear and consistent sense. To obtain the sense desired from War-
burton's emendation, we should read&mdash;&lquo;Was <I>them'd from</I> you&mdash;.&rquo; So, in <I>Tro. and
Cress.:</I> &lquo;She is a <I>theme</I> of honour and renown, A spur to valiant and magnanimous
deeds.&rquo; That he must have written <I>from,</I> appears by Antony's answer: &lquo;You do
mistake your business; my brother never Did urge me in his act.&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> &lquo;never made
<I>me</I> the <I>theme</I> for insurrection's arguing.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>M. Mason</SC>: I should suppose that some
of the words have been misplaced, and that it ought to stand thus: &lquo;&mdash;and for con-
testation Their theme was you; you were the word of war.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii):
Their contestation was not theme for Antony, but Antony was their theme for con-

<P>testation. &lquo;Was&rquo; and &lquo;for&rquo; accidentally changed places; therefore we read, &lquo;and
their contestation For theme was you.&rquo; This is all that is necessary, and it is
strange that the commentators, in their &lquo;contestation,&rquo; should not have discovered
what was required.&mdash;[Thus it stood in Collier's <I>Second Edition,</I> but in his <I>Third
Edition,</I> Collier himself failed to &lquo;discover what was required&rquo; and his text follows
the Folio, &lquo;Was theme for you,&rquo; without comment.]&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: The meaning is
apparent, though the construction is obscure and perhaps corrupt. We ought possibly
to read,&mdash;&lquo;<I>Had</I> you for theme,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>) defines &lquo;theme&rquo; in the pres-
ent passage as &lquo;a matter, an enterprise undertaken in your interest.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Deighton</SC>:
(<I>Conject. Readings,</I> p. 41): Schmidt's explanation would be excellent, if only the
words would bear that sense. Though &lquo;theme&rquo; is spelt in the Folios &lquo;theame&rquo; or
&lquo;theam&rquo; [or &lquo;theme,&rquo; F<SUB>3</SUB>], I am satisfied that it is nothing else than <I>then</I> (thenne),
perhaps sophisticated by a copyist who thought &lquo;the word of war&rquo; was explanatory
of it. [There is, possibly, one interpretation which may justify the text as it stands.
C&aelig;sar has just insinuated that Anthony while still in Egypt &lquo;practised&rquo; against him,
and is attempting to prove this, by what befell in Italy. His case would have been
weak indeed, if he could assert merely that Anthony's wife and brother, in their war,
had used Anthony's name as a pretext; in such circumstances, Anthony himself
might be as innocent as the babe unborn. To prove Anthony guilty, therefore,
C&aelig;sar must connect him, personally, with this &lquo;contestation.&rquo; He asserts, therefore,
that this very contestation was cause enough, in itself, for Anthony's practises&mdash;the
mere fact that it existed was sufficient matter for Anthony to work on, or as it stands,
in the fewest possible words, in the text, &lquo;their contestation was theme for you.&rquo;
Then, in order to involve them all, Fulvia, Lucius, and Anthony, in one common
&lquo;practise,&rquo; C&aelig;sar adds, &lquo;you were the word of war.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>57. <B>you were the word of warre</B>] <SC>John Hunter</SC>: The signal word of battle.
So in the <I>Julius C&aelig;sar</I> of North's <I>Plutarch,</I> &lquo;Brutus' men ran to give charge upon
their enemies, and tarried not the word of battle, nor commandment to give
charge.&rquo; [See, also, &lquo;death's the word,&rquo; I, ii, 158.]
<P>58, 59. <B>neuer Did vrge me in his Act</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: That is, never did make
use of my name as a pretence for the war.
<P>60. <B>reports</B>] That is, <I>reporters,</I> the abstract for the concrete. See (in this ed.)
<I>Love's Lab. L.</I> V, ii, 88, &lquo;incounters&rquo; for <I>encounterers,</I> together with the following

<P>64. <B>Hauing alike your cause</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: The meaning seems to be, &lquo;having
the same cause as you to be offended with me.&rquo; But why, because he was offended
with Antony, should he make war upon C&aelig;sar? May it not read thus: &lquo;<I>Hating</I>
alike <I>our</I> cause?&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: The old reading is immediately explained by Antony's
being the partner with Octavius in the cause against which his brother fought.&mdash;
<SC>Malone</SC>: That is, <I>I</I> having alike your cause. Did he not (says Antony) make wars
against the inclination of me also, of me, who was engaged in the same cause with
yourself? Dr Johnson supposed that <I>having</I> meant, <I>he</I> having, and hence has sug-
gested an unnecessary emendation.
<P>66. <B>As</B>] Here equivalent to <I>inasmuch as, since.</I> See I, iv, 25.
<P>66. <B>As matter whole you haue to make it with</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: The original read-
ing is without doubt erroneous.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: The old reading may be right. It
seems to allude to Antony's acknowledged neglect in aiding C&aelig;sar; but yet Antony
does not allow himself to be faulty upon the present cause alleged against him.&mdash;
<SC>Malone</SC>: I have not the smallest doubt that the correction made by Rowe is right.
The structure of the sentence, &lquo;<I>As</I> matter,&rquo; etc., proves decisively that <I>not</I> was
omitted. Of all the errors that happen at the press, omission is the most frequent.&mdash;
<SC>Knight</SC> (following the text): That is, if you'll <I>patch</I> a quarrel so as to seem the
<I>whole</I> matter you have to make it with, you must not patch it with this complaint.
<I>Whole</I> is opposed to <I>patch.</I>&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (also following the text): That is, do not find
out a cause of quarrel where none exists; do not patch a quarrel when no patching is
required, because the matter is whole.&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC>: The negative is absolutely necessary
to make sense of the passage.&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: The negative is clearly indispensable;
but to satisfy the metre, Shakespeare may have adopted the old form <I>n'have</I> instead
of <I>have not.</I>&mdash;<SC>Nichols</SC> (i, 9): The original text is right, and means, as if you have
a whole matter to make it of, and wish to preserve to it the appearance of integrity,
&mdash;of its being made out of a whole piece,&mdash;&lquo;<I>it must not be with this</I>&rquo;&mdash;for this patch
will show, will be seen. On the other hand, if [Rowe's <I>not</I>] be correct&mdash;if C&aelig;sar
did wish to &lquo;patch a quarrel&rquo;&mdash;not having matter whole to make it of, surely no better
matter could offer itself for the purpose than that which he is here expressly told he
could not use. The wife and brother of Antony had made war upon C&aelig;sar. C&aelig;sar
accuses Antony, although he was in Egypt, of having instigated them; of being, as
he says, &lquo;the word of war.&rquo; Antony denies it; and, most likely, truly; but had
C&aelig;sar wanted to make use of the facts, as far as they went, for the purpose of patch-
ing a quarrel with Antony, public opinion, notwithstanding Antony's denial, would
perhaps have gone with C&aelig;sar; and though in itself, it might not have been a suf-
ficient cause of quarrel, yet with the addition of a few other grievances, it might have
been made to constitute one. Still, it would have borne the appearance, as Antony

<P>says, of a patched quarrel, and not as made out of whole matter.&mdash;<SC>Ingleby</SC> (<I>Sh. the

to understand either &lquo;If you desire to pick a quarrel with me, you could find stronger

the phraseology is equivocal, &lquo;a forced interpretation. The meaning appears rather
to be the reverse: make trivial things&mdash;mere bits and <I>patches,</I> as it were&mdash;the ground
of quarrel. These slight occasions for disagreement are opposed to <I>matter whole,</I>

&lquo;As&rquo; is equivalent here to <I>as though;</I> compare I, ii, 110; IV, i, 1. The meaning is,
&lquo;in such a way that it will seem to be made all of a piece.&rquo; [To me the meaning
seems to be, If you'll patch a quarrel, inasmuch as you must make the patch out of
good whole material, you must not take this. I think Ingleby is entirely right in
his interpretation.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

pen, and oftner [<I>sic</I>] still by the press; such presses especially as this Poet had the
fate to come out of.

<P>71-75. <B>I know you could not lacke, . . . mine owne peace</B>] <SC>Deighton</SC>: That
is, I am certain that you could not help feeling how impossible it was for me, whose
interests were the same as yours, to regard with favourable eyes those wars which
were so opposed to my own peace. &lquo;Very&rquo; is here an adjective, <I>thorough.</I> &lquo;Attend,&rquo;
in this sense, is more commonly applied to the ears than to the eyes.
<P>74. <B>gracefull eyes</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: We still say, I could not look <I>handsomely</I> on
such or such a proceeding.
<P>75. <B>fronted</B>] <SC>Bradley</SC> (<I>N. E. D. s. v.</I> Front, <I>v.</I><SUP>1</SUP> 3): To stand face to face with;

<P>76. <B>I would you had her spirit, in such another</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: Antony means to
say, I wish you had the spirit of Fulvia, embodied in such another woman as her;
I wish you were married to such another spirited woman. By the words, &lquo;you <I>had</I>
her spirit,&rquo; etc. Shakspeare, I apprehend, meant, &lquo;you were <I>united to,</I> or possessed
of, <I>a woman with</I> her spirit.&rquo; Having formerly misapprehended this passage, and
supposed that Antony wished Augustus to <I>be actuated</I> by a spirit similar to Fulvia's,
I proposed to read&mdash;<I>e'en</I> such another, <I>in</I> being frequently printed for <I>e'en</I> in these
plays.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: The plain meaning of Antony is, I wish you had my wife's spirit
<I>in</I> another wife; <I>i. e. in</I> a wife of your own. [See <I>Appendix, Plutarch.</I>]

<P>86-88. <B>I wrote to you, . . . out of audience</B>] The feeble punctuation of the
Folio will readily give way to almost any punctuation of these lines. Dyce's, which
has been followed by the <I>Globe,</I> the <I>Cambridge,</I> and the majority of subsequent edi-
tors: &lquo;I wrote to you When rioting in Alexandria;&rquo; is somewhat objectionable,
inasmuch as it is grammatically ambiguous whether C&aelig;sar was rioting or Anthony.
There should be at least a comma after &lquo;you&rquo; (as in the Folio), but a semi-colon,
as suggested by Lloyd (<I>ap.</I> Cam.), would be better. Capell's punctuation is good: &lquo;I
wrote to you, When, rioting in Alexandria, you,&rquo; etc. All colons or semi-colons after
&lquo;Alexandria&rquo; seem to me misplaced. C&aelig;sar is enumerating Anthony's offences; to
pocket up his letters is the first distinct and separate offence; to gibe his missive is
the second; and the two should be distinguished as they are in the Folio, so it seems
to me.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>100. <B>The Honour is Sacred</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: <I>Sacred,</I> for <I>unbroken, unviolated.</I>

the true meaning; but, before I read the note, I understood it thus: Lepidus inter-
rupts C&aelig;sar, on the supposition that what he is about to say will be too harsh to be
endured by Antony; to which Antony replies&mdash;&lquo;No, Lepidus, let him speak; the
security of <I>honour on which he now speaks,</I> on which this conference is held now,
<I>is sacred,</I> even <I>supposing that I lacked</I> honour <I>before.</I>&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: Antony, in my
opinion, means to say&mdash;The theme of honour which he now speaks of, namely, the
religion of an oath, for which he supposes me not to have a due regard, is sacred; it
is a tender point, and touches my character nearly. Let him therefore urge his
charge, that I may vindicate myself.&mdash;<SC>M. Mason</SC>: I do not think that either John-
son's or Malone's explanation of this passage is satisfactory. The true meaning of

send him aid when he required it, which was contrary to his oath. Antony says, in
his defence, that he did not deny his aid, but, in the midst of dissipation, neglected to
send it: that having now brought his forces to join him against Pompey, he had
redeemed that error; and that therefore the honour which C&aelig;sar talked of, was <I>now</I>

the line should be pointed thus: &lquo;The honour's sacred that he talks on, now, Sup-
posing that I lack'd it.&rquo;&mdash;[I cannot see that anything is here implied more than that
Anthony's sacred honour having been impugned, there can be no remission of the
explicit charge, made by him who had supposed that Anthony had violated it.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>102. <B>The Article of my oath</B>] A majority of editors have followed Theobald in
placing a dash after &lquo;oath;&rquo; implying an unfinished sentence. Would not an interro-
gation point be better? Anthony is repeating C&aelig;sar's own words, and asking, I
think, an explanation.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>106, 107. <B>had bound me vp From mine owne knowledge</B>] <SC>Deighton</SC>: That
is, I had become a complete stranger to my nobler nature.
<P>109, 110. <B>nor my power Worke without it</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: Nor my greatness work
without mine honesty.&mdash;<SC>Delius</SC> prefers to consider &lquo;it&rquo; as referring not to &lquo;honesty&rquo;
but to &lquo;greatness,&rquo; and thus paraphrases the sentence: the honesty with which I
acknowledge my fault, cannot injure my greatness, cannot diminish the knowledge
of my worth; nor can it cause my power to be proved worthless.

<P>119. <B>attone</B>] <SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D. s. v.</I>): <I>Atone</I> is formed on the adverbial phrase
<I>at one</I> in its combined form as representing a simple idea, and 16th century pro-
nunciation. Short for the phrase &lquo;set or make at one.&rquo; . . . From the frequent
phrases &lquo;set at one&rquo; or &lquo;at onement,&rquo; the combined <I>atonement</I> began to take the
place of <I>onement</I> early in the 16th century, and <I>atone</I> to supplant <I>one,</I> verb, about
1550. <I>Atone</I> was not admitted into the Bible in 1611, though <I>atonement</I> had been
in since Tindale.

and 1813, and is suggested by <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 131). This oversight, unaccountable
in so careful an editor, beguiled the <SC>Cam. Edd.</SC> who record it as Dyce's conjecture
in their footnotes.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
