<P>130. <B>your Considerate stone</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: This line is passed by all the editors,
as if they understood it, and believed it universally intelligible. I cannot find in it
any very obvious, and hardly any possible meaning. I would therefore read: &lquo;Go
to then, <I>you</I> considerate <I>ones.</I>&rquo; You who dislike my frankness and temerity of
speech, and are so <I>considerate</I> and discreet, <I>go to,</I> do your own business.&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC>
(i, 33), in this instance keener than Dr Johnson, gives the meaning of Enobarbus as
that &lquo;he would, from thenceforth, be a very stone for silence, but he would think
a little.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: That is, if I must be chidden, henceforward I will be as mute
as a marble statue, which seems to think, though it can say nothing. &lquo;As silent as a
stone,&rquo; however, might have been once a common phrase.&mdash;[Hereupon follow several
examples which might be multiplied, drawn from old sources where a stone is used
as a simile of silence or stillness.]&mdash;<SC>Blackstone</SC>: The metre of this line is deficient.
It will be perfect, and the sense rather clearer, if we read (without altering a letter):
&lquo;&mdash;your consideratest one.&rquo; I doubt, indeed, whether this adjective is ever used
in the superlative degree; but in the mouth of Enobarbus it might be pardoned.&mdash;
<SC>Ritson</SC> (<I>Cursory Crit.</I> 85): As Enobarbus, to whom this line belongs, generally
speaks in plain prose, there is no occasion for any further attempt to harmonize it.&mdash;
<SC>Collier</SC> (ed. i): It may be a question whether Enobarbus means to call Antony &lquo;a
considerate stone,&rquo; or to say merely that he will be silent as a stone. If the former,
we must, with Johnson, change &lquo;your&rquo; to <I>you;</I> but the latter affords a clear mean-
ing without any alteration of the ancient text.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Remarks,</I> 246): Enobarbus
call Antony a <I>stone!</I> he would as soon have ventured to throw one at him. John-
son's proposed alteration, bad as it certainly was, did not involve such an absurdity.
&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii): That is, I will be as considerate as a stone. Johnson's notion
[where?] that Enobarbus meant to call Antony a &lquo;considerate stone,&rquo; does not seem
to us, recollecting that the words were those of a rough free-spoken soldier, such an
&lquo;absurdity&rquo; as it appeared to the Rev. Mr Dyce. In speaking of the note in our first
edition, he ought to have remembered two things, which he has entirely overlooked,
viz., that we gave the very text he supports, and that we ourselves said no change was
needed. If Mr Dyce had been more of a &lquo;<I>considerate</I> stone,&rquo; he would have saved
himself from the appearance of endeavouring to make a fault where he could not find
one. We do not at all say that the suspicion would be just, but that he has laid
himself open to it.&mdash;[Whoever wishes to hear the last word in this deplorable quarrel
between two men who had been for many years fast friends, will find it in Dyce's
<I>Strictures,</I> p. 203, where he exultantly proves that to Collier exclusively belongs the
notion that Enobarbus called Antony a stone! Time did not abate the flush of
Dyce's triumph. Seven years later he repeated these remarks in his <I>Strictures</I> at
full length, in his <I>Second Edition.</I> Apparently, so far from being crushed under
this appalling stigma of bad pree<*>minence, Collier in his <I>Monovolume</I> placidly printed
&lquo;<I>you</I> considerate stone,&rquo; and in his <I>Third Edition,</I> while returning to the old text,
reprinted the substance of the note in his <I>First Edition.</I>]&mdash; <SC>Staunton</SC>: <I>As silent as</I>

<P>131, 132. <B>I do not much dislike the matter, but The manner,</B> etc.] <SC>War-

lieutenant, that Antony himself did? Shakespeare wrote &lquo;I do not much dislike the
<I>manner,</I> but The <I>matter</I> of his speech,&rquo; etc., <I>i. e.</I> 'tis not his liberty of speech, but
the mischiefs he speaks of, which I dislike. This agrees with what follows, and is
said with much urbanity, and show of friendship.&mdash;<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 454): That is, As to the

<SC>Capell</SC> (i, 33): Here is another transposition; the words &lquo;<I>manner</I>&rquo; and &lquo;<I>matter</I>&rquo;:
the emendation was started by [Warburton], is confirm'd by what the speaker says
afterwards, and recommended by much delicacy.&mdash;[The present play was the fifth
that Capell printed (vol. i, p. 19, <I>footnote</I>). It is noteworthy how much in these

<P>137. <B>Giue me leaue C&aelig;sar.</B>] It can hardly be that the comma and dash after
&lquo;C&aelig;sar,&rquo; begun by Capell and continued by a large majority of modern editors, are
right. Where all are so courtly in this conference, it cannot be likely that C&aelig;sar
would break in upon Agrippa's first words, especially if it were merely to tell him to
continue speaking, a very needless permission; the end would have been gained
by C&aelig;sar's keeping silent. If we erase the period of the Folio, I think we should
substitute an interrogation mark.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>139. <B>a Sister by the Mothers side</B>] Octavia was C&aelig;sar's own sister, by the
same mother, Atia; but Shakespeare here follows Plutarch who says that her mother
was Ancharia. See <I>Appendix, Plutarch.</I>
<P>141. <B>Say not, say Agrippa</B>] Corrected by Rowe. This is one of the very numer-
ous instances collected by <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 314) in his fifty-eight pages of the &lquo;Sub-
stitution of Words,&rquo; generally to be attributed, as here, to proximity.
<P>141, 142. <B>your proofe</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC> said that he made &lquo;no scruple to restore
&ldquo;your <I>approof.</I>&rdquo;&rquo; <SC>Hanmer's</SC> text reads, &lquo;your <I>reproof,</I>&rquo; and a footnote has &lquo;<I>Warb.
emend.</I>&rquo; <SC>Warburton's</SC> own text, however, follows Theobald, and he has no
note on the passage. <SC>Heath</SC> (p. 451) gives a good interpretation of Theobald's
text, but there is little need to reprint it, inasmuch as Warburton's emendation has
been uniformly followed. <SC>M. Mason</SC> properly interpreted &lquo;your reproof&rquo; as &lquo;the
reproof you would undergo,&rquo; and quoted as parallel a passage from Beaumont &amp;
Fletcher's <I>Custom of the Country,</I> V, iv, where &lquo;Your great opinion in the world&rquo; is
equivalent, so he said, to &lquo;the great opinion conceived of you;&rquo; but he was herein
possibly wrong as to the exact meaning. <SC>Malone</SC> detected the source of the error
in the Folio, which lay in making the <I>r</I> in &lquo;your&rquo; do double duty, for itself and for
&lquo;reproof,&rquo; and cited as a parallel case &lquo;Mine Nightingale,&rquo; IV, viii, 24. This error
was due, so Malone said, to the transcriber's ear deceiving him.&mdash;<SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 423):

<P>206. <B>Eno. Halfe the heart,</B> etc.] <SC>Delius</SC> (<I>Sh. Jahrb.</I> V, 267): Only once in

to interject a bold word, for which he was immediately checked; but now, there-

a conversation in prose with M&aelig;cenas. But as soon as the talk rises from the
domain of mere gossip to a description of Antony's first meeting with Cleopatra, he

could this majestic masterpiece be adequately portrayed, and, therefore, the humour-

<P>213. <B>Eight Wilde-Boares,</B> etc.] See <I>Appendix, Plutarch.</I>
<P>215. <B>This was but as a Flye by an Eagle</B>] By the few editors who have taken
note of this phrase, it has been interpreted as conveying merely a comparison; the
eight boars were merely as a fly by the side of, and so in comparison with, an eagle.
Is it not capable of a different interpretation? M&aelig;cenas wonders that eight boars
should have been a breakfast for only twelve persons. Enobarbus replies, in effect,
that so far from eight boars having been considered an inordinate repast, it was no
more than a fly would be considered a hearty breakfast by an eagle.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>218, 219. <B>if report be square to her</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: That is, if report <I>quadrates</I>
with her, or suits with her merits.
<P>221. <B>vpon the Riuer of Sidnis</B>] <SC>M. Mason</SC>: This passage is a strange instance
of negligence and inattention in Shakspeare. Enobarbus is made to say that Cleo-
patra gained Antony's heart on the river Cydnus; but it appears from the conclusion
of his own description, that Antony had never seen her there; that, whilst she was
on the river, Antony was sitting alone, enthroned in the market-place, whistling to
the air, all the people having left him to gaze upon her: and that, when she landed,
he sent to her to invite her to supper.&mdash;<SC>Cowden-Clarke</SC>: The inattention is
Mason's, not Shakespeare's; the expression &lquo;upon the river of Cydnus,&rquo; is here used
to signify &lquo;the district on the shores of the river of Cydnus,&rquo; including the &lquo;city&rquo;
which &lquo;cast her people out upon her,&rquo; and its &lquo;market-place&rquo; wherein &lquo;Antony&rquo; sat
&lquo;enthroned.&rquo; The idiom &lquo;upon the Seine,&rquo; or &lquo;upon the Thames&rquo; is employed to
express the adjacent shores of those rivers, the country in their neighborhood.&mdash;<SC>Rolfe</SC>:
Mason's criticism reminds one of Yellowplush's surprise at finding Boulogne-sur-
Mer was on the shore and <I>not</I> &lquo;on the sea.&rquo;

<P>225. <B>The Barge she sat in,</B> etc.] <SC>Hazlitt</SC> (p. 97): The rich and poetical
description of Cleopatra's person seems to prepare the way for, and almost to justify
the subsequent infatuation of Antony when in the sea-fight at Actium, he leaves the
battle, and &lquo;like a doating mallard&rquo; follows her flying sails.&mdash;<SC>Hartley Coleridge</SC>
(ii, 184): Beautiful as this description is, one might almost desire that it had been
uttered by a more interesting personage. Dryden has transferred it to Antony,&mdash;copied
it pretty closely,&mdash;or perhaps kept closer to Plutarch's prose. The poetry he almost
suppresses; but he certainly introduces the story more artfully. Narration for its
own sake is not, however, a frequent fault of Shakespeare.
<P>228. <B>were Loue-sicke.</B>] <SC>Knight</SC> (ed. i and ii) virtually adheres to the punc-
tuation of the Folio, which he observes &lquo;is surely more poetical.&rquo; <SC>Dyce</SC> quotes the
observation, prints it in Italics, and affixes two exclamation marks; a cheap mode
of expressing a patronizing superiority. In Knight's <I>Second Edition, Revised,</I> the
Folio is abandoned and Capell followed.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>234. <B>cloth of Gold, of Tissue</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii): This is nonsense; it could
not be &lquo;cloth of gold&rquo; if it were &lquo;<I>of</I> tissue.&rquo; What was meant must have been that
the &lquo;cloth of gold&rquo; of the pavilion was lined with &lquo;tissue.&rquo; The contraction for &lquo;and&rquo;
was not unfrequently read <I>of</I> by old printers, and such, according to the MS, seems
to have been the case here.&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: That is, cloth-of-gold <I>on</I> a ground of tissue.
The expression so repeatedly occurs in early English books that we cannot imagine
how anyone familiar with such reading can have missed it.&mdash;[Staunton here quotes
Collier's note, which, he says, is made &lquo;with incredible simplicity.&rquo; Collier in his
<I>Third Edition</I> abandoned <I>and,</I> the reading of his MS.]

<C>[243, 244. <B>tended her i'th'eyes, And made their bends adornings</B>]</C>
<P>maids bowed with so good an air, that it added new graces to them. But this is not
what Shakespeare would say; <I>Cleopatra,</I> in this famous scene, personated <I>Venus</I> just

rounded the goddess to <I>adore,</I> and pay her homage. Agreeably to this fable Cleo-
patra had dressed her maids, the poet tells us, like Nereids. To make the whole
conformable to the story represented, we may be assured Shakspeare wrote: &lquo;And
made their bends <I>adorings.</I>&rquo; They did her observance in the posture of <I>adoration,</I>
as if she had been Venus.&mdash;<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 455): I very much doubt whether such an
affected flat expression as <I>adorings</I> came from Shakespeare. The word, <I>bend,</I> is here
used for an arch, and the <I>bends of the eyes</I> are the eye-brows. Thus the sense will
be, That these seeming nereids were employed in adjusting Cleopatra's eye-brows,
as often as they happened to be discomposed by the fanning of the boys, or any other
accident. This interpretation is confirmed by the preceding words, <I>tended her in the
eyes.</I>&mdash;[The student is entreated not to condemn Heath utterly on account of this
one aberration of mind; he is usually eminently sane.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC> (i, 33): That
is, watch'd her looks, to receive commandments from them: in the receiving of
which, the submiss inclination of body was perform'd with so much elegance, that
their other personal beauties were much set out by it. This is the obvious meaning
of &lquo;made their bends adornings.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: Perhaps &lquo;tended her <I>by th'</I> eyes,&rquo; dis-
covered her will by her eyes.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC> (<I>Var.</I> 1773): That Cleopatra personated
Venus we know; but that Shakespeare was acquainted with the circumstance of
homage being paid her by the Deities of the Sea [as stated by Warburton], is by no
means as certain.&mdash;<SC>Tollet</SC>: I think &lquo;bends&rquo; or <I>bands</I> is the same word, and
means, in this place, the several companies of Nereids, that waited on Cleopatra.&mdash;
[Although I have no idea at what age Tollet died, it is to be regretted that he did
not live long enough to withdraw this conjecture.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC> in the Var. of
1778 apprehended that &lquo;their bends&rquo; refers to Cleopatra's eyes, and that &lquo;her
attendants watched the motion of her eyes, the <I>bends</I> or movements of which added
new lustre to her beauty.&rquo; But he withdrew this interpretation in his edition of
1790, and gave in his adhesion to Warburton's <I>adorings.</I> And in the Var. of 1821,
he conceded that &lquo;tended her i'the eyes&rquo; &lquo;<I>may</I> only mean they performed their
duty in the sight of their mistress.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC> (<I>Var.</I> 1793): Perhaps &lquo;tended
her i'the eyes&rquo; may signify that the attendants on Cleopatra looked observantly into
her eyes, to catch her meaning, without giving her the trouble of verbal explana-
tion. After all, I believe it only means waited before her, in her sight. So, in <I>Ham-
let,</I> IV, iv, 5: &lquo;If that his majesty would aught of us, We shall express our duty
in his eye,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> in our personal attendance on him, by giving him ocular proof of
our respect. Henley explains it thus: &lquo;obeyed her looks without waiting for her
words.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Monck Mason</SC>: The passage, as it stands, appears to me wholly unin-
telligible; but it may be amended by a very slight deviation from the text, by read-
ing, <I>the guise,</I> instead of &lquo;the eyes,&rquo; and then it will run thus: &lquo;Her gentlewomen, like
the Nereides, So many mermaids, tended her i' the <I>guise,</I> And made their bends,
adornings.&rquo; &lquo;In the guise,&rquo; means in the form of mermaids, who were supposed to
have the head and body of a beautiful woman, concluding in a fish's tail: and by
the bends <I>which they made adornings,</I> Enobarbus means the flexure of the fictitious
fishes' tails, in which the limbs of the women were necessarily involved, in order to
carry on the deception, and which it seems they adapted with so much art as to make
them an ornament, instead of a deformity. This conjecture is supported by the very

&ldquo;made their bends adornings&rdquo; seems to be the statement that the gentlewomen were
apparelled &ldquo;like the Graces,&rdquo; and this must suggest a reference to grace in their
movements. I believe that in all that has been written on the passage, no one has
called attention to the very close paraphrase of North which Shakespeare gives:
&ldquo;Her ladies and <I>gentlewomen</I> . . . were apparelled <I>like the</I> nymphs <I>Nereids</I> (which
are the <I>mermaids</I> of the waters) and&rdquo;&mdash;after getting so far we have only to seek
a parallel for &ldquo;like the Graces;&rdquo; and may we not find it in &ldquo;made their bends
adornings?&rdquo;&mdash;made their very obeisance, as they <I>tended her,</I> like that of the Graces
waiting on Venus.&rquo; I doubt that there is any corruption in this passage. A para-
phrase by <SC>Rann</SC> has been reserved as a final word. To me it adequately expresses
the meaning of the whole phrase:&mdash;&lquo;Her gentlewomen took their orders from the
motion of her eyes, which gave her the happy opportunity of adding, by her looks,
new lustre to her beauty; and made their obeisance with the utmost imaginable
grace.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>246. <B>Swell with the touches,</B> etc.] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii) adopts the change, <I>smell,</I>
of his MS. In a note he asks, &lquo;how was &ldquo;the silken tackle&rdquo; to &ldquo;<I>swell&rdquo;?</I> The
&ldquo;flower-soft hands&rdquo; imparted a perfume to &ldquo;the silken tackle,&rdquo; and we are told just
afterwards that the &ldquo;smell&rdquo; reached even &ldquo;the adjacent wharfs.&rdquo;&rquo;&mdash;<SC>R. G. White</SC>
(<I>Sh.'s Scholar,</I> p. 450): If Mr Collier must be literal, does he not know that cordage
will swell with handling?&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Strictures,</I> etc. p. 204): Mr Collier ought certainly
to have accounted for so remarkable a circumstance [as set forth in preceding note]
on physical grounds, and also to have shown (what may be doubted) that, in Shake-
speare's days, the verb &lquo;smell&rquo; was ever followed by the preposition <I>with.</I>&mdash;<SC>Thisel-
ton</SC> (p. 13): The yielding softness of their hands gives rise to the illusion that the
silken tackle swells.&mdash;[There is to me something peculiarly disagreeable in the
emendation of Collier's MS; the idea that any <I>smell</I> results from a human touch is
offensive, and wain-ropes cannot hale me to the belief that <I>smell</I> is Shakespeare's
word. I do not forget &lquo;Since when it grows and smells, I swear, Not of itself but
thee,&rquo; and I also do not forget that the rosy wreath was perfumed because &lquo;Thou
thereon didst only breathe,&rquo;&mdash;a very different thing from smelling because it had been
handled. It is my firm belief that the silken tackle actually swelled with sheer delight
at having been clasped by those flower-soft hands.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>249. <B>Wharfes</B>] <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>): The banks of a river; as in <I>Hamlet,</I> I, v, 33:
&lquo;the fat weed that rots itself in ease on Lethe wharf.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>W. W. Skeat</SC> (<I>Academy,</I> 6
April, 1878): The root of &lquo;wharf&rquo; is the same as that which appears in Anglo-Saxon
<I>hweorfan,</I> to turn, so that <I>wharf</I> is rightly spelt with initial <I>wh.</I> But the word <I>wharf,</I>
in the sense of bank or sea-shore, is misspelt. It should rather be <I>warf,</I> and even
then it is a corruption&mdash;viz. of the Middle English <I>warth.</I> The derivation is from a
Teutonic base <I>wara,</I> meaning &lquo;sea.&rquo; Hence was formed Anglo-Saxon <I>w&aelig;roth</I> or
<I>warth,</I> meaning &lquo;sea-shore,&rquo; or &lquo;shore,&rquo; &lquo;bank.&rquo;
<P>254. <B>And made a gap in Nature</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: Alluding to an axiom in the
peripatetic philosophy, then in vogue, that &lquo;Nature abhors a vaouum.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>:
&lquo;But for vacancy&rquo; means for fear of a vacuum.&mdash;<SC>Corson</SC> (<I>Introd.</I> etc. p. 265): What
is chiefly remarkable, are the additions which Shakespeare makes to his prose original;
his imagination projects itself into inanimate things and impassions them. For ex-
ample, the winds are represented as <I>love-sick</I> with the perfumes from the sails; the
water beat by silver oars, follows faster, as if <I>amorous</I> of their strokes; the silken
tackle <I>swell with the touches of the flower-soft hands that tend them;</I> the very air of
the city, whose inhabitants had all gone out to gaze on Cleopatra, is represented as
eager to go and gaze upon her too, but that it feared to make a gap in nature! In
such a highly-colored and richly-sensuous passage, the great artist creates the atmos-
phere in which the passion-fated pair are exhibited.
<P>257. <B>Supper</B>] &lquo;With vs the nobilities, gentrie, and students, doo ordinarilie go to
dinner at eleuen before noone, and to supper at fiue, or betueene fiue and six at
afternoone. The merchants dine and sup seldome before twelue at noone, and
six at night especialie in London. . . . As for the poorest sort they generallie
dine and sup when they may.&rquo;&mdash;Harrison, <I>Description of England,</I> etc. 1587;
prefixed to Holinshed's <I>Chronicles,</I> Bk. II, cap. vi. p. 171 (p. 166, <I>New Sh. Soc.
Reprint</I>).
<P>258. <B>It should be better</B>] For this use of &lquo;should,&rquo; see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 326.

<P>260. <B>woman hard speake</B>] &lquo;Hard&rquo; is here probably a phonetic spelling of the
compositors. Possibly this pronunciation of <I>heard</I> may still exist in New England.
It was common enough fifty years ago.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>262. <B>ordinary</B>] <SC>Nares</SC>: A public dinner, where each person pays his share. The
word, in this sense, is certainly not obsolete; but it is here [<I>i. e.</I> in Nares's own
<I>Glossary</I>] inserted for the sake of observing that ordinaries were long the universal
resort of gentlemen, particularly in the reign of James I. They were, as a modern
writer well observes, &lquo;The lounging-places of the men of the town and the fantastic
gallants who herded together. Ordinaries were the exchange for news, the echoing
places for all sorts of town-talk; there they might hear of the last new play and
poem; these resorts were attended also to save charges of housekeeping.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Curiosities
of Literature,</I> iii, 82. In 1608, a common price for a genteel ordinary was two
shillings.
<P>264. <B>Wench</B>] This is by no means always a derogatory term. In the most
tragic moment of his life Othello calls his dead Desdemona &lquo;O ill-starr'd wench!&rquo;
&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

&lquo;breath&rquo; have <I>breathe,</I> and on their authority (?) the line has always, I believe, been
given thus,&mdash;&lquo;And, breathless, power breathe forth.&rquo; If we modernise the spelling,
I think we should read, what I believe to be the sense of the <I>First Folio,</I>&mdash;&lquo;And,
breathless, <I>pour</I> breath forth.&rquo; &lquo;Powre,&rquo; of the <I>First Folio</I> is the form in which the
verb <I>pour</I> is frequently there printed; as, indeed, to the present day it is still fre-
quently pronounced.&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC> (<I>Athen&aelig;um,</I> 12 April, 1873): Long before I read

the tetradrachms of Antony, was no Venus; and indeed the majority of ladies who
most successfully enslaved the hearts of princes, are known to have been less remark-
able for personal than mental attractions. The reign of insipid beauty is seldom
lasting; but permanent must be the rule of a woman who can diversify the sameness
of life by an inexhausted variety of accomplishments. To &lquo;stale&rquo; is a verb employed
by Heywood, in <I>The Iron Age,</I> 1632: &lquo;One that hath <I>stal'd</I> his courtly tricks at
home.&rquo;

<P>22. <B>Thy D&aelig;mon,</B> etc.] It verily looks as though the editor of the <I>Second Folio</I>
had here consulted North, where the corresponding passage runs thus: &lquo;&ldquo;For thy
demon,&rdquo; said he (that is to say the good angel and spirit that keepeth thee), &ldquo;is
afraid of his&rdquo;&rquo; etc. The <I>Second Folio</I> deserts the <I>First Folio</I> to an unwonted degree,
and adopts the parenthesis of North. This same predominance of C&aelig;sar's demon
over Anthony is spoken of by Macbeth:&mdash;&lquo;under [Banquo] My Genius is rebuk'd,
as it is said, Mark Anthonies was by C&aelig;sar.&rquo;&mdash;III, i, 67 (of the <I>Revised Edition</I>
of the present series), where the Editor has added a note by Prof. <SC>Baynes</SC>, who says,
&lquo;In Shakespeare, the terms angel and genius [and here, demon] are usually em-
ployed to denote the higher nature of man, the rational guiding soul or spirit, which
in connection with the mortal instruments determines his character and fate.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>22, 32. <B>spirit</B>] As to pronunciation, see I, ii, 143.
<P>23. <B>high vnmatchable</B>] Every edition, I think, since the <I>Third Folio</I> has placed
a comma after &lquo;high.&rquo; Should there be one? I think there should be a hyphen.
&lquo;High-unmatchable&rquo; is a compound adjective, like &lquo;pardon me, I am too sudden-
bold&rquo; in <I>Love's Lab. Lost,</I> and &lquo;Fools should be so deep-contemplative,&rquo; in <I>As You
Like It.</I> In the propriety of this hyphen I have the support of an Anonymous con-
jecture recorded in the Cambridge Edition.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>24, 25. <B>thy Angell Becomes a feare</B>] For &lquo;a feare&rquo; <SC>Upton</SC> (p. 192) suggested
<I>afeard,</I> and was severely criticised for it by <SC>Seward</SC> in his <I>Preface</I> to Beaumont and
Fletcher's <I>Works</I> (p. lxiv), &lquo;A Fear becomes&rquo; says Seward, &lquo;not only fearful but
ev'n <I>Fear itself.</I> The image is extremely poetical . . . God himself personizes <I>Fear;</I>
in Ezekiel, xxx, 13, He says &ldquo;I will put a Fear in the land of Egypt.&rdquo; . . . But the
instance most apposite is in <I>The Maids Tragedy,</I> where the forlorn Aspatia sees her
servant working the story of Theseus and Ariadne, and thus advises her to punish
the perfidy of the former:&mdash;&ldquo;In this place work a quick-sand . . . and then a Fear,
Do that Fear bravely.&rdquo;&rquo; <SC>Thirlby</SC>, in a letter to Theobald dated May, 1729
(Nichols <I>Illust.</I> ii, 228), anticipated Upton, whose conjecture appeared first in
print, I believe, and therefore has the prior claim. <SC>Heath</SC> upholds Upton and in
the Soothsayer's next speech: &lquo;I say again, thy spirit Is all afraid to govern thee
near him,&rquo; he says, &lquo;the reader will be pleased to observe the words, <I>I say again.</I>&rquo;
&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC> (i, 34): &lquo;A fear&rquo; has been chang'd into&mdash;<I>afeard,</I> a word that stands con-
demn'd by the sound; for whoso likes it, or can even endure it, so near in place to
&lquo;o'er-power'd,&rquo; his ear is to be pity'd: But why is &lquo;fear&rquo; to be parted with; mean-
ing only, in language of poetry,&mdash;a thing frighted or terrify'd.&mdash;<SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii,
299): What does this mean? I suspect that Shakespeare wrote <I>afear. . . .</I> I should
prefer <I>afeard,</I> the final <I>d</I> and <I>e</I> being often confounded with one another; but I can-
not away with <I>afeard&mdash;o'erpower'd.</I>&mdash;<SC>R. G. White</SC> considers Upton's conjecture
&lquo;plausible;&rquo; and <SC>Staunton</SC> observes that &lquo;the personification of fear renders the
passage more poetical; but it may be questioned, considering the old text has &ldquo;a
feare&rdquo; whether Upton's emendation is not the true reading.&rquo; [I prefer to retain
the text of the Ff with Capell's interpretation of it, in spite of Heath's strong point
in the &lquo;I say again&rquo; in line 32.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>25. <B>therefore</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.</I> 112) gives this as an instance where the stronger
accent is on the last syllable.

<P>subtle meaning that divides them; in the final resort this meaning must depend on
the verb. In the present phrase, for instance, we could here substitute <I>from</I> for
&lquo;of&rquo; without at all modifying the meaning, until we come to the verb, &lquo;beats,&rquo; and
then we perceive that &lquo;he beats thee from that natural luck&rquo; conveys a different mean-
ing from &lquo;he beats thee of that natural luck;&rquo; as when Hermione says (<I>Wint. Tale,</I>
I, ii, 42), &lquo;say this to him, He's beat from his best ward.&rquo; These prepositions are not,
therefore, here at least, interchangeable, however much they may seem so at first
sight. Nevertheless there are cases where it does seem perfectly immaterial which
one is used. Take, &lquo;His cocks do win the battle still of mine (line 41, below).
Would it not run equally well if the phrase were still <I>from</I> mine? Prospero uses
&lquo;from&rquo; after the verb &lquo;to win,&rquo; where he says (<I>Temp.</I> I, ii, 455), &lquo;hast put thyself
Upon this island as a spy, to win it From me.&rquo; This coalescence of these two prepo-
sitions has incited the grammarians to find some rule which may be a guide to their
use. <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 166) says that &lquo;<I>of</I>&rquo; is used for <I>from</I> with verbs that signify, either
literally or metaphorically, depriving, delivering, etc.&rquo; <SC>Franz</SC> (&sect; 356) is more
specific, and enumerates a considerable number of verbs where one or the other may
be used, such as, <I>discharge, deliver, rid</I> (to <I>free</I> and to <I>release,</I> on the other hand,
are used in Shakespeare only with <I>from</I>), <I>cleanse, clear, purge, wash, have, get,
receive, take, borrow, win, wrest, be, descend, come,</I> moreover, after the adjectives
<I>free, clear, secure.</I> &lquo;If,&rquo; continues Franz, &lquo;after these verbs, <I>of</I> and <I>from</I> occasion-
ally occur when they do not seem to be absolutely the same, and it may be desirable
to decide upon the difference between them, then there seems to be no principle to
be discerned in their use.&rquo; See, also, &lquo;he frets That Lepidus of the Triumpherate
should be deposed,&rquo; III, vi, 30, &lquo;Get gole for gole of youth,&rquo; IV, viii, 29.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

ing</SC> (p. 172) who says the sport &lquo;was much in vogue in Shakespeare's day.&rquo; A short
historical account of the game is to be found in Kelly's <I>Notices of Leicester,</I> p. 162.
<P>41. <B>of mine</B>] See note on &lquo;of&rquo; in line 30 above.

<P>43. <B>Beate mine (in hoopt) at odd's</B>] <SC>Seward</SC> (p. lxv): Here is evidently a sad
anti-climax. His cocks win the battle of mine when it is all to nought on my side,
and his quails, fighting <I>in a hoop,</I> beat mine when the odds are on my side. What
a falling off is there! . . . To <I>whoop</I> or hollow, might have been spelt <I>hoop,</I> without
the <I>w;</I> I read therefore: &lquo;Beat mine in <I>whoop'd-at</I> odds.&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> when the odds are so
great, that the betters on my side <I>shout</I> and <I>whoop</I> for victory. All who have been
in a Cock-pit will have a clear idea of this: Flatness and Anti-climax will be avoided,
and the soaring spirit of Shakespeare will recover its own vigour.&mdash;[Seward's reason-
ing proved too cogent for Capell, who adopted both it and his emendation.]&mdash;<SC>Heath</SC>
(p. 457): I shall only observe, that the phrase, as I apprehend, is, to beat <I>at</I> odds, not
to beat <I>in</I> odds; and that the meaning of the common reading is, Beat mine even
when put into the cage, unequally matched, with the odds very much in my favour.
&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: &lquo;Inhoop'd&rquo; is inclosed, confined, that they may fight. The modern
editions read, &lquo;Beat mine <I>in whoop'd</I> at odds.&rquo;&mdash;[The <SC>Cambridge Editors</SC> quote
this note of Johnson and remark: &lquo;No edition we know of reads thus. In Steevens
and all subsequent editions Johnson's note is repeated, &ldquo;whoop'd at&rdquo; being
hyphened.&rquo;]&mdash;<SC>Farmer</SC>: Shakespeare gives us the practice of his own time; and
there is no occasion for <I>in whoop'd-at,</I> or any other alteration. John Davies begins
one of his Epigrams <I>Vpon English Prouerbes:</I>&mdash;&lquo;He sets cocke <I>on</I> the hoope, <I>in,</I>
you would say; For cocking in hoopes is now all the play.&rquo;[&mdash;No. 287, ed. Grosart,
where it is not punctuated as intelligently as Farmer gives it.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Douce</SC> (ii, 87):
It may be doubted whether quail-fighting was practised in Shakspeare's time; but
when our poet speaks of their being <I>inhoop'd,</I> he might suppose that C&aelig;sar's or
Antony's quails, which he found in Plutarch, were trained to battle like game cocks
in a <I>ring</I> or <I>circle.</I> Quail combats were well known among the ancients, and espe-
cially at Athens. Julius Pollux relates that a circle was made in which the birds
were placed, and he whose quail was driven out of this circle lost the stake, which
was sometimes money, and occasionally the quails themselves. [Douce gives an
engraving from a Chinese miniature which] represents some ladies engaged at this
amusement, where the quails are actually <I>inhoop'd.</I>&mdash;<SC>Nares</SC> (<I>s. v. Inhoop'd</I>): The
substance of this passage is from North's Plutarch, but the &lquo;inhoop'd&rquo; is the addition
of our poet. No trace of such a mode of fighting has been found except in Davies's
<I>Epigram,</I> quoted by Farmer. Yet R. Holmes, who gives a list of terms and customs
used in cock-fighting, has no mention of <I>hoops.</I> See his <I>Acad. of Armory,</I> B. ii, ch.
11. Nor is any trace of the hoops to be found in any book on cock-fighting. If
this custom of fighting cocks within hoops could be thoroughly proved, it would also
afford the best explanation of the phrase <I>cock-a-hoop;</I> the cock perching on the <I>hoop,</I>
in an exulting manner, either before or after the battle.&mdash;[The <I>N. E. D.,</I> &lquo;in expla-
nation of <I>cock-a-hoop,</I> says that it is &lquo;a phrase of doubtful origin; the history of which
has been further obscured by subsequent attempts, explicit or implicit, to analyse it.&rquo;]
</CC>

sens the stable condition of another, is indicated, after such verbs as &lquo;to gain,&rquo; &lquo;to
encroach,&rquo; by <I>on</I> or <I>upon.</I> The preposition fulfills the same function after &lquo;to win,&rquo;
&lquo;to grow;&rquo; but the expression is, however, occasionally in Shakespeare so pregnant
as to be not always understood by a modern reader without further amplifications.
[Thus, the present phrase is equivalent to] &lquo;you will get the advantage of me by two
days.&rquo;&mdash;[See also IV, xiv, 118, &lquo;My Queen and Eros Haue . . . got upon me A
Noblenesse,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>2. <B>Musicke, moody foode,</B> etc.] <SC>Johnson</SC>: The <I>mood</I> is the <I>mind,</I> or <I>mental
disposition.</I> Perhaps here is a poor jest intended between <I>mood</I> the <I>mind</I> and <I>moods</I>
of music.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: &lquo;Moody,&rquo; in this instance, means melancholy.&mdash;[Thus in the
first line of <I>Twelfth Night,</I> &lquo;If music be the food of love, play on.&rquo;]
<P>3. <B>of vs that trade in Loue</B>] There is no thought here of <I>traffic,</I>&mdash;traffic is
mercenary. No mercenary love demands music as its food. Cleopatra means that
her sole dealing is in love; it is her very life.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

researches have shown that many things were in use in old Egypt, which, afterwards
lost, have been reinvented in modern times. But Shakespeare did not know this?
Doubtless, not; but then he knew that by using a term familiar to his audience he
would lead their thoughts to what has always followed in the train of luxury and
refinement. Suppose he had been so learned, and withal such a slave to his learn-
ing, as to use a term signifying some game which the English people had never heard

<P>Shakespeare's plays, singled out by the hypercritics, has been [this passage]. Of
late, however, certain investigators have turned the tables, and instead of leaving the
unlucky anachronism to support the Farmerian theory of Shakespeare's want of learn-
ing, or the more kindly modern belief that he wrote too impetuously to be bound by
mere chronology and scientific facts, they find in it an argument against the Shake-
spearian authorship of the plays, since as one of them says: &lquo;The human encyclo-
pedia who wrote that sentence appears to have known,&mdash;what very few people know
nowadays,&mdash;that the game of billiards is older than Cleopatra.&rquo; It may be, as asserted,
that a rudimentary game, in which ivory balls were punched with a stick into holes
in a table, after the fashion of our modern &lquo;tivoli&rquo; or &lquo;bagatelle,&rquo; was really in vogue
more than two thousand years ago, but it is very certain that Shakespeare never
bothered his head about it. He simply followed his habit, and cribbed the idea from
somebody else. In Chapman's <I>Blind Beggar of Alexandria,</I> &AElig;giale says: &lquo;Go,
Aspasia, Send for some ladies to go play with you At chess, at billiards, and at other
game.&rquo; As Chapman's play was printed in 1598, ten years before <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.</I>
was written, it is easy to see where Shakespeare got the idea that billiards was an
Egyptian game, and a favourite pastime of <I>women.</I> Whether George Chapman,
whose classical learning enabled him to translate Homer, wrote from actual knowl-
edge, or committed an anachronism, may be disputed; but the probabilities lean to
the latter conjecture, for, in this same play, the hero flourishes a pistol, smokes tobacco,
swears by &lquo;God's wounds,&rquo; and talks fair modern Spanish, in the time of the
Ptolomies.&mdash;<SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D.</I>): An adopted form of French <I>billard,</I> the game;
so named from <I>billard,</I> &lquo;a cue,&rquo; originally &lquo;a stick with curved end, a hockey-stick,&rquo;
diminutive of <I>bille,</I> piece of wood, stick. In England introduced only as the name
of the game, and made plural as in <I>draughts, skittles, bowls,</I> etc. 1591 Spenser,
<I>Mother Hubberd,</I> 803, &lquo;With all the thriftles games that may be found . . . With dice,
with cards, with balliards. 1598 Florio, <I>Trucco,</I> a kinde of play with balles vpon
a table, called billiards.&rquo;&mdash;[Then follows the present passage. In an Article in the
<I>Edinburgh Review</I> (April, 1871, p. 377) on the &lquo;Chorizontes,&rquo; the writer observes
that &lquo;Shakespeare could not have made any of his characters speak of tobacco without
being grossly anachronistic, the incidents in all his plays having occurred at remote
periods, or, at any rate, much anterior to the introduction of tobacco into Europe,
whereas Ben Jonson [who does mention tobacco] laid the plot of many a play in his
own time when tobacco was familiar to all.&rquo; This statement having been criticised
by Dr Hayman, the editor of the <I>Odyssey,</I> the author of the Article replied (<I>Athen-
&aelig;um,</I> 6 Sept. 1873), and admirably defines the distinction between anachronisms, that
might be termed permissible and those that are too &lquo;gross&rquo; to be ever tolerated.
After referring to the mention by Shakespeare of &lquo;cannon&rquo; in <I>King John,</I> a &lquo;clock
striking&rquo; in <I>Julius C&aelig;sar,</I> and &lquo;billiards&rquo; in this present play, the writer continues,
&lquo;but no dramatic author, to produce a scenic effect, would shrink from such anachro-
nisms, because they are not &ldquo;gross,&rdquo; not so &ldquo;gross&rdquo; as to be detected in an instant
by a theatrical audience, which knows nothing whatever about the origin of can-
non, clocks, and billiards. But all Shakespeare's contemporaries, even the most
ignorant, knowing that tobacco had been introduced into the old world during their
lives, would have derided the great dramatist had he represented Sir John Falstaff
consoling himself at Dame Quickly's in the reign of Henry the Fourth, with a pipe
of tobacco. . . . So a dramatist of our age could not speak of William the Conqueror
travelling by an express train, or sending a message by the electric telegraph; the

<P>anachronism would be &ldquo;gross&rdquo;; it would come immediately within the cognizance of
the audience, who know what is going on in their own generation, with some know-
ing what went on in the generation immediately preceding; and, thinking the mistake
ridiculous, they would burst into an excessive merriment. . . . But the anachronism
would not be discovered by anybody in his audience, if a dramatic author were to
represent the Egyptian Pharaoh Cheops going in a pair of boots to witness the prog-
ress of the building of the Great Pyramid, or the Jews returning in hats and shoes
from their Babylonish captivity. For where can the theatrical audience be found
that knows anything about the history of boots, hats, and shoes, when it does not com-
prise, peradventure, one man possessing sound learning and extensive information?&rquo;
&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>16. <B>Tawny fine fishes</B>] <SC>Theobald's</SC> emendation which seems obvious enough

not know why Shakespeare should have here used &lquo;tawny,&rquo; which is not, at least in
my experience, a characteristic colour of Mediterranean fishes, some of which are
extremely brilliant in hue; and he could hardly have had in mind English fish, inas-
much as he had already in <I>Much Ado</I> spoken of seeing &lquo;the fish Cut with her golden
oars the silver stream.&rquo; Possibly, it was Cleopatra's &lquo;moodiness&rquo; which tinged
everything with a sombre tint.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>21. <B>hang a salt fish on his hooke</B>] See Plutarch, <I>Appendix.</I> <SC>Grey</SC> (ii, 198)
quotes from <I>Memoirs of the English Court,</I> 1707, p. 489, a similar story of Nell

fashion.
<P>26. <B>drunke</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 339): Past indicative forms in <I>u</I> are very common in
Shakespeare. Thus <I>sang</I> does not occur, while &lquo;sung&rquo; is common as a past indicative.
<I>Sprang</I> is less common as a past tense than &lquo;sprung.&rquo; &lquo;Begun&rquo; is not uncommon
for &lquo;began,&rquo; which is also used.
<P>27. <B>Then put my Tires and Mantles on him</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: This is finely
imagined. The speaker is supposed to do this in imitation of Omphale, in her treat-
ment of Hercules, the great ancestor of Antony.
<P>28. <B>Sword Phillippan</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: We are not to suppose, nor is there any
warrant from history, that Antony had any particular sword so called. The dignify-
ing weapons, in this sort, is a custom of much more recent date. We find Antony,
afterwards, in this play, boasting of his own prowess at Philippi: see III, xi, 38.
That was the greatest action of Antony's life; and therefore this seems a fine piece
of flattery, intimating, that this sword ought to be denominated from that illustrious
battle, in the same manner as modern heroes in romance are made to give their
swords pompous names.

<P>with Octavia. She perceives at once with quickness that all is not well, and she
hastens to anticipate the worst, that she may have the pleasure of being disappointed.
Her impatience to know what she fears to learn, the vivacity with which she gradu-
ally works herself up into a state of excitement, and at length into fury, is wrought
out with a force of truth which makes us recoil.&mdash;<SC>Stapfer</SC> (p. 402): In the scene
between Cleopatra and the messenger who brings the tidings of Antony's marriage
with Octavia, her fury and unreasonableness know no bounds. Harpagon, thumping
Ma&icirc;tre Jacques, who, in obedience to his master's orders, tells him candidly what is
said of him in the town; the Viceroy of Peru, in the &lquo;P&eacute;richole&rquo; of M&eacute;rim&eacute;e, banish-
ing his secretary for a like service, are models of wisdom and coolness compared to
Cleopatra. There is some shadow of excuse for their anger, as the account given
them is not the mere simple announcement of a fact, but consists of a long preach-
ment which the secretary and Ma&icirc;tre Jacques may have flavoured with a spice of
malice of their own; but the unhappy messenger to Cleopatra is as guiltless of the
message as if he had given it to her under cover, closed and sealed. To insult him,
beat him, and threaten him with a dagger shows a capability of exercising the same
frenzy upon inanimate objects, such as pieces of furniture, mirrors, and china. No
man, however furious, vents his rage in so senseless a form as this, which would
seem to belong peculiarly to the anger of women and children. But at the same
time, we must notice how passion dignifies every movement and action; the impetu-
ous torrent of her wrath makes what is immeasurably petty, mean, and ridiculous
appear even grand. No one would ever feel inclined to laugh at this scene, in which
what might have been the subject for a comedy is transformed by the violence and
force of Cleopatra's love into tragic cries and outbursts.&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii): In the
MS this Messenger is called Elis; but whether that were the name of the actor of
the part, or of the character, as represented in some MS of the play, we cannot
determine. We know no player of that day of the name of Elis or Ellis.
<P>30. <B>Ramme</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: <I>Rain</I> of Hanmer agrees better with the epithets <I>fruit-
ful</I> and <I>barren.</I> So, in <I>Timon:</I> &lquo;Rain sacrificial whisp'rings in his ear.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>:
The term employed in the text is much in the style of the speaker; and is supported
incontestably by a passage in <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.:</I> &lquo;I go to meet The noble Brutus, <I>thrusting</I>
this <I>report Into his ears.</I>&rquo; Again, in <I>The Tempest:</I> &lquo;You <I>cram</I> these words <I>into my
ears,</I> against The stomach of my sense.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ritson</SC>: <I>Ram</I> is a vulgar word, never
used in our author's plays, but once by Falstaff, where he describes his situation in
the buck-basket. It is here evidently a misprint for <I>rain.</I> The quotation from <I>Jul.
C&aelig;s.</I> does not support the old reading at all, the idea being perfectly distinct.&mdash;
<SC>Steevens</SC>: &lquo;Ramm'd,&rquo; however, occurs in <I>King John:</I> II, i, 272.&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: The
expression in the text is quite characteristic of the speaker.&mdash;[Had Cleopatra said
sweetly and poetically &lquo;<I>rain</I> thou thy fruitful tidings in mine ears,&rquo; the succeeding
scene would never have been enacted.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>33, 34. <B>Anthonyo's dead, If thou,</B> etc.] It is all very well for sudden terror to
clutch at Cleopatra's heart and stop her pulses, but this is no excuse whatever for
not speaking rhythmically. To what trouble her heedlessness gives rise! <SC>Abbott</SC>
(&sect; 484) decides that Antony is &lquo;de - ad,&rquo; and that the villain will kill his &lquo;Misteress.&rquo;
<SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.</I> 48) does not prolong the term of Antony's demise, and twice slay
the slain, but inserts a <I>do</I> after &lquo;thou,&rquo; &lquo;If thou <I>do</I> say so;&rquo; he cannot, however, abide
plain &lquo;Mistris,&rquo; but must also pronounce it <I>Misteress.</I> <SC>Delius</SC> believes that in her
intense excitement Cleopatra uses Anthony's full dignified Latin name &lquo;Antonius,&rquo;
on the only occasion when it is used throughout the play. <SC>Keightley</SC> emits an
additional groan before &lquo;Anthonyo.&rquo; And thus all pare and protract the lines into
nice, decorous lengths to please the eye, and rhythm is smug again.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>35. <B>But well and free</B>] <SC>Rann</SC>: <I>But well; and free:</I>&mdash;Say but he is well; and
thou gain'st thy freedom.&mdash;[Rann seldom, if ever, gives any authority in his notes;
conjectures are there found of Capell, of M. Mason, and others; all mingled with
those which I believe to be his own. I think that the foregoing note is one of the
latter.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>37. <B>My blewest vaines to kisse,</B> etc.] <SC>Hazlitt</SC> (p. 99): How all the pride of
beauty and high rank breaks out in her promised reward.&mdash;[Is there not in Beaumont
&amp; Fletcher's <I>False One,</I> I, ii, a reminiscence of these lines:&mdash;&lquo;and for thy news,
Receive a favour kings have kneeled in vain for, And kiss my hand&rquo;?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>47, 48. <B>no goodnesse in thy face if Anthony Be free</B>] I cannot but consider
the punctuation of the Ff, which places a comma merely after &lquo;face,&rquo; to be far better
than <SC>Capell's</SC> colon. Cleopatra means, I think, that no one with good tidings to
impart could wear such a hang-dog look.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>48. <B>so tart a fauour</B>] <SC>Knight</SC>: How full of characteristic spirit is this passage,
in which we exactly follow the punctuation of the original. But the editors are not
satisfied with it. So they read, &lquo;<I>why</I> so tart a favour.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. ii): The &lquo;why&rquo;
added by Rowe (and by Collier's MS) is absolutely necessary for the sense of this
passage, to say nothing of the metre.&mdash;[Knight is exactly right, I think, when he says
this speech is characteristic of Cleopatra, but he seems hardly to be aware how right
he is. Twice before have we had exclamations from Cleopatra as full of scorn and
contempt as this. She said to Charmian (I, iii, 14) &lquo;Thou teachest like a fool. The
way to lose him!&rquo; and again (I, v, 86) &lquo;When I was green in judgement, cold in
blood. To say as I said then!&rquo; The present speech seems to me to be parallel. It
appears to be a fashion of speaking as peculiar to Cleopatra as little short repetitions
are to Rosalind, such as &lquo;Me believe it!&rquo; &lquo;You a lover!&rquo; etc. Rowe's didactic
&lquo;why&rquo; is to me offensive; and the pause after &lquo;healthful&rquo; makes good the metre.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>50. <B>a Furie crown'd with Snakes</B>] <SC>Deighton</SC>: The Erinyes are represented
by &AElig;schylus as having bodies all black, snakes twined in their hair, and blood drip-
ping from their eyes.
<P>51. <B>formall</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Decent, regular.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: A man in his senses.&mdash;
<SC>Bradley</SC> (<I>N. E. D. s. v.</I> &dagger; 4. c.): Normal in intellect.

<P>'Scape not the thunderbolt,&rquo; whereby it is difficult to perceive the gain. The half-

<P>101, 102. <B>Melt Egypt . . . Turne all</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 364) observes in regard to
these two verbs that it is &lquo;often impossible to tell whether we have an imperative
with a vocative, or a subjunctive used optatively or conditionally.&rquo; I hardly under-
stand what is meant by an &lquo;imperative with a vocative&rquo; in this passage. The voca-
tives can hardly be &lquo;Egypt,&rquo; or &lquo;kindly creatures.&rquo; But omitting the &lquo;vocatives,&rquo;
both verbs seem to me imperatives, like &lquo;Let Rome in Tiber melt.&rquo; <SC>Thiselton</SC>
(p. 13), in the present command of Cleopatra and in that of Anthony last quoted,
would find that &lquo;the affinity of nature between Anthony and Cleopatra is suggested
by their similar imprecations when the continuance of their connection is threatened.&rquo;
&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>103. <B>Call?</B>] Is this interrogation mark absolutely wrong? It has been discarded
by every editor since the <I>Third Folio.</I> But may it not indicate Charmian's hesi-
tation, and Cleopatra's imperious questioning of her delay? May it not be similar
to Lear's frenzied shout, &lquo;Who stirs?&rquo; when the circle of courtiers stand motion-
less with horror at the banishment of Cordelia, and Lear has already cried, &lquo;Call
France!&rquo;?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>106. <B>These hands do lacke Nobility,</B> etc.] <SC>Malone</SC>: This play was probably
not produced until after Elizabeth's death, when a stroke at her proud and passion-
ate demeanour to her courtiers and maids of honour (for her majesty used to chastise
<I>them</I> too) might be safely hazarded.&mdash;[What cared Shakespeare, at such a moment,
for Elizabeth and all her court? He was Cleopatra.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>107, 108. <B>since I my selfe . . . the cause</B>] <SC>Deighton</SC>: <I>Sc.</I> by allowing myself
to be such a slave to love for Antony.&mdash;[Or, possibly, in that she had ever allowed
Anthony to leave her.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>133. <B>That art not what th'art sure of</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: I fancy the line consists only
of abrupt starts: &lquo;That art&mdash;not what?&mdash;Thou'rt sure on't.&rquo; &lquo;That his fault should
make a knave of thee that art&mdash;<I>but what</I> shall I say thou art not? Thou art then
sure of this <I>marriage.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: <I>In Meas. for Meas.,</I> II, ii, is a passage so much
resembling this, that I cannot help pointing it out for the use of some future com-
mentator, though I am unable to apply it with success to the very difficult line before
us: &lquo;Drest in a little brief authority, <I>Most ignorant of what he's most assur'd,</I> His
glassy essence.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Tollet</SC>: That is, &lquo;Thou art not an honest man, of which thou art
thyself assured, but thou art, in my opinion, a knave by thy master's fault alone.&rquo;&mdash;
[<SC>Knight</SC> substantially adopts this paraphrase.]&mdash;<SC>M. Mason</SC>: A proper punctuation,
with the addition of a single letter, will make this passage clear; the reading <I>sure
of't,</I> instead of &lquo;sure of&rquo;: &lquo;That art not!&mdash;What? thou'rt sure <I>of't?</I>&rquo; That is,
&lquo;What? are you sure of what you tell me, that he is married to Octavia?&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>:
Cleopatra begins now a little to recollect herself, and to be ashamed of having struck
the servant for the fault of his master. She then very naturally exclaims: &lquo;O, that
his fault should make a knave of thee, That art not what thou'rt <I>sore</I> of!&rquo; for so I
would read, with the change of only one letter. &lquo;Alas, is it not strange, that the
fault of Antony should make thee appear to me a knave, thee, that art innocent, and
art not the cause of that ill news, in consequence of which thou art yet <I>sore</I> with my
blows!&rquo; If it be said, that it is very harsh to suppose that Cleopatra means to say
to the Messenger, that <I>he</I> is not himself that <I>information</I> which he brings, and which
has now made him smart, let the following passage in <I>Coriolanus</I> answer the objec-
tion: &lquo;Lest you should chance to whip your <I>information,</I> And beat the messenger
that bids beware Of what is to be dreaded.&rquo;&mdash;[IV, vi, 53.] The Egyptian queen
has beaten her <I>information.</I> If the old copy be right, the meaning is&mdash;&lquo;Strange,
that his fault should make thee appear a knave, who art not that information of which
thou bringest such certain assurance.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC> observes that the &lquo;simple change
[<I>sore</I>] proposed by Malone is more Shakespearian&rquo; than Mason's. <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. i),
who follows the punctuation of M. Mason without changing &lquo;of&rquo; into <I>of't,</I> admits
that the original text is &lquo;far from intelligible. By the words,&rquo; he continues,
&lquo;&ldquo;What! thou'rt sure of?&rdquo; Cleopatra intends to inquire of the messenger once more,
whether he is certain of the tidings he has brought.&rquo; In his <I>Second Edition,</I> how-
ever, Collier adopted Mason's <I>of't,</I> but in his <I>Third Edition</I> he returned to the
punctuation and reading of his <I>First.</I>&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Remarks,</I> p. 247): M. Mason's
punctuation, with the change of &lquo;of&rquo; to <I>of't,</I> afforded at least a sense; but Collier,
. . . has made the passage mere nonsense. I should strongly protest against any
deviation from the old eds. here. &lquo;That art not what thou'rt sure of&rquo; may mean,
&lquo;That art not the evil tidings of which thou givest me such assurance.&rquo;&mdash;[<SC>Collier</SC>
did not relish having his reading stigmatised as &lquo;mere nonsense&rquo;; accordingly in his

and so in both of Dyce's subsequent editions, Dyce denounced Collier's &lquo;discredit-
able subterfuge,&rquo; printing these two words in small capitals, which are always thus
supposed to sting like adders fanged. If it were not ludicrous, would it not be humil-
iating, to see, in the awful presence of Shakespeare, wee atomies taking themselves
so seriously?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>R. G. White</SC> (ed. i) reads &lquo;That art <I>but</I> what thou'rt sure of,&rquo;
and thus explains: That is, being merely a messenger you are to be regarded only
according to the tenor of your message . . . The universal previous punctuation of
the passage makes it not superfluous to say, that it is not an optative exclamation,
but a declaration; and that &lquo;that&rquo; in the previous line is not the conjunction, but the
definitive adjective. Cleopatra, in reply to the messenger's plea, that he only per-
forms his office, says, &lquo;O that [<I>i. e.</I> Antony's marriage], which is his fault, should
make a knave of thee, that art but what thy tidings are.&rquo;&mdash;[White retained this read-
ing in his Second Edition, with substantially the same paraphrase.]&mdash;The <SC>Cowden-
Clarkes</SC>: That is, who art not thyself that fault which thou art so sure has been
committed. The Messenger has before said, &lquo;I that do bring the news made not the
match,&rquo; and &lquo;I have made no fault.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> (reading &lquo;That art in what thou'rt
sure of&rquo;): That is, &lquo;<I>sharest</I> in, or art mixed up with, or infected by, the message
which thou art sure of.&rquo; So in I, ii, &lquo;The nature of bad news <I>infects the teller.</I>&rquo;
Cleopatra's idea seems to be, that the Messenger is made a knave by the knavish
message which he brings, and with which he shows himself to be in sympathy by
sticking to it so constantly.&mdash;<SC>C. M. Ingleby</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 1885, VI, xi, 362): The
sense is: &lquo;that ought not to be confounded with thy foul message, yet seemest to be
tarred with the same brush.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>G. Joicey</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 1891, VII, xii, 342): Read:
&lquo;That art not&mdash;what thou art sure of!&rquo; Is not Cleopatra about to say &lquo;that art not
married&rquo;? She cannot bring herself to utter the (to her) detestable word again and
paraphrases it as above. The meaning would be, &lquo;O that Antony's knavish fault of
getting married should cause thee&mdash;thee that art not married&mdash;to be treated as a
knave.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Br. Nicholson</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 1892, VIII, i, 182): I take it that the author
meant that Cleopatra,&mdash;looking to what she had just done,&mdash;would assume that such
a knave was sure to be whipped or carted. One must not look for speech other than
impulsive from an infuriated woman, still less from a Cleopatra maddened by jealous
rage; nor was Shakespeare so bad an imitator of nature as to make her talk at such
a time as thoughtfully as when debating what would best set off her charms when
robed as the Paphian queen.&mdash;<SC>Deighton</SC> (<I>Old Drama.</I> ii, 41): Perhaps &lquo;That art
<I>no whit</I> th&rquo; <I>author</I> of <I>'t': i. e.,</I> that you, who are in nowise answerable for his fault,
should be made a knave by it. This seems a suitable sense, and <I>author</I> for &lquo;art
sure&rquo; is no very violent alteration considering the writing of the time and the various
spellings of the word.&mdash;<SC>Herford</SC>: (With irony) that art innocent, forsooth, of
offence, yet sure to offend!&mdash;[This line has not proved very encouraging to those
who have lightheartedly attempted to amend it. Its most popular emendation has
but five adherents. The original text can be paraphrased hardly better, I think,
than it is by Dyce (following Malone substantially), as quoted above in his <I>Remarks.</I>
What the messenger was sure of was the ill tidings. These he himself assuredly
was not, and these it was that Cleopatra would like to tear in pieces; but as she had
maltreated him instead, all the pity she could give him was that Anthony's fault had
exposed him to the treatment of a knave.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>136. <B>em</B>] The only other instances, that I can recall (<I>Concordances</I> give no help)
of the use in the <I>First Folio</I> of this abbreviation, are in <I>The Tempest,</I> where Prospero,
speaking of his government in Naples, says &lquo;The creatures that were mine, I say, or
chang'd 'em, Or els new form'd 'em;&rquo; I, ii, 99, 100; and again, in <I>Henry V:</I> IV,
iii, 124, where Henry dismisses the French Herald who had come to demand a
ransom from him, Henry replies, &lquo;They shall have none, I swear, but these my
joints; Which if they have as I will leave 'em them, Shall yield them little,&rquo; etc.,
where the full form, <I>them,</I> would be decidedly harsh; and the reason for the abbre-
viation is plain. Again, in <I>Coriolanus,</I> II, iii, 220, the First Citizen boasts, &lquo;I
[have] twice hundred [voices] and their friends to piece 'em.&rquo; Possibly this may
indicate the low estate of the speaker. And, lastly, we find Macbeth demanding of
the witches, &lquo;Call 'em; let me see 'em.&rquo;&mdash;IV, i, 72, which may indicate his frenzied
impatience. But why this form should be used in the present line and in <I>The Tem-
pest,</I> I do not know.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>146. <B>Let him for euer go</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: She is now talking in broken sentences,
not of the Messenger, but of Antony.&mdash;<SC>Tyrwhitt</SC> (p. 11): This, I think, would be
more spirited thus:&mdash;&lquo;Let him for ever go&mdash;let him&mdash;<I>no,</I>&mdash;Charmion.&rquo;&mdash;[Adopted,
substantially, by Rann and Wordsworth.]
<P>146. <B>let him not</B>] <SC>Thiselton</SC> (p. 14): That is, hinder him not. Cleopatra
noticing that Charmian has started to bid Alexas not to bring back the Messenger,
corrects herself and tells Charmian not to interfere. The first &lquo;him&rquo; in this line
refers to the Messenger; the second to Alexas.&mdash;[Dr Johnson's interpretation seems
to me more just. Cleopatra's thoughts are not here concerned with any ignoble
messenger. It is Anthony from whom she wishes to part &lquo;for ever,&rquo; who, though he
be in one aspect like a monster, in another he is a god.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>147, 148. <B>painted one way . . . other wayes a Mars</B>] <SC>Staunton</SC>: An allusion
to the &lquo;double&rquo; pictures in vogue formerly, of which Burton says,&mdash;&lquo;they are like
these double or turning pictures; stand before w<SUP>ch</SUP>, you see a fair maid, on the one side
an ape, on the other an owl.&rquo;&mdash;[<I>Democritus to the Reader,</I> p. 73, ed. 1651.]&mdash;And
Chapman, in <I>All Fooles,</I> I, i, &lquo;But like a cousoning picture, which one way Shewes
like a Crowe, another like a Swanne.&rquo;&mdash;[Burton had once before (p. 36) thus
referred to these pictures: &lquo;&mdash;and he, and the rest are <I>hypocrites, ambodexters,</I> out
sides, so many turning pictures, a lyon on the one side, a lamb on the other.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>148. <B>wayes a Mars</B>] Is not this clearly a sophistication due to the ear?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>151. <B>Exeunt</B>] <SC>Mrs. Jameson</SC> (ii. 139): The pride and arrogance of the Egyptian
queen, the blandishment of the woman, the unexpected but natural transitions of
temper and feeling, the contest of various passions, and at length&mdash;when the wild
hurricane has spent its fury&mdash;the melting into tears, faintness, and languishment, are
portrayed with the most astonishing power, and truth, and skill in feminine nature.
More wonderful still is the splendour and force of colouring which is shed over this
extraordinary scene. The mere idea of an angry woman beating her menial presents
something ridiculous or disgusting to the mind; in a queen or a tragedy heroine it is
still more indecorous; yet this scene is as far as possible from the vulgar or the
comic. Cleopatra seems privileged to &lquo;touch the brink of all we hate&rquo; with impunity.

<P>This imperial termagant, this &lquo;wrangling queen, whom every thing becomes,&rquo; becomes
her fury. We know not by what strange power it is, that in the midst of all these
unruly passions and childish caprices, the poetry of the character, and the fanciful
and sparkling grace of the delineation are sustained and still rule in the imagination;
but we feel that it is so.

<P>23. <B>Capitoll</B>] <SC>Craik</SC> (<I>Jul. C&aelig;s.</I> II, i, 77): As an historical fact, the meeting of

Curia in which the statue of Pompey stood, being, as Plutarch tells us, one of the
edifices which Pompey had built, and had given, along with his famous Theatre, to
the public. The mistake is found also in <I>Hamlet,</I> III, ii, and [here in <I>Ant. &amp;
Cleop.</I>].

<P>34. <B>Thou dost ore count me,</B> etc.] <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 35): &lquo;O'er-count&rquo; in this speech

<P>35, 36. <B>since the Cuckoo . . . Remaine,</B> etc.] <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 35): Where is the

the cuckoo, that seizes the nests of other birds, you have invaded a house which you

only come to him he would have &lquo;endowed his purposes with words.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>38. <B>from the present</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: That is, foreign to the object of our present
discussion.&mdash;[For many examples where &lquo;from&rquo; means <I>apart from, away from,</I> with-
out a verb of motion, see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 158.]
<P>42. <B>it is worth imbrac'd</B>] It is within the bounds of possibility that the omission
of a full stop after &lquo;imbrac'd&rquo; is intentional, and indicates that C&aelig;sar in his eager-
ness interrupts Anthony. That C&aelig;sar begins his sentence with &lquo;and&rquo; adds a faint
tinge of probability to this doubtful surmise. Where we have an undoubted inter-
ruption, as in line 87, the dash is portentous.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>47. <B>greed</B>] It is not necessary in a modernised text to print this <I>'greed;</I> it is a
regular past participle of the verb, <I>to gree,</I> which is, according to <SC>Bradley</SC> (<I>N. E. D.
s. v.</I>), an aphetized form of the verb, <I>agree,</I> in use from the time of Wyclif. See II,
i, 50; <I>Mer. of Ven.</I> II, ii, 97.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>49. <B>Our Targes vndinted</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.</I> 253): Palpably <I>targe'.</I> [Where
the apostrophe marks an abbreviated plural, like <I>business', mightiness'</I>]; and so write
in <I>Cymbeline,</I> V, v, 5,&mdash;&lquo;Stept before targes of proof, cannot be found.&rquo; <I>Targe</I> in
the singular would not be Elizabethan English. [Of this last remark of Walker,
<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. ii) says] I am not sure that I understand [it];&mdash;but compare the fol-
lowing passages of Chapman's <I>Homer:</I>&mdash;&lquo;As from his chariot he leapt downe,
beneath his <I>targe</I> of brasse.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Iliad,</I> B. xi, p. 150, ed. Folio; &lquo;And (with his lance)
strooke through the <I>targe</I> of that braue Lycian king.&rquo;&mdash;B. xii, p. 167; &lquo;With sword
and fire they vext for them their <I>targes</I> hugely round,&rquo;&mdash;B. xii, p. 168. In a note on
the line in <I>Cymbeline</I> Mr Singer (<I>Shakespeare,</I> ed. 1856) observes: &lquo;The plural
<I>targes</I> seems to have been formerly a monosyllable [<I>targs</I>], as in French, where its
oldest form is <I>targues.</I>&rquo; That Chapman at least did not use it as a monosyllable is
shown by the third of the passages just cited from his <I>Homer.</I>&mdash;[<SC>Hudson</SC> adopted
<I>targs.</I>]
<P>55. <B>by telling. You must know</B>] <SC>Theobald's</SC> excellent restoration of the punc-
tuation reveals the meaning of &lquo;You must know,&rquo; which is <I>I must tell you,</I> and can-
not be <I>it must have been already known to you.</I>

<P>87. <B>Appolodorus carried</B>] <I>C&aelig;sar</I> . . . therupon secretly sent for <I>Cleopatra</I> which
was in the country to come vnto him. She only taking <I>Apollodorus</I> <SC>Sicilian</SC> of all
her friends, tooke a litle bote, &amp; went away with him in it in the night, and came
and landed hard by the foote of the castle. Then hauing no other mean to come
into the court without being knowen, she laid herselfe down vpon a mattresse or
flockbed, which <I>Apollodorus</I> her friend tied and bound vp together like a bundle
with a great leather thong, &amp; so tooke her vp on his backe, and brought her thus
hamperd in this fardle vnto <I>C&aelig;sar,</I> in the castle gate.&mdash;North's <I>Plutarch: Julius
C&aelig;sar,</I> p. 781, ed. 1595 (Leo's <I>Photolithograph</I>).
<P>88. <B>Eno. No more that: he did so</B>] <SC>Orger</SC> (p. 98): It is hard to under-
stand what Enobarbus can mean by trying to suppress a topic by the words, &lquo;no
more of that,&rquo; and then continuing to narrate it. It seems as if there is a faulty dis-
tribution of parts. In the next scene, line 9, the servant describes Lepidus, &lquo;He
cries out, &ldquo;no more,&rdquo; reconciles them to his entreaty, and himself to the drink,&rquo;
which justifies us in supposing that it is he who endeavours to stifle the scandal, and
we should divide as follows:&mdash;&lquo;<I>Lepidus.</I> No more of that. <I>Eno.</I> He did so. [<I>aside
to Pompey.</I>]&rquo;&mdash;[I think it is not impossible to imagine the action here. Pompey's
allusion to &lquo;fine Egyptian cookery&rquo; is unfortunate, especially when he speaks of it to
Anthony who is just married to Octavia; but his next reference to Julius C&aelig;sar and
his feasting is worse. Anthony tries to stop him by saying &lquo;you've heard altogether
too much.&rquo; Thereupon Pompey blunders still further by asserting that he really did
not mean anything bad, that he had fair meanings. &lquo;Then,&rquo; retorts Anthony, &lquo;see
that you put them in fair words.&rquo; But Pompey's ill-timed references are not yet
ended, &lquo;bad is begun but worse remains behind,&rquo;&mdash;he refers to Cleopatra's first love-
affair. Hereupon Enobarbus takes in the situation, and, instantly silencing Pompey,
says aside to him, &lquo;Hush, no more of that!&rquo; adding &lquo;you are quite right,&mdash;Apollo-
dorus did so.&rquo; &lquo;What?&rquo; asks the bewildered Pompey, who then recognizes Eno-
barbus. And thereafter the dialogue continues without obstruction. Anthony had
evidently turned away abruptly; he does not speak again during the scene.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>2. <B>Enter,</B> etc.] <SC>Freytag</SC> (p. 235): One of the most beautiful <I>ensemble</I> scenes of
Shakespeare is the [present] banquet scene. It contains no chief part of the action,
and is essentially a situation scene, a thing not occurring frequently in the tragic part
of the action in Shakespeare. But it receives a certain significance, because it is
at the close of the Second Act, and also stands in a place demanding eminence,
especially in this piece, in which the preceding political explanations make a varie-
gated and animated picture very desirable. The abundance of little characterising
traits which are united in this scene, their close condensation, above all, the technical
arrangement, are admirable. The Scene is introduced by a short conversation among
servants, as is frequently the case in Shakespeare, in order to provide for the setting
of the tables and the arrangement of the furniture on the stage. The Scene itself is
in three parts. The first part presents the haughty utterances of the reconciled Tri-
umvirs and the pedantry of the drunken simpleton, Lepidus, to whom the servants
have already referred; the second, in terrible contrast, is the secret interview of
Pompey and Menas; the third, introduced by the bearing out of the drunken Lepidus,
is the climax of the wild Bacchanalia and rampant drunkenness. The connecting
of the three parts, as Menas draws Pompey aside, as Pompey again in the company
of Lepidus, resuming, continues the carouse, is quite worthy of notice. Not a word
in the whole Scene is without its use and significance; the poet perceives every
moment the condition of the individual figures, and of the accessory persons; each
takes hold of the action effectively; for the manager, as well as for the r&ocirc;les, the
whole is adapted in a masterly way. From the first news of Antony across the
Nile,&mdash;through which the image of Cleopatra is introduced even into this scene,&mdash;
and the simple remark of Lepidus, &lquo;You have strange serpents there,&rquo; through which
an impression is made on the mind of the hearer that prepares for Cleopatra's death
by a serpent's sting, to the last words of Antony, &lquo;Good; give me your hand, sir,&rquo; in
which the intoxicated man involuntarily recognizes the superiority of Augustus C&aelig;sar,
and even to the following drunken speeches of Pompey and Enobarbus, everything
is like fine chiseled work on a firmly articulated metal frame. A comparison of this
scene with the close of the banquet act in <I>The Piccolomini</I> is instructive.&mdash;<SC>Corson</SC>
(p. 285): Of Pompey's entertainment, made by Shakespeare so dramatically impor-
tant a scene in the Play, Plutarch simply says, &lquo;and there&rquo; (meaning on his galley)
&lquo;he welcomed them and made them great cheer.&rquo; But Shakespeare, knowing that
wine reveals as well as disguises, that <I>in vino est veritas,</I> made this banquet the
means of characterising and contrasting the Triumvirs, and the poor relic of republi-

<P>6. <B>high Conlord</B>] This gross misprint which was corrected in the Second Folio,
<SC>Gould</SC> (p. 45) accepts as the genuine word, and asserts that &lquo;high-coloured&rquo; is &lquo;one
of the most absurd alterations&rquo; he &lquo;ever met with.&rquo; He then goes on to explain
that Lepidus &lquo;was one of the triumviri or conlords, and this is the subject of con-
versation.&rquo; Many years ago I regretfully announced that my patience was exhausted
by the ignorance and presumption of <SC>Zachary Jackson, Andrew Becket, Lord
Chedworth</SC>, and <SC>E. H. Seymour</SC>, and that thereafter, save in exceptional cases,
no space on these pages should be sacrificed to their notes. After the foregoing
note on &lquo;conlord&rquo; would a single voice be raised in censure if George Gould be
added to the list?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>7. <B>Almes drinke</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: A phrase, amongst good fellows, to signify that
liquor of another's share which his companion drinks to ease him. But it satirically
alludes to C&aelig;sar and Antony's admitting him into the Triumvirate, in order to take
off from themselves the load of envy.&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii): Meaning wine that did
not properly belong to his share, but which each had contributed, in order to intoxi-
cate Lepidus.&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>): It evidently means here the <I>leavings.</I>&mdash;<SC>Murray</SC>
(<I>N. E. D.</I> 4. b.): The remains of liquor reserved for alms-people.&mdash;[Apparently,
this is the only known instance of the use of this phrase in the language. It is the
solitary example furnished by Murray. Everyone is entitled, therefore, to give it any
meaning that in his opinion harmonises with the eternal fitness of things. To me,
Collier's definition seems the closest. Just as an <I>alms-penny</I> means, as Murray
says, &lquo;a penny given in charity or as a gratuity,&rquo; so an &lquo;alms-drink&rquo; may be a drink
that is given as a charity or as a gratuity. Inasmuch as there is here no question
of charity, we may take it as a gratuity, and a gratuity bestowed by more than one.
Lepidus then drank not only his own share, but &lquo;they&rquo; plied him with wine, which,
like the contents of a poor-box, was the result of many gratuitous contributions.&mdash;
<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>8. <B>As they pinch one another by the disposition</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: A phrase
equivalent to that now in use, of &lquo;touching one in a sore place.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC> (i, 35):
This signifies, attack for their foibles, the foibles each is <I>dispos'd</I> to.&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (ed.
ii): This seems to refer to the sign they give each other regarding &lquo;the disposition&rquo;
of Lepidus to drink.&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: &lquo;By the disposition&rquo; is a very questionable
expression. We ought perhaps to read, &lquo;by the <I>disputation,</I>&rquo; that is, <I>in the contro-
versy.</I>&mdash;The <SC>Cowden-Clarkes</SC>: That is, &lquo;as they try each other's temper by banter,&rquo;
&lquo;as they gall or plague each other's sensitiveness by their mutual taunts.&rquo; <SC>Schmidt</SC>
(<I>Lex.</I>) here defines &lquo;pinch&rquo; as &lquo;to make ridiculous, to serve a trick.&rquo; &lquo;By the dis-
position&rquo; means, he also says, &lquo;by their foible,&rquo; adding, &lquo;a servant's speech.&rquo; [I find
it, however, a little difficult to combine the two definitions into a coherent and appli-
cable paraphrase of the whole sentence. Is it: they serve one another a trick by
their foibles?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>J. Crosby</SC> (<I>Shakespeariana,</I> Feb. 1884, p. 122): The servant
has said [in effect], they have made him drink not only his own wine, but a share
of theirs also. And now as they <I>dispose of</I> and <I>set before</I> him, their full goblets to
quaff, they pinch one another, or wink significantly, at the imposition they are prac-
tising on the good-natured reveler. And this harmonises with the context, &lquo;he
cries, &ldquo;No more;&rdquo; reconciles them to his entreaty, and himself to the drink.&rquo; &lquo;Not
another drop, gentlemen, I beseech you; I am not so well as I should be, but I'll
ne'er out;&rquo; to all of which they assent; and he forthwith proceeds to drain the cups,
that raise &lquo;the greater war between him and his discretion.&rquo; I formerly thought we
should read &lquo;as they pinch one another <I>at the imposition.</I> But the explanation I
have given seems sufficient.&mdash;<SC>Thiselton</SC> (p. 15): In order to ply Lepidus suf-
ficiently with liquor and at the same time keep sober themselves, his companions
give him &lquo;Almes drinke,&rquo; thereby stinting themselves (&lquo;pinch one another by the dis-
position&rquo;). By this means, he has their shares as well as his own, and, being satisfied
with such good measure, and, perhaps, feeling some awkwardness at drinking alone
in company, he cries out &lquo;No more,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> &lquo;enough.&rquo; They, having so far gained
their object, comply, while he proceeds to drink the wine that has been so served to
him. . . . The passage has been confused by . . . the assumption that &lquo;reconciles&rquo;
necessarily imports the inferiority of the wine served to Lepidus, when it probably
indicates a slight touch of conscience on his part at continuing to drink alone.
&lquo;One another&rquo; is certainly used somewhat loosely for <I>themselves,</I> but it must be
borne in mind that it is a servant who speaks.&mdash;<SC>Deighton</SC>: This seems to mean, as
they ply each other hard with the mischievous desire of seeing one another under the
table, Lepidus, affecting to have had as much as he can carry, cries out &lquo;enough;&rquo;
yet all the same, while getting them to accept his excuses, finds it possible to quiet
his scruples against further indulgence; though perhaps &lquo;'twere to consider too curi-
ously to consider&rquo; the servant's speech as having any very exact sense.&mdash;[If &lquo;one
another&rquo; can be regarded as the same as <I>themselves,</I> Thiselton's interpretation seems
to be the most plausible. The excuse, first suggested by Schmidt, for any looseness of
