<P>16-18. <B>To be call'd into a huge Sphere, . . . pittifully disaster the cheekes</B>]
<SC>Johnson</SC>: This speech seems to be mutilated; to supply the deficiencies is impossi-
ble, but perhaps the sense was originally approaching to this: &lquo;To be called into a
huge sphere, and not to be seen to move in it,&rquo; is a very ignominious state; &lquo;great
offices&rquo; &lquo;are the holes where eyes should be, which (if eyes be wanting), pitifully
disaster the cheeks.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>M. Mason</SC>: The thought, though miserably expressed, appears
to be this: That a man called into a high sphere, without being seen to move in it,
is a sight as unseemly as the holes where the eyes should be, without the eyes to fill
them.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: I do not believe a single word has been omitted. The being
called into a huge sphere, and not being seen to move in it, these two circumstances,
says the speaker, resemble sockets in a face where eyes should be [but are not],
which <I>empty</I> sockets, or holes without eyes, pitifully disfigure the countenance. &lquo;The
sphere in which the eye moves&rquo; is an expression which Shakespeare has often used.
Thus, in his 119th <I>Sonnet:</I> &lquo;How have mine eyes out of their <I>spheres</I> been fitted,&rquo;
etc. Again, in <I>Hamlet:</I> &lquo;Make thy two eyes, like stars, start from their <I>spheres.</I>&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Rolfe</SC> here finds in &lquo;sphere&rquo; an &lquo;allusion to the old Ptolomaic astronomy, accord-
ing to which the heavenly bodies were set in hollow crystal spheres, by the revolu-
tion of which they were carried round.&rquo; And &lquo;disaster,&rquo; he observes, &lquo;was an astro-
logical term and is probably suggested here by the figure that precedes.&rquo; [Both of
these suggestions are, to me, somewhat doubtful. &lquo;Sphere&rquo; and &lquo;disaster&rquo; had been

<P>19. <B>A Sennet</B>] <SC>Nares</SC>: A word chiefly occurring in the stage-directions of the
old plays, and seeming to indicate a particular set of notes on the trumpet or cornet,
different from a flourish. &lquo;Trumpets sound a florish, and then a sennate.&rquo;&mdash;Decker's
<I>Satiromastix</I> [p. 222, ed. Pearson]. In Beaumont and Fletcher's <I>Knight of Malta,</I>

pets.&rquo; But we see from Decker's play that they were different. It appears to have
been a technical term of the musicians who played those instruments.
<P>20. <B>Enter C&aelig;sar,</B> etc.] <SC>Knight</SC> (<I>Supp. Notice,</I> p. 357): This scene is one of
those creations which render Shakspere so entirely above, and so utterly unlike, other
poets. Every line is a trait of character. Here we see the solemn, &lquo;unmeritable&rquo;
Lepidus; the cautious C&aelig;sar; the dashing, clever, genial Antony. His eye dances;
his whole visage &lquo;doth cream and mantle;&rquo; the corners of his mouth are drawn down,
as he hoaxes Lepidus about the crocodile with the most admirable fooling. The
revelry grows louder and louder, till &lquo;the Egyptian bacchanals&rquo; close the scene.
Who can doubt that Antony bears &lquo;the holding&rquo; the loudest of all? <I>These</I> are not
the lords of the world of French tragedy. Grimm, who, upon the whole, has a
leaning to Shakspere, says:&mdash;&lquo;Il est assez ridicule sans doute de faire parler les
valets comme les h&eacute;ros; mais il est beaucoup <I>plus ridicule encore</I> de faire parler aux
h&eacute;ros le langage du peuple.&rquo; To make them drunk is worse even than the worst of
the ridiculous. It is impossible to define such a sin. We think, with Dogberry, it
is &lquo;flat burglary as ever was committed.&rquo;

be fallen, and downe again. By these, the seed time is much of it spent, for that
the earth is too wet. By the other there is none at all, by reason that the ground is
dry and thirsty. The prouince taketh good keep and reckoning of both, the one as
well as the other; For when it is no higher than 12 cubits, it findeth extream famine:
yea, and at 13 it feeleth hunger still, 14 cubits comforts their hearts, 15 bids them take
no care, but 16 affoordeth them plenty and delicious dainties. . . . And so soon as any
part of the land is freed from the water, straight waies it is sowed.&rquo;&mdash;Holland's

upon the seventeenth of June, when Nilus beginning to overflow, the water thereof
conveied by the said sluce into the channel, increaseth daily. If the water reacheth
only to the fifteenth cubit of the said <I>piller,</I> they hope for a fruitful yeere following;
but if [it?] stayeth between the twelfth cubit and the fifteenth, then the increase of the
yeere will prove but mean: if it resteth between the tenth and twelfth cubits, then
it is a sign that corne will be solde ten ducates the bushel.&rquo;
<P>23. <B>Pyramid</B>] <SC>W. W. Lloyd</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 1897, VII, xi, 283) quotes &lquo;Though
palaces and pyramids do slope Their heads to their foundations.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Macb.</I> IV, i, 56;
the present passage, and &lquo;rather make My Countries high pyramides my Gibbet.&rquo;&mdash;
V, ii, 71, and then from them infers that by &lquo;pyramid,&rquo; Shakespeare &lquo;understands not a
proper pyramid, but an obelisk.&rquo; It is certainly not impossible; both terms were used
vaguely, in accordance with the conception in the popular mind of the objects them-
selves. Thus, for instance, Cotgrave defines an &lquo;obelisque&rquo;: &lquo;a great, high, and
square stone, broad at the bottome, and lessening towards the top like a Pyramides.&rquo;
&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>24. <B>or the meane</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: That is, the middle.
<P>25. <B>Foizon</B>] <SC>Bradley</SC> (<I>N. E. D.</I>): Adopted from Old French <I>foison, fuson</I> =
Proven&ccedil;al <I>foison,</I> regular phonetic descendant from popular Latin <I>f&ubreve;si&omacr;n-em</I> for
Latin <I>f&umacr;si&omacr;n-em,</I> a pouring, noun of action formed on <I>fund&ecaron;re</I> to pour. 1. Plenty,
abundance, a plentiful supply.
<P>28. <B>And shortly</B>] The <I>Cambridge Edition</I> records an Anonymous conjecture:
&lquo;And <I>'t</I> shortly,&rquo; which is highly probable.
<P>28. <B>Haruest</B>] <SC>Corson</SC> (p. 287): There's an air of solidity in this speech, which
indicates a consciousness on the part of the speaker, that he has imbibed quite freely,
and therefore assumes a solid tone of speech.&mdash;[Or it may be merely the assurance
of one who speaks of that whereof he knows. Anthony befittingly assumes to be an
authority on things Egyptian.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>31, 32. <B>Your Serpent . . . your mud . . . your Sun . . . your Crocodile</B>] If
any student desires other instances of this idiom, common at this day, he may find

<P>35. <B>I am not so well,</B> etc.] Lepidus takes the &lquo;health&rquo; literally and replies that
he is not very well, but he will not on that account leave the circle, which is what he
means, I suppose, by &lquo;I'll ne'er out;&rquo; Enobarbus, in an <I>Aside,</I> perverts it, however,
into meaning that he will not be out of his debauch until he can sleep it off.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>39, 40. <B>Pyramisis</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: <I>Pyramis</I> for <I>pyramid</I> was in common use in our
author's time. So, in Bishop Corbet's <I>Poems,</I> 1647: &lquo;Nor need the chancellor boast,
whose <I>pyramis</I> Above the host and altar reared is.&rquo; From this word Shakspeare
formed the English plural, <I>pyramises,</I> to mark the indistinct pronunciation of a man
nearly intoxicated, whose tongue is now beginning to &lquo;split what it speaks.&rquo;&mdash;[This
suggestion of Malone, that the pronunciation &lquo;pyramises&rquo; indicates the fumes of
wine, has been silently adopted by several commentators since his day. There is not
the smallest objection to allowing Lepidus to reach the utmost limits of intoxication,
but I do not see that in the present speech he has advanced as far as Malone would
have him. First, he does not say &lquo;pyramises;&rquo; this plural form Capell unwarrantably
puts in his mouth. He says &lquo;pyramisis,&rquo; which, if he shared Bishop Corbet's appar-
ent belief that <I>pyramis</I> is an English singular, is no bad attempt to form a regular
English plural; certainly not so bad as to say that his tongue splits what it speaks.
Secondly, Shakespeare does not depend on bad spelling to add comicality to language.
All spelling in his day was too lawless. This does not apply, of course, to dialectic
words like &lquo;chill&rquo; for <I>I will,</I> and the like. If Lepidus's tongue were too &lquo;thick,&rquo; in
modern, not Shakespearian, speech, to pronounce <I>pyramides,</I> how comes it that
immediately afterward he pronounces without difficulty a word quite as hard: &lquo;contra-
diction&rquo;? Lastly, in the very speech in which C&aelig;sar says his &lquo;own tongue splits,&rquo;
</CC>

<P>50, 51, 54. <B>it owne</B>] According to <I>The Bible Word-Book</I> (Eastwood and Wright)
<I>yt</I> or <I>it</I> is used in the Folio fourteen times for <I>its;</I> <SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D. s. v.</I> Its) says
fifteen times; <I>its</I> occurs ten times, whereof five (spelled <I>it's</I>) are in <I>The Winter's Tale.</I>

I, ii, 183, of this ed. <I>Its</I> does not occur in the Authorised Version of the Bible,
1611. <I>It</I> in place of <I>its</I> occurs in <I>Levit.</I> xxv, 5, where is the same phrase as in the
present passage: &lquo;That which groweth of it owne accord;&rquo; this was changed to &lquo;its
own&rquo; in an edition of the Bible printed, according to Murray (<I>loc. cit.</I>), in 1660.
Milton, who died in 1674, does not use <I>its.</I> <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 228) says that <I>it</I> is &lquo;occasion-
ally&rquo; found for <I>its,</I> &lquo;when a child is mentioned, or when anyone is contemptuously
spoken of as a child.&rquo; If this be one of the &lquo;occasional&rquo; instances, it is not without
meaning that Anthony now uses it to Lepidus.

<P>77. <B>Hast thou drunke well</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 36, reading &lquo;Thou hast&rquo;): A sar-
castical affirmation of Pompey's; and no interrogation, as the moderns have made it,
by putting a mark after &lquo;<I>well</I>&rquo; which they did not find in the two elder Folio's; whose
only mistake, in this instance, was&mdash;a transposition of &lquo;<I>hast</I>&rquo; and &lquo;<I>thou.</I>&rquo;&mdash;[It would
not be difficult to express sarcasm by a question as well as by an affirmation, and the
text of the Folio be still preserved.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>80. <B>the Ocean pales</B>] Should any poet nowadays venture on using this verb in
connection with the ocean he would be, it is to be feared, severely criticised. But
as in the beginning of this scene we had to pardon some expressions because
uttered by servants, so here point device phrases are hardly to be expected from a
pirate.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>83. <B>Competitors</B>] The same word is used in I, iv, 5; V, i, 52; see I, i, 21.
<P>84. <B>Let me cut the Cable</B>] See Plutarch, <I>Appendix.</I>
<P>86. <B>All there is thine</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: This may mean, <I>all in the vessel.</I>&mdash;<SC>Rolfe</SC>:
&lquo;There&rquo; may be accompanied with a gesture towards the company they have left.&mdash;
[Pope's specious <I>then</I> has beguiled excellent editors. Rolfe's interpretation is, to
me, just; &lquo;there&rquo; is spoken <G>deiktikw_s.</G> (This pedantic word will, I trust, be pardoned.
I know no English word precisely equivalent; <I>demonstratively</I> comes, perhaps, the
nearest, but this could be applied to a clenched fist, to which the Greek word, with
its implied wave of the hand, would be, I think, quite inapplicable.)&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

[? oin] <I>gasquim oim hespaignol oim malvoysi,</I> that is, will you drink a quart of Gas-

<P>114. <B>strike the Vessells</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Try whether the casks sound as empty.&mdash;
<SC>Steevens</SC>: This means no more than &lquo;chink the vessels one against the other, as a
mark of our unanimity in drinking,&rquo; as we now say <I>chink glasses.</I>&mdash;<SC>Holt White</SC>:
<I>Vessels</I> probably mean <I>kettle-drums,</I> which were beaten when the health of a person
of eminence was drank; immediately after we have, &lquo;make battery to our ears with
the loud musick.&rquo; They are called <I>kettles</I> in <I>Hamlet:</I> &lquo;Give me the cups; And let
the kettle to the trumpet speak.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Boswell</SC>: In Fletcher's <I>Monsieur Thomas,</I> we
meet with a passage which leaves no doubt, as Weber has observed, that to <I>strike</I>
the vessels means to <I>tap</I> them: &lquo;Home, Launce, and strike a fresh piece of wine.&rquo;&mdash;
V, x.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>) reiterates Boswell's assertion that Weber had rightly explained
the meaning of &lquo;strike&rquo; in this line, and adds an example of its use &lquo;with the same
signification in a well-known modern poem: &ldquo;L' Avare, not using half his store,
Still grumbles that he has no more; Strikes not the present tun, for fear The vintage
should be bad next year.&rdquo; &rquo;&mdash;Prior's <I>Alma,</I> C. iii. The <SC>Cowden-Clarkes</SC> while
granting that &lquo;strike&rquo; at times means to <I>tap,</I> do not believe that it has this meaning
here, because &lquo;Antony would hardly bid them broach more wine where Pompey is
the entertainer; and, moreover, at this stage of the entertainment there would be no
question of any one giving such an order.&rquo; They, therefore, adopt Steevens's inter-
pretation. [If Shakespeare had meant that the revellers should merely <I>clink</I> the
glasses, as in Iago's song: &lquo;Let me the cannikin clink,&rquo; I doubt that he would have
used so strong a word as &lquo;strike.&rquo; As regards courtesy, Anthony was almost invited
by Pompey to call for more wine by his complaint that they had not yet reached
the height of an Alexandrian feast.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>117. <B>and it grow fouler</B>] <SC>Singer</SC> reads &lquo;<I>an</I> it grow fouler,&rquo; which, as <SC>Dyce</SC> (ed.

<P>118. <B>a Child o'th'time</B>] That is, submit like a child to the humour of the hour.
Compare Lady Macbeth's words (for I believe them to be hers) to her husband:
&lquo;Away, and mock the time with fairest show, False face must hide what the false
Heart doth know.&rquo;&mdash;I, vii, 94. Lady Macbeth and Anthony use &lquo;time&rquo; in the same
sense, that is, &lquo;the company about you.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>119. <B>Possesse it</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii, reading <I>Profess it</I> from his MS, thus ex-
plains): That is, Profess to be a child of the time, and I'll do the same. Although
the meaning of <I>Profess</I> here may not be very evident, &lquo;Possess&rquo; seems to offer no
consistent sense. In <I>King Lear,</I> I, i, we have seen the opposite error, for there
&lquo;possesses&rquo; was misprinted <I>professes.</I>&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> in his <I>Third Edition</I> returned to the
original text, &lquo;Possess,&rquo; with the brief note: &lquo;So the old copies, <I>s. q. Pass</I> it, viz.,
the cup.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Anon.</SC> (<I>Blackwood,</I> Oct. 1853, p. 467): C&aelig;sar's meaning is quite obvious;
he means, <I>Be master of it.</I> &lquo;Be a child of the time,&rquo; says Antony. &lquo;Rather be its
master, say I,&rquo; rejoins C&aelig;sar,&mdash;a sentiment much more likely to come from the lips
of the great dictator than the paltry rejoinder which [Collier's MS] puts into his
mouth&mdash;&lquo;<I>Profess it,</I>&rquo;&mdash;that is, profess to be the child of the time.&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC> (<I>Sh. Vind.</I>
291): C&aelig;sar may mean, &lquo;Possess it&rquo; rather than waste it, like a child o'the time in
drunkenness.&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: There is some ambiguity in the word &lquo;possess,&rquo; which,
if not a misprint, is employed here in a sense we are unaccustomed to; but the mean-
ing of the passage is plain enough. In former days it was the practice, when one
good fellow drank to another, for the latter to &lquo;do him right&rquo; by imbibing a quantity
of wine equal to that quaffed by the health-giver. Antony proposes a health to
C&aelig;sar, but C&aelig;sar endeavours to excuse himself, whereupon Antony urges him by
saying, &lquo;Be a child o'the time,&rquo; <I>i. e. do as others do; indulge for once.</I> C&aelig;sar then
consents to pledge the health, and says, &lquo;<I>possess</I> it,&rquo; or <I>propose</I> it,&mdash;I'll do it justice.
&mdash;<SC>Thiselton</SC> (p. 16): This simply means, &lquo;Have your wish.&rquo;&mdash;[I prefer the inter-
pretation of Anon. in <I>Blackwood</I> (who is said to have been Lettsom).&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>130. <B>The holding euery man shall beate</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: The company were to
join in the burden, which the poet styles the <I>holding.</I> But how were they to <I>beat</I>
this with their <I>sides?</I> I am persuaded the poet wrote: &lquo;The holding every man
shall <I>bear,</I> as loud As his strong sides can volley.&rquo; The breast and <I>sides</I> are immedi-
ately concerned in straining to sing as loud and forcibly as a man can. So in the
Huntsman's <I>Song</I> in <I>As You Like It,</I> we find the marginal direction: &lquo;The rest
shall bear this Burthen.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: &lquo;<I>Beat</I>&rquo; might have been the poet's word,
however harsh it may appear at present. In <I>Henry VIII.</I> we find a similar expres-
sion: &lquo;&mdash; let the musick <I>knock</I> it.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: &lquo;The holding every man shall beat.&rquo;
That is, Every man shall accompany the chorus by drumming on his sides, in token
of concurrence and applause.&mdash;[Did Dr Johnson measure every one's capacity to
drum on his sides by his own?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>&mdash;<SC>M. Mason</SC>: To <I>bear</I> the burden, or, as it is
here called, the <I>holding</I> of a song, is the phrase at this day. The passage, quoted by
Steevens, from <I>Henry VIII.</I> relates to instrumental musick, not to vocal.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>:
The meaning of <I>the holding</I> is ascertained by a passage in an old pamphlet called
<I>The Serving Man's Comfort,</I> 1598: &lquo;&mdash; where a song is to be sung the <I>under-song</I>
or <I>holding</I> whereof is, It is merrie in haul where beards wag all.&rquo;
<P>133. <B>The Song</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 36): When this play was fitted up for the stage in
the year fifty-eight by the present editor, a stanza was then added to this truly
bacchanalian song, and the song printed as follows: 1. Come, thou monarch of the
vine, Plumpy Bacchus, with pink eyne; Thine it is to cheer the soul, Made, by thy
enlarging bowl, Free from wisdom's fond controul, <I>Bur.</I> Free from &amp;c. 2. Mon-
arch, come; and with thee bring Tipsy dance, and revelling: In thy vats our cares
be drown'd; With thy grapes our hairs be crown'd; Cup us, till the world go round,
<I>Bur.</I> Cup us, &amp;c.&mdash;[When Capell warbles &lquo;Tipsy dance, and revelling,&rquo; I am afraid
he had been lately reading Milton's <I>Comus.</I>]
<P>135. <B>Plumpie</B>] <SC>Green</SC> (p. 246) believes &lquo;of a certainty&rquo; that the epithet
&lquo;plumpy&rquo; was suggested by the figures depicted in the Emblem Writers, Alciat,
Whitney, and especially in Boissard's <I>Theatrum Vit&aelig; Human&aelig;,</I> p. 213; the illus-
tration in this last book Green reproduces, and Bacchus is therein depicted as unde-
niably plump, but whether the obesity be due merely to well-nourished youth or to
convivial living, it is not easy to decide. The force of Green's argument in favour
of the Emblem Writers (and it has undeniable force), lies in his accumulation of
instances, and is not to be judged by a solitary example.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>138, 139. <B>Cup vs . . . round</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii): These last two lines, or rather
the last line and the repetition of it, are expressly called &lquo;the burden&rquo; (<I>i. e. bourdon</I>)
in the MS, and they are included in a bracket.&mdash;<SC>Dowden</SC> (p. 374): If, during this
tragic period, Shakspere retain any tendency to observe the comedy of incident in
life, the incident will be of another sort from that which moves our laughter in <I>The
Comedy of Errors.</I> It will rather be a fragment of titanic burlesque, overhung by
some impending horror, and inspired by a deep &lquo;idea of world-destruction.&rquo;<SUP>*</SUP> Such
a stupendous piece of burlesque, inspired by an idea of world-destruction, Shakspere
found in Plutarch's life of Antony. and having allowed it to dilate and take colour
in his own imagination, he transferred it to his play. Aboard Pompey's galley the
masters of the earth hold hands and dance the Egyptian bacchanals, joining in the
volleying chorus, &lquo;Cup us, till the world goes round!&rquo;; and Menas whispers his
leader to bid him cut the cable, and fall to the throats of the Triumvirs. A great
painting by Orcagna shows a terrible figure, Death, armed with the scythe, and sweep-
ing down through bright air, upon the glad and careless garden-party of noble and
beautiful persons,&mdash;men and women who lean to one another, and caress their dogs
and hawks, while they listen to the music of stringed instruments. In Shakspere's
scene of revelry, death seems to be more secretly, more intimately present, seems more
surely to dominate life; though it passes by, it passes, as it were, with an ironical
smile at the security of the possessors of this world, and at the noisy insubstantial
triumph of life, permitted for a while.

<P>140. <B>What would you more?</B>] <SC>Corson</SC> (p. 291): Every speech of Octavius in
this scene shows that, though <I>in</I> the revels, he is not <I>of</I> them. He simply endures
them as a necessary evil, for the time being. &lquo;What would you more?&rquo; shows that
he has been a reluctant but politic attendant, and is impatient to have them over.
<P>142, 143. <B>Let me request . . . Frownes at this leuitie</B>] <SC>Thiselton</SC> (p. 16):
That is, &lquo;let me request you for the sake of our graver business which frowns at this
levity.&rquo; It is better to regard this passage as supplying an instance of the suppressed
relative, than to alter &lquo;of&rquo; to <I>off,</I> and bisect the sentence.&mdash;[Does not the critic over-
look the fact that he leaves the sentence incomplete? What is it that C&aelig;sar requests?
It would be difficult, moreover, to find another example, exactly parallel to this, of
the &lquo;suppression&rquo; of a relative. I can detect none in the examples quoted by Abbott
in &sect;&sect; 244, 245, 246, on the &lquo;omission of the relative.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>the sense of &lquo;you are right and&rquo; or &lquo;yes and,&rquo; the &lquo;yes&rquo; being implied. In the pres-

<P>151. <B>you haue</B>] <SC>Pope</SC> unwarrantably changed this into &lquo;you <I>hate.</I>&rquo; Whereupon
<SC>Theobald</SC> administered to Pope a somewhat sarcastic rebuke, and then, in order to
prove that the original text is correct, &lquo;insisted,&rquo;&mdash;to quote his own words,&mdash;that there
is here an allusion to a &lquo;noted witticism&rquo; made by Pompey on the present occasion.
This witticism was founded on the fact that the splendid residence in Rome of Pom-
pey's father, at that time in the possession of Anthony, was situated on the <I>Via
Carin&aelig;</I> (&lquo;or Galley-street, as we might call it&rquo;) where even the houses themselves
were built to resemble galleys; when, therefore, Pompey said that he would enter-
tain C&aelig;sar and Anthony on his galley, there was a witty double allusion to his galley
and his house in &lquo;Galley-street.&rquo; As authorities, Theobald quoted Paterculus: &lquo;Qui
[<I>i. e.</I> Pompeius] haud absurde, cum in navi C&aelig;saremque et Antonium coena excipe-
ret, dixit, in Carinis suis se coenam dare; referens hoc dictum ad loci nomen, in quo
paterna domus ab Antonio possidebatur.&rquo;&mdash;[lib. ii, cap. lxxvii.] And also Aurelius Vic-
tor: &lquo;Pace facta, epulatus in navi cum Antonio et C&aelig;sare, non invenuste ait: <I>Hae sunt
meae carinae;</I> quia Romae in Carinis domum eius Antonius tenebat.&rquo;&mdash;[cap. lxxxiv.]
It is doubtful that even Theobald's insistence can make us believe that Shakespeare
had Pompey's &lquo;witticism&rquo; here in mind; had he ever heard it or known it, an allusion
to it would have been more appropriate in II, vi, 102, where Pompey says &lquo;Aboord
my Galley, I inuite you all.&rquo; Is it not enough that Shakespeare found in Plutarch
that Antony kept possession of Pompey's house? See <I>Appendix.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>154. <B>Take heed you fall not</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 36): Speaking to some of them (Pom-
pey, probably), whom he sees stagger: After which, the boat puts off with it's com-
pany; and Enobarbus, who has not yet had his dose, turns to Menas, and says&mdash;
&lquo;<I>Menas, I'll not on shore,</I>&rquo; and is reply'd to by Menas,&mdash;&lquo;<I>No, to my cabin.</I>&rquo; This
<I>is</I> the arrangement of the passage before us; and so palpably right, that the reader
shall not be insulted with any proofs of it: What he finds in the moderns,&mdash;or may
find, if he is so dispos'd,&mdash;took its rise from the negligent folio's.&mdash;[The <I>Text. Notes</I>
show that this arrangement of Capell is now adopted by all editors.]

<P>155. <B>these Drummes</B>] <SC>Staunton</SC> (<I>Athen&aelig;um,</I> 26 Apr. 1873), who adopts, in
common with all modern editions, the division of lines in the Var. of 1778 (see
<I>Text. Notes</I>), observes: &lquo;There is an obvious deficiency in this line. As a stop-gap,
we might read,&mdash;&ldquo;<I>Where now are</I> these drums,&rdquo; etc.&rquo; In attempting to scan these
lines, we must remember that their rhythm was not composed by Shakespeare but by

line &lquo;occurs amid regular verse.&rquo;
<P>161. <B>Exeunt</B>] <SC>Corson</SC> (p. 292): There is no other scene in all the plays of
Shakespeare, perhaps, which exhibits a more complete dramatic identification on
the part of the poet, than this banquet scene. There must have been at the time
of his writing it, the fullest sympathetic reproduction within himself, of the several
characters.&mdash;<SC>Stapfer</SC> (p. 416): Voltaire's indignation is well known at Shake-
speare's so-called tragedies which are only &lquo;farces in which the burlesque and the
horrible are united,&rquo; and in which we see &lquo;the lowest rabble appearing on the stage
by the side of princes, and princes often using the same language as the mob.&rquo;
Judgements of this kind belong to a period in which the characters of a tragedy were
merely regarded as so many lay figures, who were expected to act in a solemn and
ceremonious manner, especial care being taken that they should speak in the most
courtly style and be able to make court-curtseys; and they belong moreover to a
country in which the spirit of society and of high-bred manners has always been
peculiarly cultivated and prized, and this differs as widely from the humourous spirit
as one of our garden plants does from a foreign wild flower. These adverse opinions,
however, do not prevent the banquet on board Pompey's vessel from being a most
excellent scene, and one even more thoroughly Shakespearian perhaps than the
passages most celebrated for beauty in his plays, since in this particular kind of
humourous presentation he is not only unrivalled, but has neither follower nor fore-
runner. &lquo;Vanity of vanities, all is vanity;&rquo; what more amazing or more grotesque
commentary on this philosophical truth, which lies at the basis of the spirit of humour,

<P>1. <B>Ventidius</B>] See Plutarch, <I>Appendix.</I>
<P>1. <B>as it were in triumph</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii) opines that it is all the more needful
that the phrase, &lquo;as it were in triumph&rquo; should be retained, because &lquo;Plutarch tells us
that Ventidius was the only Roman who, up to that day, &ldquo;had triumphed of the
Parthians.&rdquo; &rquo; <SC>Delius</SC>, however, interprets (<I>Sh. Jhrb.</I> viii, 200) the phrase some-
what differently. He thinks that Shakespeare, in using this phrase, meant to indi-
cate that the comrades and subordinates of the General appeared also in the pro-
cession. In this connection Delius suggests with ingenuity that we may infer from
the somewhat fuller stage-directions in the present play, that Shakespeare was not
himself personally concerned in its performance; and that, therefore, he wrote out
the directions to the actors more explicitly.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>3. <B>darting Parthya</B>] <SC>Wordsworth</SC> cites two classical passages wherein darts are
representative of the Parthians. The first is &lquo;Miles [timet] sagittas et celerem fugam
Parthi.&rquo;&mdash;Horace, <I>Odes,</I> II, xiii. The second, &lquo;Addam . . . Fidentemque fuga Par-
thum versisque sagittis.&rquo;&mdash;Virgil, <I>Georgics,</I> iii, 31.&mdash;<SC>Deighton</SC>: A reference to the
Parthian method of fighting, their horsemen pouring in a shower of darts as they
swarmed round the enemy, and then, as they fled to avoid close combat, turning in
their saddles and discharging flights of arrows.
<P>3. <B>art thou stroke</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Alludes to &lquo;darting.&rquo; Thou whose darts have so
often struck others, art struck now thyself.

<P>&lquo;For learn this, Silius: Better &verbar; To leave undone, than by our deed acquire,&rquo; etc.
He then suggests another arrangement: &lquo;Better to leave undone, &verbar; Than by our
deed acquire too high a fame, &verbar; When him we serves away.&rquo; Whereby, disregarding
the plight in which he leaves two trimeter couplets: &lquo;May make too great an act,&rquo;
and &lquo;When him we serves away,&rquo; he has in reality accomplished nothing. He
has eliminated no discord; there is no discord to be eliminated,&mdash;the lines are
rhythmical howsoever they are divided. Unless the lines are uttered in the veriest
sing-song, no ear can detect how or where they are divided. I cannot doubt that
had Walker lived to revise his work, he would have omitted much that was merely
the passing fancy of the moment. Yet <SC>Dyce</SC>, who is extremely chary of notes, reprints
in full these suggestions of Walker. <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 498) observes: &lquo;We might arrange
&ldquo;Better l&egrave;ave &verbar; und&ograve;ne, &verbar; than b&ygrave; &verbar; our d&egrave;ed &verbar; acqu&igrave;re.&rdquo; Or [line 18] might be
(but there is not pause enough to make it probable) a trimeter couplet.&rquo; Lastly,
<SC>Wordsworth</SC> amends and divides: &lquo;For learn, 'tis better &verbar; To leave undone, than
by our deed acquire &verbar; Too high a fame when him we serve's away.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>19. <B>when him we serues away</B>] For other examples of &lquo;him&rquo; used for <I>he,</I> by
attraction to <I>whom</I> understood, see, if need be, <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 208.
<P>21. <B>More in their officer, then person</B>] It is possible that in the final <I>n</I> of
&lquo;then&rquo; there is an absorption of <I>in:</I> &lquo;then&rquo; person.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>24. <B>by'th'minute</B>] <SC>Deighton</SC>: That is, each minute.
<P>28. <B>which darkens him</B>] After &lquo;him,&rquo; <SC>Keightley</SC> marks an omission, as of an

<P><SC>ton</SC>: &lquo;Grant,&rquo; for <I>afford.</I> The sense is this: &lquo;Thou hast that, Ventidius, which if
thou didst want, there would be no distinction between thee and thy sword. You
would be both equally cutting and senseless.&rquo; This was wisdom or knowledge of
the world. Ventidius had told him the reasons why he did not pursue his advan-
tages; and his friend, by this compliment, acknowledges them to be of weight.&mdash;
<SC>Capell</SC> (i, 36): Meaning&mdash;wisdom or knowledge of the world: &lquo;without which,&rquo;
the soldier affords scarcely anything to distinguish him from his sword; the sword,
in that case, doing nearly as much service, and being of equal value with himself.
This maxim, and others with which the scene is embellish'd, are form'd out of very
slight hints the Poet found in his Plutarch; which, if they are turn'd to, will shew
with how sharp a judgment he look'd into the authors he dealt with. [See <I>Ap-
pendix.</I>]
<P>39. <B>iaded</B>] <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>): That is, to treat like a jade, to spurn, to kick.
<P>41-43. <B>He purposeth . . . passe along</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 300): Arrange,
perhaps:&mdash;&lquo;He purposeth &verbar; To Athens; whither with what haste the weight &verbar; We
must convey with's will permit, we shall &verbar; Appear before him,&mdash;On, there; pass
along.&rquo;
<P>42. <B>with's</B>,] <SC>Thiselton</SC> (p. 17): The Folio punctuation is here quite in con-
sonance with Elizabethan usage, the comma after &lquo;with's&rquo; marking the end of the
relative clause.

<P>14. <B>thou Arabian Bird</B>] &lquo;There is another sacred bird, called the ph&oelig;nix, which
I myself have seen only in a picture; for, as the citizens of Helios say, it visits them
only periodically, every five hundred years; they state that it always comes on the
death of its sire. If it at all resembles its picture, it is thus and so: some of its
feathers are golden-hued, and some are red; in shape and figure it most resembles
the eagle and in size also. They say, but I cannot credit it, that this bird contrives
to bring from Arabia to the temple of Helios the body of its father plastered up in
myrrh, and there buries it. The mode of carrying it is as follows:&mdash;first, he plasters
together an egg of myrrh as large as he is able to carry, after he has tested his
strength by carrying it; this trial having been made, he hollows out the egg suf-
ficiently to place his father within, then with fresh myrrh he fills up the space
unoccupied by his father's body: the egg thereby becomes of the same weight as
before, and thus plastered up he transports it to Egypt to the temple of Helios. Such
things, they say, this bird can accomplish.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Herodotus,</I> Lib. ii, cap. 73.

<P>18-20. <B>Hearts, . . . number</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Not only the tautology of &lquo;bards&rquo; and
&lquo;poets,&rquo; but the want of a correspondent action for the &lquo;poet,&rquo; whose business in the
next line is only to &lquo;number,&rquo; makes me suspect some fault in this passage, which I
know not how to mend.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: I suspect no fault. The ancient <I>bard</I> sung
his compositions to the harp; the <I>poet</I> only commits them to paper. Verses are often
called <I>numbers,</I> and to &lquo;number,&rquo; a verb (in this sense) of Shakspeare's coining, is
<I>to make verses.</I> This puerile arrangement of words was much studied in the age of
Shakspeare, even by the first writers. So, in <I>An Excellent Sonnet of a Nimph,</I> by
Sir P. Sidney; printed in <I>England's Helicon,</I> 1600:

<P>33. <B>peece of Vertue</B>] This phrase bears a double meaning; &lquo;piece&rquo; may mean a

the better meaning here, as it is also in <I>The Tempest,</I> &lquo;Thy Mother was a peece of
vertue.&rquo;&mdash;I, ii, 69.

<P>47. <B>The Elements be kind to thee</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: This is obscure. Its seems to

means only, &lquo;May the four elements of which this world is composed, unite their
influences to make thee cheerful.&rquo; [Or it] may, indeed, mean no more than the
common compliment which the occasion of her voyage very naturally required. He
wishes &lquo;that serene weather and prosperous winds may keep her spirits free from
every apprehension that might disturb or alarm them.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>M. Mason</SC>: Octavia was
about to make a long journey both by <I>land</I> and by <I>water.</I> Her brother wishes that
both these elements may prove kind to her; and this is all.&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: There is
a passage, altogether forgotten by the commentators, in <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.</I> V, v, which is
entirely confirmatory of Dr Johnson's interpretation: &lquo;His life was gentle; and <I>the
elements</I> So mix'd in him, that Nature might stand up, And say to all the world, <I>This
was a man!</I>&rquo;&mdash;[It seems useless to contend over the meaning of &lquo;Elements&rquo; in this
sentence; its meaning must be determined by the context. &lquo;The elements&rquo; mean,
in general, earth, water, air, and fire, and of these man is supposed to be composed;
&lquo;the due proportion and commixture whereof in his composition,&rquo; says <SC>Nares</SC> (<I>s. v.</I>
Elements) &lquo;were what produced in him every kind of perfection, mental and bodily.&rquo;
Thus Cleopatra says, &lquo;I am Fire, and Ayre; my other Elements [<I>i. e.</I> earth and
water] I give to baser life.&rquo;&mdash;V, ii, 341. Sir Toby Belch asks, &lquo;Does not our liues
consist of the foure elements?&rquo;&mdash;<I>Twelfth Night,</I> II, iii, 11. Or as Anthony in the
present play says of the Crocodile, &lquo;the elements once out of it, it Transmigrates.&rquo;&mdash;
II, vii, 52. The four elements may also exist external to man, and when used in the
singular, &lquo;the element&rquo; may mean the <I>air</I> or the <I>sky,</I> as in <I>Twelfth Night,</I> where
Valentine says of Olivia, &lquo;The Element itselfe, till seuen yeares heate, Shall not

<P>behold her face.&rquo;&mdash;I, i, 31. Again, where Viola says to Olivia, &lquo;O you should not
rest Betweene the elements of ayre, and earth,&rquo; etc. Or &lquo;the element&rquo; may mean
<I>water,</I> as where the Queen in <I>Hamlet</I> says of Ophelia, when fallen in &lquo;the weeping
brook,&rquo; that she was &lquo;like a creature native and indued Unto that element.&rquo;&mdash;IV,
vii, 180. It is, therefore, quite possible in the present passage that &lquo;the elements&rquo;
may mean either those which are external to man or those of which he is composed.
If the former, then C&aelig;sar means no more than &lquo;may you have a comfortable journey&rquo;;
an objection to this meaning is that a comfortable journey does not of necessity
create cheerful spirits; there is the well-known line &lquo;C&aelig;lum non animum mutant,&rquo;
etc., which suggests a sorrow ever-present, however comfortable the voyage. If
by &lquo;the elements&rquo; C&aelig;sar means those of which Octavia's nature is composed, then
Johnson's interpretation is just, and it would be presumptuous to attempt to better
his paraphrase.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>but are not an illustration of them, but of a reflection that was then springing up upon
the state of Octavia's heart; divided between love to her brother and love to him,
and unable to give the preference to either.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC>: Very delicate imagery, but

between her brother and her husband, so that she cannot tell which she loves most.
&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC> refers to a similar image in <I>2 Henry IV:</I> II, iii, 63: &lquo;As with the tide

<P>62. <B>were he a Horse</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: A horse is said to have &lquo;a cloud in his face,&rquo;
when he has a black or dark-coloured spot in his forehead between his eyes. This
gives him a sour look, and being supposed to indicate an ill-temper, is of course
regarded as a great blemish. The same phrase occurs in Burton's <I>Anatomy of
Melancholy,</I> &lquo;Every lover admires his mistress, though she be very deformed of her
self . . . thin, lean, chitty face, have clouds in her face, be crooked,&rquo; etc.&mdash;[p. 519,
ed. 1651.]&mdash;<SC>R. G. White</SC>: An allusion to the dislike horse-fanciers have to white
marks or other discolorations in the face of that animal.&mdash;<SC>Madden</SC> (p. 255): Eno-
barbus' grim jest would have prospered better in the ear of a Smithfield horse-courser
than it has fared with some of the critics. The horse-courser could have told [Mr
Grant White] that the words meant the exact opposite [to what he has said they
mean]. The horse with a cloud in his face was one with no white star. Fitz-
herbert, in his <I>Boke of Husbandrie,</I> commends the white star. &lquo;It is an excel-
lent good marke also for a horse to have a white star in his forehead. The horse
that hath no white at all upon him is furious, dogged, full of mischiefe and mis-
fortune.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Cavalarice,</I> G. Markham. . . . In the common language of the stable such
a horse was said to have a cloud in his face. <I>Equus nebula</I> (<I>ut vulgo dicitur</I>) <I>in
facie, cujus vultus tristis est et melancholicus, jure vituperatur,</I> says the learned
Sadlerius in his work, <I>De procreandis,</I> etc., <I>equis,</I> 1587. From Sadler's words <I>ut
vulgo dicitur,</I> the expression &lquo;cloud in the face&rquo; seems to have been in general use.
Those who had not Shakespeare's intimate knowledge of the language of the stable
probably used it without any clear idea of its meaning, as Burton may have done
when he wrote [the passage quoted by Steevens].

<P>68. <B>he was</B>] This is one of the examples furnished by <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> ii, 203),
illustrating his observation that &lquo;<I>Thou wert, you were, I was,</I> etc. occur frequently

<P>68. The <I>Text. Notes</I> show a remarkable number of <I>vari&aelig; lectiones</I> within twenty
or thirty lines, in <SC>Staunton's</SC> <I>Photolithograph.</I> There can be no question that this
reproduction faithfully sets forth its original, which could be at once pronounced one
of the very earliest, if not the earliest, copy to leave the press, were it not that Staun-
ton had two copies to print from: the copy in Bridgewater House and that in the
National Library, and we do not know to which copy this page belongs.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>70. <B>till I weepe too</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: I have ventur'd to alter the tense of the verb
here, against the authority of all the copies. There was no sense in it, I think, as it
stood before. Enobarbus would say, &lquo;Indeed, Antony seem'd very free of his tears
that year; and, believe me, bewail'd all the mischief he did, till I myself wept too.&rquo;
This appears to me very sarcastical. Antony's tears, he would infer, were dissembled;
but Enobarbus wept in real compassion of the havock and slaughter committed on
his countrymen.&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC> (i, 37): Which he thought would be never: so that, tak-
ing them thus, the words are only a fresh and more positive assertion of what he had
been saying before. <I>Wept</I> (a word adopted by two modern editors) can not be
allow'd of; the sense which that would convey, being a manifest violation of
character.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: I am afraid there was better sense in this passage as it origi-
nally stood, than Theobald's alteration will afford us. &lquo;Believe it (says Enobar-
bus), that Antony did so, <I>i. e.</I> that he wept over such an event, till you see me weep-
ing on the same occasion, when I shall be obliged to you for putting such a con-
struction on my tears, which, in reality (like his), will be tears of joy.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>M. Mason</SC>:
I should certainly adopt Theobald's amendment, the meaning of which is, that
Antony wailed the death of Brutus so bitterly, that I [Enobarbus] was affected by
it, and wept also. Steevens's explanation of the present reading is so forced, that I
cannot clearly comprehend it.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC>: Steevens and Capell vainly endeavour to

<P>4. <B>Go too, go too</B>] <SC>Wordsworth</SC> (p. 341): I have ventured to alter the com-
mon text into &lquo;Go to him, go,&rquo; because the former, which is &lquo;a phrase of exhortation
or reproof&rquo; (Schm. &lquo;Lex.&rquo;), does not appear to give the meaning here required;
unless indeed we can suppose it to signify,&mdash;&lquo;Don't tell me of his being afeard. I
insist upon seeing him;&rquo; which puts at least an awkward strain upon the words.
&mdash;<SC>Deighton</SC> excellently paraphrases it as &lquo;nonsense, nonsense.&rquo;
<P>5. <B>the Messenger</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii): He is again called Elis in the MS. [See
II, v, 29.]&mdash;<SC>Mrs Jameson</SC> (p. 140): The man is afterwards brought back, almost
by force, to satisfy Cleopatra's jealous anxiety, by a description of Octavia:&mdash;but this
time, made wise by experience, he takes care to adapt his information to the humours
of his imperious mistress, and gives her a satirical picture of her rival. The scene
which follows, in which Cleopatra&mdash;artful, acute, and penetrating as she is&mdash;becomes
the dupe of her feminine spite and jealousy, nay, assists in duping herself; and after
having cuffed the messenger for telling her truths which are offensive, rewards him
for the falsehood which flatters her weakness&mdash;is not only an admirable exhibition
of character, but a fine moral lesson.
<P>6. <B>Herod of Iury</B>] See I, ii, 31. Alexas refers to the ferocious tyrant of the old
mystery plays; Cleopatra's thoughts wander to the living Herod.

<P>12. <B>Did'st thou behold Octauia?</B>] <SC>Saint-Marc Girardin</SC> (iv, 403): The
scene which follows is comical, but of a vulgar comicality. Cleopatra exhibits the
unrest and curiosity of a rival; she shows none of that confidence in herself which
constituted an element of her power.
<P>17. <B>as tall as me</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 210): Probably &lquo;as&rquo; was used with a quasi-prepo-
sitional force.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC> here refers to Melvil's <I>Memoirs</I> (see II, v, 143) and <SC>Rit-
son</SC> shows, by the date of the publication of these <I>Memoirs,</I> how extremely improbable
it is that there can be here any allusion to Queen Elizabeth's interview with Melvil,
and concludes his note with the remark that &lquo;such enquiries [as Elizabeth put to
Melvil concerning the personal appearance of the Queen of Scots] are, no doubt,
perfectly natural to rival females, whether queens or cinder-wenches.&rquo;
<P>20. <B>shrill tongu'd</B>] <SC>Thiselton</SC> (p. 17): Cleopatra is evidently wishing to com-
pare Octavia with &lquo;shrill-tongu'd Fulvia.&rquo; See I, i, 45.
<P>22. <B>That's not so good: he cannot like her long</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: Cleopatra per-
haps does not mean&mdash;&lquo;That is not so good a piece of intelligence as your last;&rquo; but,
&lquo;<I>That, i. e.</I> a low voice, is not so good as a shrill tongue.&rquo; That a low voice (on
which our author never omits to introduce an eulogium when he has an opportunity)
was not esteemed by Cleopatra as a merit appears from what she adds afterwards,
&mdash;&lquo;<I>Dull of tongue,</I> and dwarfish!&rquo; Perhaps the author intended no connection
between the two members of this line; and that Cleopatra, after a pause, should
exclaim&mdash;&lquo;He cannot like her, whatever her merits may be, for any length of time.&rquo;

thoughts. The description given of her by a contemporary, about twelve years after
her death, strongly confirms this supposition. &lquo;She was (says the Continuator of
Stowe's <I>Chronicle</I>) <I>tall of stature,</I> strong in every limb and joynt, her fingers small
and long, her <I>voyce loud and shrill.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: It may be remarked, however, that

latter part of the line is not at all consequent on what has just been said, but expresses
the secret anxiety of the woman by her emphasis in uttering it. It would be better,
perhaps, to print it as a separate sentence.&mdash;[This last interpretation is, to me, the
true one. Cleopatra was thinking of herself, not of any quality of voice, and was,

<P>45. <B>forehead</B>] <SC>Nares</SC> (<I>s. v.</I> Forehead): A high forehead was formerly accounted
a great beauty, and a low one a proportionable deformity; so completely has taste
changed in this respect. &lquo;Her eyes are grey as glass, and so are mine; Ay, but <I>her
forehead's low</I> and <I>mine's as high.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<I>Two Gent.</I> IV, iv, 197. &lquo;For this is handsome-
ness, this that draws us Body and bones; Oh, <I>what a mounted forehead,</I> What eyes
and lips, what every thing about her.&rquo;&mdash;Beaumont and Fletcher's <I>Mons. Thomas,</I> I, i.
&lquo;Her iuorie <I>forhead,</I> full of bountie braue, <I>Like a broad table</I> did it selfe dispred,
For Loue his loftie triumphes to engraue, And write the battels of his great godhed.&rquo;
&mdash;Spenser, <I>Faerie Queene,</I> II, iii, 213. This is part of the description of a perfect
ideal beauty:&mdash;&lquo;Her <I>forehead smooth, full, polish'd, bright,</I> and <I>high,</I> Bears in itself
a graceful majesty.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Witts Recreations,</I> sign. V 2, b. Thus also Sir Philip Sidney
describes the beautiful Parthenia:&mdash;&lquo;For her great gray eye, which might seeme full
of her own beauty; <I>a large, and exceedingly faire forehead,</I> with all the rest of her
face and body, cast in the mould of noblenesse, was yet attired,&rquo; etc.&mdash;Book i, p. 59.
A lady jocularly setting forth her own beauty, enumerates, &lquo;True complexion If it be
red and white, a <I>forehead high.</I>&rquo;&mdash;Beaumont and Fletcher's <I>Woman Hater,</I> III, i.
Cleopatra, when full of jealousy, is delighted to find that her rival has a <I>low forehead.</I>
[The phrase], as low &lquo;as she would wish it&rquo; is said ironically, for much lower. The
dialogue would be improved a little in spirit, if we might read it thus: &lquo;<I>Mess.</I> Brown,
Madam. <I>Cleop.</I> And her <I>forehead?</I> &verbar; <I>Mess. As low as she could wish it.</I>&rquo; A <I>low fore-
head</I> is humorously mentioned as the most striking deformity of apes:&mdash;&lquo;And all be
turn'd to barnacles, or to apes, With <I>foreheads villainous low.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<I>Tempest,</I> IV, i.

<P>In Kemble's Acting Copy this scene follows and continues the next scene, Scene v,
which is then transposed so as to follow Scene ii. Scene vii closes Act II.
<P>5. <B>New Warres</B>] <SC>Deighton</SC>: That is, contrary to the agreement between us,
and without asking my assent.
<P>5. <B>Made his will,</B> etc.] According to Plutarch (see <I>Appendix</I>), it was Antony's
Will which C&aelig;sar removed from the custody of the Vestal nuns; after reading it him-
self and noting &lquo;certain places worthy of reproach,&rquo; C&aelig;sar &lquo;assembled all the Senate
and read it before them all. Whereupon divers were marvellously offended.&rquo; Of
course there is some corruption in the text. Anthony could have no possible cause
of complaint if C&aelig;sar chose to make his own Will and read it in public. The cor-
ruption lies in the words &lquo;made his&rquo; for which he who lists may easily substitute any
words that will make the text conform to Plutarch.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>5, 6. <B>will, . . . it, . . . of me,</B>] <SC>Thiselton</SC> (p. 17) calls attention to these commas
as indications of the &lquo;impetuosity of Antony's utterance.&rquo; It is possible that Thisel-
ton is right, but at the same time we must remember that no great dependence is
to be placed on the punctuation of the Folio, which is somewhat remote from any
authoritative contact with Shakespeare's own hand.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>6. <B>scantly</B>] That is, slightingly.

then&rquo; into &lquo;vented <I>them,</I>&rquo; have been unanimously adopted by all succeeding editors.

<P>Tolerable sense can be made even in the present text, with its present punctuation,
until we come to the colon after &lquo;measure,&rquo; which leaves &lquo;lent me&rquo; inexplicable, unless
we suppose that it bears a meaning unknown elsewhere. <SC>Knight</SC> alone, among edi-
tors, retains the colon after &lquo;giuen him.&rquo; In Booth's <I>Reprint</I> there is a semi-colon
after &lquo;measure,&rquo; not a colon, as in my copy of F<SUB>1</SUB>.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>10. <B>he not look't</B>] <SC>Thirlby's</SC> emendation, &lquo;he not <I>took't,</I>&rquo; which has been adopted
by nearly all editors, is to be found, without comment, in Nichols (<I>Illust.</I> ii, 228). It
means, of course, that Anthony did not take the &lquo;best hint,&rquo; and receives some con-
firmation, albeit very slight, from the spelling in the Folio, where the apostrophe in
&lquo;look't,&rquo; as an abbreviation of <I>looked,</I> is somewhat unusual. <SC>Knight</SC> and <SC>Collier</SC>
(ed. ii) are the only modern editors who adhere to the Folio. The former does not
believe that the &lquo;best hint&rquo; is here referred to, but &lquo;on the contrary&rquo; he says, &lquo;although
it was hinted to C&aelig;sar when speaking that he should mention Antony with terms of
honour, he lent him most narrow measure&mdash;cold and sickly. His demeanour is
then more particularly described. He <I>looked</I> not upon the people as one who is
addressing them with sincerity&mdash;he <I>spoke</I> from his teeth, and not with the full utter-
ance of the heart.&rquo; <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii) retained <I>look't</I> because, I suppose, it had not
been changed by his MS corrector, who had, however, changed &lquo;not look't&rquo; to &lquo;<I>but</I>
look't,&rquo;&mdash;an emendation which Collier did not adopt, because he doubted &lquo;if there
were any confusion here, for what Antony means to say is apparent enough as the text
stands: C&aelig;sar would not look to avoid taking the least hint, or if he did look, and took
the hint, his praise was superficial and insincere.&rquo; On this reading of Collier's MS Cor-
rector, <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Notes,</I> p. 153) remarks that &lquo;it has not only great obscurity of expres-
sion, but is also unsuited to what immediately follows: &ldquo;he but look'd, <SC>Or</SC> did it from
his teeth.&rdquo; I have little doubt,&rquo; he adds, &lquo;that Thirlby's much simpler emendation
(<I>which alters only a single letter</I>) restores the genuine reading.&rquo; Later, in his edition,
Dyce is more emphatic and pronounces the emendation of Collier's MS &lquo;little better
than nonsense.&rquo; Later still, in his <I>Strictures</I> (p. 205) he criticises not the emendation
of Collier's MS, but Collier himself for following the Folio. &lquo;What,&rquo; he asks, &lquo;could
induce Mr Collier to adopt here, in his new edition, the ridiculous reading of the
folio, which admits of nothing but a ridiculous explanation?&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Anon.</SC> (<I>Blackwood,</I>
Oct. 1853, p. 467; supposed to be <SC>Lettsom</SC>): &lquo;We may be pretty sure that
[Thirlby's emendation] is the right reading, as it is assuredly the only one which
makes sense.&rquo;&mdash;[Thirlby's change is so trifling, while the gain is so marked, that I
think it may be adopted without heinous disloyalty to the Folio.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>16, 17. <B>Praying . . . presently</B>] It is &lquo;infinitely distressing&rquo; (as Sydney Smith
would say) to note the attempts which have been here made to amend what is deemed
the defective metre of these two fragmentary lines. That the emotion of the speaker
should have here any influence is not to be for a moment considered; in all circum-
stances Shakespeare should be made to know that lines must have five feet, and to
attain this end his words are to be at will lengthened, or compressed, or even omitted
altogether. <SC>Rowe</SC> and his followers read as one line, &lquo;Praying for both parts: the
good Gods will mock me,&rquo; and omit &lquo;presently.&rquo; <SC>Steevens</SC>, in 1778, runs the two
lines into an interminable one of fourteen syllables, and is followed in the union
of the lines by <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 301), who, however, reduces the number of sylla-
bles by omitting &lquo;good,&rquo; and by reading (can it be conceived?) &lquo;praying&rquo; as a
monosyllable! (I had rather be a pagan, suckled in a prose outworn, than think
heaven could be moved by <I>pra'ng.</I>) In 1793, Steevens reverts to the division of the
Folio, but pieces out the second line with an <I>and,</I> &lquo;<I>And</I> the good Gods,&rquo; etc. <SC>Dyce</SC>
follows Steevens, but rejects his <I>and,</I> and substitutes instead, &lquo;<I>Sure</I> the good Gods,&rquo;
etc. Finally, <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 484), retaining the division of the Folio, refuses both
Steevens's <I>and</I> and Dyce's <I>sure,</I> and beautifully counteracts Walker's irreverent
<I>pra'ng</I> by a pious prolongation of &lquo;good&rquo;: &lquo;The <I>g&oacute;</I> &verbar; <I>od</I> g&oacute;ds &verbar; will m&oacute;ck &verbar; me pr&eacute;s &verbar;
entl&yacute;.&rquo; The &lquo;vnhappie Lady's&rquo; broken heart and broken speech are all forgotten.
&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>30. <B>Shall staine your Brother</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: But, sure, Antony, whose business
here is to mollify Octavia, does it with a very ill grace: and 'tis a very odd way of
satisfying her, to tell her the war, he raises, shall &lquo;stain,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> cast an odium upon her
brother. I have no doubt, but we must read, with the addition only of a single letter
&mdash;&lquo;Shall <I>strain</I> your brother;&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> shall lay him under constraints; shall put him
to such shifts, that he shall neither be able to make a progress against, or to preju-
dice me. Plutarch says, that Octavius, understanding the sudden and wonderful
preparations of Antony, was astonished at it; for he himself was in many wants, and
the people were sorely oppressed with grievous exactions.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: I do not see
but &lquo;stain&rquo; may be allowed to remain unaltered, meaning no more than <I>shame</I> or
<I>disgrace.</I>&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: So, in some anonymous stanzas among the poems of Surrey
and Wyatt: &lquo;here at hand approacheth one Whose face will <I>stain</I> you all.&rquo; Again,
in <I>Shore's Wife,</I> by Churchyard, 1593: &lquo;So Shore's wife's face made foule Browneta
blush, As pearle <I>staynes</I> pitch, or gold surmounts a rush.&rquo; Again, in Churchyard's
<I>Charitie,</I> 1595: &lquo;Whose beautie <I>staines</I> the faire Helen of Greece.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: I
believe a line betwixt these two has been lost, the purport of which probably was,
&lquo;unless I am compelled in my own defence, I will do no act that <I>shall stain,</I>&rquo; etc.
After Antony has told Octavia that she shall be a mediatrix between him and his
adversary, it is surely strange to add that he will do an act that shall disgrace her
brother.&mdash;<SC>Rann</SC> ingeniously reads '<I>stain,</I> and explains it as standing for <I>sustain,</I> that
is, &lquo;in defence of him.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Boswell</SC>: Perhaps we should read: &lquo;Shall <I>stay</I> your
brother;&rquo; shall check and make him pause in his hostile designs.&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC>: To
&lquo;stain&rquo; is not here used for to shame, or disgrace, as Johnson supposed; but for to
eclipse, extinguish, throw into the shade, to put out; from the Old French <I>esteindre.</I>
In this sense it is used in all the examples quoted by Steevens.&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC> agrees
with Singer as to the meaning of &lquo;stain,&rquo; but adds that &lquo;<I>stay,</I> suggested by Boswell,
is more accordant with the context, and may easily have been misprinted &ldquo;stain.&rdquo;&rquo;
&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. i): If &lquo;stain&rquo; be right, it is equivalent to&mdash;<I>throw into the shade;</I> in
which sense the word was formerly very common; <I>e. g.</I> &lquo;She stains the ripest virgins
of the age.&rquo;&mdash;Beaumont and Fletcher's <I>Cupid's Revenge,</I> II, ii; &lquo;I saw sixe gallant

show beside C&aelig;sar's that it will overpoweringly eclipse it or stain it, as also that it

would be to evoke thoughts of peace, and not of somewhat excusable anger, Dr
Nicholson's interpretation would be faultless and carry conviction. Unfortunately,
however, prognostication is here doubtful, and &lquo;stain&rquo; cannot but convey a meaning
which is, to say the least, uncomfortable. Hence the struggles of the critics to soften
it. But is there any need of softening it? Be it as offensive as it will, it still remains
the word of the text. Anthony's bearing towards Octavia is not deferential&mdash;hardly
gentle. When he enters he is irritably dissenting from her, and we can see that he
is providing for the speedy desertion of her, for which we were prepared, in the first
hours after he was married, by his resolve to go to Egypt; where his pleasure lay.&mdash;
II, iii, 43.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>8. <B>presently</B>] <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>) includes this &lquo;presently&rquo; in his list of examples
meaning not <I>immediately,</I> but <I>shortly.</I> Of course, the decision will largely depend
on our estimate of C&aelig;sar's character. I prefer to think that C&aelig;sar acted with his
accustomed promptitude, and, as soon as Lepidus ceased to be of any use to him,
instantly deposed him. In <I>Rich. III:</I> IV, ii, 26, there is a striking instance of
the use of &lquo;presently&rquo; in the sense of <I>immediately,</I> where we should assuredly expect
the meaning <I>shortly:</I> Richard demands an immediate consent of Buckingham to the
murder of the two young princes; Buckingham pleads for delay, for &lquo;some breath,
some little pause&rquo; and concludes with the promise &lquo;I will resolve you herein pres-
ently.&rquo; Assuredly, this can mean nothing else but <I>shortly,</I> and yet the Qq, which a
majority of the editors believe have preserved the purer text, read &lquo;immediately.&rquo;
&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>14, 15. <B>they'le grinde the other</B>] In referring to the emendation, &lquo;they'll grind
<I>the one</I> the other,&rquo; <SC>Lettsom</SC> (Walker, <I>Crit.</I> ii, 259, <I>footnote</I>) observes that it &lquo;seems
to be the joint property of Capell and Johnson.&rquo; Johnson assuredly proposed it in
his edition published in 1765. Capell's edition (in which the emendation appears
in the text printed in black letter as an indication that it is not in the original)
is undated, but his Preface is dated 1767; and in a note on p. 18 of his <I>Intro-
duction,</I> he gives the dates at which his volumes went irregularly to the press: &lquo;the
first sheet of this work,&rquo; he says, &lquo;(being the first of volume 2) went to the press in
September, 1760: and this volume was follow'd by volume 8 [the volume contain-
ing the present play], 4, 9, 1, 6, and 7; the last of which was printed off in August,
1765.&rquo; Guided by this note, I have hitherto uni$ormly assumed that vol. 8 was
printed in 1761, four years before Johnson's edition. But Capell nowhere says that
his volumes were issued in the years they were printed; hence, for aught we can
tell, they may have all appeared on the same day in 1766 or 1767, a full year lag of
Johnson's. The fact, therefore, appears to be that, as regards the present emen-
dation, to Capell belongs the priority of devising and of printing, and to Johnson
the priority of publication, and it is publication that confers the prize and decides the
ownership. Unfortunately for both critics, however, it is to be feared that their claims
may be somewhat shorn of their glory. Heath's <I>Revisal of Shakespeare's Text</I>
appeared in 1765, before either Johnson's edition or Capell's,&mdash;both refer to it. On
p. 458, Heath remarks that there seemed to be an error in the present phrase which
&lquo;may be thus corrected, &ldquo;They'll grind <I>one</I> th' other,&rdquo;&rquo; which certainly contains the
germ, afterwards expanded by both Capell and Johnson into &lquo;<I>the one</I> the other;&rquo;

<P>their &lquo;joint property&rquo; turns out, therefore, to be the priceless asset of the definite

<P>16. <B>in the garden thus</B>] Wherever in Capell's text there appears a dagger
inserted between words or phrases, it is an indication of some action to be taken by
the speaker. For instance, where Cleopatra says to the Messenger, &lquo;there is gold,
and here My bluest veins to kiss,&rquo; the lines thus appear in Capell's text: &lquo;there is &dagger;
gold and here &dagger; My bluest veins to kiss,&rquo; indicating that Cleopatra extends one hand
with gold and the other to be kissed; it would be truly deplorable were an actress to
suppose that Egypt's queen uses her feet on this occasion, and against this easy error
Capell kindly does all he can to protect her. In the present line, after &lquo;garden&rquo;
Capell unsheaths a dagger, which means, I suppose, that Eros imitates Anthony's
impatient strides. Here the little dagger is not too intrusive, albeit the end would
have been gained by a dash, which <SC>Steevens</SC>, possibly taking the hint from Capell,
adopted, and has been followed herein by all editors ever since.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>21. <B>more Domitius</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: I have something more to tell you, which I
might have told at first and delayed my news. Antony requires your presence.&mdash;
[In a note on &lquo;Conlord,&rquo; II, vii, 6, I stated that the ignorant haphazard guesses of
George Gould would possibly cumber these pages no more. If anything be needed
to justify this decision, a note on &lquo;Domitius&rquo; by that critic will supply it. It is as
follows: &lquo;This is a curious misrendering of manuscript, as there are only Eros and
Enobarbus, whom he is addressing, on the scene, and as there is no Domitius in the
play. Eros simply tells Enobarbus that Antony is waiting for him.&rquo; There is no
need to moralise the spectacle of attempts to amend the language of Shakespeare by
one who has not even read over the <I>Dramatis Person&aelig;</I> in any common edition. As
far as George Gould is concerned, in these pages, the rest is silence.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>24. <B>'Twillbe naught</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 38): This has no relation to Eros' last words,
but means,&mdash;the event will be naught; and is spoke with a look of much thought-
fulness, and after a silence of some length.

<P>2, 3. <B>Contemning Rome . . . of't</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 38): The punctuation of former
editions, old and new, sets this line and the next in a light that is not true, the truth
of it being as follows. C&aelig;sar enters in converse with some to whom he has been
giving various instances of Antony's ill behaviour, and goes on to another and greater
that happen'd at Alexandria; and, in ent'ring upon it, puts into their hands the dis-
patch he receiv'd it by.&mdash;[Of Capell's punctuation of this passage no note appears to
have ever been taken; possibly because, being a matter of Capell's individual prefer-
ence, it is impossible to gainsay it. It is like Henderson's reading &lquo;many a time,&mdash;
and oft on the Rialto.&rquo; Capell thus reads: &lquo;Contemning Rome, he has done all this:
And more; &verbar; In Alexandria,&mdash;here's the manner of it,&mdash; &verbar; I'the market-place,&rquo; etc.
(In Capell's version, which he made for Garrick, the lines read: &lquo;Contemning Rome,
he <I>did</I> all this: And <I>once,</I> &verbar; In Alexandria,&mdash;here's the manner of it,&rquo; etc.) Surely
this punctuation has much to commend it.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>7. <B>my Fathers Sonne</B>] Julius C&aelig;sar was the great uncle of Octavius. That he
is here called his &lquo;father&rquo; is, possibly, due to a passage in Plutarch's <I>Life of Brutus</I>
(p. 1063, ed. 1595; p. 123, ed. Skeat) where we find that Octavius C&aelig;sar &lquo;was the
sonne of lulius C&aelig;sars Nece, whom he had adopted for his sonne, and made his
heire, by his last will and testament. But when Iulius C&aelig;sar his adopted father
was slaine, he was,&rquo; etc. At the first glance, it seems as though there were here two
separate legal acts: an adoption as a son and the making of an heir; in reality there
was but one. It was only by C&aelig;sar's Will that Octavius became an adopted son,
and this was evidently so unusual and doubtful a process that Octavius afterward had
the adoption confirmed by the curi&aelig;. &lquo;The phrase of &ldquo;adoption by testament&rdquo;
(Cic. <I>Brutus,</I> 58) seems,&rquo; says Prof. <SC>George Long</SC> (Smith's <I>Dict. Greek and Roman
Antiquities,</I> s. v. <I>Adoptio</I>) &lquo;to be rather a misapplication of the term; for though a

<P>man or woman might by testament name a heres, and impose the condition of the
heres taking the name of the testator or testatrix, this so-called adoption could not
produce the effects of a proper adoption. It could give to the person so said to be
adopted, the name or property of the testator or testatrix, but nothing more. Niebuhr
(<I>Lectures,</I> vol. ii, p. 100) speaks of the testamentary adoption of C. Octavius by
C. Julius C&aelig;sar, as the first that he knew of; but the passage of Cicero in the <I>Brutus</I>
and another passage (<I>Ad</I> Hirt. viii, 8) show that other instances had occurred before.
A person on passing from one gens into another, and taking the name of his new
familia, generally retained the name of his old gens also, with the addition to it
of the termination <I>-anus</I> (Cic. <I>ad Att.</I> iii, 20, and the note of Victorius). Thus,
C. Octavius, afterwards the Emperor Augustus, upon being adopted by the testa-
ment of his uncle, the dictator, assumed the name of Caius Julius C&aelig;sar Octavianus;
but he caused the adoption to be confirmed by the curi&aelig;. As to the testamentary
adoption of C. Octavius, see Drumann, <I>Geschichte Roms.</I> i, 337, and the references
there given.&rquo; Were there any proof that Shakespeare had ever read Dion Cassius, I
should not have referred to Plutarch as the possible source of this use of &lquo;father.&rquo;
Dion Cassius speaks over and over again of Julius C&aelig;sar as the father of Octavius.
&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<SC>M. Mason</SC> calls attention to line 76 of this scene where &lquo;Bochus&rquo; is called &lquo;the
King of Lybia,&rquo; thereby proving that &lquo;the present reading [Lydia] is right.&rquo;

<P>things which fitted out or made able for war.&mdash;<SC>Ibid</SC>. (<I>s. v.</I> Habiliment, 4 plural):
The apparel, vestments or garments appropriate to any office or occasion. (In this

<P>30, 31. <B>he frets That Lepidus of the Triumpherate, should be depos'd</B>]
See II, iii, 30, where Abbott and Franz are quoted, who would explain this &lquo;of&rquo; as
grammatically following &lquo;should be deposed.&rquo; This use of &lquo;of&rquo; after &lquo;depose&rquo; is
the accepted idiom; see the examples in the <I>N. E. D.</I> (<I>s. v.</I> depose, &dagger; 4, &dagger; b). At the
same time it may be observed from the punctuation of the Ff (nowhere followed since
Rowe, ed. ii), that the compositor did not recognize this idiom, but supposed the
sense to be, as it is quite possible it may be, &lquo;he frets that Lepidus, he of the Tri-
umvirate, should be deposed.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>32. <B>And being that, we detaine</B>] The <I>Text. Notes</I> reveal the various punctu-
ations to which these words have been subjected, without, it must be acknowledged,
greatly affecting the sense. The most idiomatic appears to be that of <SC>Theobald</SC>,
adopted by the majority of editors. <SC>Abbott's</SC> remark (&sect; 404, quoted at II, ii, 42)
then applies, which explains &lquo;being&rquo; as equivalent to <I>it being so.</I>

<P>34. <B>Messenger</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.</I> 200) scans this word as a &lquo;quasi-disyllable.&rquo;
Does there not lie in this &lquo;quasi&rquo; a confession of weakness, nay, timidity? What
honest man who loves the music of his English tongue would openly assert that we
must adopt, in poetry (of all loves!), such words as <I>messgers, passgers?</I> <SC>Abbott</SC>
(&sect; 468) follows Walker and observes that &lquo;any unaccented syllable of a poly-
syllable may be sometimes softened and almost ignored,&rquo; and would fain have us
imagine that the tripping dactyl &lquo;messenger&rquo; is <I>softened</I> when uttered as a grim
spondee, <I>messger.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>42. <B>with her Traine</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> omitted these words because, I presume, he noted
that C&aelig;sar says to Octavia &lquo;you are come A market-maid to Rome;&rquo; in this omission he
was followed by every editor down to Collier, who revives the present stage-direction
and remarks, &lquo;there can be no possible reason for following the example of modern
editors by omitting these words. It must have been a small train; she had not &ldquo;an
army for an usher,&rdquo; as appears by what follows, but she was not wholly unattended,
according to the practice of the stage when the Folio was printed.&rquo;
<P>43. <B>Haile C&aelig;sar, and my L.</B>] <SC>Deighton</SC>: Her salutation is to him not only as
C&aelig;sar, ruler of Rome, but as one to whom as the head of her family she owes
allegiance.
<P>47. <B>The wife of Anthony,</B> etc.] <SC>Corson</SC> (p. 296): The extravagance of C&aelig;sar's
language is evidently designed to exhibit his insincerity.

<P>56. <B>The ostentation</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: I dare say the poet wrote: &lquo;The <I>ostent,</I>&rquo; <I>i. e.</I>
the shewing, token, demonstration of our love; and he uses it both in these accept-
ations, and likewise to signify <I>ostentation.</I> The Alexandrine therefore is wholly
unnecessary. [Theobald here gives examples of <I>ostent</I> from the <I>Mer. of Ven.</I> and
<I>Hen. V.</I> <SC>Steevens</SC> appropriated this emendation of Theobald, even to the illus-
trations from the <I>Mer. of Ven.</I> and <I>Hen. V.;</I> these, he calmly remarks, &lquo;sufficiently
authorize [<I>ostent</I>] the slight change I have made.&rquo; Not unnaturally, <SC>Walker</SC> was
thus misled when (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 302) he made the following note]: &lquo;Steevens, perceiv-
ing the defect in the verse, reads,&mdash;<I>ostent;</I> which word, however, is always pro-
nounced by Shakespeare <I>ost&eacute;nt;</I> neither am I sure that he would have used it in this
sense. I suspect that the true reading is <I>ostention</I> (properly <I>ostension</I>). This is
nearer to the common text. Shakespeare is continually coining words from the
Latin.&rquo;
<P>57. <B>Is often left vnlou'd</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii): &lquo;Is often <I>held</I> unlov'd,&rquo; says the
MS; but with doubtful fitness.&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC> (<I>Sh. Vind.</I> p. 293): The word <I>felt,</I> by a
common accident at press, may have been jumbled into &lquo;left,&rquo; consisting of the same
letters.&mdash;<SC>Anon.</SC> (<I>Blackwood,</I> Oct. 1853, p. 467): If either of these emendations were
adopted, we should require to read, &lquo;is often felt <I>unloving,</I>&rquo; and this the measure will
not permit. We therefore stand by the old text, the meaning of which we conceive to
be&mdash;love which is left unshown is often left <I>unreturned.</I>&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: With more
likelihood we should read, &lquo;Is often left <I>unpriz'd.</I>&rquo; &lquo;Unlov'd&rquo; is a very problemati-
cal expression here, and appears to have been partly formed by the compositor from the
word &lquo;love&rquo; in the preceding line.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> [adopting Singer's <I>felt</I>]: The passage

<P>learned German is, I think, far astray when he holds the present phrase to be an
instance of the common construction of a verb with its cognate accusative; nor are
either of the examples which he quotes parallels to the present phrase. He was
misled, I think, by the jingle of the words. Adriana asks, &lquo;what ruins are there in
me which cannot be found to have been made ruins by him?&rquo; So, too, Cordelia
deserves to experience the want of that affection in which she had herself been
wanting. In what respect are these two examples parallel in construction to &lquo;the
ostentation of love which when left unshown is not felt&rquo;? Of course, in the three
paraphrases just given, cognate accusatives cannot be found, and for the simple reason
that they do not exist in the original sentences; herein lay Dr Schmidt's error. In
the interpretation of the present phrase it seems to me that there has been a mis-
apprehension of the person by whom the love is felt. The generally accepted mean-
ing seems to be that if there is no expression of love, love will soon cease to exist.
This, however, implies the possibility that C&aelig;sar's love for his &lquo;dearest sister&rquo; might
grow cold, which is hardly an expression of deep fraternal feeling. It amounts
almost to a threat. Whereas, C&aelig;sar is pleading tenderly for himself, with gentle
reproaches because Octavia has given him no chance to show his love for her, and
urges that if there is no demonstration of his love she will soon cease to care whether
he loves her or not, his love will be no longer prized; it becomes unvalued, &lquo;unloved.&rquo;
&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>might have used it for a <I>disjunctive.</I> I believe there is no such substantive as
<I>obstruct:</I> besides, we say, an obstruction <I>to</I> a thing, but not <I>between</I> one thing and
another. As Mr Malone, however, is contented with Dr Warburton's reading, I

to hold to the original, seeing that Shakespeare sometimes employs words with a
meaning peculiar to himself. His boldness may not be justified by example,&mdash;but
his meaning has always reference to the original sense of the word.&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC>: An
<I>abstract between</I> is surely nonsense.&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii): &lquo;Abstract&rquo;&mdash;a mere mis-

return.&rquo; Anthony gladly granted Octavia's return to Rome, because therein lay an
abridgement or curtailing of the hindrances between his lust and him; that is,
between the lovers now separated by Octavia's presence. The majority of editors
refer &lquo;abstract&rquo; to Octavia, instead of properly to &lquo;which.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex. s. v.</I>
Abstract): That is, the shortest way for him and his desires, the readiest opportunity
to encompass his wishes.&mdash;[To me, Delius's definition of &lquo;abstract,&rquo; with its reference

Schmidt's paraphrase is weak and inferior to that of Delius, from which it is, not
improbably, derived. I cannot find &lquo;abstract,&rquo; as here used, in the <I>N. E. D.;</I> of
<I>obstruct,</I> Dr Murray says, &lquo;not otherwise known&rquo; than here in Theobald's emendation.
In a choice between a word coined by Shakespeare and one coined by Theobald, I
prefer the former, even were it as dark as ignorance.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>102. <B>abhominations</B>] <SC>Ellis</SC> (p. 220): This was a common orthography in the
<SC>xvi</SC> th century, and the <I>h</I> seems to have been occasionally pronounced or not pro-
nounced. There was no <I>h</I> in the Latin, although in the Latin of that time <I>h</I> was
