nacyon,</I> abhominacio&rquo; and Levins, 1570, &lquo;<I>abhominate,</I> abhominari,&rquo; as if the words
referred to <I>ab-homine</I> instead of <I>ab-omine.</I>&mdash;[See <I>Love's Lab. Lost,</I> V, i, 26, of this
edition, where this note is also given.]
<P>103. <B>potent Regiment to a Trull</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: &lquo;Regiment,&rquo; is <I>government, au-
thority;</I> he puts his <I>power</I> and his empire into the hands of a false woman. It may
be observed, that &lquo;trull&rquo; was not, in our author's time, a term of mere infamy, but
a word of slight contempt, as <I>wench</I> is now.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: &lquo;Trull&rquo; is used in <I>1 Henry
VI:</I> II, ii, 28 as synonymous to <I>harlot.</I> There can therefore be no doubt of the
sense in which it is used here.
<P>104. <B>That noyses it</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: Milton has adopted this uncommon verb in his
<I>Paradise Regained;</I> &lquo;though noising loud And threat'ning nigh,&rquo; iv, 488.&mdash;[It is
not the verb itself which is so &lquo;uncommon&rquo; (it occurs elsewhere in Shakespeare,
and several times in the <I>New Testament</I>), but it is its present sense which is so
unusual, conveying, as it does, the idea of loud-voiced and turbulent opposition. I
think that Steevens might have cast, not unprofitably, a side-glance on the verb, more
than &lquo;uncommon,&rquo; which Rowe, Pope, Theobald, Hanmer, and Warburton accepted
as the true one in this passage (see <I>Text. Notes</I>), imparting, as it does, a novel and
coquettish charm to the infinite variety already ascribed to Cleopatra.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>7. <B>If not, denounc'd against vs</B>] <SC>Tyrwhitt's</SC> emendation, adopted by Steevens,
will be found in the <I>Text. Notes.</I> <SC>Malone</SC>, in 1790, read, &lquo;If not, denounce <I>'t</I> against
us,&rquo; but remarked, &lquo;I am not, however, sure that the old reading is not right, &ldquo;If
there be no particular denunciation against me, why should we not,&rdquo; etc. There is,
however, in the Folio, a comma after the word &ldquo;not&rdquo; and no point of interrogation
at the end of the sentence; which favours the emendation now made.&rquo; In the Vari-
orum of 1821, Malone restored the text of the Folio, omitting the comma after &lquo;not,&rquo;
adding an interrogation at the end, and giving the foregoing paraphrase. The
earlier commentators and their modern followers accept &lquo;denounce&rquo; in the sense of
&lquo;publicly arraign,&rquo; or &lquo;censure.&rquo; <SC>Monck Mason</SC>, alone among them, seems to have
caught what is apparently its true meaning, namely, &lquo;proclaim,&rquo; and referred it not to
Cleopatra but to the wars. &lquo;Cleopatra means to say,&rquo; he remarks, &lquo;&ldquo;Is not the war
denounced against us? Why should we not then attend in person?&rdquo;&rquo; <SC>Delius</SC>
agrees as far as referring &lquo;denounce&rquo; to the war, but gives a different paraphrase:
&lquo;If it is not fit, yet inasmuch as the war has been proclaimed against me, why should
I not be there in person?&rquo; Naturally <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>) adopts the view of Delius; so

<P>10. <B>meerly</B>] Used in its derivative sense, wholly, utterly, purely.
<P>15. <B>What should not then</B>] Very plausible is Walker's conjecture (<I>Crit.</I> iii,

<P>17. <B>Photinus an Eunuch</B>] The name of this eunuch in the original Greek is
&lquo;Pothinus,&rquo; both here and in the <I>Life of C&aelig;sar.</I> In the latter, North has correctly repro-
duced it; but here, in the <I>Life of Antonius,</I> it is rendered <I>Photinus.</I> The error began,
I think, with Amyot; in an edition of his translation, printed in Paris as late as 1811,
the name is <I>Photinus.</I> Of course, Shakespeare followed North, and what the true name
might be, he cared, probably, very little, and we, assuredly, care still less. Whatever
his name, <I>Photinus</I> or <I>Pothinus,</I> he ought to be dead; Julius C&aelig;sar put him to death
some years before the present events. <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.</I> 173) calls attention to the fact
that in Beaumont and Fletcher's <I>False One</I> &lquo;the name is everywhere pronounced as
it is now,&rquo; that is, Phot&iacute;nus, with the accent on the penult. The position of the

<P>33, 34. <B>Which might . . . slacknesse</B>] These words, which express Anthony's
hearty assent to Cleopatra's rebuke by asserting that the best of men might have used
them in upbraiding sloth, <SC>Blumhof</SC> takes as a peevish rejoinder to Cleopatra's irri-
tating remark, and regards as a separate sentence and as an exclamation of surprise,
&lquo;To taunt at slackness!&rquo; &lquo;Slackness&rquo; is lengthened into three syllables by both
<SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.</I> 20) and <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 477): &lquo;slackeness.&rquo; But would not the pro-
nunciation be almost as rhythmical, and quite as slovenly, were it uttered &lquo;<I>se</I>lack-
ness? The pause necessitated by the change of address supplies the rhythm.
Walker finishes the line and begins the next thus &lquo;Canidius, come We'll fight,&rquo; etc.
See <I>Text. Notes</I> for Hanmer's emendation.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>37. <B>Why will</B>] The accent is designedly thrown on &lquo;will.&rquo;

<P>46. <B>Impresse</B>] See &lquo;prest&rquo; in the extract from North in the preceding note.&mdash;
<SC>Skeat</SC> (<I>Concise Etymol. Dict.</I>): &lquo;Press&rquo; is a corruption of the old word <I>prest,</I> ready;
whence <I>prest-money,</I> ready money advanced to a man hired for service, earnest money;
also <I>imprest,</I> a verb (now <I>impress</I>), to give a man earnest money. When it became
common to use <I>compulsion</I> to <I>force</I> men into service, it was confused with the verb
<I>to press. Prest money</I> was money lent, derived from Old French <I>prester</I> (French
<I>pr&ecirc;ter</I>) to lend, advance money.
<P>48. <B>yare</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: So in North's <I>Plutarch:</I> &lquo;C&aelig;sar's ships were not built for
pomp, high and great, . . . but they were light of yarage.&rquo; &lquo;Yare&rquo; generally sig-
nifies, <I>dextrous, manageable.</I>
<P>49. <B>Shall fall you</B>] That is, befall you. For other words where prefixes are
dropped, see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 460.
<P>54. <B>Distract your Armie</B>] In North's <I>Plutarch,</I> Canidius tells Antony, among
other things, that he &lquo;would weaken his army by dividing them into ships.&rquo; Possi-
bly this explains the present phrase.

<P>84, 85. <B>his whole action growes Not in the power on't</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 39):
&lquo;Action&rquo; is here <I>enterprize,</I> the enterprize then in hand; no part of which, says
Canidius, &lquo;grows in the power on't,&rquo; is conducted as it might be, or suitably to the
means that we have in our power.&mdash;[Capell refers &lquo;on't&rquo; to &lquo;action.&rquo; Dr <SC>Johnson</SC>,
on the other hand, refers it to &lquo;right&rquo; in the Soldier's speech. &lquo;That is,&rquo; he says,
&lquo;his whole conduct becomes ungoverned by the right, or by reason.&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC> gives
what is essentially Capell's interpretation and points out Johnson's oversight. &lquo;I
think,&rquo; he observes, &lquo;that Canidius means to say, His whole conduct in the war is
not founded upon that which is his greatest strength (namely, his <I>land force</I>), but on
the caprice of a woman, who wishes that he should fight by sea. Dr Johnson refers
the word <I>on't</I> to <I>right</I> in the preceding speech. I apprehend, it refers to <I>action</I> in
the speech before us.&rquo; <SC>Hudson</SC> says that &lquo;This speech may refer, not merely to the
present action, but Antony's whole course of late, where his action grows, takes its
shape, not from the power that executes it, that is, himself, but from the will of
another.&rquo; The phrase is certainly obscure. Possibly, it may mean that Anthony's
course of action does not grow through its own native force, there are other influences
at work&mdash;his deeds are not self-evolved.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>85. <B>so our Leaders leade</B>] <SC>Theobald's</SC> change, &lquo;our leader's led,&rquo; which has
been adopted by every subsequent editor, is pronounced needless by <SC>Thiselton</SC>
(p. 19), and, I cannot but think, justly. If Cleopatra is herself a Leader, her power
is more direct, and the soldiers are more emphatically her men, than if this power
were exercised only indirectly through Anthony. Moreover, by the plural, &lquo;women,&rquo;
there is an implication that even Anthony himself has lost his manliness and is become
a woman, which is missed if &lquo;Leader&rquo; be restricted to Anthony alone.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>89. <B>Ven.</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii) conjectured that this abbreviation stood &lquo;perhaps for
<I>Vennard,</I> an actor in the part of Canidius.&rquo; <SC>Dyce</SC> repeated this conjecture without
comment.&mdash;<SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> ii, 185) says that the speech &lquo;is given to <I>Ventidius</I>
instead of to Canidius.&rquo;

<P>1. <SC>Bradley</SC> (p. 71): To come then to real defects:&mdash;one may be found in places
where Shakespeare strings together a number of scenes, some very short, in which
the <I>dramatis person&aelig;</I> are frequently changed; as though a novelist were to tell his
story in a succession of short chapters, in which he flitted from one group of his
characters to another. This method shows itself here and there in the pure tragedies
(<I>e. g.</I> in the last act of <I>Macbeth</I>), but it appears most decidedly where the historical
material was undramatic, as in the middle part of <I>Antony and Cleopatra.</I> It was
made possible by the absence of scenery, and doubtless Shakespeare used it because
it was the easiest way out of a difficulty. But, considered abstractedly, it is a defec-
tive method, and, even as used by Shakespeare, it sometimes reminds us of the
merely narrative arrangement common in plays before his time.
<P>8. <B>iumpe</B>] <SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D. s. v.</I> &dagger; 6): The decisive moment of plunging
into action of doubtful issue; dangerous critical moment, critical point, crisis. (Latin,
<I>discrimen.</I>) The notion is evidently that of making a jump or taking a plunge into
the unknown or untried.
<P>3. <B>battaile</B>] <SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D. s. v.</I> 8): A body or line of troops in battle array,
whether composing an entire army, or one of its main divisions. &lquo;What may the
kings whole Battaile reach vnto?&rquo;&mdash;<I>1 Hen. IV:</I> IV, i, 129.
</CC>

<P>3. <B>the noise of a Sea fight</B>] Our ignorance of the kind of noise which accom-
panied sea-fights, and enabled an audience to distinguish it, when heard behind the
scene, from that of a land-fight, is to be regretted. It may be that there were vociferous
commands to the rowers and the sound of crashing boards; but see IV, xii, 1.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>6. <B>Thantoniad</B>] &lquo;The Admiral galley of <I>Cleopatra,</I> was called Antoniade.&rquo;&mdash;
North's <I>Plutarch</I> (see <I>Appendix</I>). [&lquo;Thantoniad&rquo; betrays the ear of the com-
positor.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>7. <B>flye, and turne the Rudder</B>] <SC>Stapfer</SC> (p. 405): What had happened was
very simple; it was only that Cleopatra had felt frightened: she was not a woman
of heroic type, and her nerves were not strong enough to bear the excitement of a
battle for any length of time,&mdash;that was the whole secret. Those who seek for any
other explanation of the defeat at Actium, do so because they start with the notion
that on great occasions Cleopatra could be truly brave, the splendid manner of her
death having acquired for her a false reputation for courage; but her supposed hero-
ism is only a brilliant theatrical cloak wrapped round the most feminine little person,
presenting the most complete contrast to all manliness of character that ever wore a
crown. We have only to study closely her ending, as it is given by Shakespeare, and
the mask falls&mdash;the woman remains and the heroine vanishes.&mdash;<SC>Anatole France</SC>
(iv, 130): This flight, Admiral Jurien de la Gravi&egrave;re holds to be a skilfull man&oelig;uvre
and M. Victorien Sardou has given to it a highly dramatic effect by representing the
enamoured queen as effecting thereby the defeat and disgrace of her lover, in order to
keep him completely her own.

<P>12. <B>Cantle</B>] <SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D. s. v.</I> Medi&aelig;val Latin, <I>cantellus,</I> diminutive of
<I>cant, canto, cantus,</I> corner. 3 &dagger; c.): A segment of a circle or sphere. [Present line

<P>16. <B>the Token'd Pestilence</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: The death of those visited by the
plague was certain, when particular eruptions appeared on the skin; and these were
called <I>God's tokens.</I>&mdash;<SC>Halliwell</SC> (<I>Love's Lab. Lost,</I> V, ii, 470): &lquo;The spots
[indicative of the plague], otherwise called <I>God's tokens,</I> are commonly of the big-
nesse of a flea-bitten spot, sometimes much bigger. . . . But they have ever a circle
about them, the red ones a purplish circle, and the others a redish circle.&rquo;&mdash;Brad-
well's <I>Physick for . . . the Plague,</I> 1636.&mdash;<SC>Elton</SC> (p. 468, footnote): Allusions to
the &lquo;tokens&rquo; of pestilence in Shakespeare are not uncommon after the great outbreak
of plague in the winter of 1602, which, between Christmas and Christmas, killed
in London and its liberties more than 30,000 people. The tokens were redder than
in former pestilences; hard spots of a bright flaming red were accounted a fatal
symptom.
<P>17. <B>Yon ribaudred Nagge</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 39): Meaning, indeed,&mdash;brazen hack-
ney: and calling her so in his anger, by reason of her forwardness and her prosti-
tutions: and from hence, the propriety of the imprecation he immediately makes on
her,&mdash;&lquo;Whom leprosy o'er-take!&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: &lquo;Ribaudred&rquo; is, I believe, no more
than a corruption. Shakespeare, who is not always very nice about his versification,
might have written, &lquo;Yon <I>ribald-rid</I> nag,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> Yon strumpet, who is common to
every wanton fellow.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: I have adopted the happy emendation proposed by
Mr Steevens. <I>Ribaud</I> was only the old spelling of <I>ribald:</I> and the misprint of
&lquo;red&rquo; for <I>rid</I> is easily accounted for. By <I>ribald,</I> Scarus, I think, means the lewd
Antony in particular, not &lquo;<I>every</I> lewd fellow,&rquo; as Mr Steevens has explained it.&mdash;
<SC>Tyrwhitt</SC> (p. 9): I believe we should read, &lquo;yon ribauld <I>Hag.</I>&rquo; What follows
seems to prove it:&mdash;&lquo;The noble ruin of her <I>magick, Antony,</I>&rquo; etc.&mdash;[This emendation
</CC>

<HE>218 <I>THE TRAGEDIE OF</I> [<SC>act iii, sc.</SC> x.</HE>

<CC>
<C>[17. <B>Yon ribaudred Nagge of Egypt</B>]</C>
<P>is repeated in Collier's ed. ii, not, however, as Tyrwhitt's, but as that of Collier's
corrected Folio, which, as Collier observes, has &lquo;ribaudred&rquo; altered to <I>ribald,</I> and
&lquo;nag&rquo; to <I>hag. Ribald,</I> he continues, &lquo;requires no explanation, whereas no instance
of the use elsewhere either of &ldquo;ribaudred&rdquo; or &ldquo;ribauldred&rdquo; can be produced.
There are, no doubt, such words as <I>ribaldry</I> and <I>ribaldrous,</I> but the employment of
them by old authors proves nothing, since they are not the word wanted. &ldquo;Nag&rdquo;
for <I>hag</I> was clearly a misprint, and it will be observed that, even amending the word
&ldquo;ribaudred&rdquo; to <I>ribaldrid,</I> as was done by Steevens, gives the line a syllable too
much.&rquo; Tyrwhitt's change of &lquo;nag&rquo; into <I>hag</I> was followed a second time, this time
by <SC>Singer</SC>, who exclaims that &lquo;the poet would surely not have called Cleopatra a
<I>nag!</I>&rquo; Any change in &lquo;ribaudred,&rquo; Singer deems quite unnecessary. &lquo;&ldquo;Ribaudred&rdquo;
is,&rquo; he says, &lquo;<I>obscene,</I> indecent in words or acts. Thus Barett [<I>Alvearie,</I> 1580]:&mdash;
&ldquo;a Ribaudrous and filthie tongue. <I>Os incestum, obsc&oelig;num, impurum, &amp; impudicum.
Vide Filthie.</I>&rdquo;&mdash;[where we find] &ldquo;Villanie in actes, or words; ribauldrie, filthinesse,
vncleannesse. <I>Obsc&oelig;nitas,</I>&rdquo; etc.&rquo; To Singer's exclamation that &lquo;the poet&rquo; would
not have called Cleopatra a <I>nag,</I> <SC>Dyce</SC> replies, that &lquo;since she has been previously
called &ldquo;a trull,&rdquo; I see no reason for wondering that she should now be called
&ldquo;<I>nag,</I>&rdquo; <I>i. e.</I> jade, hackney. (&ldquo;Know we not Galloway <I>nags?</I>&rdquo; exclaims Pistol,
alluding to Doll Tearsheet.&mdash;<I>2 Hen. IV:</I> II, iv.)&rquo; Furthermore, in reference to
this use of &lquo;nag,&rquo; <SC>R. G. White</SC> (ed. i) quotes Leontes, who, &lquo;in his jealous fit, exclaims,
&ldquo;Then say my wife's a <I>hobby-horse!</I>&rdquo;&rquo;]&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: &lquo;Ribaudred nag&rquo; means filthy
strumpet.&mdash;<SC>Keightley</SC> (<I>Exp.</I> 317): There is no need of change&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC>: &lquo;Ribau-
dred&rquo; damages the metre; and I cannot perceive the sense of <I>red</I> thus tagged on to
<I>ribaud . . .</I> Bishop Hall has <I>ribaldish,</I> and so, I suspect, the Poet wrote here. [P. 90],
Of course the epithet <I>ribald</I> is applied to Cleopatra to express her notorious profligacy.
It seems to me, also, that the Poet meant &lquo;nag&rquo; in reference to her speedy flight
from the battle, carrying Antony off, as it were, on her back. And the words, &lquo;the
breese upon her,&rquo; and &lquo;like a cow in June&rquo; naturally infer that such was the image
intended.&mdash;<SC>Thiselton</SC> (p. 19): Read <I>riband-red</I> for &lquo;ribaudred&rquo; on the following
grounds. (1) No such word as &lquo;ribaudred&rquo; is known. (2) In the preceding line
&lquo;the Fight&rquo; is likened to &lquo;the Token'd Pestilence,&rquo; the reference being to the Plague,
of which there were three varieties; the red, the yellow, and the black. It is Cleo-
patra's red ribands that suggest the figure of the red plague to Scarrus. (3) Red
ribands would match a dark complexion and the actor who played the part of Cleo-
patra may be presumed to have worn them. (4) Cleopatra will then be likened to
a nag decked with red ribands as for a fair, anything but an &lquo;Arme-gaunt steede.&rquo;
(5) &lquo;Riband-red&rquo; enhances the force and appropriateness of the imprecation in the
next line, &lquo;Whom Leprosie o'er-take,&rquo; that disease being characterised by whiteness
of the skin. (6) In the Folio the <I>u</I> in the word usually given as &lquo;ribaudred&rquo; is
raised above the level of the preceding and succeeding letters, and would therefore
seem to be in reality an inverted <I>n.</I>&mdash;[Suggestions from this critic are worthy of
respectful consideration. But is it any more easy to apprehend the meaning of &lquo;a
riband-red nag&rquo; than it is of &lquo;a waistcoat-white gentleman&rquo;? In <I>Mer. of Ven.</I> III,
ii, 103, we find the phrase, &lquo;the guiled shore&rquo;; in <I>Meas. for Meas.</I> III, i, 121:
&lquo;the delighted spirit&rquo;; in <I>Othello,</I> I, iii, 320: &lquo;delighted beauty&rquo;; in <I>1 Hen. IV:</I>
I, iii, 183: &lquo;disdain'd contempt.&rquo; In all these cases, and many more could be added,
the past participles convey the meaning that the nouns which they qualify are abun-
dantly supplied with that which the participles represent. Thus, &lquo;the guiled shore&rquo;

<P>22. <B>Hoists Sailes, and flyes</B>] <SC>Staunton</SC> (<I>Athen.</I> 26 Apr. 1873): To say nothing

<I>tail</I> and flies.&rquo; Those familiar with old typography know well how readily &lquo;sails&rquo;

committed by several modern editors in reading <I>hag</I> for &lquo;nag.&rquo;

<P>49. <B>The wounded chance of Anthony</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: I know not whether the
author, who loves to draw his images from the sports of the field, might not have
written: &lquo;The wounded <I>chase</I> of Antony.&rquo; The allusion is to a deer wounded and
chased, whom all other deer avoid. <I>I will,</I> says Enobarbus, <I>follow Antony,</I> though
<I>chased</I> and <I>wounded.</I> The common reading, however, may very well stand.&mdash;
<SC>Malone</SC>: The wounded chance of Antony, is a phrase nearly of the same import as
&lquo;the broken fortunes of Antony.&rquo; The old reading is indisputably the true one. So,
&lquo;Or shall I show the cinders of my spirits, Through th' ashes of my chance.&rquo; [V,
ii, 204.]&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: Mr Malone has judiciously defended the old reading. In
<I>Othello</I> we have a phrase somewhat similar to &lquo;wounded chance&rquo;; viz. &lquo;<I>mangled</I>
matter.&rquo; [I, iii, 196.]
<P>50. <B>Sits in the winde</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 39): The word &lquo;sits&rquo; shews the phrase to
be taken from field-sports; the pursuers of which know,&mdash;that scents coming down
the wind, or from game that sits or lyes in the wind, are always the strongest.
<P>2. <B>Hearke,</B> etc.] What phenomenon in nature was it to which Antony here refers,
and interprets according to his own despairing mood? Can it have been the wild
tumult on land caused by &lquo;the great boisterous wind,&rquo; which, according to Plutarch,
troubled Anthony's ships more than aught else after he had deserted them?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>4. <B>lated</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Alluding to a benighted traveller.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: Thus, in
<I>Macbeth,</I> III, iii, 10: &lquo;Now spurres the lated traueller apace.&rquo;

<P>9. <B>I haue fled my selfe</B>] Does this mean, &lquo;I myself have fled,&rquo; or &lquo;I have fled
<I>from</I> myself&rquo;? Romeo says (I, i, 190): &lquo;I have lost myself. I am not here.&rquo;
Further on, Anthony says, &lquo;Let [that] be left which leaves itself.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>12. <B>Which has no neede of you. Be gone</B>] This line lacks two syllables.
Several ingenious expedients have been proposed to correct this serious error.
<SC>Capell</SC> reiterates &lquo;Be gone&rquo;; <SC>Steevens</SC> suggested, &lquo;Be gone, <I>I say</I>&rquo;<I>;</I> <SC>Keightley</SC>,
&lquo;Be gone, <I>I pray</I>&rquo; or &lquo;<I>I pray you.</I>&rquo; And <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 507) asserts that &lquo;the best way
of arranging&rquo; it is to print &lquo;Begone&rquo; in a separate line. Is it to be supposed that
Shakespeare was unable to detect the loss of two syllables, and that his resources
were insufficient to supply what any child could suggest? Or is it to be supposed
that, after Shakespeare's audience had shuddered on hearing the maimed utterance
on the stage, their lacerated feelings were soothed by seeing &lquo;Begone&rquo; printed as a
separate line?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>17, 18. <B>Friends be gone, . . . some Friends</B>] On the supposition that there is
some corruption in the repetition of &lquo;Friends,&rquo; <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 288) proposed, &lquo;per-
haps, &ldquo;<I>Fellows,</I> begone&rdquo; (<I>socii</I>).&rquo; Whereupon, <SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. ii) comments: &lquo;Here
Walker would alter what an earlier line (the second) of this speech proves to be quite
right. Whether or not there be any error in &ldquo;some friends&rdquo; I cannot determine.&rquo;

<P>Capell is right, I think, in his interpretation of these words. Anthony is utterly
unconscious of the world about him; but roused, for a second, by the voice, or,
possibly, the respectful hand of Eros, he answers at random with instinctive courtesy,
which, indeed, is pathetic in the circumstances, &lquo;Yes, my lord, yes.&rquo; <SC>Staunton</SC>,
however, apparently hears in the expression a somewhat petulant tone. &lquo;This kind
of rejoinder,&rquo; he remarks, &lquo;sometimes in play, sometimes in petulance, is not unfre-
quent in our old dramas. See <I>Mer. of Ven.</I> II, ix, 89, 90,&rquo;&mdash;where a Messenger
enters and asks, &lquo;Where is my Lady?&rquo; and Portia gaily replies, &lquo;Here, what would
my Lord?&rquo; As instances similar to this reply of Portia, <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Remarks,</I> p. 55)
quotes <I>ad loc.</I> from <I>1 Hen. IV:</I> II, iv: &lquo;<I>Hostess.</I> O Jesu! <I>my lord</I> the prince.
<I>P. Henry.</I> How now, <I>my lady,</I> the hostess.&rquo; From <I>Rich. II:</I> V, v: &lquo;<I>Groom.</I>
Hail, royal <I>prince! King Richard.</I> Thanks, noble <I>peer.</I>&rquo; And from <I>The Hogge
hath Lost his Pearle,</I> 1614, sig. <SC>h</SC>: &lquo;<I>Enter Peter with a candle. Peter.</I> Where are
you, <I>my Lord? Hog.</I> Here, <I>my Lady.</I>&rquo; Of these three instances, that from <I>Rich.
II.</I> should be eliminated, I think. There is neither gaiety nor petulance in Richard's
reply to the Groom, but sarcasm, as the context shows. In his note on this same
reply of Portia, Staunton says: &lquo;a dozen instances may be cited, where a similar
expression is used by an individual of station to one of very inferior rank&rquo;; but
he merely repeats those already given by Dyce, without any addition. In default,
therefore, of more examples, we can hardly accept these three, Portia's, Prince
Hal's, and Hog's, as sufficient to warrant the belief that this mode of expression
was common; and the fact that in all of them there lies banter or sarcasm, is
quite enough to deprive them of any similarity to Anthony's present words, which, I
think, stand quite alone, and have been rightly interpreted by Capell. <SC>Hudson</SC>,
however, gives a different meaning to them. &lquo;Antony,&rquo; he says, &lquo;is muttering to
himself under an overpowering sense of shame. In &ldquo;Yes, my lord, yes,&rdquo; he is
referring to C&aelig;sar: &ldquo;Yes, C&aelig;sar, you have done me now, and can have things all
your own way.&rdquo;&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>38, 39. <B>he at Philippi kept His sword e'ne like a dancer</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: In the
Morisco, and perhaps anciently in the Pyrrhick dance, the dancers held swords in
their hands with the points upward.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: I believe it means that C&aelig;sar
never offered to draw his sword, but kept it in the scabbard, like one who dances
with a sword on, which was formerly the custom in England.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: That Mr
Steevens's explanation is just, appears from a passage in <I>All's Well;</I> Bertram,
lamenting that he is kept from the <I>wars,</I> says&mdash;&lquo;Creaking my shoes . . . Till honour
be bought up, and no <I>sword worn,</I> But one to <I>dance</I> with.&rquo; [II, i, 31.] The word
<I>worn</I> shows that in both passages our author was thinking of the English, and not
of the Pyrrhick, or the Morisco, dance (as Dr Johnson supposed), in which the
sword was <I>not worn</I> at the side, but held in the hand with the point upward.&mdash;
<SC>Staunton</SC> (Note on <I>All's Well,</I> II, i, 31): As it was the fashion in Shakespeare's
time for gentlemen to dance with swords on, and the ordinary weapon was liable to
impede their motions, rapiers, light and short, were made for the purpose:&mdash;&lquo;when
our Gentlemen went simply . . . without Cuts or gards, bearing their heauy Swordes

<P>38-43. <SC>Hazlitt</SC> (p. 100): The passage after Antony's defeat by Augustus where
he is made to [utter these words] is one of those fine retrospections which shew us
the winding and eventful march of human life. The jealous attention which has
been paid to the unities both of time and place has taken away the principle of per-
spective in the drama, and all the interest which objects derive from distance, from
contrast, from privation, from change of fortune, from long-cherished passion; and
contracts our view of life from a strange and romantic dream, long, obscure, and
infinite, into a smartly contested, three hours' inaugural disputation on its merits by
the different candidates for theatrical applause.
<P>41. <B>the mad Brutus</B>] <SC>Upton</SC> (p. 296): Why does Antony call Brutus &lquo;mad&rquo;?
Plato seeing how extravagantly Diogenes acted the philosopher, said of him <I>That
he was Socrates run mad.</I> There is also a maxim drawn from the depth of philoso-
phy by Horace, <I>Epist.</I> I, vi, 15: &lquo;<I>Insani</I> sapiens nomen ferat, &aelig;quus iniqui, Ultra
quam satis est virtutem si petat ipsam.&rquo; Now if this be the opinion of philosophers
themselves concerning philosophy, that it may be pursued with so much ardor and
enthusiasm, that even the over-strained pursuit may border on madness; how agree-
able it is to the character of the wild, undisciplin'd Antony, to call even Brutus <I>Mad,</I>
the sober Brutus, the philosopher and patriot? Such as Antony look on all virtue
and patriotism as enthusiasm and madness.
<P>42. <B>Dealt on Lieutenantry</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: I know not whether the meaning is,
that C&aelig;sar acted only as lieutenant at Philippi, or that he made his attempts only on
lieutenants, and left the generals to Antony.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: I believe it means only,&mdash;
&lquo;fought by proxy,&rquo; made war by his lieutenants, or <I>on</I> the strength of his lieutenants.
So, in a former scene, Ventidius observes&mdash;&lquo;C&aelig;sar and Antony have ever won <I>More in
their officer,</I> than person.&rquo;&mdash;[III, i, 20.]&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: In the <I>Life of Antony,</I> Shakspeare
found the following: &lquo;&mdash;they were always more fortunate when <I>they made warre by
their lieutenants,</I> than by themselves&rquo;;&mdash;[see III, i, 16] which fully explains the
present passage. The subsequent words also&mdash;&lquo;and no practice had,&rquo; etc. show that
Mr Steevens has rightly interpreted this passage.&mdash;<SC>M. Mason</SC>: Steevens's explanation
of this passage is just, and agreeable to the character here given of Augustus. Shak-
speare represents him, in the next Act, as giving his orders to Agrippa, and remain-
ing unengaged himself: &lquo;Go forth, Agrippa, and begin the fight . . . .&rquo; Again: &lquo;Go,
charge, Agrippa.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: Or it may mean <I>traded in war's theory:</I>&mdash;&lquo;I met
just now a usurer, that only <I>deals upon</I> ounces.&rquo;&mdash;<I>The Witty Fair One,</I> V, i.&mdash;
<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex. s. v.</I> Deal): Acted by substitutes.

<P><I>Ant. &amp; Cleop.,</I> a simile. Had the case been reversed, the writer of the passage in
the former play would necessarily have said, &ldquo;He no more needs me than <I>the</I> ocean
needs a few drops&rdquo;; while Shakespeare would have said, just as necessarily, &ldquo;I am
a dew-drop to <I>his</I> grand sea.&rdquo;&rquo;&mdash;[There can be no doubt that the sentence is intelli-
gible. Hanmer's emendation is, I think, logically just. It is extremely probable
that the error is Shakespeare's. But it is one which demands some little mental
analysis to detect and correct, in which, if we indulge, while sitting at the play,
Euphronius will have delivered his message and departed before we have settled
the propriety of his opening speech. And there are minds of a cast so ignoble as to
prefer, where the sense is perfectly obvious, an incorrect word of Shakespeare to a
correct one of Hanmer.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>17. <B>Requires</B>] <SC>Deighton</SC>: This verb is seldom used in Shakespeare in the

it shall please you to declare,&rquo; etc., said by Wolsey to the king.

emphasis which the feeble <I>lessens</I> would hardly carry, but which the metaphorical

<P>3. <B>Thinke, and dye</B>] In North's <I>Plutarch</I> mention is made of a convivial club,

which has had but two admirers: Warburton and Capell. Both adopted it in their
text, and the latter pronounced it &lquo;most true and ingenious.&rquo; <SC>Johnson</SC> did &lquo;not
advance it into the page, not being convinced that it is necessary. &ldquo;Think and
die&rdquo;; that is, <I>Reflect on your folly, and leave the world,</I> is a natural answer.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Tyr-
whitt</SC> (p. 9): I grant it would be, <I>according to</I> [Johnson's] <I>explanation,</I> a very
proper answer from a moralist or a divine; but Enobarbus, I doubt, was neither the
one nor the other. He is drawn as a <I>plain, blunt soldier;</I> not likely, however, to
offend so grossly in point of delicacy as Hanmer's alteration would make him. I
believe the true reading is: &lquo;<I>Wink,</I> and die.&rquo; When the ship is going to be cast
away, in <I>The Sea Voyage</I> of Beaumont and Fletcher (I, i), and Aminta is lamenting,
Tibalt says to her: &lquo;&mdash; Go, take your gilt prayer-book, and to your business;
<I>Wink, and die:</I>&rquo; insinuating plainly, that she was afraid to meet death with her eyes
open. And the same insinuation, I think, Enobarbus might very naturally convey
in his return to Cleopatra's desponding question.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: The old reading may

<P>in <I>Com. of Errors,</I> <SC>Malone</SC> gives a quotation which he deems conclusive; it is from
<I>The Choice of Change . . .</I> by S. R. Gent, 1598, as follows: &lquo;Three things used by
monks, which provoke other men to laugh at their follies. 1. They are shaven and
notched on the head, like fooles.&rquo; It is probable that here &lquo;fooles&rquo; refers, not to the
domestic or &lquo;allowed fools,&rquo; but to idiots. <SC>Douce</SC> (ii, 323), in his exhaustive essay
<I>On the Clowns and Fools of Shakespeare,</I> says that, &lquo;The head was frequently shaved
in imitation or perhaps ridicule of a monk's crown. This practice is very ancient, and
can be traced to the twelfth century. In one instance, the hair exhibits a sort of triple
or Papal crown.&rquo; The reference, in the present line, is a coarse one, but then Enobarbus
was of coarse fibre. From what we know of the neglected personal habits of Fools,
the inference is not strained that they were liable to cutaneous ailments, and of such
ailments the only one that could &lquo;nick&rquo; anything was the &lquo;itch,&rquo; and the only thing it
could nick was the hair. <I>Possibly,</I> this nicking was so common among Fools as to
make the term almost synonymous with folly. In the Pathology of those days all irri-
tating cutaneous diseases were called the &lquo;itch,&rquo; but this term is not now applied to
affections of the scalp. In answer to my question on the subject, I received from my
friend, Dr <SC>L. A. Duhring</SC>, an acknowledged authority on <I>Cutaneous Diseases,</I> the fol-
lowing reply:&mdash;&lquo;The affection referred to, in the passage you quote from <I>Antony and
Cleopatra,</I> is not the itch, or scabies, but, without question, the common &ldquo;ringworm of
the scalp,&rdquo; a frequent and well-defined affection, which causes the destruction of the
hair, giving to the area invaded a nicked or cropped appearance, and in my works I
describe the hair (as do many other writers) as seeming to have been &ldquo;nibbled off.&rdquo;
It is due to a fungus, and the sensation of itching accompanies it.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>11, 12. <B>he being The meered question</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: &lquo;The <I>mered</I> question&rquo; is a
term I do not understand. I know not what to offer, except &lquo;The <I>mooted</I> question.&rquo;
That is, the <I>disputed</I> point, the subject of debate. <I>Mere</I> is indeed a <I>boundary;</I> and
the <I>meered question,</I> if it can mean anything, may, with some violence of language,
mean, the <I>disputed boundary.</I>&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: So, in Stanyhurst's translation of Virgil,
b. iii. 1582: &lquo;Wheare too ioynctlye <I>mearing</I> a cantel of Italye neereth.&rquo; Barrett, in his
<I>Alvearie,</I> 1580, interprets a <I>meere</I>-stone by <I>Terminalis lapis.</I> &lquo;Question&rquo; is certainly
the true reading. So, in <I>Hamlet,</I> I, i: &lquo;&mdash;the king That was and is the <I>question</I>
of these wars.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>M. Mason</SC>: Possibly Shakspeare might have coined the word
<I>meered,</I> and derived it from the adjective <I>mere</I> or <I>meer.</I> In that case, the <I>meered
question</I> might mean, the only cause of the dispute&mdash;the only subject of the quarrel.
&mdash;<SC>Knight</SC>: <I>Mere</I> is a boundary; and <I>to mere</I> is to mark, to limit.&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (ed.
ii): It is altered to <I>mooted</I> in the MS; but as &lquo;mered&rquo; may be taken in the sense
of <I>sole,</I> or <I>mere</I> question, we make no change.&mdash;<SC>R. G. White</SC> (ed. i): It is quite
possibly a misprint for <I>mooted.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ibid.</SC> (ed. ii): An amazing participial adjective,

<P>36, etc. <B>I see mens Iudgements,</B> etc.] <SC>Thiselton</SC> (p. 20): This speech is
excellently punctuated in the Folio. Modern editors not seeing that &lquo;that&rquo; in line
39 introduces the ground of Enobarbus' inference (see Abbott, &sect; 284), and in their
abhorrence of anything like a long sentence, place a full stop after &lquo;alike,&rquo; and a note
of exclamation after &lquo;emptinesse,&rquo; and so weaken the tension of the style. It may
be safely asserted that no one can derive an adequate conception of the energy of
Shakespeare's style from the study of a modern text.&mdash;[To follow here the punctu-
ation of Shakespeare's printers is, I think, to rob the speech of its vigour, and convert
into a philosophic, didactic observation what was intended to be indignant astonish-
ment. Rowe's dramatic instinct revealed to him the derision, nay, almost the con-
tempt, which lay in the words, &lquo;That he should dreame,&rquo; etc. We hear the same
indignant, derisive tones in Cleopatra's &lquo;To say as I said then!&rquo; (I, v, 88); or in
&lquo;The way to lose him!&rquo; (I, iii, 14); or &lquo;so tart a fauour To trumpet such good
tidings!&rquo; (II, v, 48.)&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>40. <B>Knowing all measures</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes,</I> etc. p. 497, ed. ii) records <I>miseries</I>
as the correction of his MS and explains that thereby &lquo;Enobarbus refers to the woe-
ful plight and prospects of Antony at the time he dared C&aelig;sar to &ldquo;lay his gay com-
parisons apart,&rdquo; and meet him &ldquo;sword against sword.&rdquo;&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Anon.</SC> (<I>Blackwood,</I> Oct.
p. 467, 1853): That is, it is surprising that Antony, who has experienced every
measure of fortune, has drunk of her fullest as well as of her emptiest cup, should
dream that the <I>full</I> C&aelig;sar will answer his <I>emptiness.</I> Here the words <I>full</I> and
<I>emptiness</I> prove to a demonstration that &lquo;measure&rquo; is the right word; yet Collier's
MS alters it to <I>miseries!</I>
<P>40. <B>full</B>] Thidias, line 107, calls C&aelig;sar &lquo;the fullest man,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> the most perfect.
<P>46. <B>blowne Rose . . . their nose</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 305): Shakespeare would
not have tolerated this cacophony; besides, the old grammar requires <I>noses.</I>&mdash;<SC>Lettsom</SC>
(Footnote to preceding): Walker is, I think, mistaken [Unquestionably.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] in this
latter observation, though I agree with the preceding part of the note.&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>
(<I>Athen&aelig;um,</I> 26 Apr. 1873): Walker has noticed the insufferable cacophony of &lquo;rose&rquo;
and &lquo;nose,&rquo; which assuredly Shakespeare would never have endured. But his pro-
posal to read <I>noses</I> is not a convincing remedy. My belief is that the line originally
stood &lquo;&mdash; may stop their <I>sense.</I>&rquo; That is, their sense of smelling; which, not being
understood, was changed into &lquo;nose.&rquo;&mdash;[Hereupon Staunton gives several quotations
where <I>sense</I> is applied to seeing, to hearing, to smelling; the most apposite is, &lquo;You
<I>smell</I> this business with a <I>sense</I> as cold,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<I>Wint. Tale,</I> II, i. But it is to be doubted
that any number of quotations would justify a change of the text. The cacophony
may be possibly softened, if, in reading the line, the emphasis be strongly laid on
&lquo;blown&rquo;:&mdash;&rquo;Against the <I>blown</I> rose may they stop their nose.&rquo; Was it not for this
purpose that Shakespeare threw the ictus on &lquo;blown&rquo;?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>49. <B>The Loyalty well held to Fooles,</B> etc.] <SC>Theobald</SC>: After Enobarbus has
said, that his honesty and he begin to quarrel, (<I>i. e.</I> that his reason shews him to be
mistaken in his firm adherence to Antony) he immediately falls into this generous
reflection: &lquo;Tho&rquo; loyalty, stubbornly preserved to a master in his declin'd fortunes,
seems folly in the eyes of fools; (<I>i. e.</I> men, who have not honour enough to think
more wisely), yet he, who can be so obstinately loyal, will make as great a figure on
record, as the conqueror.&rquo; I therefore read: &lquo;<I>Tho</I>&rquo; loyalty, well held, to fools does
make Our faith mere folly,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: I have preserved the old reading:
Enobarbus is deliberating upon desertion, and finding it is more prudent to forsake a
fool and more reputable to be faithful to him, makes no positive conclusion.&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC>
(i, 41): The change of &lquo;The&rquo; into&mdash;<I>Tho',</I> robs this speech of it's greatest beauty;
by destroying, or less'ning at least, that air of unsettledness that is much more visible
in it when the propositions are not connected: a good speaker would shew this,
sooner than words; by making a pause after &lquo;folly,&rquo; and pronouncing &lquo;yet&rquo; with an
<I>ictus,</I> with the force of&mdash;and yet.

<P>59. <B>Enob. He needs as many,</B> etc.] <SC>Malone</SC>: I suspect that this speech belongs
to Cleopatra, not to Enobarbus. Printers usually keep the names of the persons, who
appear in each scene, ready composed; in consequence of which, speeches are often
attributed to those to whom they do not belong. Is it probable that Enobarbus
should presume to interfere here? The whole dialogue naturally proceeds between
Cleopatra and Thyreus, till Enobarbus thinks it necessary to attend to his own
interest, and says what he speaks when he goes out. The plural number (<I>us</I>),
which suits Cleopatra, who throughout the play assumes that royal style, strengthens

<P>my conjecture. The words, &lquo;our master,&rquo; it may be said, are inconsistent with this
supposition; but I apprehend, Cleopatra might have thus described Antony, with
sufficient propriety. They are afterwards explained: &lquo;Whose he is, <I>we</I> are.&rquo;
Antony was the master of her fate.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: Enobarbus, who is the buffoon of
the play, has already presumed to interfere between the jarring Triumvirs, and might
therefore have been equally flippant on the occasion before us. For this reason, as
well as others, I conceive the speech in question to have been rightly appropriated
in the old copy. What a diminution of Shakspeare's praise would it be, if four lines
that exactly suit the mouth of Enobarbus, could come with equal propriety from the
lips of Cleopatra!
<P>60. <B>Or needs not vs</B>] <SC>Heath</SC> (p. 461): The poet's meaning is this: In his
present fortune Antony needs as many friends as C&aelig;sar hath, or else he needs not
even us, whose small number and want of power render us incapable, without other
assistance, of being of any service to him. If C&aelig;sar so pleases, our master will leap
to be his friend; for, as you know very well, though we are indeed our master's
friends, yet both he and we are at present pretty much at C&aelig;sar's discretion.
<P>60. <B>Or needs not vs. If C&aelig;sar please,</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: All sense is lost in this
false pointing, which should be reformed thus: &lquo;Or needs not us if C&aelig;sar please.&rquo;
That is, while he is at enmity with C&aelig;sar he needs a power equal to C&aelig;sar's; but
if he pleases to receive Antony into his friendship he will then want no other sup-
port. This is sensible and polite.&mdash;[For all its sense and politeness, no editor or
commentator has paid any attention to it.]
<P>61. <B>For vs you know</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 41. See <I>Text. Notes.</I>): Upon reading this
speech in former editions, the annotator was struck with seeing, in the last line but
one, a consequence drawn from premises that can never fairly be made to yield it:
he observ'd too, that the causal particle &lquo;For&rquo; was printed with a great letter; and&mdash;
concluding from both these circumstances, that no consequence was intended,&mdash;
thought rashly that &lquo;For&rquo; was a mistake, and to be amended by&mdash;<I>Or:</I> But, looking
into the folio's again, while this note was in penning, he found a word in the first
of them (overslipt in collation) that makes amendment unnecessary, and even injuri-
ous; for by reading, as that does,&mdash;&lquo;For us,&rquo; (<I>i. e.</I> As for us,) this member of the
speech has another aspect, and is so clear as to need no explaining.&mdash;[Which, being
interpreted, means that he withdraws the emendation in his text: <I>Or, as.</I>]

clause has been interpreted as a reference to &lquo;Harts Royal,&rquo; which, by the Forest
Laws, were suffered to roam where they pleased, protected from all molestation.
To the majority of Shakespeare's audience, every term in Venery was as familiar, I
suppose, as the names of vegetables. Can it be that here, in &lquo;right Royal&rquo; there is
an allusion, readily caught by the audience, to &lquo;harts royall,&rquo; the undisputed lords of
the forest?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>&lquo;spirit&rquo; does not here apply; and yet the verse seems to require it. See I, ii, 143.

<P>86. <B>And put your selfe vnder his shrowd</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 505): Lines with four
accents are, unless there is a pause in the middle of the line, <I>very</I> rare. The fol-
lowing, however, seem to have no more than four accents.&mdash;[Among the examples
then given by Abbott is found the present line (it has been printed as a separate line
in every edition since 1778), and it has seemed, apparently, in Abbott's eyes so
unmistakeably of four accents and pauseless withal, that he has queried if it be not
corrupt. But is it pauseless? Is Thidias so little of a diplomatist that he fails to $eel
his way? His keen eyes are reading every emotion that flits over Cleopatra's face.
He has won her ear. He has represented C&aelig;sar as almost cringing before her. He
has ventured perilously near to the assertion that she bears no love to Anthony, and
he has met no scornful denial; and now approaches the supreme moment, the sole
object of his mission, when, with her own consent, he is to get her into C&aelig;sar's power.
&lquo;And put yourself,&rquo; he slowly says, and pauses, watching, and would have said
&lquo;beyond temptation,&rquo; or &lquo;far from Anthony's power,&rquo; or anything else to that effect,
had he read a trace of cold suspicion in the eyes before him. But what he read so
far emboldened him that he then, and not till then, dared complete the sentence,&mdash;
&lquo;under his shrowd.&rquo; I venture to hope that a dramatic necessity is here shown for a
pause long enough to remove the line from Abbott's list of anomalies and to purge
it from corruption.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>86. <B>shrowd</B>] Derived from Anglo-Saxon <I>scr&umacr;d,</I> a garment, clothing. Secondly,
a winding sheet, etc. In the present line it means protection.&mdash;<I>Century Dictionary.</I>
[The only instance given by <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>) of this noun thus used. Compare
Milton, <I>Comus,</I> 147, where Comus bids his troop, &lquo;Run to your shrouds within these
brakes and trees.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>93. <B>from his all-obeying breath</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: &lquo;Doom&rquo; is declared rather by an
<I>all-commanding,</I> than an &lquo;all-obeying breath.&rquo; I suppose we ought to read&mdash;&lquo;all-
<I>obeyed</I> breath.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Craik</SC> (<I>Note on</I> &lquo;a labouring day,&rquo; <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.</I> I, i, 4): An expression
used by Cowper (in his verses composed in the name of Alexander Selkirk), &lquo;the
sound of the church-going bell&rquo; has been passionately reprobated by Wordsworth.
&lquo;The epithet <I>church-going</I> applied to a bell,&rquo; observes the critic (in an Appendix
upon the subject of <I>Poetic Diction</I>), &lquo;and that by so chaste a writer as Cowper, is an
instance of the strange abuses which poets have introduced into their language, till
they and their readers take them as matters of course, if they do not single them out
expressly as matters of admiration.&rquo; A <I>church-going bell</I> is merely a bell for church-
going; and the expression is constructed on the same principle with a thousand
others that are and always have been in familiar use;&mdash;such as a marauding or a
sight-seeing expedition, a banking or a house-building speculation, a fox-hunting
country, a lending library, a fishing village, etc. What would Wordsworth have
said to such a daring and extreme employment of the same form as we have in Shake-
speare, where he makes Cleopatra say, speaking of the victorious C&aelig;sar,&mdash;&lquo;From his
<I>all-obeying</I> breath I hear The doom of Egypt?&rquo; But these audacities of language
are of the very sould of poetry.
<P>96, 98. <B>Wisedome and Fortune . . . may shake it</B>] That is, if, when wisdom
and chance are opposed, the former ventures to exercise all its power, no mischance
can thwart it.
<P>98. <B>Giue me grace</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Grant me the favour.
<P>100. <B>Your C&aelig;sars Father</B>] Julius C&aelig;sar was the grand-uncle of Octavius. See
note on the relationship, III, vi, 7.
<P>101. <B>taking kingdomes in</B>] Compare, &lquo;Take in that Kingdome, and Infranchise
that,&rquo;&mdash;I, i, 35, or &lquo;He could so quickly cut the Ionian Sea And take in Troine.&rquo;&mdash;
III, vii, 28.

<P>119. <B>Whip him</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 499) finds that this line belongs to a class of &lquo;appar-
ent Alexandrines, which are sometimes regular verses of five accents preceded or
followed by a foot, more or less isolated, containing one accent.&rquo; &lquo;Whip him&rquo; is
the isolated foot here, as, I suppose, &lquo;what's her name&rquo; is the isolated one in line
121. It is the same old story; Anthony, even in the whiff and wind of foaming rage,
will pay no attention to his rhythm. . . . I now find that <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 497) has a differ-
ent scansion for the &lquo;apparent Alexandrine&rquo; of line 121. It is to be effected by &lquo;the
omission of unemphatic syllables,&rquo; thus:&mdash;&lquo;So s&aacute;ucy &verbar; with <I>the</I> h&aacute;nd &verbar; of sh&eacute; &verbar; here
&mdash;wh&aacute;t's &verbar; her n&aacute;me?&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>121. <B>hand of she heere</B>] &lquo;She&rquo; instead of <I>her</I> is used in supreme contempt.
Collier's dash before it is, I think, well devised. Hanmer's &lquo;<I>her</I> here&rquo; is to me
intolerable.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>122. <B>Since she was Cleopatra</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 132): Perhaps the meaning is
&lquo;Whip him for being saucy with this woman, <I>since</I> (though she is not now worthy
of the name) she once <I>was</I> (emphatical) Cleopatra.&rquo; Else &lquo;What is her new name
since she ceased to be Cleopatra?&rquo; If &lquo;since,&rquo; in the sense of <I>ago,</I> could be used
absolutely for <I>once,</I> a third interpretation would be possible: &lquo;What's her name?
<I>Once</I> she was Cleopatra.&rquo;
<P>127. <B>the Iacke</B>] <SC>Pope</SC> changed &lquo;the&rquo; to <I>this,</I> and has been followed by a majority
of editors. We have already had &lquo;this Jack&rquo; where Thidias is regarded as simply
an offensive menial without any qualification other than the contemptuous &lquo;this.&rquo;
But here he is &lquo;the Jack of C&aelig;sar,&rquo; and it is because he is C&aelig;sar's Jack that he is to
be made a servile messenger. There is enough contempt in the fact that he came as
C&aelig;sar's ambassador and returns as an errand-bearer. It seems to me that &lquo;the&rquo;
should be retained. The ictus falls on &lquo;Jack.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>133. <B>By one that lookes on Feeders?</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>, by an obliquity that will some-
times befall the keenest, supposed that this refers to Thidias, and that Anthony was
abused by a man who looked on while others were feeding; consequently he para-
phrased the words by: &lquo;one that waits at the table while others are eating,&rquo; which is
true enough if the words are taken literally, but the &lquo;one that looks on&rquo; (that is, looks
on <I>with favour</I>) is Cleopatra, and &lquo;feeders&rquo; are servants. When Corin offers to
establish Rosalind and Celia in their cottage he says, &lquo;I will your very faithfull
Feeder be.&rquo;&mdash;<I>As You Like It,</I> II, iv, 105.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>135. <B>boggeler</B>] <SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D.</I>): The verb <I>to boggle</I> is apparently formed
on <I>boggle,</I> a variant of <I>Bogle,</I> a spectre (such as horses are reputed to see). In later
times there has been a tendency to associate the word with <I>bungle,</I> which appears in
sense 4, and in the derivatives. 1. <I>intr.</I> To start with fright, to shy as a startled
horse, to take alarm, etc. 2. To raise scruples, hesitate, demur, stickle (<I>at,</I> etc.).
3. &lquo;To play fast or loose,&rquo;&mdash;Johnson; to palter, quibble, equivocate. 4. To fumble,
bungle, make a clumsy attempt. [Hence] <I>Boggler</I> is one who boggles, or hesitates;
a stickler [whereof the present line is quoted as an example].
<P>136-139. <B>when . . . errors</B>] That is, when we become hardened in our vicious
courses the wise gods so blind us that we lose the power of judging clearly concern-
ing our own moral defilement, and end with adoring our very errors. I am haunted
with the memory of a sentiment similar to this in the Old Testament, and mention it
in the trust that some one may be more fortunate than I in recalling it. We must
remember that <I>filth, filthy,</I> etc. are much stronger terms now than in the time of
Shakespeare.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>137. <B>our eyes</B>] Surely a debt of gratitude is due to Warburton for his punctuation
here, when we find a critic as keen as <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 305) &lquo;imagining,&rquo; that
Knight was &lquo;right&rquo; in substantially following the Folio. In the circumstances,

drop.</I> Whereas, under Warburton's corrected punctuation, the subject of &lquo;drop&rquo; is

<P>142, 143. <B>a Morsell, cold vpon . . . a Fragment</B>] <SC>Whiter</SC> (p. 136): The
rapid imagination of the unwary Poet, even when it is employed on sentiments the
most tender and pathetic, is sometimes imperceptibly entangled in a chain of imagery,
which is derived from the meanest subjects and the lowest occupations. [Hereupon
follow several illustrations of the way in which an image, drawn from the culinary
art, influences the train of thought; as here the word &lquo;morsel&rquo; leads to &lquo;fragment.&rquo;]
&lquo;In old English,&rquo; continues Whiter, &lquo;&ldquo;fragments&rdquo; and <I>broken</I> meat were synonymous.
In the vulgar translation of the Bible we have, &ldquo;and they took up of the <I>broken</I> meat
that was left seven baskets.&rdquo;&mdash;<I>Mark</I> viii, 8. In other places we find <I>fragments</I> used
for these <I>broken</I> relicts.&rquo;

<P>154, 155. <B>the hill of Basan, to out-roare The horned Heard</B>] Cruden's <I>Con-
cordance</I> gives the following references, where mention is made of the high hill of
Bashan and of its bulls:&mdash;<I>Psalms,</I> xxii, 12; lxviii, 15; <I>Ezekiel,</I> xxxix, 18; <I>Amos,</I>

<P>167. <B>The white hand</B>] Can it be that it is an unsavory commentary on the personal
cleanliness of the ladies of his time that Shakespeare lays so much stress, as some-
thing distinctive, on the &lquo;white hands&rquo; of his heroines? Rosaline has a &lquo;white hand;&rquo;
so has Rosalind, also Olivia; the Duke of Orleans in <I>Henry the Fifth</I> swears by his
&lquo;lady's white hand.&rquo; Hermione's hand was white, so also Helen of Troy's, hers
was &lquo;marvelous white&rquo;; the hand of Lucrece was a &lquo;perfect white,&rquo; and here in
the present line, by implication, Cleopatra has a &lquo;white hand.&rquo; The respective
references may be found in Bartlett's <I>Concordance.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>175. <B>Orbes</B>] This is not used for <I>orbit,</I> as has been stated, but refers to the nine
concentric crystalline spheres, in which, according to the Ptolomaic system, the seven
planets (of which the sun is one), the fixed stars, and the <I>Primum Mobile</I> moved
about the earth. What the <I>Primum Mobile</I> is, is a little vague, beyond the belief
that it moved and controlled the rest. Anthony's &lquo;good stars&rquo; were probably in the
eighth Orb of fixed stars; they were hardly likely to be in any of the planetary Orbs.
It is to this Ptolomaic theory that Cleopatra refers when she says &lquo;Oh Sunne Burne
the great Sphere thou mou'st in,&rquo;&mdash;IV, xv, 16, and again &lquo;His voyce was propertied
As all the tuned Spheres,&rquo;&mdash;V, ii, 102, in the next line Shakespeare used &lquo;Orbe&rquo;
for the whole world, as he does in <I>Twelfth Night</I> (and probably elsewhere) where
Feste says to Viola: &lquo;Foolery sir, does walke about the Orbe like the Sun,&rquo;&mdash;III, i,
39. Anthony says &lquo;shot their Fires,&rquo; to which there is a similar expression in <I>Mid.
N. Dream,</I> where Oberon says, &lquo;And certaine starres shot madly from their Spheares.&rquo;
&mdash;II, i, 158.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>180. <B>to quit me</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: To repay me this insult; to requite me.
<P>183. <B>our Terrene Moone</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 42): This will be understood by most
readers, of the moon in the heavens; which, they will think, might be call'd&mdash;
&lquo;terrene,&rquo; as being the earth's attendant, or satellite: But the speaker means it of
Cleopatra, who was call'd&mdash;the new Isis, and wore often the attires of that goddess;
[III, vi, 18] and she, in the Egyptian theology, was the same as the moon. It is to
this circumstance, in part, that Cleopatra herself alludes, in these words of hers,
&lquo;Now the fleeting moon No planet is of mine.&rquo;&mdash;[V, ii, 291.&mdash;It is Warburton who
says that Cleopatra in the last Act refers to Isis when she speaks of the &lquo;fleeting
moon,&rquo;&mdash;a thoroughly Warburtonian suggestion; and evidently the source whence

<P>and it be worth while, consider a little of it; for I have objections against it, and let
me know your opinion of it; and whether Shakespeare ever uses the word <I>discatter.</I>
&mdash;<SC>Theobald</SC>: From the corruption [of the Folios] both Dr Thirlby and I saw, we
must retrieve the word with which I have reform'd the text. . . . The congealing of
the water into hail he metaphorically calls <I>candying;</I> and it is an image he is fond
of. So in the next Act of this very play:&mdash;&lquo;The hearts, . . . do discandy, melt
their sweets,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>Knight</SC>: But how is &lquo;discandy&rquo; used in the next Act? &lquo;The
hearts . . . to whom I gave Their wishes, do <I>discandy,</I> melt their sweets, On blos-
soming C&aelig;sar.&rquo; The expletive <I>melt their sweets</I> gives us the peculiar and most forci-
ble meaning in which the word is here used. But the pelleted storm, which makes
Cleopatra's brave Egyptians lie graveless, is utterly opposed to the melting into
sweetness of the word <I>discandying.</I> See note in <I>The Mer. of Ven.</I> I, iii, upon the
passage: &lquo;other ventures he hath <I>squandered</I> abroad.&rquo; To <I>squander</I> is to scatter;
and so Dryden uses the word:&mdash;&lquo;They drive, they <I>squander</I> the huge Belgian fleet.&rquo;
To <I>dis-scander,</I> we believe then, is to <I>dis-squander. . . .</I> We, therefore, without hesi-
tation, restore the original &lquo;discandering,&rquo; in the sense of <I>dis-squandering.</I>&mdash;[<SC>Dyce</SC>
gives the reading of the Folios, and then, without quoting Knight's note, adds: &lquo;which
Mr Knight &ldquo;without hesitation restores.&rdquo;&rquo; After &lquo;restores,&rquo; Dyce indulges in a
good heartsome exclamation mark, which saves thought and does not spare feelings,
&mdash;Knight, gentlest of men, whose epitaph Douglas Jerrold said should be &lquo;Good
Night,&rquo; must, sooner or later, have known of this contemptuous treatment of his well-
considered opinion; he outlived Dyce.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>204. <B>threatning most Sea-like</B>] <SC>Thiselton</SC> (p. 21): The Navy is here regarded
as partaking of the nature of the Sea, so at home does it appear to be in that
element.
<P>205. <B>Where hast thou bin my heart? Dost thou heare Lady?</B>] To Anthony's
first question, which is that of a lover, jealous of every minute passed by his mistress
while out of sight, Cleopatra returns no answer. Whereupon follows the second
question, which would not have been asked had she not evidently been lost in thought.
During her interview with Thidias she had been true to Anthony and had encouraged
C&aelig;sar's ambassador only that she might discover the full extent of his master's plans.
But now this outburst of Anthony's Berserker wrath could not but have its effect on
her, and give her food for reflection. When the play opens, the question with her
was how she should keep Anthony by her side; now the question looms up whether
or not she should keep by the side of Anthony. C&aelig;sar's offer was perilously attrac-
tive. Small wonder that she was so abstracted that Anthony had to say, &lquo;Dost thou
hear, Lady?&rquo; She emerges from this reverie, true to her love, and from this hour
her fate and Anthony's were to be the same.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>207. <B>in Blood</B>] That is, in full vigour, in perfect condition, a phrase derived from
the chase. See, if need be, the note (in this edition) on &lquo;The Deare was (as you
know) sanguis in blood,&rquo;&mdash;<I>Love's Lab. Lost,</I> IV, ii, 4.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>209. <B>There's hope in't yet</B>] For the sake of the metre, <SC>Hanmer</SC>, with a fol-
lowing that is certainly respectable, changed this into the demure and deliberate
&lquo;There is hope in it yet.&rquo; Happily, no editor since Knight's day has thus trans-
gressed.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>211. <B>trebble-sinewed, hearted, breath'd</B>] <SC>Malone</SC> points out that &lquo;trebble&rquo;
qualifies both &lquo;hearted&rquo; and &lquo;breath'd.&rquo;

<P>230. <B>his pestilent Sythe</B>] <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>): &lquo;Pestilent sythe&rquo; is here equivalent
to the scythe of pestilence, the deaths occasioned by pestilence.&mdash;[That is, I will rival

<P>230. <B>Exeunt</B>] <SC>Vischer</SC> (p. 125): And thus Antony commits the extraordinary
blunder of allowing himself to be won over. But how? It is hardly conceivable
that he should have done so, after Cleopatra's baseness in yielding herself to C&aelig;sar
and in giving his messenger her hand to be kissed. The question arises whether or
not an intermediate scene be lost. The conclusion, that this is the case, is almost
inevitable. And why does Cleopatra here display so little charm? Did the Poet
intend that she should here appear insipid?&mdash;[Never insipid, but dazed, and think-
ing very fast. She is at the parting of the ways.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>231, 232. <B>Now hee'l . . . moode</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 306): Arrange, &lquo;Now
he'll outstare &verbar; The lightning. To be furious, is to be &verbar; <I>Affrighted</I> out of fear; and,
in that mood,&rquo; etc.
<P>233. <B>Estridge</B>] <SC>Douce</SC> (i, 435, note on &lquo;estridges,&rquo; <I>1 Hen. IV:</I> IV, i, 97):
Although it is admitted that the <I>ostrich</I> was occasionally denominated <I>estridge</I> by our
old writers, it is by no means certain that this bird is here meant. Throughout the
many observations on these difficult lines, it has been quite overlooked that <I>estridge</I>
signifies a <I>goshawk.</I> In this sense the word is used in [the present passage in <I>Ant.
&amp; Cleop.</I>]. It would be absurd to talk of a dove pecking an ostrich; the allusion is
to the practice of flying falcons at pigeons. Falconers are often called <I>ostregers</I> and
<I>ostringers</I> in the old books of falconry, and elsewhere. <I>Estridge</I> for <I>ostrich</I> or <I>ostridge</I>
is a corrupt spelling that crept into our language at the commencement of Queen
Elizabeth's reign, and it appears that after that period the two words were very often
confounded together, and used one for the other.&mdash;<SC>Madden</SC> (p. 155, footnote):
Douce was the first to point out that Shakespeare wrote of the estridge or goshawk,
not of the ostrich [in the present passage]. The same idea was present to the mind
of Clifford when he thus taunted Richard, Duke of York: &lquo;So cowards fight when

<P>common use was known as an estridge.&mdash;[On the other hand, <SC>Bradley</SC> (<I>N. E. D.</I>)

as <I>goshawk</I> is mentioned by him. Every reference that he gives clearly refers to
the ostrich, except the present, and two others, of which one is dated 1450, and the
second, dated 1649, is doubtful. The derivation which <SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D.</I>) gives
of <I>Ostreger, Ostringer,</I> has no reference to <I>Estridges,</I> but the word comes, con-
clusively, from Asturia, in Spain. The image of a dove in its fright pecking at an
African ostrich is to me so infinitely absurd that I would welcome any bird or beast
that can prove a more rational substitute. The case of the ostrich is by no means
improved when the quality is noted for which it is chiefly distinguished in the days
of Shakespeare. Some of the examples in the <I>N. E. D.</I> of the use of <I>estridge</I> refer
to its plumes, but the majority to a comfortable and enviable digestion, which success-
fully copes with nails and horse-shoes. It is hardly too much to say that in any
allusion by Shakespeare to an ostrich, an audience of his day would be at once
reminded of the bird's voracity, and, consequently, should a dove peck at an ostrich,
the allusion would be at once interpreted as referring to a defence, not of eggs or
young, but of nails or horse-shoes. After all, the question is of small moment. It is
enough that Enobarbus, after his profoundly true saying that &lquo;to be furious Is to be
frighted out of fear,&rquo;&mdash;one of those &lquo;jewels, five words long,&rquo; which sparkle for ever,
&mdash;draws his illustration from the image of a dove, the type of timidity, which attacks,
under the influence of fear, that from which it would otherwise fly in terror,&mdash;this,
I prefer to believe, is a hawk, the dove's most terrible foe.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>7. <B>I haue many other wayes to dye</B>] <SC>Upton</SC> (p. 240): What a reply is this to
Antony's challenge? 'tis acknowledging he should die under the unequal combat.
But if we read, &lquo;<I>He hath</I> many other ways to die; mean time <I>I</I> laugh at his chal-
lenge.&rquo; By this reading we have poignancy, and the very repartee of C&aelig;sar.&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC>
(i, 42): The Plutarch that Shakespeare dealt with, speaking of Antony's challenge,
says,&mdash;&lquo;<I>C&aelig;sar</I> aunswered him, that he had many other wayes to dye then so,&rquo; which
words are ambiguous, and might be taken wrong by the Poet, and occasion that reply
which is in all the editions except the Oxford one [<I>i. e.</I> Hanmer's]: But this is so
unfit a reply to be made by C&aelig;sar, that the editor could not but acquiesce in the
Oxford correction; which, besides that it is not violent, gives us the true reply as
found in the original. &lquo;I&rquo; in the next line [see <I>Text. Notes</I>], is taken from the
same edition: but the line should be further amended by the insertion of another
word,&mdash;<I>fond,</I> between &lquo;his&rquo; and &lquo;challenge&rquo;; otherwise the metre will not proceed
right.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: I think this emendation [<I>He hath</I>] deserves to be received.&mdash;
<SC>Farmer</SC>: Most indisputably this is the sense of Plutarch, and given so in the modern
translations, but Shakespeare was misled by the ambiguity of the old one: &lquo;C&aelig;sar
answered him, that he had many other ways to die, than so.&rquo;&mdash;[<SC>Dyce</SC> quotes with
approval this note of Farmer.]&mdash;<SC>Maginn</SC> (<I>Fraser's Maga.</I> Sept. 1839, p. 264): I
am not quite so sure that Shakespeare wrote [this passage] as we have it. [Maginn
here quotes it, but reads line 9 as &lquo;C&aelig;sar must <I>know.</I>&rquo;] Taking the repartee <I>liter-
ally</I> as it appears in North, Shakespeare's ordinary practice may afford a better read-
ing: &lquo;Let the old ruffian know &verbar; He hath many other ways to die than so. &verbar; Mean-
time, I laugh at's challenge. <I>Mec.</I> C&aelig;sar must know,&rquo; &verbar; . . . Is it any very violent
conjecture to imagine that Shakespeare had seized the spirit of Plutarch and had
written the <I>exact</I> words of North, without alteration of a letter, except the necessary
change of ha<I>th</I> for ha<I>d,</I> and that some printing or editorial blundering has jumbled
the pronouns. The supposition is in complete conformity with Shakespeare's prac-
tice, and it removes the metrical difficulty.&mdash;[It is patent that North's translation is

<P>4. <B>No?</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 42): &lquo;No.&rquo; So is this monosyllable pointed in the three
latter moderns [Theobald, Hanmer, Warburton], and rightly; for this sullen affirm-
ative negation expresses admirably the state of the speaker's mind at this time.
<P>6. <B>twenty times of better fortune</B>] For other instances of the &lquo;transposition of
adverbs,&rquo; such as &lquo;of twenty times better,&rquo; see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 420, and Shakespeare,
<I>passim.</I>
<P>11. <B>Woo't thou</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 241): <I>Thou</I> is often omitted after <I>would'st,</I> or per-
haps merged, in the form &lquo;woo't,&rquo; as &lquo;wilt thou&rquo; becomes <I>wilta.</I> Sometimes <I>thou</I> is
inserted [as here]. See IV, xv, 76.&mdash;<SC>Franz</SC> (&sect; 20 a): The sporadic forms <I>wot,
wo't, woo't</I> for <I>wilt,</I> and <I>wooll</I> for <I>will,</I> correspond to the Middle English <I>wolt</I> and
<I>wol;</I> in the following list [containing the present passage] the <I>l</I> is suppressed, as in
the present English <I>would.</I>
<P>12. <B>Take all</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Let the survivor take all. No composition; victory or
death.

the sense in which it is uttered every day by every mouth, elegant and vulgar; yet
Warburton, in his rage of Gallicism, changes it to <I>traits.</I>

is not &ldquo;me&rdquo; implied in the old text?&rquo;&mdash;<SC>R. G. White</SC> (<I>Studies,</I> p. 371) also quotes
Walker's question, and replies, &lquo;Not at all. The sense is perfect, like the rhythm,
as anyone may see.&rquo;

<P>38. <B>Perchance</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 43): This line is not one bit the better, for perfect-

umph, taunting. 4. Repeated <I>ho! ho!</I> or <I>ho! ho! ho!</I> it expresses derision or
derisive laughter. As in Puck's call to Demetrius: &lquo;Ho, ho, ho; Coward, why
com'st thou not?&rquo;&mdash;<I>Mid. N. D.</I> III, ii, 421.&mdash;[<SC>Boswell</SC> says that this laughter of
Anthony, like Cleopatra's &lquo;Ha, ha, give me to drink mandagora,&rquo;&mdash;I, v, 4, is hysterical,
which, if true (and I doubt hysterics in both cases), gives us no clue as to the tone in
which it was uttered. To me, it sounds like an honest laugh, merely somewhat
forced, with no tinge of derision in it,&mdash;how could there be any derision or con-
tempt, when it is followed by, &lquo;Grace grow where these drops fall!&rquo; Under &lquo;Ho,

<P>25. <B>whom Anthony loued</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 43): The words are right, and should
not have been chang'd by the moderns into&mdash;<I>who lov'd Antony;</I> for thus the author
who furnish'd them,&mdash;&lquo;they thought that it was the god unto whom Antonius bare
singular devotion:&rquo; But the Poet has put a wrong god, and perhaps by design; for
Bacchus, the god his author intended, could not stand in his verse along with these
words: Hercules, he knew, was honour'd by Antony, as well as Bacchus; and he
might think it a matter indifferent, which god these same signs were ascrib'd to: 'tis
observable, he speaks only of &lquo;musick&rquo;; and has omitted the other signs mention'd,
which determine them to have proceeded from Bacchus.

<P>6. <B>Come good Fellow</B>] <SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. ii): That the word which has dropt out of
the folio in this line was <I>my</I> (Rowe's addition) is proved by Antony's next speech
but one, &lquo;Seest thou, <I>my good fellow?</I>&rquo;
<P>6. <B>put thine Iron on</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: &lquo;Thine iron&rquo; is the iron which thou hast in
thy hand, that is, Antony's armour.&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (<I>Notes,</I> etc. p. 498): Surely &lquo;thine&rquo;
ought to be as the MS renders it, &lquo;Put <I>mine</I> iron on.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Anon.</SC> (<I>Blackwood,</I> Oct.
1853, p. 468, thus answers Collier): Not at all; either word will do; but &lquo;thine&rquo; is
more consonant with ordinary usage. A gentleman asks his butler, not &lquo;have you
cleaned <I>my</I> plate?&rquo; but &lquo;have you cleaned <I>your</I> plate?&rquo; meaning my plate of which
<I>you</I> have the charge. Eros had the charge of Antony's armour.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. ii):
[&lquo;Thine&rquo; of the Folio, with Malone's note,] is an utterly improbable reading and
explanation, since just before Antony has twice said &lquo;<I>mine</I> armour.&rquo; Nor, as the
context shows, is Antony here speaking of <I>Eros's armour,</I>&mdash;he afterwards bids Eros
&lquo;put on his defences.&rquo;&mdash;[The reason given by Dyce which renders &lquo;thine&rquo; &lquo;utterly
improbable&rquo; is to me precisely the reason which renders it extremely probable. It
would be &lquo;damnable iteration&rquo; indeed, to have called out &lquo;mine armour&rquo; three times.
Is it not universal that an exclamation or a question is varied at the second or third
repetition of its substance? It is, to me, eminently natural that Anthony should have
changed his twice-uttered impatient summons, &lquo;mine armour,&rquo; into &lquo;thine iron.&rquo; If
&lquo;thine&rquo; is to be changed to <I>mine</I> why should not, by Dyce's rule, &lquo;iron&rquo; be changed
to <I>armour?</I> An adequate reason why &lquo;thine&rquo; refers to Anthony's armour, and not
Eros's, is given, I think, by &lquo;Anon.&rquo; who, it has been said, was Lettsom.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>12. <B>Sooth-law</B>] <SC>Earle</SC> (&sect; 197): &lquo;La&rquo; is that interjection which in modern
English is spelt <I>lo.</I> It was used, in Saxon times, both as an emotional cry and as
a sign of the respectful vocative . . . The &lquo;la&rquo; of Saxon times has none of the
indicating or pointing force which <I>lo</I> now has, and which fits it to go so naturally
with an adverb of locality, as &lquo;Lo here,&rquo; or &lquo;Lo there.&rquo; While <I>lo</I> became the liter-
ary form of the word, &lquo;la&rquo; has still continued to exist more obscurely, at least down
to a recent date, even if it be not still in use. &lquo;La&rquo; may be regarded as a sort of
feminine to <I>lo.</I>&mdash;[Also see <I>Twelfth Night,</I> III, iv, 104; <I>Love's Lab. Lost,</I> V, ii,
460; <I>Wint. Tale,</I> II, iii, 64, where the foregoing note substantially appears.]
<P>12. <B>Thus it must bee</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii): These words have usually been
assigned to Cleopatra, but it appears by the MS that they belong to Antony, who is
instructing Cleopatra, and who adds &lquo;well, well,&rquo; when what he wished has been
accomplished by her.&mdash;[Cleopatra has made one blunder, and then having adjusted
a piece of armour correctly, exclaims exultingly: &lquo;Thus it <I>must</I> be!&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>15. <B>Briefely Sir</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: That is, <I>quickly,</I> sir.&mdash;[Or does it not mean, &lquo;in a
minute&rquo;? or &lquo;presently,&rquo; as we now use the word?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>49. <B>Determine</B>] <SC>Charles Allen</SC> gives a valuable chapter wherein many instances
are gathered of Shakespeare's legal knowledge whereto parallel instances are to be
found in contemporary writers; from which the conclusion fairly follows that Shake-
speare's legal knowledge, on which much stress has been laid, is not more extraordi-
nary than that of his eminent contemporaries. On p. 55 Allen notes that &lquo;&ldquo;Deter-
mine&rdquo; is twice used by Shakespeare in its legal sense as signifying the end, namely,
in <I>Coriolanus</I> (V, iii, 119): &ldquo;I purpose not to wait on fortune till These wars deter-
mine.&rdquo; [and in the present passage.] A similar use is found in Jonson's <I>Alchemist:</I>
&ldquo;For here Determines the indenture tripartite.&rdquo; (V, ii.) Donne also, in <I>Anatomy
of the World,</I> says: &ldquo;Measures of times are all determined.&rdquo; (I, &sect; 40.)&rquo;
<P>50. <B>Then Anthony; but now</B>] <SC>Kreyssig</SC> (ii, 73): To this woman Anthony
gave more than any man should dare to give: his honour. He cannot complain if
he is taken at his own valuation. The recollection of the flight of the &lquo;doting mal-
lard&rquo; from the sea-fight, although it cannot morally justify Cleopatra's faithlessness,
makes it &aelig;sthetically endurable. When she is arming him for his last battle, her
determination is already taken. She knows well enough that what must here decide
is not the heroic courage of a warrior, but wary judgement and essential superiority.
But, at that very moment, her fine, &aelig;sthetic temperament pays homage to the man who
is even in that instant betrayed.&mdash;[The <SC>Editor</SC> begs leave to remark that he is not
responsible for the opinions of commentators.]

<P>4. <B>Our will is Anthony be tooke aliue</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: It is observable with
what judgment Shakspeare draws the character of Octavius. Antony was his hero;
so the other was not to shine: yet being an historical character, there was a necessity
to draw him <I>like.</I> But the ancient historians, his flatterers, had delivered him down
so fair, that he seems ready cut and dried for a hero. Amidst these difficulties Shak-
speare has extricated himself with great address. He has admitted all those great
strokes of his character as he found them, and yet has made him a very unamiable
character, deceitful, mean-spirited, narrow-minded, proud, and revengeful.
