<P>7. <B>The time of vniuersall peace is neere</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 44): The Poet had not
this from his Plutarch, but from ecclesiastical histories (probably) or some bible com-
mentator: The return of Augustus to Rome was signaliz'd by three triumphs in the
course of one month, for victories obtain'd in Dalmatia, at Actium, and this at Alex-
andria: after which, he shut up the temple of Janus, in token that all wars were
over; an event which those histories dwell upon, as the precursor of Christ's birth,
according to prophesy.
<P>8. <B>Proue this</B>] For instances where the inversion of the subject indicates a con-
ditional sentence, see <SC>Franz</SC>, &sect; 487, <I>Anmerkung,</I> 4. c.
<P>8. <B>the three nook'd world</B>] On this puzzling phrase we get but small light from
the commentators. It is not difficult to draw an explanation from the &lquo;depths of one's
consciousness,&rquo; as Theobald and Capell seem to have drawn from theirs, and say, with
them, that according to primitive geography there were but three countries in the world:
Europe, Asia, and Africa, and that these made the &lquo;three angles.&rquo; But three angles
do not make three nooks; they may make only two. From Malone to the present day
there has been quoted, as parallel to the present passage, the closing lines in <I>King John,</I>
where the Bastard says, &lquo;Come the three corners of the world in arms, And we shall
shock them.&rquo; But, even in this passage, what the &lquo;three corners&rquo; are, is very doubtful;
it has been even suggested that they may have been the Pope, France, and Spain.
Whatever they were, England is supposed to be the fourth corner, which alone, I think,
removes the parallelism with &lquo;three nook'd.&rquo; Again it has been surmised that the
present allusion is to the fact that the world had been divided among C&aelig;sar, Anthony,
and Lepidus. If this be so, it is extremely difficult, to me at least, to imagine why
C&aelig;sar, Anthony, and Lepidus should be termed &lquo;nooks.&rquo; There is, however, one pos-
sible source of information, namely, in Shakespeare's supposed familiarity with the
Emblem writers. The proofs of this familiarity which <SC>Green</SC> has gathered on this sub-
ject are, when taken singly, of doubtful value, but become respectable by accumulation.
On p. 350 of his <I>Shakespeare and the Emblem Writers,</I> we find the following: &lquo;Curious
it is to note how slowly the continent which Columbus discovered became fully recog-
nised as an integral portion of &ldquo;the inhabited world.&rdquo; . . . Brucioli's <I>Trattato della
Sphera,</I> Venice, 1543, . . . in dividing the globe into climates, does not take a single
instance except from what is named the Old World; in fact the New World of America
is never mentioned. Somewhat later, in 1564, when Sambucus published his <I>Emblems,</I>
and presented <I>Symbols of the parts of the Inhabited Earth,</I> he gave only three [parts:
Europe, Asia, and Africa, as comprising the whole world.] . . . Shakespeare's geog-
raphy, however, though at times defective, extended further than its &ldquo;symbols&rdquo; by
Sambucus. He refers to America and the Indies in <I>Com. of Err.</I> III, ii, 131, and
to the East and West Indies in <I>The Merry Wives,</I> I, iii, 64. Yet in agreement with
the map of Sambucus, [where] the three Capes prominent upon it, are the Gibraltar
Rock, the Cape of Good Hope, and that of Malacca, Shakespeare, on other occasions,
ignores America and all its western neighbours. At the consultation by Octavius,
Antony, and Lepidus about the division of the Roman Empire, Antony, on the
exit of Lepidus, asks, &ldquo;is it fit, The three-fold world divided, he should stand One
</CC>

map of Sambucus presents only three great nooks in the world, one is formed by the
Mediterranean, a second by the Red Sea, and a third is hard to identify, but is possi-
bly the Bay of Bengal. According to this small map or Emblem (for the three
divisions of the earth are dominated by animals), the world can assuredly be styled
&lquo;three nooked.&rquo; Whether or not Shakespeare ever saw it is a question which is open
to all the doubt that anyone may choose to apply to it. That Shakespeare was, at
least, familiar with Emblems has very lately received a conspicuous proof by the dis-
covery of a payment to him and to Burbadge for designing an impresa for the sixth
Earl of Rutland.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>9. <B>Shall beare the Oliue freely</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: That is, shall spring up every-
where spontaneously and without culture.&mdash;<SC>M. Mason</SC>: To &lquo;bear&rquo; does not mean
to <I>produce,</I> but to carry; and the meaning is, that the world shall then enjoy the
blessings of peace, of which olive-branches were the emblem. The success of
Augustus could not so change the nature of things as to make the olive-tree grow
without culture in all climates, but it shut the gates of the temple of Janus. This
explanation is supported by the following lines from <I>2 Hen. IV:</I> IV, iv, 87, where
Westmoreland says, &lquo;There is not now a rebel's sword unsheath'd, But peace puts
forth her olive every where.&rquo;

&lquo;Go and enjoin Agrippa to plant those that,&rquo; etc.

from adequate to Enobarbus's deep emotion. And yet I have none better to offer,
except by hermeneutical torture. To give it force, Dr Johnson has to add, &lquo;so that
it will quickly break,&rquo; but this is wholly his addition, and is not, of necessity, inherent
in the simple word &lquo;blows.&rquo; Unquestionably, Shakespeare frequently uses &lquo;blow&rquo;
in the sense of <I>swell, puff up,</I> etc.; and there is a passage in <I>Lear</I> which seems
strongly to strengthen this sense in the present sentence. It is where Lear says, &lquo;O,
how this mother swells up toward my heart!&rquo;&mdash;(II, iv, 54.) And yet I am not
satisfied. The hermeneutical torture, as pedantic schoolmen would say, to which I
referred, is based on the right to use any extreme, legitimate interpretation. Now
Shakespeare does, once or twice, use &lquo;blow&rquo; in the sense of <I>break, shatter,</I> as the
result of an explosion. Hamlet says, &lquo;'tis the sport to have the enginer Hoist with

<P>7. <B>Scarrus</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 45): It is worth remarking, concerning this Scarus,&mdash;
that his name is of the Poet's invention, and himself a person of his creating: One
(he saw) must be had, to be about Antony when deserted by Enobarbus and the
rest, and no fit one was presented by story: he therefore had recourse to invention;
and by bringing in his foundling before among Antony's other followers at the battle
of Actium, gives his introduction in this scene an easy appearance, and hides it's

<P>10. <B>With clowts about their heads</B>] <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>) asks whether or not
&lquo;clouts&rquo; be here &lquo;equivalent to cuffs,&rquo;&mdash;a question which surely requires no answer
from any English reader. &lquo;Clouts&rquo; here are bandages for wounds.
<P>12. <B>that was like a T</B>] <SC>Delius</SC>: We must suppose that the T was lying on its
side, T, and by one or two more slashes was changed to an H.&mdash;[This is certainly
ingenious, and the only attempt I have found to explain the conversion of the letter
T into a letter H. <SC>Staunton</SC> (<I>Athen&aelig;um,</I> 26 Apr. 1873), however, gives the true
interpretation, namely, that there was no actual conversion of one letter into another;
the pun consists in that Scarus had received a T-shaped wound which, &lquo;by being
undressed and exposed to the air, had begun to pain him.&rquo; The noun <I>ache</I> and the
letter H were pronounced alike; see the next note.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>13. <B>now 'tis made an H</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC> (Note on <I>Much Ado,</I> III, iv, 52): Hey-

&lquo;H is worst among letters in the crosse row, For if thou finde him either in thine
elbow, In thine arme, or leg, in any degree, In thine head, or teeth, in thy toe or
knee, Into what place soever H may pike him, Where euer thou finde ache, thou
shalt not like him.&rquo;&mdash;[The verb was pronounced <I>ake;</I> the noun <I>aitch,</I> like the letter,
or, possibly, <I>atch.</I> For a fuller discussion of this pronunciation, see, if need be, <I>The
Tempest,</I> I, ii, 433; <I>Much Ado,</I> III, iv, 52, of this edition.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>20. <B>Ride on the pants triumphing</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: Alluding to an Admiral

202, after quoting the foregoing note): There are some points which our Professed
Critic should never touch; for, whenever he does, he only shews his ignorance about
them. He quite mistakes the nature of the &lquo;pants&rquo; here, as well as the &lquo;chain&rquo;
above. But why <I>triumphing</I> like an admiral ship after a storm? I thought victories
gained, not storms escaped, had been the matter of triumphs; and, I suppose, other
ships dance on the billows, just after the same manner as an Admiral's does.
<P>24. <B>Mine Nightingale</B>] This is an example, even more striking than &lquo;your
reproof&rquo; (II, ii, 141), of confusion of sound in the ear of the compositor, who failed
to detect, in the pronunciation of his reader, the difference between &lquo;my nightingale&rquo;
and &lquo;mine nightingale.&rquo; See also &lquo;Unarme Eros,&rquo; IV, xiv, 45; and &lquo;mine Nailes,&rquo;
V, ii, 268; &lquo;hither,&rquo; III, vi, 14; &lquo;your so,&rquo; III, iv, 27, etc.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>24. <B>Nightingale</B>] <SC>Deighton</SC>: A compliment to the fascination of her voice.

<P>6. <B>a shrew'd one</B>] <SC>Craik</SC> (p. 141): Both <I>to shrew</I> and <I>to beshrew</I> are used by
our old writers in the sense of to curse, which latter verb, again, also primarily and
properly (from the A.S. <I>cursan</I> or <I>cursian</I>) signifies to vex or torment. Now, it is
a strong confirmation of the derivation of <I>shrewd</I> from the verb <I>to shrew</I> that we find
<I>shrewd</I> and <I>curst</I> applied to the disposition and temper by our old writers in almost,
or rather in precisely, the same sense. Shakespeare himself affords us several
instances. Thus, in <I>Much Ado About Nothing</I> (II, i), Leonato having remarked to
Beatrice, &lquo;By my troth, niece, thou wilt never get a husband if thou be so <I>shrewd</I> of
thy tongue,&rquo; his brother Antonio adds, assentingly, &lquo;In faith, she's too <I>curst.</I>&rquo; So, in
<I>A Midsummer Night's Dream</I> (III, ii), Helena, declining to reply to a torrent of abuse
from Hermia, says, &lquo;I was never <I>curst;</I> I have no gift at all in <I>shrewishness.</I>&rquo; And
in <I>The Taming of the Shrew</I> (I, ii), first we have Hortensio describing Katharine
to his friend Petruchio as &lquo;intolerable <I>curst,</I> and <I>shrewd,</I> and froward,&rquo; and then we
have Katharine, the shrew, repeatedly designated &lquo;Katharine the <I>curst.</I>&rquo; At the end
of the Play she is called &lquo;a curst shrew,&rquo; that is, as we might otherwise express it, an
ill-tempered shrew. . . . As it is in words that ill-temper finds the readiest and most
frequent vent, the terms <I>curst,</I> and <I>shrew,</I> and <I>shrewd,</I> and <I>shrewish</I> are often used
with a special reference to the tongue. But sharpness of tongue, again, always
implies some sharpness of understanding as well as of temper. The terms <I>shrewd</I>
and <I>shrewdly,</I> accordingly, have come to convey usually something of both of these
qualities,&mdash;at one time, perhaps, most of the one, at another of the other. The sort
of ability that we call <I>shrewdness</I> never suggests the notion of anything very high:
the word has always a touch in it of the sarcastic or disparaging. But, on the other
hand, the disparagement which it expresses is never without an admission of some-
thing also that is creditable or flattering. Hence it has come to pass that a person
does not hesitate to use the terms in question even of himself and his own judg-
ments or conjectures. We say, &lquo;I shrewdly suspect or guess.&rquo; or &lquo;I have a shrewd
guess, or suspicion,&rquo; taking the liberty of thus asserting or assuming our own intel-
lectual acumen under cover of the modest confession at the same time of some little
ill-nature in the exercise of it. Even when <I>shrewd</I> is used without any personal
reference, the sharpness which it implies is generally, if not always, a more or less
unpleasant sharpness. &lquo;This last day was a shrewd one to us,&rquo; says one of the
Soldiers of Octavius to his comrade, in [the present passage], after the encounter in
which they had been driven back by Antony near Alexandria.

<P>39. <B>Drummes demurely wake</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: That is, &lquo;demurely,&rquo; for <I>sol-
emnly.</I>&mdash;[In the propriety of this definition the Shakespearian world seems to be
gradually acquiescing, after a temporary flurry started in 1853 by the publication of
the MS emendations in <SC>Collier's</SC> Second Folio. The change, therein prescribed,
from &lquo;demurely&rquo; to <I>do early,</I> coupled with Collier's assertion that the adverb
&lquo;demurely&rquo; &lquo;is surely ill suited to the sound of drums,&rquo; seems to have demurely
wakened the sleeping critics, always so zealously at hand to help Shakespeare express
his thoughts and endow his purposes with words. The <I>Text. Notes</I> show the result.
As none of these emendations has been approved by anybody but the emenders them-
selves, it seems needless to rehearse the arguments by which they are maintained.
The latest interpretation, fully in accord with Warburton's, is authoritative, and with
many critics will close all discussion once and for ever. Dr <SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D. s. v.</I>
&dagger; b.) thus defines &lquo;demurely&rquo; in the present passage: &lquo;In a subdued manner.&rquo; Why
&lquo;demurely&rquo; is thus appropriate is set forth by Dr <SC>B. Nicholson</SC> (<I>Notes &amp; Qu.</I> IV.
viii, 41): C&aelig;sar, like Antony, would renew the combat, and taking advantage of
&lquo;the shining&rquo; of the cloudless night, and a precaution from it, ordered the embattl-
ing of his forces to begin as early as 2 <SC>a.m.</SC> It would, therefore, only be in accord
with his careful and exact discipline that any notes of preparation should, in pres-
ence of a hostile and almost victorious force, be made in a subdued tone. Other-
wise the enemy might have unnecessary information and forewarning, or even make
such notes of preparation their signal of attack, and come upon him while defiling
out of camp and before his line of battle had been taken up. But there is yet
another and second meaning which may be given to the word <I>demure.</I> If not now,
yet at all events in 1814 the drum-reveill&eacute; of the non-Latin races was not a lively,
merry, or clamorous din, but a measured and somewhat solemn beat; and, judging
from this and from the discipline of Gustavus Adolphus and other considerations, it
seems not unlikely that the drum-reveill&eacute; of the Low Country, or German Protestant
armies of Elizabeth's time, was of the same character, even if it were not founded on

<P>a psalm tune. In one of those inartificial touches of reality and circumstance which
give such a charm to the tales of Erckmann and Chatrian, the soldier-conscript of
the first Napoleon (<I>Waterloo,</I> ch. xviii) incidentally tells us&mdash;&lquo;Notre diane com-
mence toujours avant celle des Prussiens, des Russes, des Autrichiens, et de tous nos
ennemis; c'est comme le chant de l'alouette au tout petit jour. Les autres, avec leurs
larges tambours, commencent apr&egrave;s leurs roulements sourds, qui vous donnent des
id&eacute;es d'enterrement.&rquo; (&lquo;The others, with their big drums, begin later, and their
dull-sounding rolls awake in one the remembrance of a burial.&rquo;) Now this I take to
be a perfect gloss on <I>demurely</I> in the sense of solemnly, as explained by Warburton.
But the one meaning does not exclude the other, and both would be easily under-
stood by an audience, since they were interpreted by actual beat of drum within.
This piece of stage arrangement furnishes, moreover, another important argument in
their favour. Even an inferior artist would not foolishly mar with the ill accord of
a lively rataplan the close of so touching and effective a scene. Nor could Shake-
speare do so; but he would make use of that which he knew would harmonise with
and heighten the feelings he had produced, and the measured, low-toned and far-off
beats that demurely woke the sleepers were heard as the knell of one whom the hand
of death had already raught, the funeral march for the erring but repentant soldier.

<P>9, 10. <B>They haue put forth the Hauen: Where their,</B> etc.] <SC>M. Mason</SC>: I

sense. As the passage stands, Antony appears to say, &lquo;that they could best discover
the appointment of the enemy at the haven after they had left it.&rquo; But if we add
the words <I>Further on,</I> his speech will be consistent: &lquo;As they have put out of the

next page but one he says&mdash;&lquo;Where yonder pine does stand, I shall discover all.&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Malone</SC> [reading, <I>Let's seek a spot</I> after &lquo;Hauen:&rquo;]: The defect of the metre in
the old copy shows that some words were accidentally omitted. In that copy there
is a colon at &lquo;haven&rquo;&mdash;an additional proof that something must have been said by
Antony, connected with the next line, and relative to the place where the enemy
might be reconnoitred. The <I>haven itself</I> was not such a place; but rather some hill
from which the haven and the ships newly put forth could be viewed. What Antony
says upon his re-entry, proves decisively that he had not gone to the haven, nor had
any thoughts of going thither. &lquo;I see (says he), they have not yet joined; but I'll
now choose a more convenient station near yonder pine, and I shall discover all.&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Knight</SC>: The sentence,&mdash;&lquo;Order for sea is given They have put forth the haven,&rquo;&mdash;
is parenthetical. Omit it, and Antony says, that the foot soldiers shall stay with
him, upon the hills adjoining the city, &lquo;Where their appointment we may best dis-
cover.&rquo; The editors allow nothing for the rapidity of utterance, and the modulation
with which such parenthetical passages are given upon the stage; and they, therefore,
corrupt the text by the feeble addition of <I>Let's seek a spot,</I> etc. This is Malone's
cobbling.&mdash;[<SC>Collier, Staunton</SC>, and <SC>Singer</SC> approve and adopt this interpretation,
the first two with acknowledgement, the last, <I>more suo,</I> without.]&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC>: I think

call certain poor women, which ever lay in cabins not far off, to do the household

Kinsmen,</I> I, i,&mdash;&lquo;Lend us a knee; <I>But</I> touch the ground for us no longer time,&rquo; etc.

<P>1. <B>Alarum afarre off, as at a Sea-fight</B>] Since printing the note on III, x, 3, I
have found that <SC>Gifford</SC> (<I>Silent Woman,</I> IV, ii) asserts that fights at sea &lquo;were

<P>26, 27. <B>That pannelled me at heeles, to whom I gaue Their wishes, do
dis-Candie, melt their sweets,</B> etc.] <SC>Whiter</SC> (p. 138): This passage and the
succeeding quotations are well worthy of the reader's attention:&mdash;&lquo;No, let the

&lquo;Why, what a <I>candy</I> deal of courtesy This <I>fawning greyhound</I> then did proffer
me!&rquo;&mdash;<I>1 Hen. IV:</I> I, iii, 251. These passages are very singular. The curious
reader will observe that the <I>fawning obsequiousness</I> of an animal, or an attendant, is
connected with the word <I>candy.</I> The cause of this strange association I am unable
to discover; though the reader must know but little of the human mind&mdash;of Shak-
speare&mdash;or even of the ordinary doctrine of <I>chances,</I> if he imagines that these matters
were in <I>four</I> passages connected by <I>accident.</I> When the reader shall be convinced
respecting the truth of this observation; his curiosity will be much gratified by the
following lines from the <I>Tempest;</I> in which he will perceive that the same associ-
ation still occupied the mind of the Poet, though a single <I>word</I> only is apparent, which
relates to one portion of the preceding metaphor. &lquo;<I>Seb.</I> But, for your conscience?
<I>Ant.</I> Ay, sir; where lies that? if 'twere a <I>kibe,</I> 'Twould put me to my slipper: but
I feel not This deity in my bosom: twenty consciences, That stand 'twixt me and
Milan, <I>candied</I> be they And <I>melt</I> ere they molest!&rquo;&mdash;<I>Tempest,</I> II, i, 275. Surely
the reader cannot doubt but that the introduction of the word <I>kybe</I> is to be referred to
the former expressions, &lquo;page thy <I>heels,</I>&rquo;&mdash;&lquo;spaniel'd me at <I>heels,</I>&rquo;&mdash;&lquo;spaniel'd me at <I>heels,</I>&rquo; though it is applied
to a very different metaphor. Let me add, that the quaintness of the imagery is an
argument for the remoteness of the original. Though I cannot explain to the reader
the cause of this association between the term <I>candy</I> and the <I>fawning of a dog;</I> I
can diminish his surprise respecting its existence, by producing another case, which
contains a direct union between this animal and an idea equally remote; and which
certainly would have appeared altogether as extraordinary, unless we had possessed
a clue to unravel the mystery. What should we say, were we to find in an ancient
Greek writer a combination between the <I>fawning of a dog</I> and the <I>cleansing of hands.</I>

substance, which they sometimes used for cleansing of the hands, is derived from

<P>30. <B>Oh this false Soule of Egypt! this graue Charme</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: By &lquo;this
<I>grave</I> charm,&rquo; is meant, &lquo;this sublime, this majestick beauty.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC> (i, 45; whose
text reads <I>soil</I> for &lquo;Soule&rquo;): The former reading was&mdash;&lquo;Soule&rquo;; and the sentence,
with that word in it, can be understood only of Cleopatra: but they who can but
barely imagine&mdash;she could be spoke of in so vulgar a phrase, and that by Antony,
have not pierc'd very deeply either into him or the poet. The moderns retain the
old reading: and, that the finishing part of the line might have no cause to triumph
over that it began with, the four last of them alter &lquo;grave&rquo; into&mdash;<I>gay;</I> that is, the
most noble and masculine epithet in all Shakespeare, into one the poorest and most
unworthy, of him, the speaker, and the occasion, that even study could help them to.
&lquo;Grave charm&rquo; is&mdash;a charm or enchantment that leads to death or the grave, too
truly applicable to the person intended; and they are the only words in the line that
are aim'd directly at her: The other member of it, is, as the reader sees, an exclam-
atory reflection,&mdash;growing out of the words that precede it,&mdash;on the perfidies of
Egyptians in general; so numerous, and almost continual, that he thinks their <I>soil</I>
itself is in fault; and that they are made the people they are, by some contagion that
springs out of that.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: I believe &lquo;grave charm&rquo; means only <I>deadly,</I> or
<I>destructive piece of witchcraft.</I> In this sense the epithet &lquo;grave&rquo; is often used by
Chapman, in his translation of Homer. So, in the 19th book: &lquo;but not far hence the
fatal minutes are Of thy <I>grave</I> ruin.&rquo; [lines 394, 395.] Again, in the 22d Odyssey:
&lquo;and then flew Minerva, after every dart, and made Some strike the threshold, some
the walls invade; Some beate the doores, and all acts rendred vaine Their <I>grave</I>
steel offer'd.&rquo; [lines 322-326.] It seems to be employed in the sense of the Latin
word <I>gravis.</I>&mdash;[<SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii) pronounces the reading of his MS: &lquo;this false <I>spell

of Collier's MS is very plausible; but &lquo;<I>great</I> charm,&rquo; from the same source, is infinitely
less expressive and appropriate than &lquo;grave charm,&rquo; <I>i. e. pernicious, deadly, fatal</I>
sorceress.&mdash;<SC>Keightley</SC> (p. 319): In my edition, yielding to an impulse I could not

<P>33. <B>at fast and loose</B>] <SC>Sir J. Hawkins</SC>: This is a term to signify a cheating
game, of which the following is a description. A leathern belt is made up into a
number of intricate folds, and placed edgewise upon a table. One of the folds is
made to resemble the middle of the girdle, so that whoever should thrust a skewer
into it would think he held it fast to the table; whereas, when he has so done, the
person with whom he plays may take hold of both ends, and draw it away. This trick
is now known to the common people, by the name of <I>pricking at the belt</I> or <I>girdle,</I>
[or <I>garter,</I> according to Gifford] and perhaps was practised by the Gypsies in the time
of Shakespeare.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: This supposition is confirmed by the following Epigram
in an ancient collection called <I>Run and a great Cast,</I> by Thomas Freeman, 1614:
&lquo;<I>Epig.</I> 95. &lquo;Charles the <I>&AElig;gyptian,</I> who by jugling could Make <I>fast</I> or <I>loose,</I> or what-
soere he would,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>Reed</SC>: That the &AElig;gyptians were great adepts in this art before
Shakspeare's time, may be seen in Scot's <I>Discoverie of Witchcraft,</I> 1584, p. 336,
[<I>Of fast or loose, how to knit a hard knot upon a handkercher, and to undoo the same
with words.</I>&mdash;Bk. 13, Chap. xxix.] where these practices are fully explained.&mdash;[It is
mentioned twice in <I>Love's Lab. Lost,</I> I, ii, 150, and III, i, 108.]
<P>34. <B>very heart of losse</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: To the utmost loss possible.&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC> (i,
46): This is a phrase importing&mdash;the most perfect and absolute loss, <I>i. e.</I> ruin; and
is taken from trees, whose heart and centre is commonly perfecter than their extreams.
&mdash;[This Capellesque gem ought not glow unseen.]
<P>39. <B>Vanish</B>] Shakespeare applies this verb to many objects, but especially, I think,
to witches, dreams, ghosts, exhalations, etc. Cleopatra in the last scene applies it
to Iras's departing life. Here Anthony, in thus using it, continues the image, &lquo;Thou
Spell! Avaunt!&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>44. <B>For poor'st Diminitiues, for Dolts</B>] In a letter to Theobald, in May, 1729
(Nichols, <I>Illust.</I> ii, 228) the Rev. <SC>Styan Thirlby</SC> proposed the change of &lquo;dolts&rquo;
to <I>doits.</I> Theobald, in his edition refers to Warburton's knowledge of this emen-
dation; when Warburton's edition appeared, in 1747, he made no reference to
Thirlby, but put forth the emendation as his own, and to him it has been wrongly
accredited ever since, until the appearance of the <I>Text. Notes</I> in the <I>Cam. Ed.</I>
Theobald's own note on the word thus concludes, after giving his reasons for reject-
ing <I>doits:</I> &lquo;Perhaps the Poet's meaning may be, that Cleopatra should become a
show, a spectacle to the scum and rabble of Rome; to blockheads, and people of the
lowest rank. Cleopatra speaks twice afterwards to the same effect [see V, ii, 65,
and 252].&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Warburton</SC>: As the allusion here is to monsters carried about in
shows, it is plain, that the words, &lquo;for poorest diminutives,&rquo; must mean for the least
piece of money. We must therefore read: &lquo;for <I>doits,</I>&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> farthings, which shows
what he means by &lquo;poorest diminutives.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC> (i, 46, reading <I>doits</I>): Had
&lquo;dolts&rquo; been the word, the Poet would have said, <I>to</I> dolts, <I>to</I> poor'st diminutives; as
he has, two lines higher, &lquo;<I>to</I> the shouting plebeians&rquo;; which very words led him to
&lquo;for&rquo; and to <I>doits,</I> to avoid a co-incidence of thoughts and expression in lines so
near one another.&mdash;<SC>Tyrwhitt</SC> (in answer to Warburton's note): There was surely
no occasion for the poet <I>to show what he meant</I> by <I>purest diminutives.</I> The expres-
sion is clear enough, and certainly acquires no additional force from the explana-
tion. I rather believe we should read: &lquo;For poor'st diminutives, <I>to dolts;</I>&rquo; This
aggravates the contempt of her supposed situation; to be shown, <I>as monsters are,</I> not
only <I>for the smallest piece of money,</I> but <I>to the most stupid and vulgar spectators.</I>&mdash;
<SC>Malone</SC>: I have received the emendation made by Warburton, because the letter <I>i,</I>
in consequence of the dot over it, is sometimes confounded with <I>l</I> at the press. It
appears to me much more probable that &lquo;dolts&rquo; should have been printed for <I>doits,</I>
than that &lquo;for&rquo; should have been substituted for <I>to.</I> Whichsoever of these emen-
dations be admitted, there is still a difficulty. Though monsters are shown to the
stupid and the vulgar for &lquo;poor'st diminutives,&rquo; yet Cleopatra, according to Antony's
supposition, would certainly be exhibited to the Roman populace <I>for nothing.</I> Nor
can it be said that he means that <I>she</I> would be exhibited <I>gratis,</I> as monsters are

<P>shown for small pieces of money; because his words are &lquo;monster-like, be [thou]
shown for poor'st diminutives.&rquo; I have sometimes therefore thought that Shakspeare
might have written: &lquo;<I>Fore</I> poor diminutives, <I>fore</I> dolts.&rquo; The following passage in
<I>Tro. and Cress.</I> adds some support to my conjecture: &lquo;How the poor world is
pestered with such waterflies, <I>diminutives</I> of nature!&rquo; [V, i, 38.]&mdash;<SC>Knight</SC>: We
believe that the &lquo;poor'st diminutives&rquo; are the lowest of the populace, as the &lquo;dolts&rquo; are
the most stupid. We must therefore understand &lquo;for&rquo; to mean, for the gratification
of; or adopt Malone's suggestion of &lquo;be shown <I>fore,</I>&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> pronounces this
explanation of Knight &lquo;very curious,&rquo; quotes Knight's understanding of &lquo;for,&rquo; and
subjoins his favourite exclamation mark.&mdash;<SC>Deighton</SC> (reading <I>doits</I>): With the
reading [of the Folio] &lquo;for&rquo; could only have the sense of &lquo;for the gratification of,&rquo;
a very forced one; while Malone's objection that Cleopatra would be shown for
nothing is of little value, since Shakespeare was evidently thinking of the exhibition
of monsters, strange fishes, etc., at fairs, etc., in his own country. Compare <I>Tempest,</I>
II, ii, 28-34.&mdash;<SC>Rolfe</SC> (reading &lquo;dolts&rquo;): But the reference is to Cleopatra's being led
in triumph through the streets of Rome, a &lquo;free show&rquo; for the rabble, not to her being
exhibited for a fee. Besides it seems more natural for Antony to emphasize the low
character of the spectators than the pettiness of the price charged, if there were any.
The only other instance of &lquo;diminutives&rquo; is in <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.</I> V, i, 38, where it
means insignificant persons. &lquo;Monster-like&rquo; is equivalent to as a monstrosity; but
it is not necessary to see any reference to the fact that monsters were exhibited for
money.&mdash;[The defence of the Folio may well be left in the hands of Theobald and
of Rolfe. The degradation lay in being exhibited at all, not in any sum charged
for &lquo;admission.&rquo; And it is noteworthy how deeply the taunt sank into Cleopatra's
mind by her double reference to it afterward, and how her fateful imagination mag-
nified it by her description of the atmosphere arising from the greasy mechanics, the
dolts, and poorest diminutives. Dyce calls Knight's interpretation of &lquo;for&rquo; &lquo;very
curious,&rquo; and Deighton pronounces it &lquo;very forced.&rquo; Compare, &lquo;For Banquo's issue

<P>taste of death but once.&rquo;&mdash;[I find it impossible to accept Deighton's paraphrase of
this difficult passage, and it is the only paraphrase that any editor or critic, as far as
I know, has vouchsafed us. The &lquo;many&rquo; deaths cannot refer to imaginary deaths,
as Deighton supposes; if he is correct, the inference is clear that it would be a pres-
ent mercy to kill every coward who fears to die, which would go near to depopulate
the world. Anthony does not say that Cleopatra's present death would prevent many
future deaths, real or imaginary, but his words are that her death (in time past)
&lquo;<I>might have prevented</I> many&rquo; (others, of soldiers slain in battle). In this case, &lquo;bet-
ter 'twere thou fell'st&rquo; is equivalent to &lquo;better 'twere thou shouldst have fallen,&rquo;&mdash;
the sequence of tenses will hardly permit &lquo;fell'st&rquo; to be the perfect indicative. Can
it be that in Anthony's present conviction of Cleopatra's treachery there rise in his
memory past occasions when he mistrusted her, notably her reception of C&aelig;sar's
messenger? and he now sees that it would have been better had she fallen under his
fury then? and by one death &lquo;might have prevented many&rquo;?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>51, etc. <B>The shirt of Nessus,</B> etc.] <SC>Heath</SC> (p. 463): While Antony is contem-
plating his present inevitable ruin, brought upon him, as he thought, by the treachery
of the woman who was dearest to him, his imagination presents to him his supposed
ancestor Hercules in circumstances exactly parallel, wrapped up, by the instrumen-
tality of Deianira's deceived jealousy, in the poisoned shirt of Nessus, from which it
was impossible he could ever extricate himself alive. Upon this point, his imagi-
nation taking fire transports him almost to a delirium. He fancies himself to be a
real Hercules, and the shirt of Nessus to be actually upon him; and, after invoking
his ancestor to inspire him with the same rage, with which he was actuated on the
like occasion, he is instantly on the wing to exert it in the very same effects, in the
lodging Lichas on the horns of the moon, and in subduing his worthiest self, with
those very Herculean hands that grasped the heaviest club. All which, when
stripped of those violent figures in which his heated imagination had cloathed it,
terminates in no more than this, the taking the severest vengeance on the instrument
of his ruin, and putting an end to his life by his own hands. The most exception-
able expression perhaps is, the bestowing the epithet, <I>worthiest,</I> on himself; but even
this exaggeration will appear excusable at least, if not justifiable, when it is con-
sidered, that it is not seriously intended as a vain-glorious vaunt, but proceeds wholly
from a transport of the fancy, which represents him to himself for that moment as
the very Hercules in person.&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC> (i, 46): Lichas was not lodg'd by Hercules
quite upon &lquo;the horns of the moon,&rquo; but was thrown from the top of Mount Oeta
into the sea: Antony's exaggeration in this place, and the puffiness of what he speaks
next, should be consider'd as specimens of that Asiatick tumour of diction, which
the Poet (using Plutarch's authority) has made a part of his character; throwing it
into some of his speeches as occasion presented, and most properly into this.

<P>11. <B>Pageants</B>] <SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D. s. v.</I>): Origin and history obscure. 1. A
scene acted on the stage; specially, one scene or act of a medi&aelig;val mystery play.
&dagger; 2. A stage or platform on which scenes were acted or tableaux represented; espe-
cially in early use, the movable structure or &lquo;carriage,&rquo; consisting of stage and stage
machinery, used in open air performances of the mystery plays. 3. A tableau, repre-
sentation, allegorical device, or the like, erected on a fixed stage or carried on a
moving car, as a public show; any kind of show, device, or temporary structure,
exhibited as a feature of a public triumph or celebration. (This sense, in which
&lquo;scene&rquo; and &lquo;stage&rquo; are combined, may have been the intermediate link between 1
and 2.)&mdash;[In conclusion Dr Murray gives an extremely valuable <I>Note,</I> wherein is
discussed the two main early senses of the word, which were &lquo;a scene displayed on
a stage&rquo; and &lquo;a stage on which a scene is exhibited or acted.&rquo; Unfortunately this
purely philological question is not germane to these pages. It is not to be sup-
posed that in using the word &lquo;Pageants&rquo; Shakespeare had in mind the uncouth
clumsy structures or the barbarous acting of the early <I>Moralities</I> or <I>Mysteries.</I> The
pageants of his day were elaborate, allegorical, and superbly furnished. <SC>Warton</SC>
(ii, 365) says &lquo;the frequent and public exhibition of personifications in the <I>Pageaunts,</I>
which anciently accompanied every high festivity, greatly contributed to cherish the
spirit of allegorical poetry, and even to enrich the imagination of Spenser. [<I>Foot-
note.</I>] And of Shakespeare. There is a passage [the present,] in <I>Antony and Cleo-
patra,</I> where the metaphor is exceedingly beautiful; but where the beauty both of the
expression and the allusion is lost, unless we recollect the frequency and the nature
of these shews in Shakespeare's age.&rquo; On p. 202, <I>et seq.</I> of the same volume, War-
ton gives, from contemporary sources, an account of the magnificence of Pageants
in which even royal personages took part. <SC>Whiter</SC>, also, writes to the same effect.
&lquo;It is impossible,&rquo; he says (p. 199), speaking of Pageants presented at Court, &lquo;for
the reader to form an adequate notion of these performances, or to conceive their
impression on the minds of those to whom they were familiar, unless he will himself
consult the original narratives, which describe their exhibition. When he reflects on
the immense sums which were lavished on these occasions; and considers that the
most celebrated artists and poets of the age were employed in displaying before a
voluptuous Court the most consummate specimens of their skill, he will readily

<P>14. <B>the Racke dislimes</B>] <SC>Whiter</SC> (p. 195): This is a continuation of the

<I>Masque of Hymen:</I> &lquo;Here the upper part of the scene, which was all of clouds, and
made artificially to swell, and ride like <I>the rack,</I> began to open,&rquo; etc. [p. 59, ed.
Gifford. It is more than probable that Whiter is here right in saying that this is a
continuation of the allusion, although Anthony's speech throughout deals with actual

instance, as in another occurring in <I>Ant. &amp; Cleop.,</I> was thinking not more of the
actual clouds than of those gauzy semblances, which, in the pageants of his day, as
in the stage-spectacles of ours, were often used partly or totally to obscure the scene

<P><B>Enemies triumph</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: Shakspeare has here, as usual, taken his meta-
phor from a low trivial subject; but has enobled it with much art, by so contriving
that the principal term in the subject from whence the metaphor was <I>taken,</I> should
belong to, and suit the dignity of the subject to which the metaphor is <I>transferred:</I>
thereby providing at once for the integrity of the figure, and the nobleness of the
thought. And this by the word <I>triumph,</I> which either signifies Octavius's conquest,
or what we now call, contractedly, the <I>trump</I> at cards, then called the <I>triumph</I> or the
<I>triumphing sort.</I>&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: This explanation is very just; the thought did not
deserve so good an annotation.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: I believe Warburton here, as in many
other places, saw more than his author meant. Shakspeare, I think, only intended
to say, that Cleopatra, by collusion, played the great game they were engaged in
falsely, so as <I>to sacrifice Antony's fame to that of his enemy.</I> The playing false to
the adversary's <I>trump card</I> (as Warburton explains the words) conveys no distinct
idea. The plain sense of the passage will appear from the following dialogue in
Florio's <I>Second Frvtes,</I> 1591: &lquo;S. What a shooffling doo you keepe with those
cardes? A. <I>I plaie faire plaie,</I> and shooffell them as I ought. S. Me thinkes
you <I>pack</I> and set them.&rquo; [p. 69. Assuredly, Malone is right. To play false to your
opponents trump can do no harm to anybody but the player and his partner. Possi-
bly, the sentence may be thus paraphrased:&mdash;She &lquo;stacked&rquo; the cards in C&aelig;sar's
favour, and then, by her cheating, converted my glory into an enemy's triumph.
Warburton's note renders needless the many comments on the conversion of &lquo;the
triumph card&rquo; into &lquo;the <I>trump</I> card.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>24. <B>C&aelig;sars</B>] For the superfluous <I>s</I> see I, iv, 11.
<P>29. <B>she has rob'd me of my Sword</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 47): Words that should not
be taken metaphorically, as some have suppos'd, but literally; for that he had no
sword of his own, appears by what he says to Eros [line 94], and he afterwards dies
by his sword: nor is it any objection, that this sword is call'd by Dercetas Antony's
sword [V, i, 30]; who only gives it that name as knowing 'twas the sword that he
dy'd by, and look'd no farther. Cleopatra's action proceeded from tenderness: she
saw the rage he was in; and, fearing the effects of it, withdrew (or caus'd to be
withdrawn), the instrument of his harm.&mdash;[If there were any special meaning in ask-
ing Eros to use his own sword, it may have been that there was therein less thought
of suicide. Later on Anthony asks Diomed also to draw his sword and give suf-
ficing strokes for death; possibly, in this case, because the sword of Eros was still in
the wound. Cleopatra had robbed Anthony of his sword just as the belief in Des-
demona's infidelity had robbed Othello of his occupation.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>50. <B>The battery from my heart</B>] <SC>Boswell</SC>: This means, I apprehend, &lquo;the
battery <I>proceeding from</I> my heart, which is strong enough to break through the seven-
fold shield of Ajax; I wish it were strong enough to cleave my sides and destroy
me.&rquo;&mdash;[Anthony is unarming, and, as Eros &lquo;plucks off&rquo; his breastplate, is reminded
of the folly of supposing that such a mere sheet of metal could protect his heart from
a battery against which Ajax's seven-fold shield would have proved vain. Then,
as he breathes freer, and his chest expands, he prays his heart to cleave his sides,
that for once it may find relief in breaking. Boswell's note is to me incompre-
hensible, and what is still more incomprehensible is that five, at least, of recent edi-
tors should have adopted it in whole or in part. A shield is for the protection of
the bearer. Who, one may ask, was the bearer of Ajax's shield, who was to be pro-
tected from the battery &lquo;proceeding from&rquo; Anthony's heart? Against whom was
Anthony about to open a battery from his heart? and with what object? His own
heart was the citadel from which the battery could not be kept.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>50, 51. <B>cleaue my sides. Heart</B>] I utterly mistrust the period in the Folio after
&lquo;sides,&rquo; which has been practically retained by every editor. It makes Anthony
adjure his sides to cleave, <I>scil.</I> themselves. This intransitive or reflexive use of
&lquo;cleave&rquo; is rare; see Murray (<I>N. E. D.</I>) where comparatively few examples of it
are given. Replace the period with a comma, and &lquo;cleave&rquo; then becomes the
imperative of a transitive verb with &lquo;sides&rquo; as an object, and &lquo;Heart&rquo; as the subject:
&lquo;Oh, Heart, cleave my sides!&rquo; Then, in a manner thoroughly Shakespearian, the
idea is repeated, but in a different form: &lquo;for once be stronger than thy continent,
crack thy frail case.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>51. <B>Continent</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: That is, the thing that contains thee. [Of which
Schmidt's <I>Lex.</I> will furnish many examples.]
<P>57. <B>length</B>] <SC>Halliwell</SC> (<I>Select. Notes,</I> p. 35): This word may stand for <I>length
of life.</I>&mdash;[Assuredly. And for length of time, of breathing, of heart-beats, of every-
thing. It is what it is: length in the abstract.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>58-60. <B>Now all labour Marres what it does: yea, very force entangles It

<P>60. <B>Seale then</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: Antony had offended Cleopatra with his suspicions;
he is about doing something to deserve her pardon: and he thinks stabbing himself
will <I>seal</I> that pardon.&mdash;<SC>Warburton</SC>: Metaphor taken from civil contracts, where,
when all is agreed on, the sealing compleats the contract; so he hath determined to
die, and nothing remained but to give the stroke.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: I believe the reading
is: &lquo;<I>seel</I> then, and all is done.&rquo; To <I>seel hawks,</I> is to close their eyes. The mean-
ing will be: &lquo;Close thine eyes <I>for ever, and be quiet.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: The old read-
ing is the true one. Thus, in <I>Henry V:</I> &lquo;And so espous'd to death, with blood he
<I>seal'd</I> A testament of noble-ending love.&rquo; [IV, vi, 26.]
<P>64. <B>Dido, and her &AElig;neas</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: But Dido's fondness did not reach to
the other world; she then despised &AElig;neas, and returned to her old affection for
Sich&aelig;us. I should think, therefore, that the Poet wrote, &lquo;Dido and her <I>Sich&aelig;us.</I>&rquo;
And the rather, because the comparison of Antony to Sich&aelig;us is remarkably apposite.
Sich&aelig;us was murdered by his brother Pygmalion for his wealth, on which his wife,
Dido, fled into Africa: So Antony was fought with and defeated at Actium by his
brother Octavius, for his share of the dominion of the world, whereon Cleopatra fled
from the victor's rage into Egypt. [&lquo;and there is salmons in both.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC>
(i, 47): The Poet did not stay to consider, whether Dido's love for &AElig;neas did or
did not follow her into the other world; it was very sufficient for his purpose&mdash;that
the loves of her and &AElig;neas were of great fame, which made them a fit couple to
be rank'd with those he is talking of.

<P>69, 70. <B>the Gods Detest my basenesse</B>] <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> ii, 311): In the
writers of that age <I>detest</I> is used in the sense which as then it still retained from its
original, <I>detestari,</I> being indicative of something spoken, not of an affection of the
mind.&mdash;[Among other examples of this use Walker quotes the present passage, and
here defines &lquo;detest&rquo; as <I>cry out against;</I> which is, possibly, correct; at the same
time, there are many passages in Shakespeare where the idea of simple abhorrence
obtains, as in Lear's &lquo;Detested kite! thou liest.&rquo; The range of readings which
the <I>N. E. D.</I> affords would have shown Walker that his interpretation was too
restricted. Dr <SC>Murray</SC> distinguishes three meanings in the use of &lquo;detest.&rquo; The
third: &lquo;To renounce solemnly or under oath&rquo; is <I>obsolete</I> and rare, and does not concern
us here. The two other meanings, under which there are venerable and abundant
examples in proof, are: &lquo;1. <I>transitive.</I> To curse, calling God to witness; to express
abhorrence of, to denounce, execrate [Walker's meaning]. 2. To feel abhorrence
of; to hate or dislike intensely; to abhor, to abominate.&rquo; The latter meaning is
certainly applicable to the present passage.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>72. <B>With Ships, made Cities</B>] Compare, <I>Henry V:</I> III, Chorus, line 14: &lquo;behold
A city on the inconstant billows dancing; For so appears this fleet majestical, Hold-
ing due course to Harfleur.&rquo; <SC>Deighton</SC>, however, understands it differently, and
paraphrases, &lquo;his vessels being so capacious as to carry in each of them the popu-
lation of a city.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>72, 73. <B>condemne my selfe, to lacke The Courage . . . lesse Noble minde</B>]
<SC>Malone</SC> conceived that &lquo;less noble mind&rquo; as well as &lquo;courage&rquo; was the object of
&lquo;lack&rquo; and that, consequently, Antony said what he did not mean. But he took
heart of grace in the supposition that the construction was one of Shakespeare's
&lquo;peculiar inaccuracies&rquo; on which we must look leniently and in which &lquo;the poet&rquo;
must be humoured. Finally, he received great contentment from finding that &lquo;how-
ever inaccurate, the text is not corrupt,&rquo;&mdash;in North's <I>Plutarch</I> occur the very same
words! Thus Antony there says, &lquo;I am sorrie that having been so great a captaine
and emperour, I am indeede <I>condemned</I> to be <I>judged</I> of <I>lesse corage and noble minde</I>
than a woman.&rquo; <SC>Steevens</SC> then remarks that &lquo;&ldquo;Condemn myself <I>to lack,</I>&rdquo; however
licentiously, may have been employed to signify, &ldquo;condemn myself <I>for lacking</I> even
the courage of a woman.&rdquo;&rquo; <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 356) supplies many and many an instance
of the infinitive thus indefinitely used. That &lquo;less noble mind&rquo; (or mind<I>ed,</I>&mdash;it makes
little difference) is still governed by &lquo;I,&rquo; in line 70 (&lquo;I, that with my sword,&rquo; etc.),

<P>might have been made a little clearer had the punctuation of the Folio been followed.
But every editor since Rowe has placed a semi-colon or a colon after &lquo;Woman,&rquo; and so
disjointed the sentence. <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 310) says &lquo;Read &ldquo;less <I>noble-minded.</I>&rdquo;&rquo;

<P>78. <B>Th'ineuitable prosecution of disgrace and horror</B>] This line, with its
eight feet catalectic, has given much metrical trouble. Its predecessor and suc-
cessor are adequately correct, but this line is certainly a notable violation of the laws
of blank verse. To utter these words, proclaiming his open shame, must have cost
Anthony's proud spirit a fierce struggle; every word is a torture, and his emotion
must have been almost uncontrollable before he could bring himself to utter &lquo;disgrace&rquo;
and &lquo;horror.&rquo; Wherefore, disregarding all metrical laws whatsoever, I would, with
a long pause after &lquo;of,&rquo; put &lquo;disgrace and horror&rquo; in a separate line, and allow the
other lines to remain undisturbed. Although this arrangement is, in effect, for the
benefit of the eye, yet through the eye it conveys an intimation of the way in which,
as I think, it should be spoken.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>81. <B>Put colour in thy Cheeke</B>] Elsewhere Shakespeare makes us see how terror
blanches the cheek. &lquo;Out, you tallow-face,&rquo; says old Capulet to Juliet when he tells
her she must marry Paris. &lquo;What soldiers, whey-face?&rquo; asks Macbeth of the Ser-
vant who brings the news of the approach of ten thousand English. <SC>John Hunter</SC>
paraphrases it, however, &lquo;Rouse the blood into thy face through eagerness to defeat
C&aelig;sar.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
</CC>

<P>113. <B>Why there then</B>] After these words <SC>Theobald</SC> inserted the stage direc-

of the next line, <I>Dyes.</I> This slaying of the slain was faithfully copied by <SC>Warbur-

slavishly, from his edition.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

deeds. See Franz's note on II, iv, 11, &lquo;you'le win two dayes vpon me.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>124. <B>The Guard, how</B>] <SC>Malone</SC> lays stress on his having early &lquo;suspected&rquo; that

his own discrimination in acutely distinguishing <I>ho</I> from &lquo;how.&rquo; Through two
editions <SC>Collier</SC> bravely clung to &lquo;how,&rquo; but, in his <I>Third Ed.</I> yielded to <I>ho,</I> possi-
bly in consequence of Dyce's home-question (<I>Strict.</I> p. 207): &lquo;If Mr Collier did
not intend to make Antony &ldquo;<I>call</I> the guard,&rdquo; I should like to know what meaning he
would have us attach to &ldquo;The Guard!&rdquo; The modern editors who printed <I>ho</I> for
&ldquo;how&rdquo; were evidently right.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>7-9. <B>our size of sorrow . . . which makes it</B>] As <SC>Deighton</SC> justly remarks, this

agrees well enough with what precedes.&mdash;[Is &lquo;thither&rquo; merely &lquo;well enough&rquo; when
it refers to <I>that</I> place, away from the speaker, on the other side of the monument?
Is it possible, in such circumstances, that <I>hither</I> can be right?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>17. <B>Burne the great Sphere thou mou'st in</B>] <SC>Heath</SC> (p. 464): According to
the philosophy which prevailed from the age of Aristotle to that of Shakspeare, and
long since, the sun was a planet, and was whirled round the earth by the motion of
a solid sphere in which it was fixed. If the sun therefore was to set fire to the sphere,
so as to consume it, the consequence would be, that itself, for want of support, must
drop through, and wander in endless space; and in that case, the earth would be
involved in endless night. [See note on III, xiii, 175.]
<P>18. <B>The varrying shore o'th'world</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: That is, of the earth, where
light and darkness make an incessant variation.&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC> (<I>Athen&aelig;um,</I> 26 Apr.
1873): We have here a painful proof of the injury which the change of a word can
do to the finest passage. Cleopatra's magnificent invocation is turned into sheer non-
sense by that miserable misprint &lquo;shore.&rquo; What is the varying shore? . . . Read
&lquo;The varying <I>star</I> o'th' world.&rquo; The varying <I>star</I> of the world, spelt of old <I>starre,</I>

<P>32. <B>I dare not</B>] This is one of the lines, enumerated at IV, viii, 9, which <SC>Walker</SC>
(<I>Crit.</I> iii, 307) says has lost something at the end. The <I>Text. Notes</I> bear witness
that something has happened. After devising an addition (to supply what is sup-
posed to be lost), which will never be generally accepted, and after the counting of
syllables in order to convert these impassioned lines into smug pentameters, the zeal-
ous critics must have retired with &lquo;fingers weary and worn,&rquo;&mdash;and without adding
anything toward the better comprehension of a line already adequately clear.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>35. <B>Be brooch'd with me</B>] <SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D.</I>) gives the present passage as
the only example of the use of this verb, except one other reference of a date as late
as 1865. Its meaning is &lquo;to adorn as with a brooch.&rquo; The substantive &lquo;brooch&rquo; is
&lquo;the same as <I>broach,</I> the difference of spelling being only recent, and hardly yet
established.&rquo; Its meanings are &lquo;1. An ornamental fastening, consisting of a safety
pin, with the clasping part fashioned into a ring, boss, or shield, or other device of
precious metal or other material, artistically wrought, set with jewels, etc. Now used
mainly as a (female) ornament; but always for the ostensible purpose of fastening
some part of the dress. &dagger; 2. Formerly also in a more general sense; according to
Johnson &ldquo;a jewel, an ornament of jewels.&rdquo; In earlier times applied to a necklace,
a bracelet, and other trinkets.&rquo;
<P>35, 36. <B>Knife, Drugges, Serpents haue Edge, sting, or operation</B>] To make
this &lquo;respective construction&rquo; exact, the order of the second line should run: &lquo;Edge,
operation, or sting,&rquo; as Hanmer has it, but it does not run smoothly. In the reference
to &lquo;serpents,&rquo; have we an anticipation?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>39. <B>Demuring vpon me</B>] This is the only example given by <SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D.</I>)

<P>51. <B>Dye when thou hast liu'd</B>] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. i) is the only editor, since Pope,
who ventured to retain &lquo;when&rquo; of the Folio, and even his courage deserted him before
his <I>Second Edition.</I> He interpreted &lquo;Die, when thou hast liv'd&rquo; as meaning &lquo;in
consequence of being quickened, or restored, by my kissing thee.&rquo;
<P>52. <B>Quicken with kissing</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: That is, revive by my kiss.
<P>58. <B>That the false . . . breake her Wheele</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: This despicable line
has occurred before. [Where? The nearest approach to it that I can find is the
one suggested by Malone, and it is in prose. &lquo;Let us sit and mock the good hous-
wife, Fortune, from her wheel,&rquo; as Celia says to Rosalind. <SC>Knight</SC> quotes Johnson
and then drily remarks, &lquo;There are not many such &ldquo;despicable&rdquo; lines in <I>Irene.</I>&rquo;]&mdash;
<SC>Staunton</SC>: &lquo;Huswife&rquo; is here used in the loose sense, which it often bore, of <I>hussy,</I>
or <I>harlot.</I> So in <I>Hen. V:</I> V, i, Pistol asks,&mdash;&lquo;Doth Fortune play the huswife with
me now?&rquo;&mdash;[I doubt that &lquo;Huswife,&rquo; in Shakespeare's days, retained, to any large
extent, the idea of a <I>house-wife,</I> that is, one who devoted herself to household cares.
It was an opprobrious epithet, rather than a literal one. Otherwise, we might infer
that Shakespeare, at least here and in <I>As You Like It,</I> supposed that Fortune's wheel
was a spinning-wheel. Possibly, in popular belief it was so, owing to some con-
fusion with Clotho's distaff. Fluellen, however, had a perfectly correct idea of it.
&lquo;Fortune,&rquo; he says, &lquo;is painted also with a wheel to signify to you . . . that she is turn-
ing, and inconstant, and mutability, and variation; and her foot, look you, is fixed
upon a spherical stone, which rolls, and rolls, and rolls.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Hen. V:</I> III, vi, 34.
Why Fortune should have two similar symbols of revolution, it is hard to say. Both
are found in early Etruscan times. Possibly, the wheel was merely an added
emblem or badge of the tribe of Leucomones. See Creuzer, <I>Symbolik,</I> iii, 664,
footnote.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>76, etc. <B>Noblest of men,</B> etc.] <SC>Mrs Jameson</SC> (ii, 150): Cleopatra's speech, after
Antony has expired in her arms, I have always regarded as one of the most wonder-
ful in Shakspeare. Cleopatra is not a woman to grieve silently. The contrast
between the violence of her passions and the weakness of her sex, between her
regal grandeur and her excess of misery, her impetuous, unavailing struggles with
the fearful destiny which has compassed her, and the mixture of wild impatience
and pathos in her agony, are really magnificent. She faints on the body of Antony,
and is recalled to life by the cries of her women.

<P>92. <B>Peace, peace, Iras</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: Cleopatra is fallen into a swoon; her
maids endeavour to recover her by invoking her by her several titles. At length,
Charmian says to the other, &lquo;Peace, peace, Iras&rquo;; on which Cleopatra comes to her-
self, and replies to these last words, &lquo;No, you are mistaken, I am a mere woman like
yourself.&rquo; Thus stands this senseless dialogue. But Shakespeare never wrote it so.
We must observe then, that the two women call her by her several titles, to see
which best pleased her; and this was highly in character; the Ancients thought,
that not only men, but Gods too, had some names which, above others, they much
delighted in, and would soonest answer to; as we may see by the hymns of Orpheus,
Homer, and Callimachus. The Poet, conforming to this notion, makes the maids
say, Sovereign Lady, Madam, Royal Egypt, Empress. And now we come to the
place in question: Charmian, when she saw that none of these titles had their effect,
invokes her by a still more flattering one: &lquo;Peace, peace, <SC>Isis</SC>!&rquo; for so it should be
read and pointed: <I>i. e.</I> peace, we can never move her by these titles: Let us give
her her favourite name of the Goddess <SC>Isis</SC>. And now Cleopatra's answer becomes
pertinent and fine: &lquo;No more but a mere woman,&rquo; etc. <I>i. e.</I> I now see the folly of
assuming to myself those flattering titles of divinity. My misfortunes, and my impo-
tence in bearing them, convince me I am a mere woman and subject to all the passions
of the meanest of my species. Here the Poet has followed history exactly, and what
is more, his author Plutarch, who says, that Cleopatra assumed the habit and attributes
of that Goddess, and gave judgements, or rather oracles to her people under the quality
of the <SC>New Isis</SC>.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: Of this [foregoing note] it may be truly said, that it
at least deserves to be right, nor can he, that shall question the justness of the emen-
dation, refuse his esteem to the ingenuity and learning with which it is proposed. I
suppose, however, that we may justly change the ancient copy thus, &lquo;No more, but
<I>e'en</I> a woman.&rquo; I am inclined to think that she speaks abruptly, not answering her
woman, but discoursing with her own thoughts: &lquo;No more&mdash;but <I>e'en</I> a woman. I
have no more of my wonted greatness, but am even a woman, on the level with other
women; were I what I once was, it were for me to throw my scepter,&rquo; etc. &lquo;Peace,
peace, Iras,&rquo; is said by Charmian, when she sees the Queen recovering, and thinks
speech troublesome.

<P>1. <B>Menas</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC> (ed. ii): Menas and Menecrates, we may remember, were

<P>4, 5. <B>Being so frustrate, tell him, He mockes the pawses,</B> etc.] <SC>Steevens</SC>
(<I>Variorum</I> of 1778): &lquo;He mocks the pauses that he makes&rquo; means that he plays

to me, are mere idle mockery. &lquo;He mocks the pauses&rquo; may be a licentious mode

<C>[4, 5. <B>Being so frustrate, tell him,</B> etc.]</C>
<P>of expression for,&mdash;<I>he makes a mockery of us by these pauses; i. e.</I> he trifles with us.
&mdash;In the <I>Variorum</I> of 1785, <SC>Malone</SC> expressed the belief that the defect in metre
proved that some words had been omitted which would have rendered the line
intelligible. &lquo;When Antony himself made these pauses, would he mock,&rquo; Malone
asks, &lquo;or laugh at them? and what is the meaning of <I>mocking a pause?</I>&rquo; He there-
fore conjectured that <I>us by</I> were the omitted words, and in his own later edition, in
1790, thus prints the line: &lquo;Being so frustrate, tell him, he mocks <I>us by</I> The pauses,&rquo;
etc. In this same edition of 1790 Malone rather disingenuously conveys the
impression that the note by Steevens (quoted above), had been written after the line
had been rendered intelligible by the emendation <I>us by.</I> I have, therefore, dated
Steevens's note to show that it was written before Malone had, in his own estimation,
amended the line. In Steevens's edition of 1793 appeared the following additional
note by him:&mdash;I have left Malone's emendation in the text; though, to complete
the measure, we might read,&mdash;&lquo;frustrate<I>d,</I>&rquo; or &lquo;Being so frustrate, tell him <I>that</I> he
mocks,&rquo; etc.; as I am well convinced we are not yet acquainted with the full and
exact meaning of the verb <I>mock,</I> as sometimes employed by Shakespeare. [From
<SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii) we learn that this change, suggested by Steevens, &lquo;tell him <I>that,</I>&rquo; is
also given by the MS. Collier thereupon remarks]: The expression <I>to mock pauses</I>
is far from intelligible; and it seems pretty certain that the old printer made some con-
fusion between &lquo;mocks&rquo; and <I>makes,</I> words so much alike in old MSS. Malone added
<I>us by,</I> and they appear necessary in order to render the sense clear; at all events
that object has been obtained, and the regularity of the verse preserved.&mdash;<SC>Ritson</SC>
(<I>Cursory Crit.</I> p. 88): The two last words [&lquo;<I>us by</I>&rquo;] of this line are added by the
present Irish editor, who observes that &lquo;the defect of the metre,&rquo; of which he knows
as much as a superannuated jack-ass, &lquo;shows that something was omitted.&rquo; Former
editors [see <I>Text. Notes</I>] supplied the measure by reading, &lquo;Being so frustrat<I>ed,</I> tell
him he mocks&rquo;; which, it must be confessed, does not afford an easy sense. Shake-
speare, however, would never have written the above hobbling line [Malone's]
which has no sort of pretensions to metre. We may read, &lquo;Being so frustrated, he
mocks us by.&rquo;&mdash;[<SC>Knight</SC> reluctantly approves of Malone's emendation, and prints
it in brackets in his text. <SC>R. G. White</SC> (ed. i) approves but does not adopt. <SC>Hud-
son</SC> approves heartily and adopts, and does &lquo;not see how it is possible to strain any
sense at all out of the original reading.&rquo; For my part, I think Steevens supplies us
with a sense when he says, in effect, that Anthony's pauses, now that he is utterly
vanquished, are a mockery.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>4. <B>frustrate</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 342) gives a list of verbs, ending in <I>-te, -t,</I> and <I>-d,</I>
which &lquo;on account of their already resembling participles in their terminations, do not
add <I>-ed</I> in the participle. . . . Words like &ldquo;miscreate,&rdquo; &ldquo;create,&rdquo; &ldquo;consecrate&rdquo;
[&lquo;frustrate&rquo;] being directly derived from Latin participles, stand on a different foot-
ing, and may themselves be regarded as participial adjectives, with the addition of <I>-d.</I>&rquo;
<SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.</I> 8) includes the present &lquo;frustrate&rquo; in his list of words illustrating the
rule that, &lquo;Words such as <I>Juggler, tickling, kindling, England, angry, children,</I> and
the like are,&mdash;as is well known,&mdash;frequently pronounced by the Elizabethan poets as
though a vowel were interposed between the liquid and the preceding mute.&rquo; Of the
present line, he asks, &lquo;Can a good sense be made out of the original reading? the
play of words seems a very strong argument in its favour; indeed, it seems impossible
that this should be accidental. So&mdash;though it seems hardly worth while to accumu-
late instances of the same word used in the same manner,&mdash;Massinger, Middleton,

<P>6. <B>I shall</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: I make no doubt but it should be marked here that Dolla-

command; so that the speeches placed to him in the sequel of this scene, must be
transferred to Agrippa, or he is introduced as a mute. Besides, that Dollabella
should be gone out, appears from this, that when C&aelig;sar asks for him, he recollects
that he had sent him on business. [For this use of &lquo;shall&rquo; for <I>will,</I> both here and
in line 82, below, see, if need be, <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 315.]

<P><B>into ciuill streets</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: I think here is a line lost, after which it is in vain to
go in quest. The sense seems to have been this: &lquo;The round world should have
shook,&rquo; and this great alteration of the system of things should send &lquo;lions into
streets, and citizens into dens.&rquo; There is sense still, but it is harsh and violent.&mdash;
<SC>Steevens</SC>: I believe we should read, &lquo;A greater crack <I>than this:</I> The <I>ruin'd</I>
world,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> the general disruption of elements should have <I>shook,</I> etc. Shakespeare
seems to mean that the death of so great a man ought to have produced effects
similar to those which might have been expected from the dissolution of the universe,
when all distinctions shall be lost. Perhaps, however, Shakespeare might mean
nothing more here than merely an earthquake, in which the shaking of the <I>round
world</I> was to be so violent as to toss the inhabitants of woods into cities and the
inhabitants of cities into woods.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: The defect of the metre strongly sup-
ports Dr Johnson's conjecture, that something is lost. Perhaps the passage origin-
ally stood thus: &lquo;The round world should have shook; <I>Thrown hungry</I> lions into
civil streets,&rquo; etc. . . . The words omitted were perhaps in the middle of the line,
which originally might have stood thus in the MS: &lquo;Lions <I>been hurtled</I> into civil
streets,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>Tyrwhitt</SC>: The sense, I think, is complete and plain, if we consider
&lquo;shook&rquo; (more properly <I>shaken</I>) as the participle past of a verb <I>active.</I>&mdash;[That there
is here an omission is also the opinion of <SC>Collier, Dyce, R. G. White, Staunton,
Deighton, Rolfe</SC>, and of <SC>Walker</SC> (see IV, viii, 9). But as the meaning is per-
fectly clear, and forcibly expressed, for my part, the tears live in an onion that shall
water the sorrow for any loss.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>change adds much force and grace to the tribute Dercetas is paying to his dead
master.
<P>33. <B>Looke you sad Friends</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: It is requisite to transpose the comma
[after &lquo;you&rquo; in Pope's edition, and place it after &lquo;sad&rquo;; because] Octavius's friends
would probably avoid showing any concern on the news of Antony's death, lest it
should give displeasure to C&aelig;sar; which C&aelig;sar observing, it shows a noble humanity
in him to bid them share in such a sorrow, and to tell them it is a calamity that ought
to draw tears even from the eyes of Princes. Young Prince Henry, upon his father's
death, speaks just in the same manner to his brothers; and tho' he would not have
them mix fear with their affliction, he encourages them in their sorrow&mdash;&lquo;Yet be sad,
good brothers, For, by my faith, it very well becomes you.&rquo;&mdash;<I>2 Hen. IV:</I> V, ii, 49.
<P>34. <B>but it is Tydings</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: That is, may the gods rebuke me, <I>if this be
not</I> tidings to make kings weep. &lquo;But&rquo; again, for <I>if not.</I> [Johnson probably here
refers to III, xi, 50, which see, and also IV, xi, 2. &lquo;Tidings&rquo; has already been used
as a singular noun in &lquo;this tidings&rquo; IV, xiv, 137; which justifies those editors who
prefer the reading of F<SUB>2</SUB>, if they need any justification.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>35. <B>To wash the eyes of Kings</B>] <SC>Craik</SC> (p. 194): &lquo;Wash,&rquo; an Anglo-Saxon
word (preserved also in the German <I>waschen</I>), is used in what is probably its primi-
tive sense of immersing in or covering with liquid. Thus we say to <I>wash</I> with gold
or silver.
<P>36. <B>Dol. And,</B> etc.] <SC>Daniel</SC> (p. 83): I would continue this speech to C&aelig;sar,
and, in line 38, for &lquo;<I>per$i$ted</I>&rquo; would read, <I>perfited.</I>&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC> accepted this dis-
tribution of speeches; &lquo;surely,&rquo; he says, &lquo;this speech comes more fitly from C&aelig;sar&rquo;
[than from Agrippa, to whom it had been assigned by Theobald].

<P>46, etc. <B>I haue followed . . . we do launch,</B> etc.] <SC>Steevens</SC>: &lquo;Launch&rquo; was
the ancient, and is still, the vulgar pronunciation, of <I>lance.</I> Nurses always talk of
<I>launching</I> the gums of children, when they have difficulty in cutting teeth. &lquo;I have
followed thee,&rquo; says C&aelig;sar, &lquo;to this&rquo;; <I>i. e.</I> I have pursued thee, till I compelled thee
to self-destruction. But, adds the speaker (at once extenuating his own conduct, and
considering the deceased as one with whom he had been united by the ties of relation-
ship as well as policy, as one who had been a part of himself), the violence, with
which I proceeded, was not my choice; I have done but by him as we do by our
own natural bodies. I have employed force, where force only could be effectual. I
have shed the blood of the irreclaimable Antony, on the same principle that we <I>lance</I>
a disease incurable by gentler means.

<P>the last word in the fourth. We should read the passage thus: &lquo;And it is great To
do the thing that ends all other deeds; Which shackles accidents, and bolts up
change; [<I>Lulls wearied nature to a sound repose;</I>] Which sleeps, and never palates
more the <I>dugg:</I> The beggar's nurse and C&aelig;sar's.&rquo; That this line in hooks was the
substance of that lost, is evident from its making sense of all the rest: which are to
this effect. &lquo;It is great to do that which frees us from all the accidents of humanity,
lulls our over-wearied nature to repose (which now sleeps and has no more appetite
for worldly enjoyments), and is equally the nurse of C&aelig;sar and the beggar.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Seward</SC>
(Note on <I>The False One,</I> IV, ii, p. 139): When we speak in contempt of anything,
we generally resolve it into its first principles: Thus, man is dust and ashes, and
the food we eat, the dung, by which first our vegetable, and from thence our animal,
food is nourished. Thus Cleopatra finding she can no longer riot in the pleasures
of life, with the usual workings of a disappointed pride, pretends a disgust to them,
and speaks in praise of suicide [as in the present lines]. From the observations
above, nothing can be clearer than this passage: &lquo;both the beggar and C&aelig;sar are
fed and nursed by the dung of the earth.&rquo; Of this sense there is a demonstration in
[I, i, 48].&mdash;<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 466): That is, which sleeps, and hath no further relish for
the trash and dung of this earth, which dung is equally necessary to the support of
C&aelig;sar, as of the meanest beggar. In what sense Warburton could understand death
to be equally the nurse of C&aelig;sar and the beggar, or indeed to be the nurse of either,
is inconceivable.&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC> (i, 49): The sentiment in line 8 is not unlike one in I,
i, 48, and the expressions which that is couch'd in, shew plainly what &lquo;dung&rquo; means
in this line, viz.&mdash;the earth, and it's <I>dungy</I> productions; and to mark her contempt
of them, and of C&aelig;sar too at the same time, she calls them&mdash;the nourses or nourishers
both of him and the beggar.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: The difficulty of the passage, if any difficulty
there be, arises only from this, that the act of suicide, and the state which is the effect
of suicide, are confounded. Voluntary death, says she, is an act <I>which bolts up
change;</I> it produces a state, &lquo;Which sleeps, and never palates more the dung, The
beggar's nurse and C&aelig;sar's.&rquo; Which has no longer need of the gross and terrene
sustenance, in the use of which C&aelig;sar and the beggar are on a level. The speech
is abrupt, but perturbation in such a state is surely natural.&mdash;<SC>Boswell</SC>: &lquo;The beg-
gar's nurse and C&aelig;sar's&rquo; means, I apprehend, &lquo;death&rquo; (as Warburton has observed),
and not, as Johnson supposed, the gross substance on which C&aelig;sar and the beggar
were fed.&mdash;[<SC>Knight</SC> agrees with Boswell that the &lquo;beggar's nurse is, unquestionably,

<P>death.&rquo;]&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii): This [<I>dug</I>] is an admirable, though merely literal
emendation in the MS. What Cleopatra says is, that self-destruction prevents all
change, and no longer requires, or &lquo;palates&rquo; the <I>dug,</I> which affords nutriment to all
mankind, whether high or low.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. ii): To me the word &lquo;nurse&rquo; is almost
alone sufficient evidence that &lquo;dung&rquo; is a transcriber's or printer's mistake for <I>dug,</I>&mdash;
which was the more liable to be corrupted, as it was formerly often spelt <I>dugge</I> (so the
folio has, in <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I> I, iii, &lquo;on the nipple of my <I>Dugge</I>&rquo;). The sense I conceive
to be, &lquo;and never more palates that dug which affords nourishment as well to the beg-
gar as to C&aelig;sar.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Anon.</SC> (<I>Blackwood,</I> Oct. 1853, p. 469): The sense probably is,
&mdash;&lquo;It is great to do the thing (suicide) which causes us to sleep, and never more to
taste the produce of the earth, which nourishes alike C&aelig;sar and the beggar. The
MS correction [Warburton's] certainly does not mend matters. This reading affords
no extrication of the construction, &lquo;which sleeps,&rquo; which we have ventured to explain
as &lquo;which <I>lays us</I> asleep, and <I>causes us</I> never more to palate or taste,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>R. G.
White</SC> (ed. i): As I am unable to discern what is the dug which is &lquo;the beggar's
nurse and C&aelig;sar's,&rquo; and as the word in the text is expressive of the speaker's bitter
disgust of life, I make no change.&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: &lquo;Dung&rquo; for <I>dug</I> is an obvious mis-
print, though not wanting defenders.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC>: &lquo;Nurse&rquo; appears to be used here
for <I>nourishment.</I> Cleopatra is speaking contemptuously of this life, as if anything
that depends upon such coarse, vulgar feeding were not worth keeping. But Cleopatra
has never <I>palated</I> the <I>dug</I> since she was a baby; and the sense of the passage clearly
requires some contemptuous word for the <I>common</I> supports of human life, as such,&mdash;
the food she has to palate every day.&mdash;<SC>Deighton</SC>: That is, which produces a state
in which one sleeps a lasting sleep and has no need to taste the dug by which poor
and rich, great and small, are nourished, <I>i. e.</I> no need of the sustenance of life. . . .
There seems a considerable difference between speaking of the earth as fertilized by
manure into furnishing food, and a human being feeding on dung.&mdash;<SC>Irving Edition</SC>:
It seems more natural to suppose that the word &lquo;dung&rquo; is simply a periphrasis for the
fruits of the fertilizing earth, used, certainly in a spirit of bitter mockery and supreme
contempt.&mdash;<SC>Thiselton</SC> (p. 25): A reminiscence of Anthony's words in I, i, 48.
Nowhere are such reminiscences used with more effect than in the close of this trag-
edy where they suggest the integrity of Cleopatra's attachment to Anthony. Shake-
speare meant us to leave Cleopatra, notwithstanding her failings, with feelings of
sympathy and admiration, and that our last thoughts should be of &lquo;the glory of her
womanhood.&rquo;&mdash;[There is a strength in the very coarseness of the word &lquo;dung&rquo;
which, to me, strongly commends it. Only a poet, strong in his own strength, and
conscious of his own supremacy, and &lquo;nearness to the eternal verities,&rquo; would have
dared to use it. This elemental vigour is, to me, wholly lacking in Warburton's
substitution. Surely it does not need either natural death or suicide to cause us to
cease from palating the dug. The palating of it ceases with weaning. It is while
we palate it, before we are weaned, that an aversion to it can be created. When we
cease to have any love for it, death can then produce no aversion. In order, there-
fore, to change love for the dug into indifference to it, should not suicide be restricted
to babes at the breast?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

just the thing to make C&aelig;sar feel sure of having her at his command, and so he will
be less secret as to his purpose, or what he means to do with her; which is what she
most of all desires to learn.

<P>missively.&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC>: The meaning is, when you sue to him for mercy, as to a
