<P>35, 36. <B>I send him The Greatnesse he has got</B>] <SC>Capell</SC> (i, 49): Homage
of great people to persons greater than them, was (and still is), in many countries,
accompany'd with presents: Cleopatra, in her reply, acknowledges herself C&aelig;sar's
vassal, and that she ow'd him homage as such; but that, having nothing in way of
present to send him, she sent him <I>his own greatness;</I> intimating&mdash;that he was master
of hers, and of the fortunes of all the world, and could not be disturb'd in them.&mdash;
<SC>Johnson</SC>: I allow him to be my conqueror; I own his superiority with complete
submission.&mdash;<SC>M. Mason</SC>: Johnson has mistaken the meaning of this passage, nor will
the words bear the construction he gives them. It appears to me, that by <I>the great-
ness he has got,</I> she means her crown which he has won; and I suppose that when
she pronounces these words, she delivers to Proculeius either her own crown, or some
other ensign or royalty.&mdash;[I prefer Johnson's interpretation, which is, substantially,
that of Capell.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

her clothes for feare of any poyson hidden about her.&rquo;&mdash;[See <I>Appendix, Plutarch.</I>
I have not recorded in the <I>Text. Notes</I> all the stage-directions given by the early
editors in their vain reachings after those which would satisfy all requirements; nor
have I recorded all the minor variations of the modern editors. For my own part, I
see no need of any stage-direction at all. It is, at least for me, quite sufficient to see
that the Romans rush in and seize the Queen. In these thrilling moments, how they
got in, I neither know nor care. Nor does any one in the audience ever know how
they entered, and would not know, unless the stage-manager came forward and
read aloud Plutarch, or Malone's directions.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>42, 43. <B>Pro. You see how easily . . . C&aelig;sar come</B>] The Ff, followed by
<SC>Rowe</SC> and <SC>Pope</SC>, give this speech to Charmian. <SC>Theobald</SC>, however, attributed
this distribution to the two latter editors, and remarks: This blunder was for want
of knowing, or observing, the historical fact. When C&aelig;sar sent Proculeius to the
queen, he sent Gallus after him with new instructions; and while one amused Cleo-
patra with propositions from C&aelig;sar, through the crannies of the monument, the other
scaled it by a ladder, entered it at a window backward, and made Cleopatra, and
those with her, prisoners. I have reformed the passage, therefore (as, I am per-
suaded, the author designed it), from the authority of Plutarch.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: This
line, in the first edition, is given to Proculeius; and to him it certainly belongs, though
perhaps misplaced. I would put it at the end of his foregoing speech: &lquo;Where he
for grace is kneel'd to. <I>Aside to Gallus.</I> You see how easily she may be surpriz'd&rquo;;
Then, while Cleopatra makes a formal answer, Gallus, upon the hint given, seizes
her, and Proculeius, interrupting the civility of his answer: &lquo;&mdash;your plight is pitied
Of him that caus'd it,&rquo; cries out: &lquo;Guard her till C&aelig;sar come.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: It is
clear, from the passage quoted from Plutarch in the preceding note, that this [&lquo;<I>Pro.</I>&rquo;]
was an error of the compositor's at the press, and that it belongs to Gallus; who,

<P>after Proculeius hath, according to his suggestion, ascended the monument, goes out
to inform C&aelig;sar that Cleopatra is taken. That C&aelig;sar was informed immediately of
Cleopatra's being taken, appears from Dolabella's first speech to Proculeius on his
entry: &lquo;Proculeius, What thou hast done, thy master C&aelig;sar knows,&rquo; etc. [See lines
77, 78.] This information, it is to be presumed, C&aelig;sar obtained from Gallus. The
stage-directions being very imperfect in this scene in the old copy, no <I>exit</I> is here
marked; but as Gallus afterwards enters along with C&aelig;sar, it was undoubtedly the
author's intention that he should here go out.&mdash;<SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> ii, 177) has an Article
on &lquo;Instances in which Speeches are assigned in the Folio to Wrong Characters,&rquo; in
the course of which he remarks (p. 185) that, &lquo;Errors in the assignment of speeches,
&mdash;including cases in which two speeches have been confused into one, or the like,&mdash;
are remarkably frequent in the Folio. I have just cited sixty or more instances [sixty-
six, by my counting.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] in which this has taken place, even according to the uni-
versally received text. This being the case, there is no reason why we should be
scrupulous in asserting the same of other passages, where the context clearly
indicates it. [The present line is among the sixty-six.]&mdash;<SC>Thiselton</SC> (p. 26): If it
were desired to follow Plutarch, the simplest way would be, perhaps, to regard this
line as the commencement of a new scene the interval being taken up with the move-
ments of Proculeius, but the fact that Gallus, whose presence talking with Cleopatra
is essential to Plutarch's account, does not enter till later shows that Shakespeare did
not intend to follow his authority slavishly. It therefore seems preferable to suppose
that the ladder was fixed by the soldiers during Proculeius&rquo; previous conversation
with Cleopatra, and that he, instead of going to C&aelig;sar as he pretended, climbed up
the ladder with the soldiers and almost immediately appeared behind Cleopatra and
her companions who were still standing at the gate. This view will account for the
two speeches in succession being attributed to Proculeius by the Folio.
<P>49. <B>Releeu'd, but not betraid</B>] <SC>Peck</SC> (p. 254): Instead of &lquo;betray'd,&rquo; I think,
we should read <I>bereav'd.</I> This reading, I am sure, agrees better with Cleopatra's
next words, . . . where <I>betray'd of death</I> is a forced expression, but <I>bereav'd</I> is very
natural. Besides in her present condition she finds herself already <I>bereav'd</I> of her
crown, and, therefore, thinks it harder to be <I>bereav'd of death,</I> or the liberty to kill
herself.&mdash;[Seven years after the publication of the foregoing note by Peck, <SC>War-
burton</SC> proposed the same emendation, except that he transferred the change to
&lquo;Releeu'd&rquo;; his text reads &lquo;<I>Bereav'd,</I> but not betray'd.&rquo; His note thereon is of
small consequence.]

<P>may mean <I>sometimes.</I> The meaning of Cleopatra seems to be this: If <I>idle talking</I> be
sometimes necessary to the prolongation of life, why I will not <I>sleep</I> for fear of <I>talk-
ing idly in my sleep.</I> The sense, designed, however, may be&mdash;If it be necessary, for
once, to talk of performing impossibilities, why, I'll not sleep neither. I have little
confidence, however, in these attempts, to produce a meaning from the words under
consideration.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: The explications above given appear to me so unsatisfac-
tory, that I have no doubt that a line has been lost after the word <I>necessary,</I> in which
Cleopatra threatened to observe an obstinate silence. The line probably began
with the word <I>I'll,</I> and the compositor's eye glancing on the same words in the line
beneath, all that intervened was lost. The omitted line might have been of this
import: &lquo;If idle talk will once be necessary, <I>I'll not so much as syllable a word;</I> I'll
not sleep neither,&rquo; etc. The words, &lquo;I'll not sleep neither,&rquo; contain a new and dis-
tinct menace.&mdash;<SC>Ritson</SC>: I agree that a line is lost, which I shall attempt to supply:
&lquo;If idle talk will once be necessary [<I>I will not speak; If sleep be necessary</I>], I'll
not sleep neither.&rquo; The repetition of the word <I>necessary</I> may have occasioned the
omission.&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii) says, in effect, that, according to the MS, Cleopatra
adds &lquo;that she will hasten her death by perpetual watchfulness, if &lquo;idle talk&rquo; will
contribute to it, or be <I>accessary</I> to it.&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: We adopt Hanmer's <I>accessary.</I>
The sense is plainly,&mdash;&lquo;I'll neither eat nor drink, and, if idle talk will, <I>for the nonce,</I>
be assistant, I'll not sleep.&rquo;&mdash;[The obscurity in these lines is removed, I think, by
the paraphrases of Heath and of Johnson.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>97, etc. <B>His face was as the Heau'ns,</B> etc.] In all the similes throughout this
&lquo;dream,&rquo; <SC>Whiter</SC> discerns allusions to pageants and processions. &lquo;Let it be
remembered,&rquo; he says (p. 190), &lquo;that an imitation of the sphere of the Heavens,
with the attributes and ornaments belonging to it, the sweetness of its music, and
the noise of its thunder, the Sun, the Moon, and the Earth, colossal figures,&mdash;
armorial bearings,&mdash;a magnificent procession of monarchs and their attendants,&mdash;
floating islands,&mdash;and a prodigal distribution of wealth and honors, are the known
and familiar materials which formed the motley compound of the Masque, the
Pageant, or the Procession.&rquo; See IV, xiv, 11.
<P>99, 100. <B>The little . . . Creature</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: What a blessed limping verse
these two hemistichs give us! Had none of the Editors an ear to find the hitch in
its pace? 'Tis true, there is but a syllable wanting, and that, I believe verily, was
but of a single letter; which the first Editors not understanding, learnedly threw it
out as a redundance. I restore, <I>The little O o'th' Earth, i. e.</I> the little orb or circle.
And, 'tis plain, our Poet in other passages chuses to express himself thus, &lquo;Ros. O,
that your face were not so full of O'es.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Love's Labour's Lost,</I> V, ii, 46, <I>i. e.</I> of
round dimples, pitts with the smallpox. &lquo;Can we cram, Within this wooden O,
the very casques,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<I>Prol.</I> to <I>Henry V.</I> 12. &lquo;Fair Helena, who more engilds the
night Than all you fiery O's and Eyes of light.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Mid. N. D.,</I> III, ii, 195, <I>i. e.</I>
the circles, orbs of the stars.&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC>: [Notwithstanding Theobald's amendment,
the text of the folio] may, after all, be the true reading.

<P>105-107. <B>For his Bounty, There was no winter in't. An Anthony it was,
That grew the more by reaping</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: There was certainly a contrast
both in the thought and terms, designed here, which is lost in an accidental cor-
ruption. How could an Antony grow the more by reaping? I'll venture, by a very
easy change, to restore an exquisite fine allusion; which carries its reason with it too,
why there was no <I>winter</I> in his bounty: &lquo;For his bounty, There was no <I>winter</I>
in't; an <I>autumn</I> 'twas, That grew the more by reaping.&rquo; I ought to take notice,
that the ingenious Dr Thirlby likewise started this very emendation, and had marked
it in the margin of his book. The reason of the depravation might easily arise from
the great similitude of the two words in the old spelling, <I>Antonie</I> and <I>Automne.</I> [The
name is spelt <I>Anthony</I> in this play in the Folio without an exception, I think;
which injures the literal &lquo;similitude&rquo; not a little.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] Our author has employed
this thought again in [his 53rd <I>Sonnet</I>]: &lquo;Speak of the spring and foison of the
year; The one doth shadow of your beauty show, The other as your bounty doth
appear; And you in every blessed shape we know.&rquo; 'Tis plain that &lquo;foison&rquo; means
<I>Autumn</I> here, which pours out its profusion of fruits bountifully; in opposition to
<I>Spring,</I> which only shews the youthful beauty, and promise of that future bounty.&mdash;
<SC>Corson</SC> (<I>The Nation,</I> 28 Aug., 1873): If &lquo;An Anthony it was&rquo; is not right, &lquo;an
autumn 'twas&rquo; is certainly wrong. It is too tame for the intensely impassioned
speech in which it occurs, or, rather, into which it has been introduced by the editors.
Again, if &lquo;autumn&rquo; could, by metonymy, be wrenched to mean the crops of autumn,
it could hardly be said that an autumn <I>grows</I> the more by reaping. But this reading
of Theobald has been silently adopted by all subsequent editors, without any con-
sideration of its tameness or of the resultant incongruity. In &lquo;An <I>Anthony</I> it was,&rquo;
&lquo;it&rquo; stands, of course, for &lquo;Bounty.&rquo; His Bounty was an <I>Anthony,</I> &lquo;that grew the
more by reaping.&rquo; Now, could the &lquo;less Greek&rquo; which, Ben Jonson tells us, Shake-
speare possessed, have enabled him to see in &lquo;Anthony&rquo; the word <G>a)\nqos?</G> His
Bounty had no winter in it; it was a mead of perennial luxuriance, affording a

<P><I>flowering</I> pasturage (<G>*a)nqo/nomos</G>), and &lquo;that grew the more by reaping.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>James
Spedding</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.,</I> 1874, V, i, 303): I cannot understand Prof. Corson's objec-
tion to &lquo;autumn.&rquo; In the cursive black-letter hand of the time <I>Autumn</I> might easily
be written so as to be hardly distinguishable from <I>Antonie,</I> and surely it makes better
sense and better poetry. So far from calling it &lquo;tame,&rquo; I should instance it as one of
the noblest, boldest, and liveliest images in poetry. Keats said that poetry &lquo;ought
to surprise, by a fine excess.&rquo; This is exactly a case of such &lquo;fine excess.&rquo; &lquo;An
autumn that grew the more by reaping&rquo;&mdash;that, the more you took of its harvests,
the more there remained to take&mdash;is surely as great an image of &lquo;bounty&rquo; as the
mind in its most impassioned state ever created; quite as much so, and yet evidently
from the same mint, as Juliet's&mdash;&lquo;My bounty is as boundless as the sea, My love as
deep; the more I give to thee, The more I have; for both are infinite.&rquo; As for the
difficulty of understanding by autumn the crops of autumn, how is it more difficult
than to understand by &lquo;winter&rquo; the absence of crops? And what are we to come
to? Instead of allowing Tennyson to say&mdash;&lquo;To strip a hundred hollows bare of
spring,&rquo; we shall have to ask him to print &lquo;sprigs&rquo; for &lquo;spring.&rquo; As for the amount
of Shakespeare's Greek, of which he has left us no means of judging, the difficulty
is to understand how he could have had Greek enough to know that <G>a)\nqos</G> meant a
flower, without knowing also that Anthony could <I>not</I> mean a pasture of flowers; and
not only could not really mean it, but could not, by any process of association, legiti-
mate or illegitimate, suggest the image to an Englishman.&mdash;[Theobald asks, &lquo;how
an Antony could grow the more by reaping?&rquo; Would it not be equally perti-
nent to ask how an autumn could grow the more by reaping? Reaping in the
autumn is done when the grain is ripe, and grain thus reaped never grows again.
The farmer is not yet born who, in the temperate zone, reaps the ripe grain in the
autumn and finds it growing more vigorously for the process. To be sure, a farmer
who could keep on reaping stubble fields and find at each reaping a heavier harvest
would be, as Spedding observes, &lquo;as great an image of &ldquo;bounty&rdquo; as the mind in its
most impassioned state ever created,&rquo; and, possibly, can be paralleled only in the
<I>Arabian Nights.</I> Not thus essentially at fault are, I think, Shakespeare's similes,
which may be sometimes flagrantly open to criticism, but never to downright folly&mdash;
thus, in all humility, it seems to me. When Spedding becomes eloquent over the
beauty of &lquo;autumn,&rquo; he seems to forget that he is exalting not Shakespeare, but Theo-
bald. There is about Corson's suggestion so much refinement, elegance, and charm
that it is hard to reject it. But, unfortunately, there is nothing in common between
Anthony and Anthos but the first syllable, and there is no Greek word which will
furnish any more. Moreover, we do not reap flowers, even to make them grow.
Until an emendation is suggested, therefore, happier, as I think, than <I>autumn,</I> I
shall endeavour, for my own feeble self, to extract from &lquo;Anthony&rquo; what meaning I
may of inexhaustible perfection in face, in form, in voice, in bounty, which for Cleo-
patra so far lay in that single name that once, in order to express the height and
depth and boundlessness of her self-absorption she exclaimed, &lquo;Oh, my oblivion is a
very Anthony!&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>111. <B>As plates</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: &lquo;Plates&rquo; mean, I believe, <I>silver money.</I> So, in Mar-
lowe's <I>Jew of Malta,</I> 1633: &lquo;What's the price of this slave? two hundred crowns!
. . . And if he has, he is worth three hundred <I>plates.</I>&rquo;&mdash;[II, p. 272, ed. Dyce.]
Again: &lquo;Rat'st thou this Moor but at two hundred <I>plates?</I>&rquo;&mdash;[<I>Ibid.</I> p. 273.]&mdash;
<SC>Whalley</SC>: Steevens justly interprets &lquo;plates&rquo; to mean silver money. It is a term
in heraldry. The balls or roundels in an escutcheon of arms, according to their
different colours, have different names. If <I>gules,</I> or red, they are called <I>torteauxes;</I>
if <I>or,</I> or yellow, <I>bezants;</I> if <I>argent,</I> or white, <I>plates,</I> which are buttons of silver with-
out any impression, but only prepared for the stamp.
<P>117. <B>nor euer were</B>] <SC>Thiselton</SC> (p. 27): &lquo;Nor&rquo; has been unwarrantably changed
to <I>or,</I> owing to its being overlooked that this line is in direct contrast with the preced-
ing, and that &lquo;nor&rquo; implies an ellipsis of <I>neither</I> or <I>not.</I> Cleopatra would ask, &lquo;But
assuming for the moment you are right, how came I to dream of such a one?&rquo; And
this question she answers by saying that though Fancy could outstrip Nature, yet the
mere picture of Anthony as he actually was in Nature exceeded anything Fancy
could create. The description Cleopatra has just given was the work of fancy but in
so far as it did not tally with Anthony as he was, it was because it fell short of, not
because it exaggerated, his greatness.
<P>119. <B>To vie</B>] <SC>Staunton</SC>: This was a term at cards, and meant, particularly, to
increase the stakes, and, generally, to challenge any one to a <I>contention, bet, wager,</I>
etc.&mdash;[Undoubtedly, it was, and, perhaps, originally, a term at cards, although its
meaning is obscure. It is used in Florio's <I>Second Frutes</I> (pp. 69, 71) in a way
which is difficult to explain. But I doubt that, in the present passage, it has any
reference to cards. It is used, I think, as it is defined in the <I>Century Dictionary</I>
(<I>s. v.</I> vie, II. <I>trans.</I> 2.): &lquo;To put or bring into competition; try to outdo in; contend
with respect to.&rquo; Whereupon the present passage is quoted as an example.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>119-121. <B>yet t'imagine . . . shadowes quite</B>] <SC>Whiter</SC> (p. 194): Is it possible
to employ terms more pointed and significant than those which might be selected
from the concluding sentence to describe the nature and properties of such romantic
exhibitions? For what are the devices of the Pageant, but the creatures of a <I>dream,</I>
&mdash;the <I>strange forms</I> of an illusive <I>fancy,</I> and the empty <I>shadows</I> of a sportive
imagination?&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: We are not sure of having mastered the sense of this, or
indeed that the text exhibits precisely what Shakespeare wrote, but the meaning
apparently is,&mdash;&lquo;Nature lacks material to compete with fancy in unwonted shapes,
yet the conception of an Antony was a masterpiece of Nature over fancy, abasing
phantoms quite.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Hudson</SC>: Shakespeare sometimes uses <I>fancy</I> and <I>imagination</I> as
equivalent terms, and here he uses both for the dreaming-power. Nature lacks
material to keep up with fancy in the creation of strange forms; yet to fancy such an
actual being as Antony, a man of Nature's making, were to make Nature an over-
match for fancy, dwarfing its shadowy creatures into insignificance. The passage
is exceedingly strong and subtle, and comes appropriately from this matchless roll of
unwomanly womanhood.
<P>120, 121. <B>were Natures peece, 'gainst Fancie, Condemning shadowes quite</B>]
<SC>Warburton</SC>: The word <I>prize,</I> which I have restored, is very pretty, as figuring a
contention between <I>nature</I> and <I>imagination</I> about the larger extent of their powers;
and <I>nature</I> gaining the <I>prize</I> by producing Antony.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: The word &lquo;piece,&rquo;
is a term appropriated to works of art. Here Nature and Fancy produce each their
<I>piece,</I> and the <I>piece</I> done by Nature had the preference. Antony was in reality <I>past
the size of dreaming;</I> he was more by <I>Nature</I> than <I>Fancy</I> could present in sleep.
<P>124, 125. <B>would I . . . But I do</B>] <SC>Thiselton</SC> (p. 27): &lquo;But,&rquo; Dollabella means,
&lquo;If success in a cherished object carries with it the being infected by the grief of my
victim, as I am now by your grief, I would rather forego it.&rquo;&mdash;[Is not the &lquo;But,&rquo; in
this passage, that which follows strong asseverations, as in Othello's exclamation:
&lquo;Perdition catch my soul But I do love thee&rquo;? Thus here Dollabella says, in effect,
&lquo;Would I might never gain success, if I do not sympathise with you!&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>clash of <I>shoots</I> and &lquo;root.&rquo;&mdash;[Collier repeats this note in his ed. ii, and adds that
&lquo;suites&rquo; is corrected to <I>smites</I> in the MS.]&mdash;<SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 311): &lquo;A grief that
<I>shoots,</I>&rquo;&mdash;that is neither old nor modern English. Note, too, &lquo;shoots <I>at root.</I>&rquo; Folio,
<I>suites;</I> hence one of the commentators (I know not who), recollecting the puns on
<I>suitor</I> and <I>shooter</I> in the old dramatists, concluded it was a mistake of the printer's
ear for <I>shoots.</I> (Apropos of which, by the way, in a letter of John Alleyn, the player,
a man ignorant of spelling, ap. Collier's <I>Alleyn Papers, shaute</I> is written for <I>suite,</I>
courtship, offer of marriage.) Shakespeare wrote <I>smites. Smite</I> occurs in the very
next column; so that the word seems to have been running in his head.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC>:
<I>Smites,</I>&mdash;thus Tyrwhitt in his copy of F<SUB>2</SUB> in the British Museum.&mdash;<SC>Anon.</SC> (<I>Black-
wood,</I> Oct. 1853): &lquo;Suites&rquo; is perhaps judiciously altered into <I>smites.</I>&mdash;[Inasmuch
as there is proof, adequately conclusive (see a long discussion in <I>Love's Lab. Lost,</I>
IV, i, 122), that <I>suite</I> and <I>suitor</I> were, in Shakespeare's day, pronounced, on occasion,
<I>shoot</I> and <I>shooter;</I> and, inasmuch as &lquo;suites,&rquo; thus pronounced in the present pas-
sage makes good sense, I do not think we are justified in substituting, for one of
Shakespeare's own words, any other word, however great may be the improvement.
Is it not common enough, at the present day, to speak of physical pain as &lquo;shooting&rquo;?
Cannot poetic license apply the same verb to mental pain?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>149. <B>I cannot proiect mine owne cause</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: &lquo;Project&rquo; signifies to
<I>invent</I> a cause, not to <I>plead</I> it; which is the sense here required. It is plain that we
should read, <I>proctor.</I> The technical term, to plead by an advocate.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>:
Hanmer reads: &lquo;I cannot <I>parget</I> my own cause&mdash;.&rquo; Meaning, I cannot <I>whitewash,
varnish,</I> or <I>gloss</I> my cause. I believe the present reading to be right. To <I>project a
cause</I> is to <I>represent</I> a cause; to <I>project</I> it <I>well,</I> is to <I>plan</I> or <I>contrive</I> a scheme of
defence.&mdash;<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 466): To <I>project</I> is properly a term of perspective, signifying
to represent an object truly, according to the rules of that art. Hence it is applied
metaphorically to denote a representation of any kind whatever. So that the sense
is, I am not capable of stating my own cause in so favourable a light, as to free
myself from all blame.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: &lquo;Project&rquo; may certainly be right. Sir John
Harrington, in his <I>Metamorphosis of Ajax,</I> 1596, says&mdash;&lquo;I am not only groundedly
studied in the reformation of Ajax, which I have chosen for the <I>project</I> of this dis-
course.&rquo;&mdash;[p. 95, ed. Singer.]&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: In <I>Much Ado,</I> we find these lines: &lquo;She
cannot love, Nor take no shape nor <I>project</I> of affection, She is so self-endear'd.&rquo;&mdash;[III,
i, 59.] I cannot <I>project,</I> etc. means, therefore, I cannot shape or form my cause,
etc.&mdash;[Heath's interpretation, which is also, in fact, Johnson's, seems to be the best.
&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
</CC>

<P>166. <B>You shall aduise me in all for Cleopatra</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: You shall yourself
be my counsellor, and suggest whatever you wish to be done for your relief. So,
afterwards: &lquo;For we intend so to dispose you, as Yourself shall give us counsel.&rquo;
[lines 219, 220.]
<P>167. <B>This is the breefe,</B> etc.] <SC>von Friesen</SC> (iii, 256): Cleopatra's determination
to shut herself up in her Monument, and have her death announced to Anthony is a
step concerning which it is difficult to decide whether it was prompted by a sudden
prudence in retiring before the bitter reproaches of Antony, or an artistic stroke of
fresh <I>coquetterie.</I> But when there followed upon it an unexpected issue and Antony
had committed suicide, I am convinced that Cleopatra was smitten with a love for
the dying and for the dead hero, deeper and, possibly, more overwhelming than ever
she had felt for him when alive. Hereupon, she reveals in her opposition to Octavius
all the versatility of her shrewdness and dissimulation. Plutarch, justly enough,
does not record that she contemplated enmeshing Octavius in her charms. This
repulsive legend, started by the historians after Plutarch's time, Shakespeare could
not, therefore, have intended, even in the remotest degree, to have recalled. On the
contrary her deportment toward the Emperor from the moment of his sending Thyreus
to her displays the keenest shrewdness. In this respect, her interview with him is a
model. . . . From the very instant that she learned the Emperor's decision to carry
her as a prisoner to Rome to grace his triumph, her resolve to take her own life was
fixed and immovable. For what other purpose, forsooth, was the presentation to
Octavius of the brief of her treasures and the summons to Seleucus to testify to her
conscientious statement?

<P>168, 169. <B>'tis exactly valewed, Not petty things admitted</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>:
Sagacious editors! Cleopatra gives in a list of her wealth, says, 'tis exactly valued;
but that petty things are not <I>admitted</I> in this list: and then she appeals to her treas-
urer, that she has reserved nothing to herself. And when he betrays her, she is
reduced to the shift of exclaiming against the ingratitude of servants, and of making
apologies for having secreted certain trifles. Who does not see, that we ought to
read: &lquo;Not petty things <I>omitted?</I>&rquo; For this declaration lays open her falsehood;
and makes her angry, when her treasurer detects her in a direct lie.&mdash;<SC>Johnson</SC>: Not-
withstanding the wrath of Theobald, I have restored the old reading. She is angry
afterwards, that she is accused of having reserved more than petty things.&mdash;[In the
corresponding passage in Plutarch, Cleopatra says, &lquo;though it may be I have reserved
some jewels and trifles meet for women,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]&mdash;<SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 377): The parti-
ciple is often used to express a condition, where, for perspicuity we should now mostly
insert <I>if.</I> Thus here the meaning is, &lquo;exactly, if petty things be excepted.&rquo;&mdash;[See
III, xii, 17.]
<P>174. <B>I had rather seele my lippes</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Sew up my mouth.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>:
It means close up my lips as effectually as the eyes of a hawk are closed. To <I>seel</I>
hawks was the technical term.&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (ed. i): The commentators have under-
stood an allusion to <I>seeling</I> the eyes of a hawk; but the common expression of <I>sealing</I>
the lips requires no such explanation.&mdash;<SC>Singer</SC>: But the poet is very fond of such
allusions [to hawking], and there is surely no reason for printing <I>seal,</I> and thus sub-
stituting a word not authorised by the old copy which always prints the latter word
<I>seal</I> or <I>seale.</I>&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. ii): In III, xiii, 137, we have &lquo;the wise gods <I>seele</I> our
eyes,&rquo; etc. But here the spelling of the Folio goes for little; in <I>Lear,</I> IV, vi, 168,
the Folio has &lquo;the power to <I>seale</I> th' accusers lips&rquo;; and in <I>2 Hen. VI:</I> I, ii, 89,
&lquo;<I>Seale</I> vp your Lips.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Staunton</SC>: To <I>seal</I> one's lips was a familiar expression ages

<P>209-211. <B>when we fall, We answer others merits, in our name Are there-
fore to be pittied</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: The lines should be pointed thus:&mdash;&lquo;And when
we fall We answer. Others' merits, in our names Are therefore to be pitied.&rquo; That
is, &lquo;when any misfortune hath subjected us to the power of our enemies, we are sure
to be punished for those faults. As this is the case, it is but reasonable that we
should have the merit of our ministers' good actions, as well as bear the blame of
their bad.&rquo; But she softens the word <I>merit</I> into <I>pity.</I> The reason of her making
the reflexion was this: Her former conduct was liable to much censure from
Octavius, which she would hereby artfully insinuate was owing to her evil ministers.
And as her present conduct, in concealing her treasures, appeared to be her own act,
she being detected by her minister, she begs, that as she now answers for her
former minister's miscarriages, so her present minister's merit in this discovery, might
likewise be placed to her account: Which she thinks but reasonable.&mdash;<SC>Heath</SC>
(p. 467): That is, We, who are in possession of the supreme power, are ill thought
of for faults committed by others, without our direction or knowledge; and, when we
are stripped of this power, are obliged to answer in our own names for what those
others ought in justice to answer for themselves. Therefore we are to be pitied. I
conceive that this reflection of Cleopatra is intended to insinuate, that the deficiency
in the inventory ought to be imputed to Seleucus her accuser, and not to herself;
</CC>

<P>and that he therefore was properly answerable for it. I would beg leave to add,
that I am inclined to believe that Shakespear gave us the third line thus, And <I>answer
others merits in our names;</I> which renders the construction more explicit and per-
spicuous.&mdash;[<SC>Collier's</SC> MS marked the same change from &lquo;Are&rquo; to <I>And.</I> &lquo;Very
unnecessarily,&rquo; says <SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. ii): &lquo;In the last clause of a sentence Shakespeare
(like other old writers) sometimes omits &ldquo;and.&rdquo;&rquo;]&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC> (i, 51): The reflec-
tions contain'd in this speech are perfectly just, and their wording as clear as their
intention; which is&mdash;to exculpate the speaker, not in what has recently happen'd,
but her political behaviour in general: Nothing then is hard to conceive, but the
consequence drawn from these premises,&mdash;&lquo;in our name Are therefore to be pity'd&rquo;;
and the single difficulty there, lyes in&mdash;&lquo;<I>name</I>&rquo;<I>:</I> But how often is <I>name</I> put for&mdash;
title? and here with great energy: as importing&mdash;that greatness and dignities, high
and swelling titles, were mere vanities and a <I>name</I> only; rather worthy of pity than
envy, by reason of it's servants' abuses, and the ruin it often suffers through them.&mdash;
<SC>Johnson</SC>: &lquo;We su$$er at our highest state of elevation in the thoughts of mankind
for that which others do; and when we fall, those that contented themselves only
to think ill before, call us to answer in our own names for the merits of others. We
are therefore to be pitied.&rquo; <I>Merits</I> is in this place taken in an ill sense, for actions
meriting censure.&mdash;<SC>M. Mason</SC>: The plain meaning is this: &lquo;The greatest of us are
aspersed for things which others do; and when, by the decline of our power, we
become in a condition to be questioned, we are called to answer in our own names
for the actions of other people.&rquo; <I>Merit</I> is here used, as the word <I>desert</I> frequently
is, to express a certain degree of merit or demerit. A man may merit punishment
as well as reward.&mdash;<SC>Malone</SC>: As <I>demerits</I> was often used, in Shakspeare's time, as
synonymous to <I>merit,</I> so <I>merit</I> might have been used in the sense which we now
affix to <I>demerit;</I> or the meaning may be only, we are called to account, and to answer
in our own names for <I>acts,</I> with which others, rather than we, <I>deserve</I> to be charged.
&mdash;[From Capell's crabbed English (Dr Johnson, using Prospero's language in
reference to Caliban, said that if Capell had only come to him, he would &lquo;have
endowed his purposes with words&rquo;) I can extract more light than from any of the
other interpretations, and, in addition, his version conforms closely to the Folio.
The real difficulty lies, as he says, in the word &lquo;name,&rquo; which here, I think, means
<I>eminence, greatness</I> (as in other instances which Schmidt's <I>Lexicon</I> will supply).
The passage, then, may be paraphrased: &lquo;When we, the great ones of earth, fail,
it is not through our own fault, but through that of others, our subordinates; for the
very eminence of our position, therefore, we are to be pitied.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>218. <B>Make not your thoughts your prisons</B>] <SC>Johnson</SC>: I once wished to
read&mdash;&lquo;Make not your thoughts your <I>poison</I>&mdash;&rquo;: Do not destroy yourself by musing
on your misfortune. Yet I would change nothing, as the old reading presents a very
proper sense. &lquo;Be not a prisoner in imagination, when in reality you are free.&mdash;
[<SC>Johnson</SC> suggested <I>poison,</I> wherein he was anticipated by Hanmer ed. i. <SC>Dyce</SC>

<P>232. <B>and it is prouided</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC>: Freinshemius has observed, upon a pas-
sage in Quintus Curtius, that your best writers very often leave some things to be
understood from the consequence and implication of words, which the words them-
selves do not express. Our author observes this conduct here. Cleopatra must be
supposed to mean, she has spoke for the asp, and it is provided, tho' she says not a
word of it in direct terms.&mdash;<SC>Capell</SC> (i, 51): The Poet's art in this place is worth
noting: &lquo;it&rquo; relates covertly to the asp which she afterwards dies by; but her
further directions about it, are convey'd in a whisper,&mdash;&lquo;But hark thee, Charmian&rquo;;
which had they been openly given, a main grace of the incident that presently fol-
lows had been taken away from it, that is&mdash;it's novelty.

<P>250, etc. <B>Now Iras,</B> etc.] <SC>Mrs Jameson</SC> (ii, 152): But though Cleopatra talks
of dying &lquo;after the high Roman fashion,&rquo; she fears what she most desires, and cannot
perform with simplicity what costs her such an effort. That extreme physical coward-
ice, which was so strong a trait in her historical character, which led to the defeat
of Actium, which made her delay the execution of a fatal resolve till she had &lquo;tried
conclusions infinite of <I>easy</I> ways to die,&rquo; Shakespeare has rendered with the finest
possible effect, and in a manner which heightens instead of diminishing our respect
and interest. Timid by nature, she is courageous by the mere force of will, and she
lashes herself up with high-sounding words into a kind of false daring. Her lively
imagination suggests every incentive which can spur her on to the deed she has
resolved, yet trembles to contemplate. She pictures to herself all the degradations
which must attend her captivity; and let it be observed, that those which she antici-
pates are precisely such as a vain, luxurious, and haughty woman would especially
dread, and which only true virtue and magnanimity could despise. Cleopatra could
have endured the loss of freedom; but to be led in triumph through the streets of
Rome is insufferable. She could stoop to C&aelig;sar with dissembling courtesy, and meet
duplicity with superior art; but &lquo;to be chastised&rquo; by the scornful or upbraiding
glance of the injured Octavia&mdash;&lquo;rather a ditch in Egypt!&rquo;

In the same vein, after she has done this, she calls C&aelig;sar an &lquo;ass unpolicied.&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D. s. v.</I>): Adopted from French <I>absurde,</I> an adaptation of Latin
<I>absurd-us,</I> inharmonious, tasteless, foolish; formed on <I>ab</I> off, here intensive+<I>surdus</I>
deaf, inaudible, insufferable to the ear. 2. Out of harmony with reason or propriety;
incongruous, unreasonable, illogical. In modern sense, especially, plainly opposed to
reason and hence ridiculous, silly.&mdash;[I think Shakespeare has a right to the privi-
lege of using &lquo;absurd&rquo; in its derivative sense.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>274, 275, etc. <B>Go fetch My best Attyres,</B> etc.] <SC>Mrs Jameson</SC> (ii, 154): She then
calls for her diadem, her robes of state, and attires herself as if &lquo;again for Cydnus, to
meet Mark Antony.&rquo; Coquette to the last, she must make Death proud to take her,
and die &lquo;ph&oelig;nix like,&rquo; as she had lived, with all the pomp of preparation&mdash;luxurious
in her despair. The death of Lucretia, of Portia, of Arria, and others who died
&lquo;after the high Roman fashion,&rquo; is sublime according to the Pagan ideas of virtue,
and yet none of them so powerfully affect the imagination as the catastrophe of Cleo-
patra. The idea of this frail, timid, wayward woman, dying with heroism from the
mere force of passion and will, takes us by surprise. The attic elegance of her mind,
her poetical imagination, the pride of beauty and royalty predominating to the last,
and the sumptuous and picturesque accompaniments with which she surrounds her-
self in death, carry to its extreme height that effect of contrast which prevails through
her life and character. No arts, no invention could add to the real circumstances of
Cleopatra's closing scene. Shakespeare has shown profound judgment and feeling in
adhering closely to the classical authorities; and to say that the language and senti-
ments worthily fill up the outline, is the most magnificent praise that can be given.
<P>276. <B>Sirra Iras</B>] See IV, xv, 105.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. ii): Nearly all the modern editors
wrongly put a comma between these words.

<P>283. <B>a rurall Fellow</B>] <SC>A. C. Bradley</SC> (p. 395): The Porter [in <I>Macbeth</I>] does
not make me smile: the moment is too terrific. He is grotesque; no doubt the
contrast he affords is humorous as well as ghastly; I dare say the groundlings roared
with laughter at his coarsest remarks. But they are not comic enough to allow one
to forget for a moment what has preceded and what must follow. And I am far
from complaining of this. I believe that it is what Shakespeare intended, and that
he despised the groundlings if they laughed. Of course he could have written with-
out the least difficulty speeches five times as humorous; but he knew better. The
Grave-diggers make us laugh: the old Countryman who brings the asps to Cleopatra
makes us smile at least. But the Grave-digger scene does not come at a moment of
extreme tension; and it is long. Our distress for Ophelia is not so absorbing that
we refuse to be interested in the man who digs her grave, or even continue through-
out the long conversation to remember always with pain that the grave is hers. It
is fitting, therefore, that he should be made decidedly humorous. The passage in
<I>Antony and Cleopatra</I> is much nearer to the passage in <I>Macbeth,</I> and seems to have
been forgotten by those who say that there is nothing in Shakespeare resembling that
passage.<SUP>*</SUP> The old Countryman comes at a moment of tragic exaltation, and the
dialogue is appropriately brief. But the moment, though tragic, is emphatically one
of exaltation. We have not been feeling horror, nor are we feeling a dreadful
suspense. We are going to see Cleopatra die, but she is to die gloriously and to
triumph over Octavius. And therefore our amusement at the old Countryman and
the contrast he affords to these high passions, is untroubled, and it was right to make
him really comic. But the Porter's case is quite different. We cannot forget how
the knocking that makes him grumble sounded to Macbeth, or that within a few
minutes of his opening the gate Duncan will be discovered in his blood; nor can we
help feeling that in pretending to be porter of hell-gate he is terribly near the truth.
To give him language so humorous that it would ask us almost to lose the sense of
these things would have been a fatal mistake,&mdash;the kind of mistake that means want
of dramatic imagination. And that was not the sort of error into which Shakespeare
fell.
<FHL>
<NOTE>* Even if this were true, the retort is obvious that neither is there anything resem-
bling the murder-scene in <I>Macbeth.</I></NOTE>

<P>287. <B>What poore an Instrument</B>] <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 85): &lquo;What&rquo; is here used for
<I>how.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ibid</SC> (&sect; 422): We can say &lquo;how poor <I>an</I> instrument,&rquo; regarding &lquo;how&rquo; as
an adverb, and &lquo;how poor&rquo; as an adverbialized expression, but not, &lquo;What poor an
instrument,&rquo; because &lquo;what&rquo; has almost lost with us its adverbial force.&mdash;[In this
section Abbott gives many examples of the transposition of the Article.]
<P>291. <B>the fleeting Moone</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: Alluding to the Egyptian devotion
paid to the moon under the name of Isis.&mdash;[See III, xiii, 183.]&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>: I
really believe that the poet was not at all acquainted with the devotion that the
Egyptians paid to this planet under the name of Isis. &lquo;Fleeting&rquo; is inconstant.&mdash;
[Juliet's words are a sufficing commentary: &lquo;O, swear not by the moon, th' incon-
stant moon, That monthly changes in her circled orb.&rquo;&mdash;II, ii, 109.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>293. <B>Enter . . . Clowne</B>] <SC>Vischer</SC> (vi, p. 175): The Clown enters with the
asp, which Cleopatra had ordered. In him, Shakespeare introduces a dunderhead,
who, unwitting of the great act to which he had been summoned, cracks jokes about
the bite of the worm of Nilus, and, like the Musicians in <I>Romeo and Juliet,</I> the
Porter in <I>Macbeth,</I> and the Grave-diggers in Hamlet, supplies the contrast between
the exalted image of death and low ordinary life. It is not too distracting. Genuine
tragic emotion is often stimulated thereby, so fearfully does life love to mingle the
serious and the comic.&mdash;<SC>Delius</SC> (<I>Sh. Jahrbuch,</I> V, p. 268): This &lquo;rural Fellow&rquo;
is the Clown of the drama, and consequently uses Clown's language, which is prose
embellished with perverted words.

<P>338, 339. <B>which the Gods giue . . . after wrath</B>] <SC>Rev. John Hunter</SC>: The
notion of good fortune in this world justifying the gods in reversing it in the next
world, was founded on the parable of Dives and Lazarus, <I>Luke,</I> xvi, 25.&mdash;<SC>Words-
worth</SC>: A genuine heathen sentiment: see <I>Herod.</I> III, 40.&mdash;[Dr Wordsworth also
refers to his own Book, <I>Shakespeare's Knowledge and Use of the Bible,</I> where (p. 114,
<I>et seq.</I>) the attempt is made to show that Shakespeare is wont to make religious senti-
ments conform to the religion of the speaker, whether Heathen or Christian.]
<P>339. <B>Husband</B>] This sanctifies her love for Anthony; in this one sacred word
we hear Shakespeare's last appeal to us for her pardon,&mdash;like &lquo;the heavenly voice&rquo;
breathing forth, in Gretchen's dungeon, &lquo;sie ist gerettet!&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>341. <B>Fire, and Ayre; my other Elements</B>] <SC>Malone</SC>: So in <I>Henry the Fifth,</I>
&lquo;he is pure air and fire; and the dull elements of earth and water never appear in
him.&rquo;&mdash;[III, vii, 22. This is in the Dauphin's description of his horse, and <SC>Madden</SC>
(p. 261) shows that this reference to the elements, in this connection, has, in old
writers on farriery, more significance than is at once apparent. Cleopatra here uses
&lquo;elements&rquo; as referring to the materials of which man is composed. See note on
III, ii, 47.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

jecture was not repeated in Theobald's edition.]&mdash;<SC>Deighton</SC>: I leave to be eaten

<P>triumphing manner that Cleopatra goes off in, shews the flow of her spirits, and her

death was grief at the leave-taking,&rquo; which is also the opinion of the present Editor.
We have already had an instance in this play where a broken heart has caused death,
and, moreover, where the victim was a strong, vigorous man.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>357. <B>this knot intrinsicate</B>] <SC>Warburton</SC>: The expression is fine; it signifies
a hidden, secret (<I>intrinsecus</I>) knot, as that which ties soul and body together.&mdash;
<SC>Edwards</SC> (p. 184): How, secret <I>as</I> that which ties soul and body together? Why,
it is that very knot she speaks of. But, what a lingua franca is here! a secret
<I>intrinsecus</I> knot! How long has <I>intrinsecus</I> been an adjective? and, if it be not,
how will he construe the sentence? Had our critic read Shakspeare with any atten-
tion, he might have known, that he uses <I>intrinsecate</I> for <I>intricate, entangled,</I> or <I>tied
in hard knots;</I> &lquo;Like rats, oft bite the holy cords in twain, Too <I>intrinsecate</I> to
unloose.&rquo; Had it signified <I>hidden, secret,</I> it could no more have been <I>bitten in twain,</I>
than <I>untied,</I> before it was <I>found out.</I>&mdash;<SC>Murray</SC> (<I>N. E. D.</I>): Apparently formed on
Italian <I>intrinsecato,</I> familiar, confused in sense with <I>intricato,</I> intricate. Equivalent
to <I>intricate,</I> involved, entangled. [Four references follow: 1560, Whitehorne, <I>Arte
Warre;</I> 1599, Jonson, <I>Cynthia's Revels,</I> V, ii; Marston, <I>Scourge of Villanie;</I> and
the present passage in <I>Ant. &amp; Cleop.</I>]

<P>363. <B>at my breast</B>] <SC>Bucknill</SC> (p. 221): It is curious that Shakespeare makes
Cleopatra apply the aspic both to the breast and to the arm, since we find a discussion
in old Primrose's <I>Popular Errors,</I> on this point. Primrose does not appear to have
read Shakespeare, or with his love of reference he would certainly have shewn it.
In his chapter on the mountebank's antidote, he says:&mdash;&lquo;And now the story of <I>Cleo-

<I>Life of Antonius,</I> and out of <I>Plinie</I> likewise, that she applyed it to her arme. <I>Zon-

her arme. <I>C&aelig;sar</I> also in her statute which he carryed in triumph, applyed the aspe
to her arme: For in the armes there are great veines and arteries, which doe quickly
and in a straight way convey the venome to the heart, whereas in the paps the vessels
are slender, which, by sundry circumvolutions onely, do lead to the heart.&rquo;
<P>364. <B>That suckes the Nurse asleepe</B>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: Before the publication of
this piece, <I>The Tragedy of Cleopatra,</I> by Daniel, 1594, had made its appearance;
but Dryden is more indebted to it than Shakspeare. Daniel has the following address
to the asp: &lquo;Better than death death's office thou dischargest, That with one gentle
touch can free our breath; And in a pleasing sleep our soul enlargest, Making our-
selves not privy to our death. Therefore come thou, of wonders wonder chief, That
open canst with such an easy key The door of life; come gentle, cunning thief, That
from ourselves so steal'st ourselves away.&rquo; [See Dryden's <I>All for Love in Appendix.</I>]
<P>364. <B>asleepe</B>] <SC>Theobald</SC> proves by quotations from Lucius Florus, Solinus,
Propertius, Lucan, and Ovid, that Shakespeare was justified in thus attributing a
somnolent effect to the venom of the asp. The proof is not now needed. Batman
<I>vppon Bartholome</I> is authority sufficient for the popular belief in Shakespeare's day.
Probably, no one, however, among the early editors was as competent as Theobald
to furnish, off-hand, such an array of learning.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>leius Paterculus, Eutropius, and Lucius Florus leave this matter as much at large.
Leonardo Augustini, among his antique gems, exhibits one of Cleopatra upon an
agot, with an aspick biting her right breast. And Strada, the Mantuan Antiquary,
who gives us a medal of this princess, says, that she died by serpents applied to her
breasts. And Domitius Calderinus, upon the 59th <I>Epigram</I> of the <SC>iv</SC>th Book of
Martial, says precisely, that she procured her own death by applying Asps to her
breast and arm.
<P>368. <B>Dyes</B>] <SC>Sir Thomas Browne</SC> (<I>Vulgar Errors,</I> Book V, Chap. xii, p. 291,
ed. 1672): The picture concerning the death of <I>Cleopatra</I> with two Asps or venem-
ous Serpents unto her arms, or breasts, or both, requires consideration: for therein
(beside that this variety is not excusable) the thing it self is questionable; nor is it
indisputably certain what manner of death she died. <I>Plutarch</I> in the life of <I>Antony</I>
plainly delivereth, that no man knew the manner of her death; for some affirmed
she perished by poison, which she always carried in a little hollow comb, and wore
it in her hair. Beside, there were never any Asps discovered in the place of her
death, although two of her Maids perished also with her; only it was said, two small
and almost insensible pricks were found upon her arm; which was all the ground
that <I>C&aelig;sar</I> had to presume the manner of her death. <I>Galen</I> who was contemporary
unto <I>Plutarch,</I> delivereth two wayes of her death: that she killed her self by the
bite of an Asp, or bit an hole in her arm, and poured poison therein. <I>Strabo</I> that
lived before them both hath also two opinions; that she died by the bite of an Asp,
or else a poisonous ointment. We might question the length of the Asps, which are
sometimes described exceeding short; whereas the Chers&aelig;a or land-Asp which most
conceive she used, is above four cubits long. Their number is not unquestionable;
for whereas there are generally two described, <I>Augustus</I> (as <I>Plutarch</I> relateth) did
carry in his triumph the Image of <I>Cleopatra</I> but with one Asp unto her arm. As for
the two pricks, or little spots in her arm, they infer not their plurality: for like the
Viper, the Asp hath two teeth; whereby it left this impression, or double puncture
behind it. And lastly, We might question the place; for some apply them unto her
breast, which notwithstanding will not consist with the History; and <I>Petrus Vic-
torius</I> hath well observed the same. But herein the mistake was easie; it being the
custom in capital malefactors to apply them unto the breast, as the Author <I>De The-
riaca ad Pisonem,</I> an eye witness hereof in <I>Alexandria,</I> where <I>Cleopatra</I> died,
determineth: I beheld, saith he, in <I>Alexandria,</I> how suddenly these Serpents bereave
a man of life; for when any one is condemned to this kind of death, if they intend to
use him favourably, that is, to dispatch him suddenly, they fasten an Asp unto his
breast; and bidding him walk about, he presently perisheth thereby.

<P>tion upon the difference between the two words in point of propriety.&mdash;<SC>Steevens</SC>:
I suppose she means by this <I>wild</I> world, this world which by the death of Antony is
become a <I>desert</I> to her. A <I>wild</I> is a <I>desert.</I> Our author, however, might have writ-
ten <I>wild</I> (<I>i. e. vile</I> according to ancient spelling), for <I>worthless.</I>&mdash;<SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii):
There is not the slightest pretext for altering &lquo;wild&rquo; to the commonplace <I>vile,</I> as has
been done under the supposition that <I>vile</I> having been of old often misprinted <I>vilde</I>
(a form to which the Rev. Mr Dyce strangely adheres), it was in this place mistaken
for &lquo;wild.&rquo; Charmian might well call the world &lquo;wild,&rquo; desert, and savage, after the
deaths of Antony, Cleopatra, and others whom she loved. This passage is another
proof how the corruption of <I>vild,</I> where <I>vile</I> was intended, makes confusion in the
heads of editors, as well as in the texts of dramatists; if <I>vile</I> had not sometimes been
misprinted <I>vild,</I> nobody would have thought of amending &lquo;wild world&rquo; to &lquo;<I>vile</I>
world.&rquo; If any change were made, we should prefer here <I>wide</I> to <I>vile;</I> but in truth it
is an offence against all just rules of criticism to attempt an emendation where none
is required.&mdash;<SC>R. G. White</SC> (ed. i): There is not sufficient justification for the change
[to <I>vile</I>]. At that time the world seemed wild enough to poor Charmian.&mdash;<SC>Dyce</SC>
(ed. i): Capell saw (what is plain enough) that <I>vilde</I> had been by mistake transformed
into &lquo;wilde.&rquo; (The folio, with its usual inconsistency of spelling, has in some places
&lquo;vild&rquo; and &lquo;vilde,&rquo;&mdash;in others &lquo;vile.&rquo;)&mdash;<SC>Ibid</SC>. (ed. ii): On the above remark [of
Collier] I have to remark:&mdash;First, That I no longer &lquo;adhere&rquo; to the old spelling
<I>vild. . . .</I> Secondly, That the passages in early books where <I>vild</I> (<I>i. e. vile</I>) is mis-
printed <I>wild</I> are so very numerous, that there can be no doubt of the same error hav-
ing been committed in the passage now under consideration. We meet with the fol-
lowing examples in the plays of Beaumont &amp; Fletcher:&mdash;&lquo;I will not lose a word To
this <I>wild</I> [read <I>vild = vile</I>] woman,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<I>The Maid's Tragedy,</I> III, i; &lquo;That now
dares say I am a stranger, not the same, more <I>wild</I> [read <I>vild = vile</I>],&rquo; etc.&mdash;<I>The
Faithful Shepherdess,</I> IV, iv; &lquo;To do these <I>wild</I> [so the first 4to, the later 4tos
<I>vild,</I> folio 1679 <I>vile</I>] unmanly things.&rquo;&mdash;<I>The Scornful Lady,</I> III, i; &lquo;Or am I of so
<I>wild</I> [read <I>vild = vile</I>] and low a blood,&rquo; etc.&mdash;<I>The Little French Lawyer,</I> III, v.
Thirdly, That &lquo;<I>vile world,</I>&rquo; which Collier terms a &lquo;commonplace phrase,&rquo; occurs in a
passage of <I>2 Henry VI:</I> V, ii, a passage which (as it is not found in <I>The First Part
of the Contention,</I> etc.) we may confidently ascribe to Shakespeare:&mdash;&lquo;O, let the
<SC>vile world</SC> end, And the promis&egrave;d flames of the last day, Knit earth and heaven
together!&rquo; Fourthly, That &lquo;wide,&rquo; [Collier's suggestion,] has no propriety here,

Collier always believed that Dyce's bitter and inappeasible hostility dated from the

<P>385. <B>Is this well done?</B>] <SC>Singer</SC>: This refers to a deception. Charmian, whispered
by Cleopatra, went out to manage the introduction of the Clown with the asps.&mdash;
<SC>R. G. White</SC> gives a similar explanation, which might be accepted were it not that
the question is exactly copied from North's <I>Plutarch,</I> where the Guard could not

<P>401. <B>purposes</B>] For the concluding <I>s</I> see I, iv, 11. <SC>Dyce</SC> conjectured <I>purpose,</I>
not knowing that he had been virtually anticipated by <SC>Walker</SC>, and that Walker had
been anticipated by <SC>Pope</SC>.
<P>401. <B>and being Royall</B>] <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 290): This passage is left without any
annotation, and yet there is meaning in it which many readers might not discover.
Dollabella had alluded to the augurs. This introduces the idea of the flight of birds;
this the idea of hawking; and Cleopatra, brave in her death, is represented under
the image of a hawk levelling at the purposes of her conqueror, and rendering them
dead or ineffectual. The idea of hawking introduced the idea of other field-sports,
and to the hawk Shakespeare transfers the attribute of a <I>hart-royal,</I> which had the
privilege of roaming at large unmolested, and taking its own way to its lair. Thus
Cleopatra being &lquo;royal&rquo; had &lquo;taken her own way&rquo; in self-destruction. In <I>The
Gentleman's Recreation,</I> p. 6, the liberty of the <I>hart-royal</I> is thus described:&mdash;&lquo;If
the King or Queen shall happen to hunt or chase a hart, and he escape with life, he
shall ever after be called a <I>hart-royal;</I> but if he fly so far from the forest or chase
that it is unlikely he will ever return of his own accord to the place aforesaid, and
that proclamation be made in all towns and villages thereabout, that none shall kill
or offend him, but that he may safely return, if he list, he is then called a <I>hart royal
proclaimed.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Madden</SC> (p. 19): The male red deer is now ordinarily called a stag,
the female a hind, and the young a calf. . . . But if you would speak in the strict
language of woodcraft, you would call him in the first year &lquo;a Hind calfe, or a calfe,
the second yeere you shall call him a Broket; . . . the sixt yeere you shall call him a
Hart. . . . But if the king or queene doe hunt or chace him, and he escape away
aliue, then after such a hunting or chacing he is called Hart Royall.&rquo;&mdash;Manwood,
<I>The Forest Lawes,</I> 1598. Thenceforth, after proclamation, he was free to return to
the forest from whence he came, and no man might meddle with a hart royal pro-
claimed. Hunter suggests [as above] that when C&aelig;sar said of Cleopatra that she
&lquo;being royal, Took her own way,&rquo; the licence accorded to the hart royal to go his
own way was present to his mind; and certainly instances may be found in Shake-
speare of similar conceits. The stag, or hart, at six years of age should have acquired
&lquo;his rights,&rquo;&mdash;that is to say, the brow, bay, and trey antlers&mdash;and two points on top
of each horn. The modern use of the term &lquo;royal&rquo; to denote a stag with all his
rights and three on top, is altogether inaccurate, and without warranty of any writer
of authority on woodcraft.

<P>437. It cannot but prove interesting, I think, to read the account of the closing
</CC>
<PB N=376>
<HE>376 <I>THE TRAGEDIE OF</I> [<SC>act v, sc.</SC> ii.</HE>
<CC>
<P>events of this historical Tragedy as given by Dion Cassius (after Plutarch one of our
best historians of these days), especially since in several Dramatic Versions the two
accounts, Plutarch's and Dion Cassius's, have been interwoven. For Plutarch's
account, see, of course, the <I>Appendix.</I>&mdash;<SC>Dion Cassius</SC> (vol. iii, p. 323, trans. by Pro-
fessor H. B. Foster, 1906, Troy, N. Y.): Antony after his unexpected setback took
refuge in his fleet and prepared to have a combat on the water, or in any case to sail
to Spain. Cleopatra seeing this caused the ships to desert and she herself rushed
suddenly into the mausoleum pretending that she feared C&aelig;sar and desired by some
means to destroy herself before capture, but really as an invitation to Antony to enter
there also. He had an inkling that he was being betrayed, but his infatuation would
not allow him to believe it, and, as one might say, he pitied her more than himself.
Cleopatra was fully aware of this and hoped that if he should be informed that she
was dead, he would not prolong his life, but meet death at once. Accordingly, she
hastened into the monument with one eunuch and two female attendants and from
there sent a message to him to the effect that she had passed away. When he heard it,
he did not delay, but was seized with a desire to follow her in death. Then first he
asked one of the bystanders to slay him, but the man drew a sword and dispatched
himself. Wishing to imitate his courage Antony gave himself a wound and fell upon
his face, causing the bystanders to think that he was dead. An outcry was raised at
his deed, and Cleopatra hearing it leaned out over the top of the monument. By a
certain contrivance its doors once closed could not be opened again, but above, near
the ceiling, it had not yet been completed. That was where they saw her leaning
out and some began to utter shouts that reached the ears of Antony. He, learning
that she survived, stood up as if he had still the power to live; but a great gush of
blood from his wound made him despair of rescue and he besought those present to
carry him to the monument and to hoist him by the ropes that were hanging there to
elevate stone blocks. This was done and he died there on Cleopatra's bosom.
<P>She now began to feel confidence in C&aelig;sar and immediately made him aware of
what had taken place, but did not feel altogether confident that she would experience
no harm. Hence she kept herself within the structure, in order that if there should
be no other motive for her preservation, she might at least purchase pardon and her
sovereignty through fear about her money. Even then in such depths of calamity
she remembered that she was queen, and chose rather to die with the name and
dignities of a sovereign than to live as an ordinary person. It should be stated that
she kept fire on hand to use upon her money and asps and other reptiles to use upon
herself, and that she had tried the latter on human beings to see in what way they
killed in each case. C&aelig;sar was anxious to make himself master of her treasures, to
seize her alive, and to take her back for his triumph. However, as he had given
her a kind of pledge, he did not wish to appear to have acted personally as an
impostor, since this would prevent him from treating her as a captive and to a certain
extent subdued against her will. He therefore sent to her Gaius Proculeius, a knight,
and Epaphroditus, a freedman, giving them directions what they must say and do.
So they obtained an audience with Cleopatra and after some accusations of a mild
type suddenly laid hold of her before any decision was reached. Then they put out
of her way everything by which she could bring death upon herself and allowed her
to spend some days where she was, since the embalming of Antony's body claimed
her attention. After that they took her to the palace, but did not remove any of her
accustomed retinue or attendants, to the end that she should still more hope to
accomplish her wishes and do no harm to herself. When she expressed a desire to
</CC>
<PB N=377>
<HE><SC>act v, sc.</SC> ii.] <I>ANTHONY AND CLEOPATRA</I> 377</HE>
<CC>
<P>appear before C&aelig;sar and converse with him, it was granted; and to beguile her still
more, he promised that he would come to her himself.
<P>She accordingly prepared a luxurious apartment and costly couch, and adorned
herself further in a kind of careless fashion,&mdash;for her mourning garb mightily became
her,&mdash;and seated herself upon the couch; beside her she had placed many images
of his father, of all sorts, and in her bosom she had put all the letters that his father
had sent her. When, after this, C&aelig;sar entered, she hastily arose, blushing, and said:
&lquo;Hail, master, Heaven has given joy to you and taken it from me. But you see with
your own eyes your father in the guise in which he often visited me, and you may
hear how he honored me in various ways and made me queen of the Egyptians. That
you may learn what were his own words about me, take and read the missives which
he sent me with his own hand.&rquo;
<P>As she spoke thus, she read aloud many endearing expressions of his. And now
she would lament and caress the letters and again fall before his images and do them
reverence. She kept turning her eyes toward C&aelig;sar, and melodiously continued to
bewail her fate. She spoke in melting tones, saying at one time, &lquo;Of what avail
C&aelig;sar, are these your letters?&rquo; and at another, &lquo;But in the man before me you also
are alive for me.&rquo; Then again, &lquo;Would that I had died before you!&rquo; and still again,
&lquo;But if I have him, I have you!&rquo; Some such diversity both of words and of gestures
did she employ, at the same time gazing at and murmuring to him sweetly. C&aelig;sar
comprehended her outbreak of passion and appeal for sympathy. Yet he did not pre-
tend to do so, but letting his eyes rest upon the ground, he said only this: &lquo;Be of
cheer, woman, and keep a good heart, for no harm shall befall you.&rquo; She was dis-
tressed that he would neither look at her nor breathe a word about the kingdom or
any sigh of love, and fell at his knees wailing: &lquo;Life for me, C&aelig;sar, is neither desir-
able nor possible. This favor I beseech of you in memory of your father,&mdash;that since
Heaven gave me to Antony after him, I may also die with my lord. Would that I
had perished on the very instant after C&aelig;sar's death! But since this present fate
was my destiny, send me to Antony: grudge me not burial with him, that as I die
because of him, so in Hades also I may dwell with him.&rquo;
<P>Such words she uttered expecting to obtain commiseration: C&aelig;sar, however, made
no answer to it. Fearing, however, that she might make away with herself he exhorted
her again to be of good cheer, did not remove any of her attendants, and kept a care-
ful watch upon her, that she might add brilliance to his triumph. Suspecting this,
and regarding it as worse than innumerable deaths, she began to desire really to die
and begged C&aelig;sar frequently that she might be allowed to perish in some way,
and devised many plans by herself. When she could accomplish nothing, she feigned
to change her mind and to repose great hope in him, as well as great hope in Livia.
She said she would sail voluntarily and made ready many treasured adornments as
gifts. In this way she hoped to inspire confidence that she had no designs upon her-
self, and so be more free from scrutiny and bring about her destruction. This also
took place. The other officials and Epaphroditus, to whom she had been committed,
believed that her state of mind was really as it seemed, and neglected to keep a care-
ful watch. She, meanwhile, was making preparations to die as painlessly as possi-
ble. First she gave a sealed paper, in which she begged C&aelig;sar to order that she be
buried beside Antony, to Epaphroditus himself to deliver, pretending that it con-
tained some other matter. Having by this excuse freed herself of his presence, she
set to her task. She put on her most beauteous apparel and after choosing a most
becoming pose, assumed all the royal robes and appurtenances, and so died. No one
</CC>
<PB N=378>
<HE>378 <I>THE TRAGEDIE OF</I> [<SC>act v, sc.</SC> ii.</HE>
<CC>
<P>knows clearly in what manner she perished, for there were found merely slight
indentations on her arm. Some say that she applied an asp which had been brought
in to her in a water-jar or among some flowers. Others declare that she had smeared
a needle, with which she was wont to braid her hair, with some poison possessed of
such properties that it would not injure the surface of the body at all, but if it touched
the least drop of blood it caused death very quickly and painlessly. The supposition
is, then, that previously it had been her custom to wear it in her hair, and on this
occasion after first making a small scratch on her arm with some instrument, she
dipped the needle in the blood. In this or some very similar way she perished with
her two handmaidens. The eunuch, at the moment her body was taken up, pre-
sented himself voluntarily to the serpents, and after being bitten by them leaped into
a coffin which had been prepared by him. C&aelig;sar on hearing of her demise was
shocked, and both viewed her body and applied drugs to it and sent for Psylli,<SUP>*</SUP> in
the hope that she might possibly revive. These Psylli, who are male, for there is no
woman born in their tribe, have the power of sucking out before a person dies all the
poison of every reptile and are not harmed themselves when bitten by any such crea-
ture. They are propagated from one another and they test their offspring, the latter
being thrown among serpents at once or having serpents laid upon their swaddling-
clothes. In such cases the poisonous creatures do not harm the child and are
benumbed by its clothing. This is the nature of their function. But C&aelig;sar, when
he could not in any way resuscitate Cleopatra, felt admiration and pity for her and
was himself excessively grieved, as much as if he had been deprived of all the glory
of the victory.

Trans. ed. 1635.]</NOTE>

<C>DATE OF COMPOSITION</C>
<P><SC>Steevens</SC> is, I believe, the earliest among editors to attempt to fix the <I>Date</I> of
publication of this play. In the <I>Variorum</I> of 1785 (p. 131) he calls attention to
the following entry in the <I>Stationers' Registers</I>:
<C><B>xix&degree; die <*>rtnhris.</B> [1593]</C>
<T>
<R><CE><B>Symond water-
son.</B></CE><CE>Entred for his Copie vnder th andes of bothe the wardens a booke
intituled The Tragedye of Cleopatra .. ..</CE><CE>vjd <SUP>*</SUP></CE></R>
</T>
<P>This Symon Waterson, Steevens goes on to say, was the printer of some of Daniel's
works; the foregoing entry probably refers, therefore, &lquo;to Daniel's <I>Cleopatra,</I> of
which there are several editions.&rquo; Steevens found a second entry, of which he
remarks that &lquo;it is the first notice I have met with concerning any edition of this
play, more ancient than the folio of 1623.&rquo; It is as follows:
<C><B>20 maij</B> [1608]</C>
<T>
<R><CE><B>Edward Blount.</B></CE><CE>Entred for his copie vnder th andes of Sir George Buck knight
and Master Warden Seton A booke called. The booke of Pericles
prynce of Tyre .. .. .. .. .. ..</CE><CE>vjd</CE></R>
<R><CE><B>Edward Blunt.</B></CE><CE>Entred also for his copie by the lyke Aucthoritie. A booke
Called. Anthony. and Cleopatra .. .. ..</CE><CE>vjd &dagger;</CE></R>
</T>
<P><SC>Malone</SC>, in his edition of 1790, says, in his notice of <I>Julius C&aelig;sar</I> (vol. i, p. 369),
that &lquo;we have certain proof that <I>Antony and Cleopatra</I> was composed before the mid-
dle of the year 1608.&rquo; This certain proof is the entry in the <I>Stationers Registers</I> of
that year, but Malone gives a slightly wrong impression in saying that the 20th of May
is &lquo;before the middle of the year&rquo;; the year then began in March and the middle of
the year fell in September. As a further corroboration of this date, 1608, he observes
(p. 372) that &lquo;in Ben Jonson's <I>Silent Woman,</I> IV, iv [IV, ii, ed. Gifford], 1609, this
play seems to be alluded to: &ldquo;<I>Morose.</I> Nay, I would sit out a play, that were nothing
but <I>fights at sea,</I> drum, trumpet, and target.&rdquo;&rquo; If the reference be here to <I>Antony &amp;
Cleopatra,</I> the play which is &lquo;<I>nothing but</I> fights at sea&rquo; dwindles to a single stage-
direction &lquo;Alarum as at a sea fight.&rquo;&mdash;IV, xii, 1. The flimsiness of the pretence of
adducing this quotation from Jonson as an indication of the date of <I>Anthony &amp; Cleo-
patra</I> is thus exposed by <SC>Gifford</SC>: &lquo;Long before <I>The Silent Woman</I> was written,
nay, before Shakespeare was known to the stage, the theatres were in possession of
many rude pieces founded on the remarkable events of our history, of which battles,
etc., always formed a prominent feature. The miserable attempts to represent these
favourite scenes, were often made a subject of mirth by succeeding writers.&rquo; Never-

<NOTE>* Arber's <I>Transcript,</I> II, 638.</NOTE>
<NOTE>&dagger; Arber's <I>Transcript,</I> III, 378.</NOTE>

<P>theless, <SC>George Chalmers</SC>, the next critic who deals with the Chronology of the
Plays, repeats Malone's quotation from <I>The Silent Woman</I> without dissent; he also
accepts the proof to be drawn from the entry in the <I>Stationers' Registers</I> as conclusive,
and observes that if this tragedy were written as a sequel to <I>Julius C&aelig;sar,</I> &lquo;it may,
perhaps, have been written in the beginning of the year 1608.&rquo; He also opines
(<I>Supplemental Apology,</I> 1799, p. 432) that &lquo;like other preceding dramas, this tragedy
had been suggested to the observant mind of Shakespeare, by prior intimations. . . .
The argument of Daniel's <I>Cleopatra</I> may have furnished the more dramatic genius of
Shakespeare with several hints, which he well knew how to work into a better form.
He had seen in <I>The Devils Incarnate,</I> in 1596, which he had attentively read,
what Lodge had remarked, how &ldquo;Anthony, dallying in delights with Cleopatra,
gave C&aelig;sar opportunitie of many victories.&rdquo;&rquo;
<P><SC>Knight</SC> is the next editor to discuss the Date. In the <I>Introduction</I> to <I>Coriolanus</I>
(p. 148) he remarks: &lquo;In 1623 Blount and Jaggard, the publishers of the folio, enter
&ldquo;Mr. William Shakspere's Comedies, Histories, and Tragedies, so many of the said
copies as are not formerly entered to other men.&rdquo; Amongst these is <I>Antony and
Cleopatra.</I> All the plays thus entered in 1623 were unpublished; and not one of them,
with the exception of <I>Antony and Cleopatra,</I> had been &ldquo;formerly entered&rdquo; by name.
It is therefore more than probable that the <I>Anthony and Cleopatra</I> entered in 1608 was
not Shakspere's tragedy; and we therefore reject this entry as any evidence that Shak-
spere's <I>Antony and Cleopatra</I> was written as early as 1608. Upon the date of this
play depends, according to Malone, the date of <I>Julius C&aelig;sar.</I> We state, unhesitat-
ingly, that there is no <I>internal</I> evidence whatever for the dates of any of the three
Roman plays. We believe that they belong to the same cycle; but we would place
that later in Shakspere's life than is ordinarily done. Malone places them together,
properly enough; but in assuming that they were written in 1607, 1608, and 1610,
his theory makes Shakspere almost absolutely unemployed for the last seven years
of his life. We hold that his last years were devoted to these plays.&rquo;&mdash;[Knight's
assertion that &lquo;all the plays&rquo; entered in the First Folio list &lquo;were unpublished,&rquo; is,
possibly, a little rash, and yet it is difficult to disprove it. He is on firmer ground
when he says that it is &lquo;more than probable&rquo; that the <I>Anthony and Cleopatra</I> of 1608
is not Shakespeare's tragedy,&mdash;ground which, I think, has been examined by editors
and critics with hardly sufficient care. It raises another mystery; the ever-recurring
mysteries connected with the Quartos has a tendency to become monotonous. The
Edward Blount who entered the copy of <I>Anthony and Cleopatra</I> in 1608 is the same
Edward Blount who with William Jaggard entered the copy of the First Folio on
the eighth of November, 1623, and the terms of the latter entry expressly exclude
&lquo;soe manie&rquo; of the &lquo;Comedyes, Histories, and Tragedyes&rquo; &lquo;as are not formerly
entred to other men.&rquo; In the list which follows there stands our present <I>Anthonie
and Cleopatra.</I> Why, it may be asked, should Edward Blount include this play in
1623, seeing that he had already received the license to print it in 1608? To be
sure, it had not been entered to an &lquo;other man,&rquo; but it had been entered to himself,
and, if, in 1608, <I>it was Shakespeare's play,</I> why should he desire to take out a double
license? Why should it be mentioned at all, seeing that, <I>if the 1608 entry was the
present play</I> it was already his property? The list, as it stands in the <I>Stationers'
Registers,</I> of unlicensed plays by Shakespeare which Blount and Jaggard were
licensed to print in 1623 is as follows:<SUP>*</SUP>
