<P>As Knight says, &lquo;not one of these, with the exception of <I>Anthonie and Cleopatra,</I>
had been &ldquo;formerly entred&rdquo; by name.&rquo; And, to repeat what I have just said, if the
1608 <I>Anthony and Cleopatra</I> were Shakespeare's, and already the property of Edward
Blount, it is not clear why it should have been entered again. When, therefore,
Knight rejects the date of 1608 as a proof that Shakespeare wrote the present play in
that year, even-handed justice must acknowledge that there is colour for his rejection,
and, furthermore, all who, confiding on this date, erect their scheme of the chro-
nology of these plays, do so on a foundation which, in respect to the present play, is
not flawless.
<P><SC>G. C. Verplanck</SC> gives a late date to the three plays <I>Coriolanus, Julius C&aelig;sar,</I>
and the present play, because Shakespeare, in these tragedies, preserves throughout
&lquo;an artist-like keeping, which, combined with their dramatic skill, the constant pro-
pensity of the author to moral or political argument or reasoning, and the more
habitual and mature tone of his philosophy, as well as with the evidence of diction
and versification, gives strong attestation that they belong to that later epoch of
Shakespeare's authorship, when (to use Coleridge's discriminating criticism) &ldquo;the
energies of intellect in the cycle of genius become predominant over passion and
creative self-manifestation.&rdquo; This period I should place as beginning after the pro-
duction of <I>Lear</I> and <I>Macbeth,</I> in 1608 or 1609, or about the Poet's forty-fifth year.
Besides those reasons for ascribing the Roman dramas to this date, which appeal
only to the reader's taste and feeling, the following considerations seem also of some
weight. <I>Coriolanus</I> and its Plutarchian companions appeared first in print in the
posthumous folio of 1623, and they were then entered in the Stationers' Register as
among the plays in that volume &ldquo;not formerly entered to other men.&rdquo; This was the
case with all Shakespeare's later works, either produced or remodelled after <I>Lear;</I>
for it appears that after <I>Othello, Hamlet,</I> and <I>Lear</I> had placed him far above his con-
temporaries, his plays became of too much value to the theatrical company which held
the copies to be suffered to go into the market as mere literary property. Again:
there is no period of Shakespeare's life, except the last seven or eight years, where
we can well find room for the production of these dramas. We well know from
<PB N=384>
<HE>384 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>various sources what were the luxuriant products of his youthful genius until 1598.
During the succeeding ten years we find him with his full share of interest and
occupation in the management and pecuniary concerns of his theatre, yet employed
in the enlargement of his <I>Hamlet</I> &lquo;to as much again as it was,&rquo; the improvement and
revision of some of his comedies, and the composition of <I>As You Like It, Much Ado
About Nothing, Twelfth Night,</I> very probably of several of his English historical
plays, and of <I>Timon,</I> and certainly of <I>Othello, Measure for Measure, Troilus and
Cressida, Lear, and Macbeth.</I> It can scarcely be thought that he had then leisure
to add the Roman tragedies to all these. On the other hand, if there had been no
trace of any additional authorship after 1609, we might infer that he had been inca-
pacitated by disease, or drawn away by some other cause from composition; but as
we know that after that date he revised or greatly enlarged some dramas, and wrote
two or three new ones, we have far more reason to presume that some portion of his
leisure, after he had returned to his native village, during which he wrote the <I>Tem-
pest,</I> was also employed in the composition of these tragedies, filled like that, his
last poetic comedy, with grave and deep reflections, wide moral speculation, and the
sobered energy of mature but calm power, than to believe that they were poured
forth in the same rapid torrent of invention and passionate thought which, during the
ten preceding years of the Poet's life, had enriched English literature with more of
original dramatic character, and poetic sentiment and expression, than it owes to the
life of any other author.
<P><SC>Charles Bathurst</SC> (p. 130): Entered on the Stationers' books, May 2, 1608.
This is a valuable date, for the verse is still more checked and cut up (as in his
fourth style) than in <I>Coriolanus. Put off my helmet to My countryman, a Roman.</I>
Remarkably so, in the change of person in dialogue; but it is far from having the
same load of ideas, nor stiffness. The mind of the reader would flow on more freely,
than in <I>Coriolanus,</I> if the ear were allowed to do so. It is a far more irregular,
varied, play,&mdash;more, perhaps, than any he has written. There is, however, still much
of the crampness of a lesson out of a book, in the political parts. With this cramp-
ness goes correctness of taste. There are not the faults of carelessness or of
unchecked want of taste, which are common in the earlier plays. Mere conceits,
puns, indelicacy, we do not see much of. There are many double endings in this
play.
<P><SC>G. G. Gervinus</SC> (ii, 312, 1872. 4te Auflage): It may well be that by the &lquo;booke,&rquo;
entered by Blount, the present play is meant, and that its date of composition may be
set down as in 1607-8. Indications of a common treatment of material, certain
peculiarities of style, possibly even more than these, the poet's frame of mind at the
time, place this play near to <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.,</I> which may also tend to confirm this date.
<P>The late date of the present play is corroborated by the Metrical Tests. From
the careful Table, prepared by Prof. <SC>Ingram</SC> (<I>New Sh. Soc. Trans.</I> 1874, p. 450),
of Shakespeare's use of light and weak endings, Prof. Ingram deduces the following
results:
<P>&lquo;1. During the first three-fourths (or thereabouts) of Shakspere's poetic life, he
used the light endings [such as <I>am, are, art, be, been, can,</I> etc.] very sparingly, and
the weak endings [such as <I>and, as, at, by, for, from,</I> etc.] scarcely at all.
<P>&lquo;2. The last fourth (or thereabouts) is obviously and unmistakeably distinguished
<PB N=385>
<HE><I>DATE OF COMPOSITION</I> 385</HE>
<P>from the earlier stages by the very great increase of the number of light endings,
and, still more, by the first appearance in any appreciable number, and afterwards
the steady growth, of the weak endings.
<P>&lquo;3. Hence, in any discrimination of periods which is founded on metrical con-
siderations, this last may be called the &ldquo;weak-ending Period.&rdquo; . . .
<P>&lquo;7. The weak endings do not come in by slow degrees, but the poet seems to
have thrown himself at once into this new structure of verse; 28 examples occurring
in <I>Ant. and Cleop.,</I> whilst there are not more than two in any earlier play.&rquo;
<P>Accordingly, in Prof. Ingram's Table, <I>Ant. &amp; Cleop.</I> is the twenty-sixth in order,
and is followed only by &lquo;<I>Coriolanus, Pericles</I> (Shakspere's part), <I>Tempest, Cymbeline,
Winter's Tale, Henry VIII</I> (Shakspere's part).&rquo;
<P><SC>J. O. Halliwell-Phillipps</SC> (<I>Outlines,</I> 5th ed. p. 187): About the time that
<I>Pericles</I> was so well received at the Globe, the tragedy of <I>Antony and Cleopatra</I> was
in course of performance at the same theatre, but, although successful, it did not
equal the former in popularity. It was, however, sufficiently attractive for Blount to
secure the consent of the Master of the Revels to its publication and also for the
company to frustrate his immediate design.&mdash;[In his <I>Illustrative Notes,</I> Halliwell
attempts to substantiate the foregoing positive assertions by adducing two inferences.
On the words &lquo;although successful&rquo; there is the following note (p. 524): &lquo;This
&lquo;fact may be inferred from the entry in the Stationers&rquo; Registers of 1608, to Edward
&lquo;Blount of &ldquo;his copie by the lyke aucthoritie, a booke called Anthony and Cleo-
&lquo;&ldquo;patra.&rdquo; The &ldquo;like authority&rdquo; refers to the sanction of Sir George Buck and the
&lquo;company, as appears from the previous entry in the register, so that Blount was no
&lquo;doubt in possession of the copyright of the authentic play. If he printed it in 1608,
&lquo;no copy of the impression is now known to exist, the earliest edition which has been
&lquo;preserved being that in the collective work of 1623, of which Blount was one of
&lquo;the publishers; and although it is included in the list of tragedies &ldquo;as are not
&lquo;&ldquo;formerly entred to other men&rdquo; in the notice of the copyright of the folio, it is
&lquo;still not impossible that an earlier separate edition was issued by him. There are
&lquo;indications that the list of non-entered plays was carelessly drawn up.&rquo; It is
impossible to deny Halliwell's assertion that there are indications that this list is
carelessly drawn up; but he does not state what the indications are; this at least is
certain that it is so far careful that with but two exceptions, not a single play is given
in it which has been before even referred to in the <I>Stationers' Registers;</I> in regard to
the other plays which it specifies the list is strictly accurate. The two exceptions are
<I>As You Like It,</I> which is not entered, but mentioned only &lquo;to be staied&rquo; and the pres-
ent play of <I>Anthony and Cleopatra,</I> if the entry of 20th of May, 1608 really refers to
it. When, then, we find this list so accurate in regard to all the other plays, I do
not believe we are justified in asserting that it is inaccurate in this one solitary instance,
unless we are positively certain that the entry of 20th of May, 1608 refers to Shake-
speare's <I>Anthony and Cleopatra.</I> Knight and Verplanck believe that it does not.
And it is impossible to contradict them. There is no proof whatever that it is Shake-
speare's play. We do not even know that it was a play at all,&mdash;it may have been a
prose history. There is nothing here but inferences, as is, unfortunately, so much of
what Halliwell asserts in his <I>Outlines.</I> For instance, in the note (p. 525) on his state-
ment that <I>Anthony and Cleopatra</I> did not equal <I>Pericles</I> in popularity: &lquo;this,&rquo; he
remarks, &lquo;may be gathered from the rarity of contemporary allusions to it. The only
&lquo;extrinsic notice of the tragedy during the author's life-time appears to be a curious one
<PB N=386>
<HE>386 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>&lquo;in Anton's Philosophers Satyrs, 1616, where the latter poet blames ladies for encour-
&lquo;aging the performance of so vicious a drama by their presence.&rquo; Here, in this note,
there are two inferences which are supposed to substantiate the truth of an assertion.
In its first line, the inference is open and confessed where it is said that <I>it may be
gathered.</I> The second inference lies in assuming that Anton, when he speaks of
&lquo;Orestes incest, Cleopatres crimes&rquo; refers to Shakespeare's play of <I>Anthony and
Cleopatra.</I> That he does so, is purely a surmise on Halliwell's part. If surmises
be once allowed, why may we not surmise that the unknown date of Beaumont and
Fletcher's <I>The False One,</I> wherein Cleopatra is the heroine, be before 1616? Weber
places it before 1618. Only a little stretching will bring it into 1616, and then to it,
and not to Shakespeare, Anton's reference may apply. Moreover, Shakespeare died
in 1616. Can a work, which, like Anton's <I>Satyrs</I> is dated 1616, be stated without
qualification to contain a &lquo;notice of the tragedy during the poet's lifetime&rquo;?

<C>DURATION OF ACTION</C>
<P>It is hardly likely that Shakespeare, in his Historical Dramas, paid much attention
to the passage of time, either historical or dramatic. It was enough that in the flight
of ten years a general sequence of events was preserved. In these circumstances,
where there inevitably exists much shuffling of times, it is a task of extreme difficulty
to unravel the tangled skein and to determine the division into days of dramatic time.
<PB N=387>
<HE><I>SOURCE OF THE PLOT</I> 387</HE>

in a quite triumphant manner, as follows (His scheme had better be accepted; it is
not likely that, in the future, anyone with adequate skill and patience will be found
who can modify it.):

<C>SOURCE OF THE PLOT</C>
<P>After the painful student has waded through the preceding pages of this volume, it
seems impertinently superfluous to state that Shakespeare drew the Source of his Plot
from North's <I>Translation of Plutarch.</I> The continual references in the <I>Commentary</I>
to this portion of the <I>Appendix</I> are wearisome in their iteration. Yet, surely, that
mind must be inert, indeed, that finds no pleasure in observing the magic whereby
Shakespeare, gilding the pale stream with heavenly alchemy, transfigures the quiet
prose, at times almost word for word, into exalted poetry. In the following pages
only those passages are reprinted from the <I>Life of Antonius</I> which, in the Editor's
judgement, have any relation to the present play. In the original there are marginal
notes, in Italics, setting forth the substance of the adjoining text; in order to save
space these have been omitted, and their places supplied by references, in broad-
faced type, to Acts, Scenes, and Lines in the play.
<P>The following <I>Transcript</I> is taken from the <I>Photolithograph</I> of <I>Four Chapters of
North's Plutarch,</I> of the edition of 1595, published in 1878, by Dr <SC>F. A. Leo</SC>, of
Berlin.

<C>PLUTARCH</C>
<P><SC>The Lives &verbar; of the noble gre- &verbar; cians and romanes, compared &verbar; together
by that grave learned &verbar; philosopher and historiographer</SC>, &verbar; <I>Plutarke of
Ch&aelig;ronea:</I> &verbar; Tran$lated out of Greeke into French by <SC>Iames Amiot</SC>, Abbot of
Bello- &verbar; zane, Bi$hop of Auxerre, one of the Kings priuie coun$ell, and great &verbar; Amner
of France, and out of French into Engli$h, by &verbar; <I>Thomas North.</I> [Vignette] Imprinted
at London by Richard Field for &verbar; Bonham Norton. &verbar; 1595.
<SHL>
<P>Thereupon he left <SC>Italy</SC>, &amp; went into <SC>Grece</SC>, &amp; there bestowed the most part
of his time, sometime in warres, and otherwhile in the studie of
eloquence. He vsed a manner of phrase in his speech, called Asiat-
<MARG><B>I, iii, 67.</B></MARG>
ike, which caried the best grace and estimation at that time, and was
<MARG><B>IV, xii, 51.</B></MARG>
much like to his manners and life: for it was full of ostentation, fool-
ish brauerie, and vaine ambition. . . .
<P>But besides all this, he had a noble presence, and shewed a countenance of one
of a noble house: he had a goodly thicke beard, a broad forehead, crooke nosed,
and there appeared such a manly looke in his countenance, as is commonly seene in
<I>Hercules</I> pictures, stamped or grauen in mettall. Now it had bene a speech of old
time, that the familie of the <I>Anton&yuml;</I> were discended from one <I>Anton,</I>
the sonne of <I>Hercules,</I> whereof the family tooke name. This opinion
<MARG><B>I, iii, 105.</B></MARG>
did <I>Antonius</I> seeke to confirme in all his doings: not onely resem-
bling him in the likenesse of his bodie, as we haue saide before, but
also in the wearing of his garments. For when he would openly shewe himselfe
abroad before many people, he would alwaies weare his cassocke girt downe low
vppon his hippes, with a great sword hanging by his side, and vpon that, some ill
fauoured cloke. Furthermore, things that seeme intollerable in other
men, as to boast commonly, to ieast with one or other, to drinke like
<MARG><B>I, iv, 22, etc.</B></MARG>
a good fellow with euery bodie, to sit with the souldiers when they
dine, and to eate and drinke with them souldierlike: it is incredible
what wonderfull loue it wanne him amongst them. And furthermore, being given
to loue: that made him the more desired, and by that meanes he brought many to
loue him. For he would further euery mans loue, and also would not be angry that
men should merily tell him of those he loued. But besides all this, that which most
procured his rising and aduancement, was his liberalitie, who gaue all to the souldiers,
and kept nothing for himselfe: and when he was growen to great credite, then was
his authoritie and power also very great, the which notwithstanding himselfe did
ouerthrowe, by a thousand other faults he had. . . .
<P>Then was <I>Antonius</I> straight maruellously commended and beloued
of the souldiers, because he commonly exercised himselfe among
<MARG><B>I, iv, 22.</B></MARG>
them, and would oftentimes eate and drinke with them, and also be
liberall vnto them, according to his abilitie. . . .
<P>Afterwardes when <I>Pompeys</I> house was put to open sale, <I>Antonius</I>
<MARG><B>II, vii, 151,</B></MARG>
bought it: but when they asked him money for it, he made it very
<MARG><I>see post.</I></MARG>
strange, and was offended with them. . . .
<P>And therefore he left his dissolute manner of life, and maried
<MARG><B>I, ii, 137</B></MARG>
<I>Fuluia</I> that was <I>Clodius</I> widdow, a woman not so basely minded to
<MARG><B>II, ii, 76.</B></MARG>
spend her time in spinning and housewiuery, and was not contented
to master her husband at home, but would also rule him in his office abroade, and
<PB N=389>
<HE><I>PLUTARCH</I> 389</HE>
<P>commaund him, that commaunded legions and great armies: so that <I>Cleopatra</I> was
to giue <I>Fuluia</I> thankes for that shee had taught <I>Antonius</I> this obedience to women,
that learned so well to be at their commandement. . . .
<P>Now things remayning in this state at <SC>Rome</SC>, <I>Octauius C&aelig;sar</I>
the yonger came to <SC>Rome</SC>, who was the sonne of <I>Julius C&aelig;sars</I>
<MARG><B>III, vi, 7.</B></MARG>
Neece, as you haue heard before, and was left his lawfull heire by
will, remayning at the time of the death of his great Vncle that was
slaine, in the City of <SC>Apollonia</SC>. . . .
<P><I>Cicero</I> on the other side being at that time the chiefest man of authority and esti-
mation in the city, he stirred vp all men against <I>Antonius:</I> so that in the end he made
the Senate pronounce him an enemy to his country, and appointed yong <I>C&aelig;sar</I> Ser-
geants to cary axes before him, and such other signes as were inci-
dent to the dignity of a Consull or Pr&aelig;tor: and moreouer sent <I>Hir-</I>
<MARG><B>I, iv, 67.</B></MARG>
<I>cius</I> and <I>Pansa,</I> then Consuls, to driue <I>Antonius</I> out of <SC>Italy</SC>.
These two Consuls together with <I>C&aelig;sar,</I> who also had an army,
went against <I>Antonius</I> that besieged the city of <SC>Modena</SC>, and there ouerthrew him in
battel: but both the Consuls were slaine there. <I>Antonius</I> flying vpon this ouerthrow,
fell into great misery all at once: but the chiefest want of all other, and that pinched
him most, was famine. Howbeit he was of such a strong nature, that by patience he
would ouercome any aduersitie, and the heauier fortune lay vpon him, the more con-
stant shewed he himselfe. Euery man that feeleth want or aduersity, knoweth by
vertue and discretion what he should doe: but when indeede they are ouerlayed with
extremity, and be sore oppressed, few haue the hearts to follow that which they praise
and commend, and much lesse to auoide that they reproue and mislike. But rather
to the contrary, they yeeld to their accustomed easie life: and through faint heart, &amp;
lacke of corage, doe chaunge their first mind and purpose. And therefore it was a
wonderfull example to the souldiers, to see <I>Antonius</I> that was brought
vp in all finenesse and superfluity, so easily to drinke puddle water,
<MARG><B>I, iv, 70.</B></MARG>
and to eate wild frutes and rootes: and moreouer it is reported, that
euen as they passed the Alpes, they did eate the barkes of trees, and
such beasts, as neuer man tasted of their flesh before. . . .
<P>Thus <I>Antonius</I> being a foote againe, and growen of great power, repassed ouer
the Alpes, leading into <SC>Italy</SC> with him seuenteene legions, and tenne thousand horse-
men, besides sixe legions he left in garrison among the <SC>Gavles</SC>, vnder the charge of
one <I>Varius,</I> a companion of his that woulde drinke lustely with him, and therefore
in mockery was surnamed <I>Cotylon:</I> to wit, a bibber.
<P>But setting aside the ill name he had for his insolency, he was yet much more
hated in respect of the house he dwelt in, the which was the house of <I>Pompey</I> the
great: a man as famous for his temperance, modesty, and ciuil life,
as for his three triumphes. For it grieued them to see the gates
<MARG><B>II, vii, 151.</B></MARG>
commonly shut against the Captaines, Magistrates of the city, and
also Ambassadors of straunge nations, which were sometimes thrust
from the gate with violence. . . .
<P>When they had passed ouer the seas, and that they beganne to make warre, they
being both camped by their enemies, to wit, <I>Antonius</I> against <I>Cassius,</I> and <I>C&aelig;sar</I>
against <I>Brutus: C&aelig;sar</I> did no great matter, but <I>Antonius</I> had alway the vpper hand,
and did all. For at the first battell <I>C&aelig;sar</I> was ouerthrowen by <I>Brutus,</I> and lost his
campe, and very hardly saued him selfe by flying from them that followed him.
Howbeit he writeth himselfe in his Commentaries, that he fled before the charge was
<PB N=390>
<HE>390 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>giuen, because of a dreame one of his friends had. <I>Antonius</I> on the other side ouer-
threw <I>Cassius</I> in battell, though some write that he was not there himselfe at the bat-
tel, but that he came after the ouerthrow, whilest his men had the enemies in chase.
So <I>Cassius</I> at his earnest request was slaine by a faithfull seruant of his own called
<I>Pindarus,</I> whom he had infranchised: because he knew not in time that <I>Brutus</I>
had ouercome <I>C&aelig;sar.</I> Shortly after they fought an other battell
againe, in the which <I>Brutus</I> was ouerthrowen, who afterwardes also
<MARG><B>III, xi, 41.</B></MARG>
slue himself. Thus <I>Antonius</I> had the chiefest glory of all this vic-
tory, specially because <I>C&aelig;sar</I> was sicke at that time. . . .
<P><I>Antonius</I> being thus inclined, the last and extreamest mischiefe of all other (to
wit, the loue of <I>Cleopatra</I>) lighted on him, who did waken and stirre vp many vices
yet hidden in him, and were neuer seene to any: and if any sparke of goodnesse or
hope of rising were left him, <I>Cleopatra</I> quenched it straight, and made it worse then
before. The manner how he fell in loue with her was this. <I>Antonius</I> going to make
warre with the <SC>Parthians</SC>, sent to command <I>Cleopatra</I> to appeare personally before
him, when he came into <SC>Cilicia</SC>, to aunswere vnto such accusations as were laide
against her, being this: that she had aided <I>Cassius</I> and <I>Brutus</I> in their warre against
him. The messenger sent vnto <I>Cleopatra</I> to make his summons vnto her, was called
<I>Dellius:</I> who when he had thoroughly considered her beautie, the excellent grace
and sweetenesse of her tongue, he nothing mistrusted that <I>Antonius</I> would doe any
hurt to so noble a Ladie, but rather assured himselfe, that within few dayes she should
be in great fauor with him. Thereupon he did her great honour, and perswaded
her to come into <SC>Cilicia</SC>, as honourably furnished as she could possible, and bad her
not to be affraide at all of <I>Antonius,</I> for he was a more courteous Lord, then any that
she had euer seene. <I>Cleopatra</I> on the other side beleeuing <I>Dellius</I> words, &amp; gessing
by the former accesse and credit she had with <I>Julius C&aelig;sar,</I> and <I>Cneus Pompey</I> (the
sonne of <I>Pompey</I> the great) onely for her beautie: she began to haue good hope that
she might more easily win <I>Antonius.</I> For <I>C&aelig;sar</I> and <I>Pompey</I> knew her when she
was but a young thing, &amp; knew not then what the worlde ment: but
now she went to <I>Antonius</I> at the age when a womans beautie is at
<MARG><B>I, v, 86.</B></MARG>
the prime, and she also of best iudgement. So, she furnished her-
selfe with a world of gifts, store of gold and siluer, and of riches and
other sumptuous ornaments, as is credible enough she might bring from so great a
house, and from so wealthie and rich a realme as <SC>&AElig;gypt</SC> was. But yet she caried
nothing with her wherein she trusted more then in her selfe, and in the charmes and
inchauntment of her passing beautie and grace. Therefore when she was sent vnto
by diuers letters, both from <I>Antonius</I> himselfe, and also from his friendes, she made
so light of it and mocked <I>Antonius</I> so much, that she disdained to set
forward otherwise, but to take her barge in the riuer of Cydnus, the
<MARG><B>II, ii, 225.</B></MARG>
poope whereof was of gold, the sailes of purple, and the owers of
<MARG><B>II, ii, 243.</B></MARG>
siluer, which kept stroke in rowing after the sound of the musicke
of flutes, howboyes, cytherns, vyolls, and such other instruments as they played vpon
in the barge. And now for the person of her selfe: she was laide vnder a pauillion
of cloth of golde of tissue, apparelled and attired like the goddesse <I>Venus,</I> commonly
drawen in picture: and hard by her, on either hand of her, pretie faire boyes appa-
relled as painters doe set foorth god <I>Cupide,</I> with litle fans in their hands, with the
which they fanned winde vpon her. Her Ladies and gentlewomen also, the fairest
of them were apparelled like the nymphes <I>Nereides</I> (which are the myrmaides of the
waters) and like the <I>Graces,</I> some stearing the helme, others tending the tackle and

<HE><I>PLUTARCH</I> 391</HE>
<P>ropes of the barge, out of the which there came a wonderfull passing sweete sauor
of perfumes, that perfumed the wharfes side, pestered with innumerable multitudes
of people. Some of them followed the barge all alongst the riuers side: others also
ranne out of the citie to see her comming in. So that in the end, there ranne such
multitudes of people one after an other to see her, that <I>Antonius</I> was left post alone
in the market place, in his Imperiall seate to giue audience: and there went a rumor
in the peoples mouthes, that the goddesse <I>Venus</I> was come to play with the god <I>Bac-
chus,</I> for the generall good of all <SC>Asia.</SC> When <I>Cleopatra</I> landed, <I>Antonius</I> sent to
inuite her to supper to him. But she sent him worde againe, he should doe better
rather to come and suppe with her. <I>Antonius</I> therefore to shew himselfe curteous
vnto her at her arriuall, was contented to obey her, and went to supper to her: where
he found such passing sumptuous fare, that no tongue can expresse it. But amongst
all other things, he most wondered at the infinite number of lightes and torches
hanged on the toppe of the house, giuing light in euery place, so artificially set and
ordered by deuises, some round, some square: that it was the rarest thing to behold
that eye could discerne, or that euer bookes could mention. The next night, <I>Antonius</I>
feasting her, contended to passe her in magnificence and finenes: but she ouercame
him in both. So that he himselfe began to scorne the grosse seruice of his house, in
respect of <I>Cleopatraes</I> sumptuousnes and finenesse. And when <I>Cleopatra</I> found
<I>Antonius</I> ieasts and flents to be but grosse, and souldier like, in plaine manner: she
gaue it him finely, and without feare taunted him throughly. Now her beautie (as
it is reported) was not so passing, as vnmatchable of other women, nor yet such, as
vpon present viewe did enamor men with her: but so sweete was her companie and
conuersation, that a man could not possiblie but be taken. And besides her beautie,
the good grace she had to talke and discourse, her curteous nature that tempered her
words &amp; deedes, was a spurre that pricked to the quick. Furthermore, besides all
these, her voice and words were maruellous pleasant: for her tongue was an instru-
ment of musicke to diuers sportes and pastimes, the which she easily turned to any
language that pleased her. She spake vnto few barbarous people by interpreter, but
made them answere her selfe, or at the least the most part of them: as the <SC>&AElig;thiop-
ians</SC>, the <SC>Arabians</SC>, the <SC>Troglodytes</SC>, the <SC>Hebrves</SC>, the <SC>Syrians</SC>, the <SC>Medes</SC>,
and the <SC>Parthians</SC>, and to many others also, whose languages she had learned.
Whereas diuers of her progenitors, the kings of <SC>&AElig;gypt</SC>, could scarce learne the
<SC>&AElig;gyptian</SC> tongue only &amp; many of them forgot to speake the <SC>Macedonian</SC>. Now,
<I>Antonius</I> was so rauished with the loue of <I>Cleopatra,</I> that though his wife <I>Fuluia</I>
had great warres, and much a doe with <I>C&aelig;sar</I> for his affaires, and that the armie of
the <SC>Parthians</SC> (the which the kings Lieutenantes had giuen to the only leading of
<I>Labienus</I>) was now assembled in <SC>Mesopotamia</SC> readie to inuade <SC>Syria</SC>: yet, as
though all this had nothing touched him, he yeelded himselfe to goe with <I>Cleopatra</I>
into <SC>Alexandria</SC>, where he spent and lost in childish sports (as a man might say)
and idle pastimes, the most pretious thing a man can spend, as <I>Antiphon</I> saith: and
that is, time. For they made an order betwene them, which they called Amimetobion
(as much to say, no life comparable and matchable with it) one feasting each other
by turnes, and in cost, exceeding all measure and reason. And for proofe hereof, I
haue heard my grandfather <I>Lampryas</I> report, that one <I>Philotas</I> a Phisitian, borne in
the city of <SC>Amphissa</SC>, told him that he was at that present time in <SC>Alexandria</SC>,
and studied Phisicke: and that hauing acquaintance with one of <I>Antonius</I> cookes,
he tooke him with him to <I>Antonius</I> house, (being a young man desirous to see
things) to shew him the wonderfull sumptuous charge and preparation of one only
<PB N=392>
<HE>392 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>supper. When he was in the kitchin, and saw a world of diuersities of meates, and
amongst others, eight wild boares rosted whole: he began to wonder
at it, and saide, sure you haue a great number of guestes to supper.
<MARG><B>II, ii, 213.</B></MARG>
The cooke fell a laughing, and answered him, no (quoth he) not many
guestes, nor aboue twelue in all: but yet all that is boyled or roasted
must be serued in whole, or else it would be marred straight. For <I>Antonius</I> per-
aduenture will suppe presently, or it may be a pretie while hence, or likely enough he
will deferre it longer, for that he hath drunke well to day, or else hath had some
other great matters in hand: and therefore we doe not dresse one supper onely, but
many suppers, because we are uncertaine of the houre he will suppe in. <I>Philotas</I> the
Phisitian tolde my grandfather this tale. . . .
<P>But now againe to <I>Cleopatra. Plato</I> writeth that there are foure kinds of flatterie:
but <I>Cleopatra</I> deuided it into many kinds. For she, were it in sport, or in matters of
earnest, still deuised sundrie newe delights to haue <I>Antonius</I> at commaundement,
neuer leauing him night nor day, nor once letting him go out of her sight. For
she would play at dice with him, drinke with him, &amp; hunt commonly with him,
and also be with him when he went to any exercise or actiuitie of
body. And sometime also, when he would go vp and downe the
<MARG><B>I, i, 68.</B></MARG>
citie disguised as a slaue in the night, &amp; would peere into poore
mens windowes &amp; their shops, and scold and braule with them
within the house: <I>Cleopatra</I> would be also in a chamber maides array, and amble
vp and downe the streetes with him, so that oftentimes <I>Antonius</I> bare away both
mockes and blowes. Now, though most men misliked this manner, yet the <SC>Alex-
andrians</SC> were commonly glad of this iolity, and liked it well, saying very gallantly,
and wisely: that <I>Antonius</I> shewed them a comicall face, to wit, a merie countenance:
and the <SC>Romaines</SC> a tragicall face, to say, a grimme looke. But to reckon vp all
the foolish sportes they made, reuelling in this sort: it were too fonde a part of me,
and therefore I will only tell you one among the rest. On a time he went to angle
for fish, and when he could take none, he was as angrie as could be, because
<I>Cleopatra</I> stood by. Wherefore he secretly commaunded the fisher men, that when
he cast in his line, they should straight diue vnder the water, and put a fish on his
hooke which they had taken before: and so snatched vp his angling rodde, and
brought vp fish twise or thrise. <I>Cleopatra</I> found it straight, yet she seemed not to
see it, but wondred at his excellent fishing: but when she was alone by her selfe
among her owne people, she tolde them how it was, and bad them the next morning
to be on the water to see the fishing. A number of people came to the hauen, and
got into the fisher boates to see this fishing. <I>Antonius</I> then threw in his line and
<I>Cleopatra</I> straight commanded one of her men to diue vnder water
before <I>Antonius</I> men, and to put some old salt fish vpon his baite,
<MARG><B>II, v, 21.</B></MARG>
like vnto those that are brought out of the country of <SC>Pont</SC>. When
he had hong the fish on his hook, <I>Antonius</I> thinking he had taken
a fish in deede, snatched vp his line presently. Then they all fell a laughing.
<I>Cleopatra</I> laughing also, said vnto him: leaue vs (my Lord) <SC>&AElig;gyptians</SC> (which
dwell in the country of <SC>Pharvs &amp; Canobus</SC>) your angling rod: this is not thy pro-
fession: thou must hunt after conquering of realmes and countries.
Now <I>Antonius</I> delighting in these fond and childish pastimes, very
<MARG><B>I, ii, 102.</B></MARG>

he commeth neere vnto the other. Howsoeuer it was, the euents ensuing proued the
<SC>&AElig;gyptians</SC> words true. For, it is said, that as often as they two drew cuts for pas-

Oftentimes when they were disposed to see cockfight, or quailes that

<P>This so great and puisant army which made the <SC>Indians</SC> quake for fear, dwelling

<P>loue, that he had no other thought but of her, and how he might quickly returne

<P>Then seeing him selfe enuironned of all sides, he sent vnto the army, that they
should come and aide him: but there the Captaines that led the legions (among the
which <I>Canidius,</I> a man of great estimation about <I>Antonius</I> made one) committed

<P>Now whilest <I>Antonius</I> was busie in this preparation, <I>Octauia</I> his wife, whom he

well armed like vnto the Pr&aelig;tors bands. When <I>Niger,</I> one of <I>Antonius</I> friendes

went from her, she fell a weeping and blubbering, looked ruefully of the matter, and
still found she meanes that <I>Antonius</I> should oftentimes finde her weeping: and then
when he came sodainely vppon her, she made as though she dried her eyes, and
turned her face away, as if she were vnwilling that he should see her weepe. . . .
<P>When <I>Octauia</I> was returned to <SC>Rome</SC> from <SC>Athens</SC>, <I>C&aelig;sar</I> commanded her to

take no thought for her: for sayed she, it were too shamefull a thing, that two
famous Captaines should bring in ciuill warres among the <SC>Romains</SC>, the one for the
loue of a woman, and the other for the iealousie betwixt one another. Now as she

Furthermore, when <I>Antonius</I> sent any of his men to <SC>Rome</SC>, to sue for any office in

band, made euery man hate him, when they sawe he did so vnkindly vse so noble
a Ladie: but yet the greatest cause of their malice vnto him, was for the diuision of

<P>So <I>Antonius,</I> through the perswasions of <I>Domitius,</I> commaunded <I>Cleopatra,</I> to returne

reason to send her from this war, who defraied so great a charge: neither that it was
for his profit, because that thereby the <SC>&AElig;gyptians</SC> would then be vtterly discoraged,
which were the chiefest strength of the armie by sea: considering that he could see
no king of all the kings their confederates, that <I>Cleopatra</I> was inferior vnto, either
for wisedom or iudgement, seeing that long before she had wisely gouerned so great
a realme as <SC>&AElig;gypt</SC>, &amp; besides that she had bene so long acquainted with him, by
whom she had learned to manedge great affaires. These faire perswasions wanne
him: for it was predestined that the gouernment of all the world should fall into
<I>Octauius C&aelig;sars</I> handes. <I>Octauius C&aelig;sar</I> vnderstanding the sodaine
&amp; wonderfull great preparation of <I>Antonius,</I> he was not a litle
<MARG><B>III, iv, 30.</B></MARG>
astonied at it, (fearing he should be driuen to fight that sommer)
because he wanted many things, &amp; the great and grieuous exactions of money did
sorely oppresse the people. . . .
<P>Furthermore, <I>Titius</I> and <I>Plancus</I> (two of <I>Antonius</I> chiefest friendes and that had

themselues vnto <I>C&aelig;sar,</I> and tolde him where the testament was that
<I>Antonius</I> had made, knowing perfitly what was in it. The will was
<MARG><B>III, iv, 5.</B></MARG>
in the custody of the <I>Vestall Nunnes:</I> of whom <I>C&aelig;sar</I> demanded for
it. They answered him, that they would not giue it him: but if he
would goe and take it, they would not hinder him. Thereupon <I>C&aelig;sar</I> went thither,
&amp; hauing read it first to himselfe, he noted certen places worthy of
reproch: so assembling all the Senate, he read it before them all. . . .
<MARG><B>III, iv, 5.</B></MARG>
<P>Now after that <I>C&aelig;sar</I> had made sufficient preparation, he pro-
claimed open warre against <I>Cleopatra,</I> and made the people to
<MARG><B>III, vii, 7.</B></MARG>
abolish the power and Empire of <I>Antonius,</I> because he had before

Maister of himselfe, but that <I>Cleopatra</I> had brought him beside himselfe, by her

<P><I>peius</I>) but rather that he should doe against all reason, he hauing so great skill and

<MARG><B>III, vii, 76.</B></MARG>

<P>All that day and the three dayes following, the sea rose so high &amp; was so boister-

againe and then they rowed with force of owers in battell one against the other. . . .
<P>Now <I>Publicola</I> seing <I>Agrippa</I> put forth his left wing of <I>C&aelig;sars</I> armie, to compasse

<MARG><B>III, x, 18.</B></MARG>

<MARG><B>III, x, 29.</B></MARG>
his vtter destruction. When she knew his galley a farre off, she lift

by land was yet whole. Then <I>Antonius</I> sent vnto <I>Canidius,</I> to return with his army
into <SC>Asia</SC>, by <SC>Macedon</SC>. Now for himself, he determined to crosse

<MARG><B>III, xi, 23.</B></MARG>

<P>And thus it stood with <I>Antonius.</I> Now for his armie by sea, that fought before
the head or foreland of <SC>Activm</SC>: they helde out a long time, and
nothing troubled them more then a great boysterous winde that rose
<MARG><B>III, xi, 2.</B></MARG>
full in the prooes of their shippes and yet with much a doe, his nauie

<P>But now to returne to <I>Antonius</I> againe. <I>Canidius</I> himselfe came to bring him

her royall pallace. He was no sooner com thither, but he straight set all the citie on

had by <I>Fuluia,</I> the mans gown, the which was a plaine gowne, without gard or
embroderie of purple. For these things, there was kept great feast-
<MARG><B>III, xiii, 3.</B></MARG>
ing, banquetting and dancing in <SC>Alexandria</SC> many dayes together.
In deede they did breake their first order they had set downe, which
they called Amimetobion, (as much to say, no life comparable) &amp; did set vp another,
which they called Synapothanumenon (signifying the order and agreement of those that

the first. For their friendes made themselues to be inrolled in this order of those that
would die together, and so made great feastes one to another: for euerie man when it
came to his turne, feasted their whole companie and fraternitie. <I>Cleopatra</I> in the meane
time was verie carefull in gathering all sorts of poysons together, to destroy men.
Now to make proofe of those poysons which made men die with least paine, she tryed
it vpon condemned men in prison. For when she saw the poysons that were sodaine
and vehement, and brought speedy death with grieuous torments: &amp; in contrary
<PB N=403>
<HE><I>PLUTARCH</I> 403</HE>
<P>manner, that such as were more milde and gentle, had not that quicke speede and
force to make one dye sodainely: she afterwardes went about to proue the stinging
of snakes and adders, and made some to be applyed vnto men in her sight, some in
one sorte and some in another. So when she had daily made diuers and sundrie
proofes, she found none of them all she had proued so fit, as the biting of an Aspick,
the which causeth onely a heauines of the head, without swounding or complaining,
and bringeth a great desire also to sleepe, with a litle swet in the face, and so by litle
and litle taketh away the senses &amp; vitall powers, no liuing creature perceiuing that
the patients feele any paine. For they are so sorie when any bodie awaketh them,
and taketh them vp: as those that being taken out of a sound sleep, are very heauie
and desirous to sleepe. This notwithstanding, they sent Ambassadors vnto <I>Octauius
C&aelig;sar</I> in <SC>Asia</SC>, <I>Cleopatra</I> requesting the realme of <SC>&AElig;gypt</SC> for their children, and

<I>C&aelig;sar</I> would not let him remaine in <SC>&AElig;gypt</SC>. And because they had no other men

<MARG><B>III, xii, 9.</B></MARG>

of rowing they were come neare vnto them, they first saluted <I>C&aelig;sars</I> men: and then
<I>C&aelig;sars</I> men resaluted them also, and of two armies made but one, and then did all
together row toward the citie. When <I>Antonius</I> saw that his men did forsake him,
and yeelded vnto <I>C&aelig;sar,</I> and that his footemen were broken and ouerthrowen: he
then fled into the citie, crying out that <I>Cleopatra</I> had betrayed him vnto them, with
whom he had made warre for her sake. Th&emacr; she being affrayed of his fury, fled
into the tombe which she had caused to be made, and there locked
the doores vnto her, and shut all the springs of the lockes with great
<MARG><B>IV, xiii, 5.</B></MARG>
boltes, and in the meane time sent vnto <I>Antonius</I> to tell him that
she was dead. <I>Antonius</I> beleeuing it, sayd vnto himselfe: what
doest thou looke for further, <I>Antonius,</I> sith spightfull fortune hath taken from thee
the onely ioy thou haddest, for whom thou yet reseruedst thy life? when he had
sayd these words, he went into a chamber &amp; vnarmed himselfe, and being naked said
thus: O <I>Cleopatra,</I> it grieueth me not that I haue lost thy companie, for I will not
be long from thee: but I am sory, that hauing bene so great a Captaine and Emper-
our, I am indeede condemned to be iudged of lesse courage &amp; noble
minde, then a woman. Now he had a man of his called <I>Eros,</I>
<MARG><B>IV, xiv, 72.</B></MARG>
whom he loued and trusted much, and whom he had long before
<MARG><B>IV, xiv, 97.</B></MARG>
caused to sweare vnto him, that he should kill him when he did
commaunde him: and then he willed him to keepe his promise.
His man drawing his sword, lift it vp as though he meant to haue striken his mais-
ter: but turning his head at one side, he thrust his sword into himselfe, and fell
downe dead at his maisters foote. Then sayd <I>Antonius,</I> O noble <I>Eros,</I> I thanke
thee for this, and it is valiantly done of thee, to shew me what I should do to my
selfe, which thou couldest not do for me. Therewithall he tooke his sword, and
thrust it into his bellie, and so fell downe vpon a litle bed. The wounde he had
killed him not presently, for the bloud stinted a litle when he was layed: and when
he came somewhat to himselfe againe, he prayed them that were about him to dis-
patch him. But they all fled out of the chamber, and left him crying out &amp; torment-
ing himselfe: vntill at last there came a Secretarie vnto him called <I>Diomedes,</I> who
was commaunded to bring him into the tombe or monument where <I>Cleopatra</I> was.
Wh&emacr; he heard that she was aliue, he very earnestly prayed his men to carie his body
thither, and so he was caried in his mens armes into the entry of the monument.
Notwithstanding, <I>Cleopatra</I> would not open the gates, but came to the high win-
dowes, and cast out certaine chaines and ropes, in the which <I>Antonius</I> was trussed:
and <I>Cleopatra</I> her owne selfe, with two women onely, which she had suffered to
come with her into these monuments, trised <I>Antonius</I> vp. They that were present
to behold it, sayd they neuer saw so pitifull a sight. For, they plucked vp poore
<I>Antonius</I> all bloudy as he was, and drawing on with pangs of death, who holding
vp his hands to <I>Cleopatra,</I> raised vp himselfe as well as he could. It was a hard
thing for these women to do, to lift him vp: but <I>Cleopatra</I> stouping downe with her

<P>head, putting all her strength to her vttermost power, did lift him vp with much
a do, and neuer let go her hold, with the helpe of the women beneath that bad her
be of good courage, and were as sory to see her labour so, as she her selfe. So
when she had gotten him in after that sort, and layed him on a bed: she rent her
garments vpon him, clapping her brest, and scratching her face and stomacke.
Then she dried vp his bloud that had berayed his face, and called him her Lord, her
husband, and Emperour, forgetting her owne miserie and calamity, for the pitie and
compasion she tooke of him. <I>Antonius</I> made her ceasse her lament-
ing, and called for wine, either because he was a thirst, or else for
<MARG><B>IV, xv, 56.</B></MARG>
that he thought thereby to hasten his death. When he had dronke,
he earnestly prayed her, and perswaded her, that she would seeke
to saue her life, if she could possible, without reproche and dishonour: and that

had thrust his sword in himselfe, as they caried him into the tombes
and monuments of <I>Cleopatra,</I> one of his gard called <I>Dercet&aelig;us,</I>
<MARG><B>V, i, 7.</B></MARG>
tooke his sword with the which he had striken himselfe, and hid it:
then he secretly stale away, and brought <I>Octauius C&aelig;sar</I> the first
newes of his death, &amp; shewed him his sword that was bloudied. <I>C&aelig;sar</I> hearing these
newes, straight withdrew himselfe into a secret place of his tent, and there burst out
with teares, lamenting his hard and miserable fortune, that had bene his friend and
brother in law, his equall in the Empire, and companion with him in sundry great
exploits and battels. Then he called for all his friendes, and shewed them the letters
<I>Antonius</I> had written to him, and his aunsweres also sent him againe, during their
quarrell and strife: and how fiercely and proudly the other aunswered him, to all

commaunded him to do what he could possible to get <I>Cleopatra</I> aliue, fearing least
otherwise all the treasure would be lost: &amp; furthermore, he thought that if he could
take <I>Cleopatra,</I> and bring her aliue to <SC>Rome</SC>, she would maruellously beautifie and

although they spake together. For <I>Proculeius</I> came to the gates that were very thicke
&amp; strong, and surely barred, but yet there were some cranewes through the which
her voyce might be heard, and so they without vnderstood, that <I>Cleopatra</I> demaunded
the kingdome of <SC>&AElig;gypt</SC> for her sonnes: and that <I>Proculeius</I> aunswered her, that she
should be of good cheare, and not be affrayed to referre all vnto <I>C&aelig;sar.</I> After he
had viewed the place very well, he came and reported her answere vnto <I>C&aelig;sar.</I>
Who immediately sent <I>Gallus</I> to speake once againe with her, and bad him pur-
posely hold her with talke, whilest <I>Proculeius</I> did set vp a ladder against that high
window, by the which <I>Antonius</I> was trised vp, and came downe into the monument

sayd vnto her. One of her women which was shut in her monum&emacr;ts with her, saw
<I>Proculeius</I> by chance as he came downe, and shreeked out: O poore <I>Cleopatra,</I> thou
art taken. Then when she saw <I>Proculeius</I> behind her as she came from the gate,
she thought to haue stabbed her selfe in with a short dagger she wore of purpose by

<P>her side. But <I>Proculeius</I> came sodainly vpon her, and taking her by both the hands,

and mercie, and to giue his enemies cause to accuse the most curteous and noble Prince
that euer was, and to appeache him, as though he were a cruell and mercilesse man,
that were not to be trusted. So euen as he spake the word, he tooke her dagger
from her, and shooke her clothes for feare of any poyson hidden about her. After-
wardes <I>C&aelig;sar</I> sent one of his infranchised men called <I>Epaphroditus,</I> whom he
straightly charged to looke well vnto her, and to beware in any case that she made
not her selfeaway: and for the rest, to vse her with all the curtesie possible. . . .
<P>Therefore <I>C&aelig;sar</I> did put <I>C&aelig;sarion</I> to death, after the death of his mother <I>Cleo-
patra.</I> Many Princes, great kings &amp; Captaines did craue <I>Antonius</I> body of <I>Octauius

who did sumptuously &amp; royally bury him with her own hands, whom <I>C&aelig;sar</I> suffred
to take as much as she would to bestow vpon his funerals. Now was she altogether
ouercome with sorow &amp; passion of minde, for she had knocked her brest so pitifully,
that she had martyred it, and in diuers places had raysed vlcers &amp; inflammations, so
that she fell into a feuer withall: whereof she was very glad, hoping
<MARG><B>V, ii, 59.</B></MARG>

a booke of all these things. But <I>C&aelig;sar</I> mistrusted the matter, by many coniectures
he had, and therefore did put her in feare, and threatned her to put her children to
shamefull death. With these threates, <I>Cleopatra</I> for feare yeelded straight, as she
would haue yeelded vnto strokes: &amp; afterwards suffred her selfe to be cured and
dieted as they listed. Shortly after, <I>C&aelig;sar</I> came himself in person to see her, &amp; to
c&omacr;fort her. <I>Cleopatra</I> being layed vpon a litle low bed in poore estate, when she
saw <I>C&aelig;sar</I> come into her chamber, she sodainly rose vp, naked in her smocke, and
fell downe at his feete maruellously disfigured: both for that she had plucked her haire
from her head, as also for that she had martired all her face with her nayles, and
besides, her voyce was small and trembling, her eyes sunke into her head with con-
tinuall blubbering and moreouer, they might see the most part of her stomake torne
in sunder. To be short, her body was not much better then her minde: yet her
good grace and comelynesse, and the force of her beautie was not altogether defaced.
But notwithstanding this ougly and pitifull state of hers, yet she shewed herselfe
within, by her outward lookes and countenance. When <I>C&aelig;sar</I> had made her lye
downe againe, and sate by her beds side: <I>Cleopatra</I> began to cleare and excuse her
selfe for that she had done, laying all to the feare she had of <I>Antonius: C&aelig;sar,</I> in
contrary manner, reproued her in euery point. Then she sodainly altered her
speach, and prayed him to pardon her, as though she were affrayed to dye, and
desirous to liue. At length, she gaue him a briefe and memoriall of all the ready
money and treasure she had. But by chaunce there stood <I>Seleucus</I> by, one of her
Treasurers, who to seeme a good seruant, came straight to <I>C&aelig;sar</I> to disproue <I>Cleo-
patra,</I> that she had not set in all, but kept many things backe of purpose. <I>Cleopatra</I>
was in such a rage with him, that she flew vpon him, &amp; tooke him by the haire of
the head, and boxed him welfauouredly. <I>C&aelig;sar</I> fell a laughing, and parted the
fray. Alas, sayd she, O <I>C&aelig;sar:</I> is not this a great shame and reproche, that thou
hauing vouchsaued to take the paines to come vnto me, and hast done me this hon-

was, and there falling downe on her knees, imbracing the tombe with her women,
&lquo;the teares running down her cheekes, she began to speake in this sort: O my deare
&lquo;Lord <I>Antonius,</I> not long sithence I buried thee here, being a free woman: and now
&lquo;I offer vnto thee the funerall sprinklings and oblations, being a captiue and prisoner,
&lquo;and yet I am forbidden and kept from tearing &amp; murthering this captiue body of mine

&lquo;therefore henceforth for no other honours, offerings, nor sacrifices from me, for these

&lquo;in <SC>Italie</SC>, which shall be all the good that I haue receiued by thy country. If there-

when she had bathed and washed her selfe, she fell to her meate, and was sumptu-

<P>and began to read her lam&emacr;tation and petition, requesting him that he would let her

thither himselfe: howbeit he sent one before in all hast that might be, to see what it
was. Her death was very sodaine. For those whom <I>C&aelig;sar</I> sent vnto her ran thither
in all hast possible, &amp; found the souldiers standing at the gate, mistrusting noth-

found <I>Cleopatra</I> starke dead, layed vpon a bed of gold, attired &amp; arayed in her roy-

her other woman called <I>Charmion</I> halfe dead, and trembling, trim-

<MARG><B>V, ii, 373.</B></MARG>
the souldiers seeing her, angrily sayd vnto her: is that well done
<I>Charmion?</I> Very well sayd she againe, and meete for a Princesse

dead hard by the bed. Some report that this Aspicke was brought vnto her in the
basket with figs, &amp; that she had commaunded them to hide it vnder the figge leaues,
that when she should thinke to take out the figges, the Aspicke should bite her before
she should see her: howbeit, that when she would haue taken away the leaues for
the figges, she perceiued it, and sayd, art thou here then? And so, her arme being
naked, she put it to the Aspicke to be bitten. Other say againe, she kept it in a
boxe, and that she did pricke and thrust it with a spindle of gold, so that the Aspicke
being angerd withall, lept out with great furie, and bit her in the arme. Howbeit
few can tell the troth. For they report also, that she had hidden poyson in a hollow
raser which she caried in the haire of her head: and yet was there no marke seene
of her body, or any signe discerned that she was poysoned, neither also did they finde
this serpent in her tombe. But it was reported onely, that there were seene certaine
fresh steppes or trackes where it had gone, on the tombe side toward the sea, and
specially by the doore side. Some say also, that they found two litle pretie bytings
in her arme, scant to be discerned: the which it seemeth <I>C&aelig;sar</I> him-
selfe gaue credit vnto, because in his triumphe he caried <I>Cleopatraes</I>
<MARG><B>V, ii, 422.</B></MARG>
image, with an Aspicke byting of her arme. And thus goeth the
<MARG><B>V, ii, 429.</B></MARG>
report of her death. Now <I>C&aelig;sar,</I> though he was maruellous sory
for the death of <I>Cleopatra,</I> yet he wondred at her noble minde and
courage, and therefore commaunded she should be nobly buried, and layed by
<I>Antonius:</I> and willed also that her two women should haue honorable buriall.
<I>Cleopatra</I> dyed being eight and thirtie yeare old, after she had raigned two and
twenty yeares, and gouerned aboue foureteen of them with <I>Antonius.</I> And for
<I>Antonius,</I> some say that he liued three and fiftie yeares: and others say, six and
fiftie.

<HE>410 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<C>PREFACE.</C>
<P>The death of <I>Anthony</I> and <I>Cleopatra,</I> is a Subject which has been treated by the
greatest Wits of our Nation, after <I>Shakespeare;</I> and by all so variously, that their
example has given me the confidence to try my self in this Bowe of <I>Ulysses</I> amongst
the Crowd of Sutors; and, withal, to take my own measures, in aiming at the Mark.
I doubt not but the same Motive has prevailed with all of us in this attempt; I mean
the excellency of the Moral: for the chief persons represented, were famous patterns
of unlawful love; and their end accordingly was unfortunate. All reasonable men
have long since concluded, That the Heroe of the Poem, ought not to be a character
of perfect Virtue, for, then, he could not, without injustice, be made unhappy; nor
yet altogether wicked, because he could not then be pitied: I have therefore steer'd
the middle course; and have drawn the character of <I>Anthony</I> as favourably as <I>Plu-
tarch, Appian,</I> and <I>Dion Cassius</I> wou'd give me leave: the like I have observ'd in
<I>Cleopatra.</I> That which is wanting to work up the pity to a greater heighth, was not
afforded me by the story: for the crimes of love which they both committed, were not
occasion'd by any necessity, or fatal ignorance, but were wholly voluntary; since our
passions are, or ought to be, within our power. The Fabrick of the Play is regular
enough, as to the inferior parts of it; and the Unities of Time, Place and Action,
more exactly observed, than, perhaps, the English Theater requires. Particularly,
the Action is so much one, that it is the only of the kind without Episode, or Under-
plot; every Scene in the Tragedy conducing to the main design, and every Act con-
cluding with a turn of it. The greatest errour in the contrivance seems to be in the
person of <I>Octavia:</I> For, though I might use the priviledge of a Poet, to introduce
her into <I>Alexandria,</I> yet I had not enough consider'd, that the compassion she mov'd
to her self and children, was destructive to that which I reserv'd for <I>Anthony</I> and
<I>Cleopatra;</I> whose mutual love being founded upon vice, must lessen the favour of
the Audience to them, when Virtue and Innocence were oppress'd by it. And,
though I justified <I>Anthony</I> in some measure, by making <I>Octavia's</I> departure, to pro-
ceed wholly from her self; yet the force of the first Machine still remain'd; and the
dividing of pity, like the cutting of a River into many Channels, abated the strength
of the natural stream. But this is an Objection which none of my Critiques have
urg'd against me; and therefore I might have let it pass, if I could have resolv'd to
have been partial to my self. The faults my Enemies have found, are rather cavils
concerning little, and not essential Decencies; which a Master of the Ceremonies
may decide betwixt us. The <I>French</I> Poets, I confess, are strict Observers of these
Punctilio's: They would not, for example, have suffer'd <I>Cleopatra</I> and <I>Octavia</I> to
have met; or if they had met, there must only have pass'd betwixt them some cold
civilities, but no eagerness of repart&eacute;e, for fear of offending against the greatness of
their Characters, and the modesty of their Sex. This Objection I foresaw, and at the
same time contemn'd: for I judg'd it both natural and probable, that <I>Octavia,</I> proud
of her new-gain'd Conquest, would search out <I>Cleopatra</I> to triumph over her; and
that <I>Cleopatra,</I> thus attacqu'd, was not of a spirit to shun the encounter: and 'tis
not unlikely, that two exasperated Rivals should use such Satyre as I have put into
their mouths; for after all, though the one were a <I>Roman,</I> and the other a Queen,
they were both Women. . . .
<P>In my Stile I have profess'd to imitate the Divine <I>Shakespeare;</I> which that I
might perform more freely, I have disincumber'd my self from Rhyme. Not that I
condemn my former way, but that this is more proper to my present purpose. I hope
<PB N=411>
<HE><I>DRYDEN&mdash;ALL FOR LOVE</I> 411</HE>
<P>I need not to explain myself, that I have not Copy'd my Author servilely: Words
and Phrases must of necessity receive a change in succeeding Ages: but 'tis almost
a Miracle that much of his Language remains so pure; and that he who began Dra-
matique Poetry amongst us, untaught by any, and, as <I>Ben Johnson</I> tells us, without
Learning, should by the force of his own Genius perform so much, that in a manner
he has left no praise for any who come after him. The occasion is fair, and the sub-
ject would be pleasant to handle the difference of Stiles betwixt him and <I>Fletcher,</I>
and wherein, and how far they are both to be imitated. But since I must not be
over-confident of my own performance after him, it will be prudence in me to be
silent. Yet I hope I may affirm, and without vanity, that by imitating him, I have
excell'd my self throughout the Play; and particularly, that I prefer the Scene
betwixt <I>Anthony</I> and <I>Ventidius</I> in the first Act, to any thing which I have written
in this kind.
<SHL>
<BQ>
<C><SC>Prologue.</SC></C><LB>
<CURL>
What Flocks of Critiques hover here to day,<LB>
As Vultures wait on Armies for their Prey,<LB>
All gaping for the Carcass of a Play!<LB>
</CURL>
With Croaking Notes they bode some dire event;<LB>
And follow dying Poets by the scent.<LB>
Ours gives himself for gone; y'have watch'd your time!<LB>
He fights this day unarm'd; without his Rhyme.<LB>
And brings a Tale which often has been told;<LB>
As sad as Dido's; and almost as old.<LB>
His Heroe, whom you Wits his Bully call,<LB>
Bates of his mettle; and scarce rants at all;<LB>
He's somewhat lewd; but a well-meaning mind;<LB>
Weeps much; fights little; but is wond'rous kind.<LB>
In short, a Pattern, and Companion fit,<LB>
For all the keeping Tonyes of the Pit.<LB>
<CURL>
I cou'd name more; a Wife and Mistress too;<LB>
Both (to be plain) too good for most of you:<LB>
The Wife well-natur'd, and the Mistress true.<LB>
</CURL>
Now, Poets, if your fame has been his care;<LB>
Allow him all the candour you can spare.<LB>
A brave Man scorns to quarrel once a day;<LB>
Like Hectors, in at every petty fray.<LB>
Let those find fault whose Wit's so very small,<LB>
They've need to show that they can think at all:<LB>
Errours like Straws upon the surface flow;<LB>
He who would search for Pearls must dive below.<LB>
Fops may have leave to level all they can;<LB>
As Pigmies wou'd be glad to lopp a Man.<LB>
Half-Wits are Fleas; so little and so light;<LB>
We scarce cou'd know they live, but that they bite.<LB>
But, as the Rich, when tir'd with daily Feasts,<LB>
For change, become their next poor Tenants Ghests;<LB>
Drink hearty Draughts of Ale, from plain brown Bowls,<LB>
And snatch the homely Rasher from the Coals:<LB>
</BQ>
<PB N=412>
<HE>412 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<BQ>
So you, retiring from much better Cheer,<LB>
For once, may venture to do penance here.<LB>
And since that plenteous Autumn now is past,<LB>
Whose Grapes and Peaches have Indulged your taste,<LB>
Take in good part from our poor Poets boord,<LB>
Such rivell'd Fruits as Winter can afford.<LB>

<C><SC>Scene Alexandria</SC>.</C><LB>
<C><SC>Act.</SC> I. <SC>Scene</SC>, <I>The Temple of</I> Isis.</C><LB>
<C><I>Enter</I> Serapion, Myris, <I>Priests of</I> Isis.</C><LB>
<S>Serap.</S> Portents, and Prodigies, are grown so frequent,<LB>
That they have lost their Name. Our fruitful <I>Nile</I><LB>
Flow'd ere the wonted Season, with a Torrent<LB>
So unexpected, and so wondrous fierce,<LB>
That the wild Deluge overtook the haste<LB>
Ev'n of the Hinds that watch'd it: Men and Beasts<LB>
Were born above the tops of Trees, that grew<LB>
On th' utmost Margin of the Water-mark.<LB>
Then, with so swift an Ebb, the Floud drove backward<LB>
It slipt from underneath the Scaly Herd:<LB>
Here monstrous <I>Phoc&aelig;</I> panted on the Shore;<LB>
Forsaken <I>Dolphins</I> there, with their broad tails,<LB>
Lay lashing the departing Waves: Hard by 'em,<LB>
Sea-Horses floundring in the slimy mud,<LB>
Toss'd up their heads, and dash'd the ooze about 'em.<LB>
<C><I>Enter</I> Alexas <I>behind them.</I></C><LB>
<S>Myr.</S> Avert these Omens, Heav'n.<LB>
<S>Serap.</S> Last night, between the hours of Twelve and One,<LB>
In a lone Isle o'th'Temple while I walk'd,<LB>
A Whirl-wind rose, that, with a violent blast,<LB>
Shook all the <I>Dome:</I> the Doors around me clapt,<LB>
The Iron Wicket, that defends the Vault,<LB>
Where the long Race of <I>Ptolomies</I> is lay'd,<LB>

Burst open, and disclosed the mighty dead.<LB>
From out each Monument, in order plac'd,<LB>
An Armed Ghost start up: the Boy-King last<LB>
Rear'd his inglorious head. A peal of groans<LB>
Then follow'd, and a lamentable voice<LB>
Cry'd <I>&AElig;gypt</I> is no more. My blood ran back,<LB>
My shaking knees against each other knock'd;<LB>
On the cold pavement down I fell intranc'd;<LB>
And so unfinish'd left the horrid Scene.<LB>
<I>Alexas</I> (<I>showing himself.</I>) And, Dream'd you this? or, Did invent the Story?<LB>
To frighten our <I>&AElig;gyptian</I> Boys withal,<LB>
And train 'em up betimes in fear of Priesthood?<LB>
<S>Serap.</S> My Lord, I saw you not,<LB>
Nor meant my words should reach your ears; but what<LB>
I uttered was most true.<LB>
<S>Alex.</S> A foolish Dream,<LB>
Bred from the fumes of indigested Feasts,<LB>
And holy Luxury.<LB>
<S>Serap.</S> I know my duty:<LB>
This goes no farther.<LB>
<S>Alex.</S> 'Tis not fit it should.<LB>
Nor would the times now bear it, were it true.<LB>
All Southern, from you hills, the <I>Roman</I> Camp<LB>
Hangs o'er us black and threatning, like a Storm<LB>
Just breaking on our heads.<LB>
<S>Serap.</S> Our faint <I>&AElig;gyptians</I> pray for <I>Antony;</I><LB>
But in their Servile hearts they own <I>Octavius.</I><LB>
<S>Myr.</S> Why then does <I>Antony</I> dream out his hours,<LB>
And tempts not Fortune for a noble Day,<LB>
Which might redeem, what <I>Actium</I> lost?<LB>
<S>Alex.</S> He thinks 'tis past recovery.<LB>
<S>Serap.</S> Yet the Foe<LB>
Seems not to press the Siege.<LB>
<S>Alex.</S> O, there's the wonder.<LB>
<I>Mec&aelig;nas</I> and <I>Agrippa,</I> who can most<LB>
With <I>C&aelig;sar,</I> are his Foes. His Wife <I>Octavia,</I><LB>
Driv'n from his House, solicits her revenge;<LB>
And <I>Dolabella,</I> who was once his Friend,<LB>
Upon some private grudge, now seeks his ruine:<LB>
Yet still War seems on either side to sleep.<LB>
<S>Serap.</S> 'Tis strange that <I>Antony,</I> for some days past,<LB>
Has not beheld the face of <I>Cleopatra;</I><LB>
But here, in <I>Isis</I> Temple, lives retir'd,<LB>
And makes his heart a prey to black despair.<LB>
<S>Alex.</S> 'Tis true; and we much fear he hopes by absence<LB>
To cure his mind of Love.<LB>
<S>Serap.</S> If he be vanquish'd,<LB>
Or make his peace, <I>&AElig;gypt</I> is doom'd to be<LB>
A <I>Roman</I> Province; and our plenteous Harvests<LB>

Must then redeem the scarceness of their Soil.<LB>
While <I>Antony</I> stood firm, our <I>Alexandria</I><LB>
Rival'd proud <I>Rome</I> (Dominions other Seat)<LB>

<S>Alex.</S> Had I my wish, these Tyrants of all Nature<LB>

Each by the others Sword; but, since our will<LB>
Is lamely follow'd by our pow'r, we must<LB>
Depend on one; with him to rise or fall.<LB>
<S>Serap.</S> How stands the Queen affected?<LB>
<S>Alex.</S> O, she dotes,<LB>
She dotes, <I>Serapion,</I> on this vanquish'd Man,<LB>
And winds her self about his mighty ruins,<LB>
Whom would she yet forsake, yet yield him up,<LB>
This hunted prey, to his pursuers hands,<LB>
She might preserve us all; but 'tis in vain&mdash;&mdash;&mdash;<LB>
This changes my designs, this blasts my Counsels,<LB>
And makes me use all means to keep him here,<LB>

The state of things; no more of your ill Omens,<LB>
And black Prognosticks; labour to confirm<LB>

<C><I>Enter</I> Ventidius, <I>talking aside with a Gentleman of</I> Antony's.</C><LB>
<S>Serap.</S> These <I>Romans</I> will o'rehear us.<LB>

His fierce demeanor, and erected look,<LB>
He's of no vulgar note.<LB>
<S>Alex.</S> O, 'tis <I>Ventidius,</I><LB>
Our Emp'rors great Lieutenant in the East,<LB>

When <I>Antony</I> return'd from <I>Syria</I> last,<LB>
He left this Man to guard the <I>Roman</I> Frontiers.<LB>
<S>Serap.</S> You seem to know him well.<LB>
<S>Alex.</S> Too well. I saw him in <I>Cilicia</I> first,<LB>
When <I>Cleopatra</I> there met <I>Antony:</I><LB>
A mortal he was to us, and <I>&AElig;gypt.</I><LB>
But, let me witness to the worth I hate,<LB>
A braver Roman never drew a Sword.<LB>
Firm to his Prince; but, as a friend, not slave.<LB>
He ne'r was of his pleasures; but presides<LB>
O're all his cooler hours and morning counsels:<LB>
In short, the plainness, fierceness, rugged virtue<LB>
Of an old true-stampt Roman lives in him.<LB>
His coming bodes I know not what of ill<LB>
To our affairs. Withdraw, to mark him better;<LB>
And I'll acquaint you why I sought you here,<LB>

For fear their Souls should animate their Marbles,<LB>
To blush at their degenerate Progeny.<LB>
<S>Alex.</S> A love which knows no bounds to <I>Antony,</I><LB>
Would mark the Day with honors; when all Heaven<LB>
Labored for him, when each propitious Star<LB>
Stood wakeful in his Orb, to watch that hour,<LB>

Our Queen neglected, like a vulgar Fate,<SUP>*</SUP><LB>
That pass'd obscurely by.<LB>

Some other Prince, not him.<LB>
<S>Alex.</S> Your Emperor,<LB>
Tho grown unkind, would be more gentle, than<LB>
T'upbraid my Queen, for loving him too well.<LB>
<S>Ven.</S> Does the mute Sacrifice upbraid the Priest?<LB>
He knows him not his Executioner.<LB>
O, she has deck'd his ruin with her love,<LB>
Led him in golden bands to gaudy slaughter,<LB>
And made perdition pleasing: She has left him<LB>
The blank of what he was;<LB>
I tell thee, Eunuch, she has quite unmann'd him:<LB>
Can any Roman see, and know him now,<LB>
Thus alter'd from the Lord of half Mankind,<LB>
Unbent, unsinew'd, made a Womans Toy,<LB>
Shrunk from the vast extent of all his honors,<LB>
And crampt within a corner of the World?<LB>
O, <I>Antony!</I><LB>
Thou bravest Soldier, and thou best of Friends!<LB>
Bounteous as Nature; next to Nature's God!<LB>
Could'st thou but make new Worlds, so wouldst thou give 'em<LB>
As bounty were thy being. Rough in Battel,<LB>
As the first <I>Romans,</I> when they went to War;<LB>
Yet, after Victory, more pitiful,<LB>
Than all their Praying Virgins left at home!<LB>
<S>Alex.</S> Would you could add to those more shining Virtues,<LB>
His truth to her who loves him.<LB>
<S>Ven.</S> Would I could not.<LB>
But, Wherefore waste I precious hours with thee?<LB>
Thou art her darling mischief, her chief Engin,<LB>
<I>Antony'</I>s other Fate. Go, tell thy Queen,<LB>
<I>Ventidius</I> is arriv'd, to end her Charms.<LB>
Let your <I>&AElig;gyptian</I> Timbrels play alone;<LB>
Nor mix Effeminate Sounds with <I>Roman</I> Trumpets<LB>
You dare not fight for <I>Antony;</I> go Pray,<LB>
And keep your Cowards-Holy-day in Temples. [<I>Exeunt</I> Alex. Serap.<LB>
